# Adoption Guides

Author: Kelly Alvarez

These user guides contain guidance for practicing automation growth behaviors. In EST we have grown a culture around embracing automation and AI which is the best way to increase your productivity.

## Why Automate?

**Increase Efficiency and Speed:** Automation accelerates test execution, enabling adopters to decrease the effort per test required. Manual test procedures can be time-consuming. Complex systems often demand intermittent attention. Speedups are critical for meeting tight development timelines.

**Improved Accuracy, Consistency, and Repeatability:** Properly implemented automation will avoid human errors. Automated processes ensure consistent execution of test cases. This also helps promote standardization of procedures across teams. This leads to higher confidence in system verification and volume of regression.

**Maximize utilization with scalability and parallelization:** Automation scales to handle larger volumes of tests, allowing regression to cover multiple configurations and input parameters. With careful resource planning, it can enable more tests to run in parallel. This supports test mobilization across diverse environments and test phases.

h careful resource planning, it can enable more tests to run in parallel. This supports test mobilization across diverse environments and test phases.

**Accelerate Education:** Streamlining workflow steps and reducing tedium helps flatten the learning curve involved in new tasks. It will help quickly see cause-and-effect relationships and refine your mental models of complex processes. We can grow expertise by mastering control over more subsystems areas and learning how they interact.

# AI Assistance

Author: Kelly Alvarez

Leverage AI to boost productivity, but be aware of its limitations! AI output is not always accurate, so double-check and provide feedback when necessary.

Know the [AI usage policies](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/infrastructure-ai-guild/guidance-policy) and technology guidance, for building AI with speed and safety in IBM Infrastructure. Follow guidelines on using AI effectively, such as avoiding copying and pasting code into Copilot. Utilize IBM approved tools like [Bob](https://ibm.seismic.com/Link/Content/DCg4cRfBQ6V7G8TW3ppJ6XT8qcM3) (agentic AI) and [Watsonx](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/wca-ibm).

Consider setting up [mcp servers](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/build-server) to provide context for AI prompts. A dedicated [MCP course](https://yourlearning.ibm.com/activity/UDEMY-6632653) is available for further learning. Learn how to leverage Bob to create a MCP server and corresponding Mode for usage of existing automation tools in [this showcase](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/pit-bob/issues/16).

reate a MCP server and corresponding Mode for usage of existing automation tools in [this showcase](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/pit-bob/issues/16).

Got an AI project idea? Check out [pit-bob](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/pit-bob), a community-based GitHub platform for sharing ideas across the IBM Platform Integration & Test organization.

You can also reach out with any questions, feedback or discussion in the [est-bob Slack channel](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0AM235JGKW)!

By following these guidelines, you can effectively deploy your tools and harness the power of AI to improve productivity!

# Creating Issues

Author: Kelly Alvarez

When adding a new feature or making changes, start by creating an **issue**. An issue represents a goal such as fixing a bug, implementing or requesting a new feature, or making changes. Issues help with planning, tracking progress, and documenting work through comments. Both developers and users are encouraged to create issues. Once an issue is created, an associated branch can be created. Issues are assigned a unique issue number for reference.
![Alt Text](./images/issue.png)
- [Further documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/learning-about-issues/about-issues)

## Milestones

A [milestone](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/using-labels-and-milestones-to-track-work/about-milestones) is a collection of issues or pull requests. They can help you set a timeline for your work, make sure you are making steady progress, plan out in incremental steps, and break things up into digestible chunks.

# Deployment and Automation

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To ensure smooth deployment of tools to TOAD, refer to the documentation on the [Automation Tool Deployment Pipeline](/Automation/TOAD/how-to-contribute/build-pipeline/). When creating a new tool, add your tool to the [Automation Packages Registry](https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/automation-packages/), which lists all deployed tools in TOAD. Each tool in the registry includes links to user guides and repositories. To add to the registry, you can add to the "List of Available Automation Packages" section in the TOAD user guide [here](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/EST-User-Guide/blob/main/Automation/TOAD/how-to-maintain/README.md).

![Alt Text](./images/deployment.png)

# Documentation

Author: Kelly Alvarez

Documentation should exist for any and all automation. Documentation is written in Markdown. By prioritizing documentation, you can ensure that your tools are well-understood and easily usable by others. It's good practice to write it as you go! Here are some key aspects to focus on:

* **[Docstrings](https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/)**: Provide documentation for functions, which can be accessed by highlighting the function.
* **[Comments](../CodeQuality/how-to-comment-code.md)**: Include detailed comments within files for your reference.
* **[README](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes)**: A README.md file is a minimum requirement, and should specify any necessary requirements if they aren't specified in the repository in a requirements.txt file (see [Packages](./Repository%20Structure.md#Packaging)). Focus on user-centric information, such as info that users need to know about your tool, the indented environment, available options that your tool provides and their functionality.

on, such as info that users need to know about your tool, the indented environment, available options that your tool provides and their functionality.

* **Help Menu**: Uses a third party library called Typer to provide information on options and their usage.
* **[EST User Guide](/Automation/)**: The EST User Guide is a centralized hub for documentation on all tools, with a dedicated section for automation. The EST User Guide Task Force maintains and updates this guide to ensure it's intuitive and user-friendly. You can ask for help regarding the EST User Guide in the [EST User Guide Slack channel](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0BAA04H5K6).
* **Issues**: Use issues to document progress and provide a record of changes and discussions.

# Logging

Author: Kelly Alvarez

[Logging](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html) serves as a comprehensive audit of events that your tool has gone through, allowing for retracing processes and catching user errors. Implementing effective logging is useful for auditing events and debugging purposes.

![Alt Text](./images/logging.png)

##  Key Features:
Include:
- Timestamps in filenames or events
- Configurable log levels

## Best Practices:
- Write to a log file to prevent data loss.
- Avoid huge log files due to limited storage.
- Prevent overwriting previous logs. A good way to avoid this is adding timestamps in the file name.
- When running multiple instances of a Python program, having a single log file can make it difficult to discern which instance is generating the log output. To avoid this, consider using individual log files for each invocation of the tool.
- Use the Python logging package and implement configurable log levels. It's recommended to default to terminal output for warnings and errors only.
- Allow users to configure log levels, and write all log output to a file, regardless of the configured log level, to ensure that no information is missed.

# Planning/Proposals for Automation Projects

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To facilitate collaboration and prevent duplication of effort, Infrastructure automation project planning meetings are held and are open to anyone looking to start new projects. These meetings provide an opportunity to coordinate with others, identify existing tools that may be useful for your project, and check if similar projects are already in progress. The goal is to break down silos and come together on our automation efforts. Additionally, the [Infrastructure Automation Project Pipeline](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/Infrastructure-Automation-Projects/issues)  is a valuable resource to check if an existing solution already exists for your use case.

For new project ideas, a [template](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/automation-tool-template) is available in the Infrastructure Automation repository. This template allows you to provide an overview of the proposal, specify the mission/goal of the project, and describe the current process. Project designs are stored in a [Project Designs Box folder](https://ibm.ent.box.com/s/v85ii0uzsrce68u8ugy2kt0rlg6atcid).

# Automation Development Best Practices
Author: Eric Reid, Kelly Alvarez

Understanding developer practices is essential for both developers and anyone who wants to engage with the automation developed by EST. Producing robust tools that minimize technical debt and functional limitations requires careful consideration of development practices. While innovation is encouraged, formalizing tools and ensuring they are sustainable is crucial. The following practices aim to promote this goal. Unclean code practices are responsible for 80% of the cost associated with support and service, highlighting the importance of developing tools with best practices in mind. Let’s make sure we are developing tools in the best way possible!

If you're unsure about how to proceed, you can reach out to the Nova team, `@nova-automation` on Slack, for guidance. Additionally, each squad has an Automation Representative who stays informed about available tools. The appointed automation reps are included in the `@est-automation-reps` Slack group.

## Code Language and Repository
In general, unless there is a specific, approved technical reason not to, we should be writing all new automation in Python 3. Python is available in every major runtime environment, and provides a consistent framework in which to write automation. All code should be in repositories in [systemz](https://github.ibm.com/systemz).

## General Best Practices
When programming, strive to be object-oriented, using classes and methods to create small functions that can be re-used not only by your automation but by others. This alleviates problems down the road.

You should comment your code, and if you want others to use your Python modules, type hints should be included in your module definition (See: https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html)

## Other Useful Links
- [Index of Python Enhancement Proposals](https://peps.python.org/pep-0000/)
- [Nova GitHub team](https://github.ibm.com/orgs/systemz/teams/nova-automation)
- Nova team Slack user group: @nova-automation
- [#whitewater-github](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C3SSJ6CSE) Slack channel
- [#test-floor-automation-guild](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C03JJCXNNJG) Slack channel

# Releases and Release Notes

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To manage releases effectively, follow these best practices:

* **Bundle Fixes and Features**: Group related changes together and create a new release.
* **Write Release Notes**: Summarize the changes included in the release.
* **Dev Branch**: Create a `dev` branch off of `main` to accumulate features and fixes before merging into `main`. Branch off of `dev` to work on individual features or fixes, then merge back into `dev`.
* **[Auto-Generate Release Notes](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/automatically-generated-release-notes)**: Use GitHub's auto-generate release notes feature to create release notes based on well-defined issues and branches.

# Repository Structure

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To maintain consistency across SystemZ repositories, it's recommended to use the [template repository](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/automation-tool-template) when creating a new project. Although the template is Python-focused, its clean code structure can benefit projects in any language.

## Key Components of the Template

![Alt Text](./images/repo_structure.png)

* `src` directory: contains all source code
	+ `package_name` subdirectory: replace with your package name
	+ `main` file: kicks off the process with your tool, leveraging classes and modules
* `unittests` directory: contains automated tests for your package
* `gitignore`: The [gitignore](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore) file is where you specify file formats or files that Git should ignore, preventing them from being committed to the repository.
* `pyproject.toml`: The [pyproject.toml](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/writing-pyproject-toml/) file enables packaging your repository. It contains essential metadata, including:
	* `package_name`
	* `authors`: a list of contributors
	* `readme` and `user guide`: documentation for your tool
	* `dependencies`: external modules, third-party packages, or classes required by your tool.

## Dependencies

By specifying dependencies, you ensure that users installing your tool will also receive the necessary dependencies. Notably, the Automation Tools [package registry](https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/automation-packages/) allows you to list dependencies that are hosted outside the main [Python Package Index](https://pypi.org/) (PyPI). TOAD is configured to first check this registry for tool packages, avoiding naming conflicts with existing PyPI packages. You can still install dependencies from PyPI as needed.

## Packaging

There are [tutorials](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/tutorials/packaging-projects/) available on how to package a simple Python project. It will show you how to add the necessary files and structure to create the package, how to build the package, and how to upload it to the Python Package Index (PyPI).

## Versioning

The versioning scheme follows **Semantic Versioning**, which consists of three numbers:
1. **Major version** (first number): indicates a breaking change that may cause issues when switching between versions
2. **Minor version** (second number): represents new features or enhancements
3. **Patch version** (third number): denotes bug fixes

This versioning scheme helps ensure that changes are properly tracked and communicated.

# Unit Testing

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To ensure the reliability and stability of your code, implement unit tests using the following guidelines:

## Pytest
Use [Pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/), a feature-rich framework for running unit tests, which is easier to write and execute than the built-in Python `unittest` module.

![Alt Text](./images/unit_tests.png)

## Mocking Data
Utilize [mocking data](https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.mock.html) to simulate interactions with external sources that may not be accessible in your test environment.

# User Experience

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To create a seamless user experience, consider the following recommendations:

## Recommended Libraries:
Utilize third-party packages like:
- [Typer](https://typer.tiangolo.com/): manages command line arguments and help menus
- [Textual](https://textual.textualize.io/): creates interactive menus in the command line

## Consistency:
Strive for consistency in the use and user experience of your tools, making them intuitive and easy to use.

## Gaining Insight from Power Users:
Work with power users to gather feedback and understand the target audience. Use this input to shape your tool and improve the user experience.

# Virtual Environments

Author: Kelly Alvarez

TOAD is a test environment, NOT a development environment! To develop tools effectively, use a local environment with **[virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/venv.html) (venv)**. This approach keeps your development environment clean and organized, allows you to work on multiple tools or test different versions without conflicts, prevents unexpected dependency behavior, and enables you to easily remove or recreate environments as needed.

## Best Practices
Avoid developing tools directly in TOAD, as it's a shared environment with limited resources. Refrain from installing development tools like VS Code in TOAD to avoid conflicts with other users. Instead, use the TOAD dashboard to open an SSH connection to your container for testing purposes.

## uv: Python Packages/Projects Manager

[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is a command-line tool for managing Python environments, offering features such as installing and switching between python versions, creating virtual environments, and building Python tools. uv comes with pip package management ready to go, and you can build your package with a simple `uv build` command in your repository. uv is significantly faster than pip, making it a more efficient choice for managing your Python projects.

# Working with Branches

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To maintain a clean and organized repository, follow these best practices when working with [branches](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-branches):

* **Create a new branch for each issue**: ALWAYS create a new branch before starting any work! Limit each branch to one issue to make pull requests easy to review and integrate into the main codebase. ONLY commit related changes to a branch!
* **Keep branch names simple**: Use the corresponding issue number or a brief description of the change.
* **Delete branches after merging**: After a pull request is complete and the branch is merged, delete the branch to avoid a cluttered repository.

When creating an issue, you can:
* Create a branch directly from the issue page
* Link a pull request to the issue. The branch name will default to the issue title, but remember to keep it simple and concise!

# CIO DevEx Guide

Author: Savannah Portilla

## What is the CIO DevEx App?
[CIO DevEx](https://pages.github.ibm.com/cio-ci-cd/documentation/) (Developer Experience) is IBM’s centralized CI/CD platform, designed to standardize how applications are built, tested, and deployed across the company. It automates the end-to-end software delivery process so engineers can focus on development while the platform handles repetitive tasks like builds, vulnerability checks, security scans, deployments, and validations.

metadata.section_heading: What is the CIO DevEx App?

content:
#### CIO DevEx Pipeline Overview:
![](./images/CI_CD_Pipelines_chart.png)

## Get Started with CIO DevEx

**🔗 [CIO DevEx](https://pages.github.ibm.com/cio-ci-cd/documentation/python-library/)**

#### 🚨 Notes Before you Begin
The pipeline is configured to use the following steps/tasks:
```
00  - build-ci-image (creation of the building image)
01  - clone (cloning the repo into the building image)
01a - detect-secrets (scanning for secrets in the repository)
02  - install (refreshing dependencies, using 'poetry install')
03  - mend-scan (open-source scanning for dependency vulnerabilities)
04  - unit-test  (execute unit tests (like pytest))
05  - lint (syntax checking)
06  - git-version (writing back version information)
07  - python-version (writing back version information)
08  - sonarqube-scan (sonarqube vulnerability scan)
09  - publish (publish to artifactory)
```
**⚠️ Building packages is only supported for poetry at the moment. If your pipeline fails to publish, this is likely caused by not committing the [poetry.lock file](./Poetry.md). When the lockfile is missing, the pipeline can't identify the correct response.**

**⚠️You'll also need to set up the Detect Secrets tool, follow the steps in the [IBM Detect Secrets page](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/detect-secrets).**

### 1. Install the GitHub Application
In order to connect a pipeline to your application, the Github Application should be installed in your repository. This application will listen for push events (one or more commits) to your GitHub repository. Install the CIO DevEx GitHub App [here](https://github.ibm.com/github-apps/cio-devex/installations/select_target).

❗ Make sure that you have Owner permission, or have someone with Owner permission approves this installation.

### 2. Create your `build.yml` file

More information on this process [here](https://pages.github.ibm.com/cio-ci-cd/documentation/python-library/#creation-of-a-buildyml), view the nova_saturn_client `build.yml` [here](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/nova_saturn_client/blob/main/build.yml) as an example.

Example:
```
apiVersion: automation.cio/v1alpha1
kind: RepositoryConfig
ealImapNumber: <EAL NUMBER OF THE PROJECT>
jiraProjectName: <OPTIONAL, SEE BELOW>
notifications:
slackChannel: <OPTIONAL, SEE BELOW>
build:
strategy: simple-pipeline
pipeline: python-v3.9-micropipenv-pypi-library
version: v2
config:
    private-dependencies: <SEE DESCRIPTION BELOW>
    publish-repository-name: <NAME OF THE REPO INSIDE THE REFERRED ARTIFACTORY>
    install-packages-ci: <OPTIONAL, SEE BELOW>
```

⚠️ See instructions on generating your `private-dependencies` token [here](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/saturn-client/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) under the "Encrypting credentials for publishing with CIO DevEx Pipelines" section.

### 3. Push Code and Wait for Build
When you commit and push code changes from your feature branch on you local repository to github.ibm.com, the CIO CI/CD pipeline is triggered to build the code.

💡 If you need to restart a build, run the following command:
```
git commit --allow-empty -m "Trigger Build"
git push
```

# Formatters

Author: Kelly Alvarez

Follow the [PEP 8](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/) style guide for Python code which is referenced by Pylint. Use tools like [Autopep8](https://pypi.org/project/autopep8/#toc-entry-4), available as a [VS Code extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.autopep8), to auto-indent code, remove extraneous whitespace, ensure consistency across tools and improve maintainability.

# Linters

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To ensure clean code and prevent technical debt, utilize tools like Pylint.

[Pylint](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.pylint) helps automatically implement clean code by highlighting syntax and logic issues, providing links to explanations and solutions, enforcing coding standards, and detecting bugs and preventing errors.

# Modularity

Author: Kelly Alvarez

To promote reusability and collaboration, focus on building modular tools. By adopting a modular approach, you can create tools that are more flexible, maintainable, and reusable.

Key aspects of modularity include:

ar tools. By adopting a modular approach, you can create tools that are more flexible, maintainable, and reusable.

Key aspects of modularity include:

* **[Classes](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/classes.html)**: Group common attributes and methods into a single logical unit, utilizing [object-oriented programming](https://yourlearning.ibm.com/activity/UDEMY-1933808) principles.
* **[Modules](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/modules.html)**: Break down large programs into smaller, logically grouped units, allowing users to utilize specific parts of the tool as needed.
* **Avoid Monolithic Design**: Refrain from [combining components into a single, inseparable unit](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/system-design/monolithic-architecture-system-design/), as this can hinder scalability and maintainability.
* **[Unix Philosophy](https://cscie2x.dce.harvard.edu/hw/ch01s06.html)**: Embody the principle of "do one thing and do it well," promoting a collaborative ecosystem of tools.
* **Consider Others' Needs**: Think about how others might want to use your tool and consider incorporating aspects of other tools.

### Watch out for when tools possess these opportunities for improvement:

**The Swiss Army Knife:** A tool which offers a versatile set of functions that are implemented by embedded logic for each function. You can’t just take one piece of it and run it unattended or standalone. Suites are sweet but they should leverage modular tools that can be used in different use cases.

**Rube Goldberg Contraptions:** A monolithic tool which automates a sequence of workflow steps that involves logic or commonality with other processes. We need to strive for E2E automation but it's important that automated workflow steps can be utilized discreetly.

# Poetry Guide

Author: Savannah Portilla

## What is Poetry?
[Poetry](https://python-poetry.org/docs/) is a modern tool for Python dependency management and packaging. It simplifies creating virtual environments, adding dependencies, and publishing Python packages by consolidating everything into a single file: `pyproject.toml`.

## Why make the switch?
Poetry streamlines packaging and dependency management, allowing for a more maintainable and automated process. With Poetry, you no longer need to manage separate `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, and `requirements.txt` files. Instead, everything lives in a single `pyproject.toml` file.

If you use Poetry alongside the [CIO CI/CD pipeline (CIO DevEx)](CIO%20DevEx.md), Poetry can automatically publish your package to [Artifactory](Artifactory.md) as part of the pipeline process.

Additionally, Poetry has it's own [virtual environment](https://python-poetry.org/docs/basic-usage/#using-your-virtual-environment) that is great for testing installs and running test scripts in a clean, isolated environment.
## 🧰 Switching to Poetry

### 🏁 Install Poetry
**🔗 [Install Poetry](https://python-poetry.org/docs/#installation)**
```
pip install poetry
```
or
```
curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -
```
Then, verify the installation:
```
poetry --version
```
### 🏁 Start a New Project / Add Poetry to an Existing One

metadata.section_heading: 🏁 Start a New Project / Add Poetry to an Existing One

content:
#### → Starting a New Project
[Create a new Poetry project](https://python-poetry.org/docs/basic-usage/#project-setup):
```
poetry new my_project
```
This creates:
```
my_project/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── my_project/__init__.py
└── tests/
```

#### → Adding Poetry to an Existing Project
Delete `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `requirements.txt`, and `MANIFEST.in` if they exist. Poetry doesn’t use these.

[If you already have a Python project](https://python-poetry.org/docs/basic-usage/#initialising-a-pre-existing-project), run:
```
poetry init
```
Follow the prompts to create a `pyproject.toml`.

Or, create the file yourself. Read more about this file structure and requirements [here](https://python-poetry.org/docs/pyproject/) or view the [nova_saturn_client pyproject.toml](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/nova_saturn_client/blob/main/pyproject.toml) file for an example.

metadata.section_heading: → Adding Poetry to an Existing Project

content:
## ℹ️ `poetry.lock` File
[`poetry.lock`](https://python-poetry.org/docs/libraries#lock-file) is a lock file that records the exact versions of every package (and their dependencies) that were installed when Poetry last resolved your environment. If your teammate runs poetry install, they get the same versions you had, even if new releases are available. View the [nova_saturn_client .lock file](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/nova_saturn_client/blob/main/poetry.lock) as an example.

### How is it generated?
The `poetry.lock` file is automatically generated the first time Poetry resolves dependencies for your project.

This happens when you run either:
- `poetry install` (Installs exact versions from poetry.lock or creates it if no lock file exists yet)
- `poetry add <package>` (adding a new dependency also regenerates the lock file)
- `poetry update` (explicitly refreshes dependencies and **rewrites** the lock file)

### What's inside?
It’s a more detailed TOML-formatted file that contains:

- Exact version numbers of all dependencies
- Source info (PyPI, Artifactory, etc.)
- Package metadata (description, category, optional status, etc.)
- Hashes of distributions (so Poetry can verify integrity when installing)

⚠️ Don’t edit poetry.lock manually, only change it via Poetry commands (`add`, `update`, `remove`)
## 💡 Poetry How-To's

### 📦 Managing Dependencies
**🔗 [Managing Dependencies](https://python-poetry.org/docs/managing-dependencies/)**

Add a dependency (example: argparse):
```
poetry add <package name>
```
Add a development dependency (example: pytest):
```
poetry add --group dev <tool name>
```
Install all dependencies:
```
poetry install
```
Poetry looks at your pyproject.toml (and poetry.lock, if it exists) to decide what to install.

Update dependencies:
```
poetry update
```

### 🗺️ Virtual Environments
Poetry automatically manages [virtual environments](https://python-poetry.org/docs/basic-usage/#using-your-virtual-environment). When you run `poetry install` or `poetry shell`, Poetry automatically creates a virtual environment (if one doesn't exist yet) specifically for that project.

This virtual environment:
- Is separate from global Python installs
- Keeps dependencies isolated
- Is managed entirely by Poet-ry (no need to use venv or virtualenv manually)

#### → Where it's stored:
By default, Poetry puts virtual environments in a central cache folder, named after the project.
To see the exact path:
```
poetry env info --path
```
You can also configure Poetry to store venvs inside your project directory:
```
poetry config virtualenvs.in-project true
```
That creates .venv/ in your project root.

#### → How to use it:
Run:
```
poetry install
```
And Poetry creates .venv and installs dependencies inside it.

To drop into a shell inside that venv:
```
poetry shell
```

Any scripts run with:
```
poetry run python your_script.py
```
Are executed using the venv's Python and dependencies.

### 🛠️ Building and Publishing:
**🚨 IMPORTANT:** **Remember to increment your version!**

Build your package:
```
poetry build
```
Publish to a repository (example with Artifactory):
```
poetry publish -r sys-stg-team-pypi-local
```
🔥 Use `poetry run pre-commit run --all-files` to check formatting and style before pushing if you use the [Pre-commit Tool](./Pre-commit.md).

# Pre-commit Tool Guide

Author: Savannah Portilla

## What is the Pre-commit tool?
[`pre-commit`](https://pre-commit.com/) is a framework for managing and automatically running code checks (called hooks) before you make a commit. It helps catch common issues early, like formatting problems, syntax errors, or accidentally committed secrets, by scanning your files and blocking commits that don’t pass.

It's used to enforce standards like:
- Code style with [autopep8](https://pypi.org/project/autopep8/), [black](https://github.com/psf/black), or [flake8](https://flake8.pycqa.org/en/latest/)
- Secret scanning with [detect-secrets](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/detect-secrets)
- Linting and static analysis
- Formatting consistency

Once installed, pre-commit runs automatically every time you try to commit code, helping you keep things clean, consistent, and secure without having to remember to run checks manually.

## Using `pre-commit`
For more in depth instructions and details, view the [pre-commit website](https://pre-commit.com/).

**🚨 Ensure you have installed and set up `detect-secrets` first, follow this [guide](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/detect-secrets) for assistance.**

1. Install the tool
    ```
    pip install pre-commit
    ```

2. Add a config file. In the root of your project, create a `.pre-commit-config.yaml` file. See the nova_saturn_client file as an example [here](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/nova_saturn_client/blob/main/.pre-commit-config.yaml) or view the [pre-commit website](https://pre-commit.com/) for more details on this step.

3. Install the git hook scripts

On the project folder execute `pre-commit install` → now pre-commit will run automatically on every git commit.

4. Test that the pre-commit hooks are working by running `pre-commit run --all-files --verbose`, you will get a list of checks with their status.

✅ These steps ensure every commit goes through automated checks, helping enforce consistency and prevent common issues before code review.

# Code Quality

This section includes an overview of some tools recommended by the CIO to instill best practices, enabling the efficient creation, maintenance, and delivery of code as well as overall coding best practices guides.
## Code Quality Tools

### CIO DevEx

### Poetry

[Poetry](./Poetry.md) is a modern tool for Python dependency management and packaging. It can help with creating pyproject.toml files!

### Pre Commit

[Pre Commit](./Pre-commit.md) is a framework for managing and automatically running code checks before you make a commit to help catch common issues early.

### Formatters

[Autopep8](https://pypi.org/project/autopep8/#toc-entry-4) is a Python library and tool that automatically formats your code to conform to the [PEP 8 style guide](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/).

### Linters

[Pylint](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.pylint) is a popular static code analyzer for Python that checks for programming errors, enforces coding standards (like PEP 8), and suggests refactoring opportunities.
## Coding Best Practices

### Commenting Code

The [how-to-comment-code](./how-to-comment-code.md) guide will teach you all the basics for ensuring you are following the best practices when commenting your code.

### Modularity

To promote reusability and collaboration, focus on building modular tools. By adopting a modular approach, you can create tools that are more flexible, maintainable, and reusable.
# Code Commenting Best Practices

## Introduction

Readable code matters. Clear variable names, well-defined functions, and good structure help others (and future you) understand what your code does.

Comments are another valuable tool when used correctly. They should explain why something exists or clarify complex logic, not restate the obvious.

Too many comments add noise but too few leave readers guessing. Aim for clean, self-explanatory code, and use comments only where they add real value.
## Types of Comments

### Inline Comments: Brief notes next to code lines

- Inline comments add quick clarity to a single line of code. Keep them brief, relevant, and under ~72 characters to avoid clutter.

```python

metadata.section_heading: Inline Comments: Brief notes next to code lines

content:
# Keep only ripe apples
ripe_apples = [apple for apple in apples if apple.ripeness >= 5]
```
> ⚠️ If you’re writing a lot of inline comments, your code may need clearer names or smaller functions so the comments aren’t necessary. If your code requires a lot of comments to understand it may be time for a refactor!

### Block Comments: Longer explanations for code sections

```python

metadata.section_heading: Block Comments: Longer explanations for code sections

content: # Block comments span multiple lines and are used to

metadata.section_heading: Block comments span multiple lines and are used to

content: # explain larger sections of code.
# They’re perfect for providing context,
# describing the overall logic,

# or outlining steps in a complex algorithm.
```

metadata.section_heading: or outlining steps in a complex algorithm.

content:
### Docstrings: Descriptive comments for functions, classes, and modules

- Docstrings are structured documentation strings placed immediately after a module, class, or function definition.

```python
def example_function(apple_type:str, apple_count:int)->dict:
    """
    Explains what the function does, its inputs, and its return value.
    Docstrings must be the first statement in a function to appear in tooltips.
    """
    # If you use a comment here, python will not recognize this as a function description.
```

- A good docstring answers:
    - What the function does
    - What parameters it expects
    - What it returns
    - Any side effects or exceptions

- Document each parameter’s purpose and type, and clearly describe the return value, especially when behavior changes based on conditions.

metadata.section_heading: Docstrings: Descriptive comments for functions, classes, and modules

content: ## Best Practices

### Keep comments concise and relevant.
- Comments should explain why something exists or clarify non-obvious behavior, not narrate the code.

### Avoid obvious comments.
- If the code is clear, don’t comment it. Restating what the code already says adds noise.
- Follow **D.R.Y.** (Don't repeat yourself): don’t repeat what the code already communicates.

```python
return x # returns x -> this is an unnecessary comment.
```

### Keep comments up to date with code changes.
- Outdated comments are worse than none. Update or remove comments whenever behavior changes.

metadata.section_heading: Keep comments up to date with code changes.

content:
### Explain intent, not implementation.
- Describe why a decision was made, especially for workarounds or edge cases.

### Avoid TODO clutter.
- Use "TODO"s sparingly and always include context or a reason, not just a reminder.

### Comment before complex logic.
- Introduce hard-to-read code with a short explanation, rather than interrupting it line by line.

## Tools and Automation

**Commenting standards and linters**

- Linters help enforce consistent commenting and documentation across a codebase by catching missing or poorly formatted comments early.

- Common examples include:
    - **pylint**: Flags missing or incomplete docstrings and encourages consistent documentation.
    - **flake8**: Enforces general style rules and can be extended with plugins for docstring checks.
    - **pydocstyle**: Focuses specifically on docstring conventions, such as those defined in PEP 257.

- Running these tools in automated checks helps maintain standards without relying solely on manual code reviews.

## Conclusion
- Write code that explains what it does.

- Use comments to explain why it does it, but only when needed.

If your code needs a comment, write a good one. If it needs many, rewrite the code instead.

# Artifactory Guide

Author: Savannah Portilla

## What is Artifactory?

[Artifactory](https://jfrog.com/help/r/jfrog-artifactory-documentation/jfrog-artifactory) is IBM's internal package registry, a centralized system where we store, version, and distribute software artifacts like Python packages, Docker images, and more.

For Python developers, Artifactory acts like a private PyPI, allowing you to publish and install internal packages across teams while controlling access, tracking versions, and ensuring code security.
## Getting your Python package on Artifactory

metadata.section_heading: Getting your Python package on Artifactory

content:
### 1. Get an Artifactory token, this will act as your password when installing from or downloading to Artifactory.
- Visit the [jFrog Artifactory website](https://na.artifactory.swg-devops.com/ui/repos/tree/General) and login with your W3 credentials
- Generate token by:
    1. Click your username in the top-right
    2. Click "Edit Profile"
    4. Click "Generate Identity Token"
    5. **🚨 IMPORTANT:** **Save your token somewhere safe!** You can't view it again.
- Visit this [official guide](https://taas.cloud.ibm.com/guides/artifactory-authentication-access-tokens.md) for more information on Artifactory access tokens.

metadata.section_heading: 1. Get an Artifactory token, this will act as your password when installing from or downloading to Artifactory.

content:
### 2. Publish to Artifactory
Artifactory is not limited to a single Python packaging tool. Whether you are using poetry, setuptools or something else, you can still publish your package. In this guide I will include steps for both poetry and setuptools.

#### Method 1: Publish with Poetry
For help getting started with Poetry, read the [Poetry guide](../Poetry.md).

Once you’ve obtained your token, tell Poetry how to authenticate and where to publish.
1. Add the Artifactory source to your pyproject.toml file:
    ```
    [[tool.poetry.source]]
    name = "sys-stg-team-pypi-local"
    url = "https://na.artifactory.swg-devops.com/artifactory/api/pypi/sys-stg-team-pypi-local/simple/"
    priority = "supplemental"
    ```
2. Configure authentication (one-time setup). This securely stores your credentials in Poetry's config file.
    ```
    poetry config http-basic.sys-stg-team-pypi-local <your-w3-email> <your-token>
    ```
3. Build and Publish (**❗ONLY if NOT using CIO DevEx**):

**🚨 IMPORTANT:** **Ensure you have incremented your package version in the pyproject.toml file**.
    ```
    poetry build
    poetry publish -r sys-stg-team-pypi-local
    ```
    If using CIO DevEx CI/CD, it will automatically publish the package when the PR is merged, for help getting started, read the [CIO DevEx guide](<../CIO DevEx.md>).

#### Method 2: Publish with setuptools and Twine
1. **🚨 IMPORTANT:** Update the version in your pyproject.toml
2. Navigate to your package root (where pyproject.toml is located)
3. Install required build tools:
    ```
    pip install build twine
    ```
4. Remove any old dist builds and build the new one:
    ```
    rm -rf dist/
    python -m build
    ```
5. Upload to Artifactory with Twine:
    ```
    twine upload \
    --repository-url https://na.artifactory.swg-devops.com/artifactory/api/pypi/sys-stg-team-pypi-local/simple/ \
    dist/*
    ```
    ⚠️ You’ll be prompted to enter your IBM W3 email and Artifactory token.

metadata.section_heading: Method 2: Publish with setuptools and Twine

content:
### Step 3. Ensure your package was successfully uploaded
Under the "Artifactory" -> "Artifacts" section on the [jFrog Artifactory website](https://na.artifactory.swg-devops.com/ui/repos/tree/General/sys-stg-team-pypi-local/), you will see the "sys-stg-team-pypi-local" folder, your package will be stored there along with any older versions you have uploaded. When people install your package, the latest version will be installed by default.

metadata.section_heading: Step 3. Ensure your package was successfully uploaded

content:
### Installing your package:
Install command:
```
pip install <your_package_name> --extra-index-url='https://na.artifactory.swg-devops.com/artifactory/api/pypi/sys-stg-team-pypi-local/simple'
```
You (or your user) will be prompted to enter your IBM W3 email and Artifactory token. **🚨 IMPORTANT:** **You and your users will need an Artifactory token to install.**

# Github Releases

Author: Eric Reid

Date: 07/14/2023

## Overarching Rules

First, all releasing is conducted through Github Releases, and our users are instructed to watch changes in repositories of tools they wnat updates on. All releases MUST follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/)

## General Release Flow

1. A new piece of automation passes through initial testing and is agreed upon that it is ready for general release. What changes are made are noted, and a version number chosen accordingly. The version number is included in any setup.py files, for consistent versioning.
2. A release note is drafted, including what is changed, what (if anything) users have to do to receive the new release, and who worked on the changes.
3. A release date is chosen, if necessary
4. The development branch is merged to main, if any merge errors occur, the release is postponed to address merge conflicts.
5. Github release is created, and users now have access to the code.
6. A new development branch is created from main.

Specific delivery methods and platforms will have their own requirements, restrictions and steps. Please be sure to consult your delivery methods' guides.

## Minimum Requirements of a Release Note

1. Author of the release note, developer(s) names and contact info
2. Link to Github repository
3. Release version
4. Link to EST User's Guide Documentation
5. What fixes are in the release
6. What is new in the release

Release notes may also have instructions to migrate to the new version from the old version. This should be accompanyied with a major release version, and should be infrequent.

# HOW TO: Code Reviews
This guide outlines the best practices and procedure for reviewing automation tool code changes.

## As the Developer
1. After opening a `PR (Pull Request)` for your code changes, assign at least one reviewer. This should ideally be someone familiar with the tool, but it is also a good idea to get a fresh pair of eyes.

![](../../images/code-reviews-as-dev-1.png)

2. Allow time for the assigned reviewers to complete their review before merging your changes. You will see the status of reviews at the bottom of the PR or under the `Reviewers` section shown in the previous step.

3. If there are any checks configured for your PR, make sure all of the checks passed. You can determine this by looking at the bottom of the PR or under the `Checks` tab at the top. In the case any checks fail, review the details of the failing checks and address with additional changes as needed.

![](../../images/code-reviews-as-dev-2.png)

4. If any reviewers request changes, address any feedback by committing additional changes to the same branch and re-request the review(s) when ready.

![](../../images/code-reviews-as-dev-3.png)

any feedback by committing additional changes to the same branch and re-request the review(s) when ready.

![](../../images/code-reviews-as-dev-3.png)

5. Resolve any merge conflicts with additional commits. If so, re-request review(s). More info on merge conflicts can be found [here](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/addressing-merge-conflicts/resolving-a-merge-conflict-on-github).

6. Once all changes have been reviewed and approved, all checks have passed and all merge conflicts have been addressed you may merge the PR. If merging from a feature/fix branch, delete the branch after merging.

## As the Reviewer
1. When you're assigned as a reviewer for a `PR (Pull Request)`, you will be notified via email which provides a link to that PR. So keep an eye out for any reviews you get assigned. You can organize your inbox to filter emails from GitHub into a separate folder for better visibility.

2. Access the PR and review the description of the changes. There will often be a parent issue linked which the changes in the PR are meant to address. If the information describing the changes is insufficient, reach out to the developer that opened the PR.

3. Once you have enough context for the changes, navigate to the `Files Changed` tab of the PR.

4. If this is your first PR review, you can take a look at the display settings and see which you prefer. The default is `Unified`.

![](../../images/code-reviews-as-reviewer-1.png)

5. When reviewing changes look out for the following:

e which you prefer. The default is `Unified`.

![](../../images/code-reviews-as-reviewer-1.png)

5. When reviewing changes look out for the following:

* Do any existing supported tools already perform a similar function?
    * Do the changes accomplish the goal(s) described in the PR description or parent issue?
    * Are the changes clear and easy to understand?
    * Do the changes meet our standards?
    * Are there any potential logic improvements to suggest?
    * Do the changes potentially cause problems/breakage in code that would use it?

6. If you come across any of these, you should add review comments on the offending line(s). If it's one line you can hover over the line and click the plus sign that appears. Otherwise you can click from the first line and drag to the last line in the block you want to comment on.

![](../../images/code-reviews-as-reviewer-2.png)

7. In the prompt, add the necessary feedback. You can also add a change suggestion if you already have any idea of what should be changed.

Once you've reviewed all of the changes and added any feedback click `Review changes` at the top of the page. ![](../../images/code-reviews-as-reviewer-5.png) 10. ### PHP Api Hooks
STELAR 2.1 continues the use of api calls based in PHP. Each site and category contains its own respective api and hook call, but many categories across the different sites share an api call.

For example, the System Search Api call to search a system in Power Lab is https://stela.aus.stglabs.ibm.com/api/system/enumerate, while the System Search Api call in Z Lab is https://stela.pok.stglabs.ibm.com/api/system/enumerate. Both api calls contain **system/enumerate**, but differ in the global api call. Power Lab is **stela.aus.stglabs.ibm.com** and Z Lab is **stela.pok.stglabs.ibm.com**

# Migration Procedure for STELA 2.1
Author: Sabrina Netters
Date Updated: 01/08/2024

## Reason for Migration
The repository tool STELA has been around since 2009, where it ran on PHP APIs, basic HTML, and CSS. It was upgraded to STELA 2.0 in 2022, where the use of the PHP APIs remained, but the front end is using React and the Carbon Design System. STELA 2.0 is hosted on a server in the Austin Lab.

As the Austin Lab begins to sunset some servers, the decision came to host STELA on Cirrus Cloud, where the front end is continuing to use React and the Carbon Design System has been upgraded to version 11. This is STELA 2.1, where it will be now known as STELAR 2.1 with the addition of the Reservation tool.

## Differences between STELA 2.0 and STELAR 2.1
The main differences in STELA 2.0 and STELAR 2.1 are found in the development tools and UI.

![](../Automation%20Documentation/images/2.0vs2.1.png)

# CARTES Automation Documentation

This is a repository for developer-centric documentation of CARTES

# CARTES Data Collection

This document describes how CARTES gets its data, for user understanding. There are a lot of details here, if you are interested feel free to talk to one of the engineers about the exact mechanisms and logic, or feel free to look through the code on Github!

## Basics

CARTES is integrated into STELA, and uses many of their data harvesting systems, GUI's, and database structures. All automatically obtained Z data is through STELA. The main addition for Z data that CARTES added was to get the output of the System Input Output Configuration Analyzer (SIOCA). This is a panel in the SE, and can be run programmatically in test systems to obtain the **last IML'ed** configuration. Dynamic changes are currently not supported in CARTES (see Restrictions below).

Switch data is harvested using modified versions of Brian Jacob's Switch.py scripts, running CLI commands in the switches and interpeting the data for CARTES to use.

DASD data is achieved via API requests to the DS8K HMC's. This limits how old of DASD we are able to support (again, see Restrictions).

## System Registration and Definition

Z systems are defined to STELA through Rodney's Lifelines, and is maintained by the STELA team. A brand new system may take a day or two to enter.

Switches are defined to STELA through the Register Systems, though automatic harvesting is working on being implemented. This is managed by the [Infrastructure Team](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/ibm-z-test-development-floor-ewm-guide).

DASD are automatically harvested by subnet with standardized logins on a nightly basis.

Systems can be manually registered, but the design point is to enable automatic registartion as much as possible.

## Production Z Systems (i.e. w/o Tools)

Production Z systems currently have minimal support, since they cannot run CLI SIOCA. The CARTES team is working on methods to manually enter the data by exporting SIOCA data. A system with associated to a location with cable information can exist in CARTES even if the full system data doesn't.

## Current Restrictions

1. Dynamic I/O changes will not be picked up, only last IML'ed configuration.
2. Production Z systems have limited capabilities
3. Non-IBM DS8K storage are not supported
4. DS8K's older than 8870 have limited support since they have no API capabilities.
5. Other test hardware (Finisar's, DWDM's, etc.) are not currently supported.

# Column Filtering and Configuration

All tables in CARTES are equipped with powerful data filters that can help narrow what you are viewing to what is important to you. This guide will use an example of a CEC Systems Inventory data table, but all tables will have the same functionality. Refer to the relevant query guides to get to a table.

## Column Configuration

Tables are shown with default columns. The abiliy to select which columns should appear/disappear or to rearrange the order of the columns is known as `column config`. Column config is accessed by clicking the vertical `Columns` button found on the right hand side of all tables:

![](../../images/columnconfigcolumnbutton.png)

Clicking the `Columns` button will open up a list of all possible columns for the data you are viewing. Clicking the checkboxes will make columns appear and disappear in the table. Grabbing the small grid icon and dragging it will change the order of the columns in the table. Click the `Columns` button again to hide the menu.

![](../../images/columnsmanu.png)

### Saving your Column Configuration

For a tables customized column configurations to remain, the `Save Column Config` must be clicked. This button is found at the top right of a table under the `Save` icon.

![](../../images/columnfilteringsavecolumnconfigbtn.png)

After the `Save Column Config` is clicked, you can now save your customized queries, as well as share them. See [Save and Share Queries](../Finding%20Data/GeneralSavingQueries.md) to learn more about saving and sharing your query.

## Filtering and Searching in and Across Columns

Once you have all the columns you want, you can now search and filter inside of columns. You can sort the data by the alphabetical order by clicking on the name of a column. Clicking it again will make it reverse alphabetical order, and a third time will set it to default.

More powerful filtering is available.  Below each column is a blank box and an arrow:

![](../../images/columnsblankbox.png)

Clicking the arrow on a column will show all the possible values of the column. You can search through these with the Search and Filter boxes. Then, select and deselect whatever you want to add and remove it from the table.

![](../../images/columnfiltering.png)

You can also type in the search box below a column, then press ENTER to search for any rows in that column that have your search text in them:

![](../../images/columnssearchtext.png)

These filters, searches and selections apply across the entire table, and can be combined. An example would be to find a list of all BRINGUP systems in 'boe':

![](../../images/columndoublefilter.png)

# Save and Share Queries

CARTES provides the ability to save queries for later use. These queries can also be shared to other users.

:::caution

If you want to save or share a query that has customized column configurations (reordered or hidden/unhidden columns), you **MUST** configure the columns using the the `Column` tab on the right hand side of the table. Refer back to [Column Filtering and Configuration](../Finding%20Data/GeneralColumnFiltering.md) for configuring the columns.

:::

## Saving a Query

After creating a query and configuring the columns to your liking, you can go to the top right corner of the page and select `Save Query`.

![](../../images/savequery_new.png)

This will open up the save query modal:

![](../../images/savequery_modal.png)

Add a title, a comments and then press "Save".

This will save the modal to your user account. By default, it is not available to any other users.

## Using a Saved Query

Once you have saved a query, you can use it for later. It is important that you have to go to the same overarching category and report type to recall a query. For example, if you saved a query under CARTES PCHID, that query will not appear in CARTES DASD or CARTES Switches, you have to be in CARTES PCHID to access that saved query. Queries should be listed when you click "Search queries for ....." in the top right hand corner:

![](../../images/recallquery.png)

Select the `eye` icon to view the saved query. The `trashcan` icon will delete the saved query.

## Sharing a Query

You can send queries to other people so they can use it. On the top right, click the "Share Query" button to open the modal:

![](../../images/sharequerymodal.png)

You have the option of sharing the current query you are on or sharing one of your previously created queries. You can share via slack or by sharing the url.

# Accessing Path Reports

Path report queries are intended to work with the physical fibers between systems. This is also where individual edits to paths can be performed.

Access the path report of different systems by clicking the top left dropdown on the CARTES homepage and clicking **Path Report**.

![](./images/PathReportAccessStep1.png)

Once on the path report page, you must select a *path report type* and a *system name*, or else the query will not apply properly. System Product is **NOT** required. Once a path report type and system name have been selected, click the **Apply Query** button.

![](./images/PathReportAccessStep2.png)

For this example, we will be selecting the path report type **CARTES PCHID** and the system name **a40**. Once these are selecting, click the **Apply Query** button.

| Select Cartes PCHID                   | Select a40             |
| ----------------------- | ---------------- |
| ![select CARTES PCHID for path report type](./images/PathReportAccessStep3-1.png)            | ![selet a40 for system name](./images/PathReportAccessStep3-2.png)   |

PCHID for path report type](./images/PathReportAccessStep3-1.png)            | ![selet a40 for system name](./images/PathReportAccessStep3-2.png)   |

Now you should see a table displaying the path report for system **a40**. This includes the *Entry System*, which is a40 in this case, *Entry Port*, the *Cable Path*, the *Destination System*, *Destination Port*, as well as the *Cable Classes*.

![](./images/PathReportAccessStep4.png)

:::note

Now with the query pulled up, use any of the general guides below to help navigate the data:

[Column Filtering, Sorting, and Searching](../GeneralColumnFiltering.md)

[Saving, Searching, and Recalling Queries](../GeneralSavingQueries.md)

:::

## Data Interpetation

**Entry System** - System that starts the path in the report

**Entry Port** - PCHID, switch blade and port, and DASD SAID (or tag).

**Path** - CARTES retains the formatting of path reports from EPCT, but seperated by ',' instead of '->'.  If CARTES can recognize the EPCT text, it will include the names of each of the components in the path report in the "Classes" column.

**Destination Port** and **Destination System** - remotely sensed other end of the connnection. As of 09/29/2023, this is automatically populated in CARTES. Please open Github tickets if you also want a manual entry, but this was deemed more manual effort.

**Classes** - This is CARTES auto-detection of what type of equipment is separated by each comma in the Path report column.
## Query Examples:

#### CARTES Path Report PCHIDs:

![](./images/pathreportpchids.png)

#### CARTES Path Report Switches:

![](./images/path%20report%20switches.png)

#### CARTES Path Report DASD:

![](./images/pathreportdasd.png)

## Editing a Path in the Path Report Table

Once the path report table is visible, the ability to edit the path column is availble. Editing introduces the ability to add, modify, and delete a single path or multiple paths at a given time.

To access editing mode, click the **Edit**   ![](./images/EditPathsEditIcon.png)  icon on the top left of table.

Upon clicking the Edit icon, there will be a dropdown containing the options: *Edit Paths*, *Undo Edit*, *Redo Edit*, and *Submit Edit*. Click on **Edit Paths**.

![](./images/EditPathsStep1.png)

Once *Edit Paths* is clicked on, you should now be able to click on a path in the path column. In this example, we are on the path report for system *a40*. We will add a path to the Entry port 0140. To add a path, click on the empty path column in row 0140.

![](./images//EditPathsShowWhereEditIs.png)

:::note

You only need to click the path column **once** for the text editor to show.

:::

Once the path column is clicked on, a text editor will show. The editor is able to be resized if needed.

![](./images/EditPathStep2.png)

Inside the text editor, place `test comment`. To finish the edit, either click anywhere outside of the path column or press **Enter**.

![](./images//EditPathsStep3.png)

You should now see `test comment` in the previously empty path column for entry port 0140.
## Submit Edit

### An edit made in the table is not complete unless Submit Edit is clicked in the Edit icon dropdown.

For example, after our `test comment` is added to entry port 0140, if we refresh the table by clicking the **Apply Query** button, our edit will disappear.

![](./images/EditPathsRefreshTable.png)
![](./images/EditPathsUncompletedEdit.png)

In order for an edit to be complete and appear on the table after refreshing, the **Submit Edit** selection must be clicked in the Edit icon dropdown

![](./images/EditPathsSubmitEditSelection.png)

Let's re-enter Edit mode and add `test comment` back to the path column for entry port 0140. After the edit is made, click **Submit Edit** in the Edit icon dropdown.

Now the table can be refreshed (Reminder: click *Apply Query* button to refresh table). And your edit should now appear!

content:
### Multiple Path Edits
Because an edit is not complete unless  *Submit Edit* is clicked, it is possible to edit multiple paths at a time. For example, let's add `test comment` to entry port 0140, `test comment 2` to entry port 0141, and `test comment 3` to entry port 0154.

The steps to edit multiple paths are the same as editing a single path: click on a path to edit, edit in the text editor, then exit the text editor. Except you can edit any other row afterwards. Once entry port 0140, 0141, and 0154 have been edited, click *Submit Edit* for all edits to be finalized.

![](./images/EditPathsMultipleEdits.png)

## Undo and Redo Edit
While in editing mode (**before clicking Submit Edit**), you are able to undo and redo an edit. You can undo and redo an edit by either clicking **Undo Edit**/**Redo Edit** in the Edit icon dropdown, or you can use the Undo/Redo hotkeys (*Ctrl + Z/Command + Z for **Undo*** and *Ctrl + Y/Command + Shift + Z for **Redo***)

:::caution

The Undo and Redo hotkeys will **NOT** work unless the respective cell is in focus (the text editor is visible)!

| Correct cell view for Undo/Redo Hotkeys                   | Incorrect cell view for Undo/Redo Hotkeys               |
| ----------------------- | ---------------- |
| ![](./images/EditPathsCorrectUndoRedo.png)            | ![](./images/EditPathsIncorrectUndoRedo.png)   |

content:
## Basic Functionality

CARTES is hosted in STELAR 2.1, and uses their Carbon design. CARTES can be accessed from the CARTES tab:

![](../../images/CARTESHome.png)

On the left side is a "Search Type". Each of the guides in this folder will discuss how to find data in each of the search types in CARTES, below is an overview of what types of data or function are included in each.

### System Inventory

Systems inventory includes machine-specific data, such as CCIN, PCHIDs, CHPIDs, switch ports, and DASD ports. It doesn't show physical paths, but can show logical connections across the SAN. This can be useful to find what systems are where from detailed data found in operating systems, HMC's and SE's.

### Path Reports

Path report queries are intended to work with the physical fibers between systems. This is also where individual edits to paths can be performed.

### Systems

Systems query generates lists of systems, and boiler plate information about the systems. This information can include serial numbers, names, IP addresses, etc.

### Upload Data

This is used to upload bulk data in spreadsheets to CARTES. This data is formatted like exports from EPCT. See the [relevant procedure](/Automation/CARTES/UploadingData.md). In general, it's recommended to edit that directly in the Path Reports.

# System Inventory Queries

Systems inventory includes machine-specific data, such as CCIN, PCHIDs, CHPIDs, switch ports, and DASD ports. It doesn't show physical paths, but can show logical connections across the SAN. This can be useful to find what systems are where from detailed data.

metadata.section_heading: How to Upload Data to CARTES

content:
## Open the Upload Data Tab

In the top left corner of [CARTES](https://prod.stela.dal.app.cirrus.ibm.com/cartes/), open the `Categories` dropdown menu, then select `Upload Data`. From there, You can upload data via a file, or via a manual entry form.

You can also access it [here](https://prod.stela.dal.app.cirrus.ibm.com/cartes/uploaddata).

![](../images/CARTESUploadData.png)

## Uploading Data Via a File

Once on the `Upload Data` page, from the the `File Data Type` dropdown, either select `Path Entry` or `System Data`.

:::warning
Keep in mind that there is a file size limit of 500KB, if your file exceeds the limit, break it up into multiple files for submission.
:::

### Path Entry Uploads

For `Path Entry`, only `CSV` files in the format displayed below are valid.

By clicking the `Drag and drop files or click to upload section`, you may select files to upload.

Finally, hit the `Submit Path Entry Files` button and your files will uploaded to the CARTES database!

:::note
`Tip`: if you have multiple files to submit, drag and select them all before uploading to save time
:::

:::note
For `CECs`, the `Entry Port` should be the `PCHID` including the leading zero.
:::

:::note
`Dest Test Cell` and `Dest Port` are both optional columns.
:::

[Click here to view example Path Entry CSV](../files/path-entry-example.CSV)

### System Data Uploads

First, select the target system you want to upload system IO configuration data for from the `Select Systems` dropdown.

For `System Data`, only `zip` files are accepted.

:::note
The zip file must containe the following files collected from their respective SE panels:
* actvpda.xml
* actvpde.xml
* controlunitview.csv
* linkloadview.csv
* nodeidview.csv
* pchidlparview.csv
* pchidview.csv
:::

By clicking the `Drag and drop files or click to upload section`, you may select the zip file to upload.

Finally, hit the `Submit <System Name> System Data File` button and your file will uploaded to the CARTES database!
# Tools for Tracing Light

## Tracing Light Using a Scope

Fiber MicroScopes are the primary tools used to trace light, and are necessary to know whether or not a cable is dirty or not.

![](../images/Lightel.jpeg)

By placing an end point of a cable in the furrule on top of the device, you are running light through it for it to inspect. On the screen, a black circle should appear without any obstructions. if there is anything off about the circle or screen, it means there is dirt obstrcuting the cable. In order to clean it, there are a few devices usable depending on the size of the tip, or a sheet should be attached to the device for you to wipe the cable on.

## Using an Optical Power Meter

![](../images/OPM.jpeg)

Sometimes you may not get enough information from the microscope, for example, it can't tell you if the cable or optic is broken. In those cases, using an OPM may give you the answers you need. When dealing with a potentially damaged cable, place the left endpoint in the left side of the furrule and ensure the wavelngth is set to 1310. If the cable is working, it should display a number between 0 and -2.0 for a working cable and optic. If the number exceeds that range, you may be dealing with a broken optic or cable, which will need to be replaced.

## Cleaning MTP and LC Connnections

![](../images/MTPCleaner.png)

MTP Cleaner

![](../images/LCCleaner.jpeg)

LC Cleaner

For their respective connections, these devices clean the endpoints of cables and optics. Depending on if the cap is attached, it will either wrap around or go inside of what it needs to clean. press the cleaner into the connection and once a click is heard, the endpoint should be clean. This may need to be repeated a couple of times.

content:
## What is Light Tracing?

Light Tracing is the process of using a device known as a fiber microscope in order to determine if there is anything obstructing light through a cable.

## Finding the Dirty Cable

An example of light tracing using a path provided by CARTES

![](../images/PathReport.png)

## How To Trace Light

1. Begin by finding the Z system on the test floor using the red blue markers.

![](../images/SupportElement.png)

2. Once you have found the Z system, login to the support element, find your Z system and click on the channels tab. From there, search up the PCHID and note the location on the machine.

3. To find the port using the location, use the first section to locate the rack and card on the machine. The first letter indicates the frame, the numbers inbetween identifies the row, and the 2nd letter identifies the column. The second section in the location identifies the 'daughter'. Looking at each card, you will find a D1 and a D2, the first two characters in the second section identify which daugther you PCHID is connected to. Confirm that the proper PCHID is connected by checking the tag on the cable and referencing it to the jumper.

4. After confirming the cable connected to the optic is the one you are looking for, unplug the cable and trace light using the microscope, then clean the optic itself using the MTP cleaner.

![](../images/PathReport2.png)

looking for, unplug the cable and trace light using the microscope, then clean the optic itself using the MTP cleaner.

![](../images/PathReport2.png)

5. If the dirty cable still hasn't been identified, go to the patch panel room and use the Z patch panel port to confirm the specific cable which is connected to the port(the first character indicates the column, the second character indicates the row). Confirm that the proper cable is connected to the port by checking the tag. Then, Test for light using the microscope in that cable on both sides. If you still haven't found the dirty cable, continue to the next step.

![](../images/PathReport3.png)

6. You should also check the back side of the patch panel as well, you can do so by opening the backside and checking the tags to ensure you are unplugging the correct cable. Once you have, trace light and move on to the next step.

![](../images/PathReport4.png)

king the tags to ensure you are unplugging the correct cable. Once you have, trace light and move on to the next step.

![](../images/PathReport4.png)

7. If you still haven't found anything wrong, follow each switch identified in the switch link-outs section. Check the jumper tags to ensure you are following the proper path. Then use the switch patch panel-Port section to find the connections there and trace light for them as well.

![](../images/PathReport5.png)

8. In addition, they may be connected to an MDP patch panel, check there as well in the same manner you have checked the other 2 patch panels.

![](../images/PathReport6.png)

9. By now you have likely found the problem cable, if you still haven't, you will need to find the switch on the test floor to continue tracing light. To do so, note the test cell listed here, and use the rows and columns in the same way they are used in the patch panel room to find the cables there as well. Check their tags to ensure the path is still correct, and trace light.

![](../images/PathReport7.png)

ch panel room to find the cables there as well. Check their tags to ensure the path is still correct, and trace light.

![](../images/PathReport7.png)

10. Finally, check the DASD port by going to the corresponding test cell. Then using the first digit after the colon, locate the I/O enclosure. The second digit gives us the card location, and the third digit is the individual port. Once you have found the port, you may trace light there using the MicroScope.
