## What is CARTES?

CARTES (Connections And Records Tool for Enterprise Systems) is a powerful tool which enables users to utilize connection path data across the test floor. CARTES presents the gold standard for data presentation and collection by building off of past tools and automatically gathering data from systems on the test floor.

## Why use CARTES?

With CARTES, users can now debug I/O connection data much more efficiently and view live mapping without having to worry about reliability or integrity. CARTES provides a foundation for users to leverage data in new way by providing an all in one location for configuration data on the test floor.

## Where to Access CARTES?

CARTES lives on the STELA framework, and has a tab dedicated to it. When in STELA, click on the CARTES tab. Alternatively, you can find it [here](https://prod.stela.dal.app.cirrus.ibm.com/cartes). You can also access the github repository at this [link](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/CARTES)

**_NOTE:_** You will need to have access to STELA before using CARTES. You can request STELA access [here](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/stela/stela-quick-reference/request-access).

# Visualizing CARTES Data

Author: Eric Reid
Date: 05/30/2024

## Introduction

Humans are visual creatures. CARTES provides a wealth of data, but visualizing the data can halp planners, architects and others understand their environment.
This procedure talks about using an open source tool, [Gephi](https://gephi.org/users/) for visualizing SAN connections.

Gephi is a very poweful tool, and at this time I've exploited maybe 10% of its capabilities. I encourage you to play around.

## Download and Install

Choose the version of Gephi for your operating system: https://gephi.org/users/download/

Download the application, and install it on your laptop.  Once it's installed, run it, you should get to the home page:

![image](./images/gephi_home.png)

## Overview of the Process

The easiest way to make Gephi do things is to import a CSV file where one column is labelled as "Source" and another as "Target". This will build points and lines connecting these columns.  You can do this multiple times, changing which columns are Source/Target. Gephi will glue together things if the text is the same. Be careful with this - it's a clean match, so you may need to "clean" your data beforehand to make sure that entities have exactly the same text.  As an example, Gephi will consider `SW20` and `20` as two different things, even if you think they are the same.

Once the data is imported, you have to run algorithms to have it separate the data points from each other to form a readable map, and do things like add labels. Out of the gate, all of the data points will be clumped together and not labelled.

## A Walkthrough for Z -> Switch -> DASD

This is designed as an example walkthrough for a common case - to graph your SAN at the "system" level, connecting each Z you want to each switch and to all DASD those switches are connected too.

metadata.section_heading: A Walkthrough for Z -> Switch -> DASD

content:
### Step 1: Download Z Data from CARTES and into Gephi

In CARTES, select "System Inventory", then search for CARTES PCHIDs. Execute the query, and when CARTES returns the data, filter the System Name for whatever system(s) you want to get data from.

![image](./images/system_filter.png)

Then, in the top right of the table, click the "Export Table" button, and export as a CSV. This will download the file to your computer.

Open the file in Excel. Change the name of the "System Name" columen to "Source", and the "Switch" to "Target":

![image](./images/edit_columns.png)

Save the spreadsheet. In Gephi, on the top left choose File -> Import Spreadsheet. Navigate to the CSV file you downloaded and edited.

This should open a window that shows you a snippet of your data. Make sure that the "Seperator" is "Comma", and "Import As" is set to "Edges Table":

![image](./images/import_csv1.png)

metadata.section_heading: Step 1: Download Z Data from CARTES and into Gephi

content:
ws you a snippet of your data. Make sure that the "Seperator" is "Comma", and "Import As" is set to "Edges Table":

![image](./images/import_csv1.png)

Press "Next". It's recommended to uncheck all of the other data on the next screen, it may mess up the program and won't add any value here. Then press "Finish". Gephi will think for a second, parsing the data. On the next screen, press "OK". You may see many errors, this is from rows that have no switch, which is expected. You should then see a collection of points and arrows that don't make sense. That's OK, we'll clean it up later.

### Step 2: Switch and DASD Data

Next, the easiest way to see the rest of the SAN is to use the switch data from CARTES. Go to CARTES, and I recommend refreshing the page. Then, go "System Inventory", data source is CARTES Switches.

You'll need a list of what switches your Z's connect to. You can get this from CARTES or from Excel, and use that list to filter switches in CARTES. It's recommended to skip switches 20 and 21, those are IPL fabric switches that you likely don't need to include to get a picture of your environment.

Then in CARTES, filter by the model type of the remote port. You can use this to filter things in or out, like Z connections. If you are unsure, just choose type "2107". Then, download this data from CARTES using "Export Table" -> export as CSV.

Set the Source as the Switch ID column. Then, insert a new column to the right of Remote Machine Serial. Enter the following equation on row 2: `=RIGHT(P2,5)` in column Q. This cleans up the fact that Cisco and Brocade report the DASD S/N's slightly differently. Name the new column Q Target. Save your spreadsheet.

![image](./images/switches_dasd_grephi.png)

Brocade report the DASD S/N's slightly differently. Name the new column Q Target. Save your spreadsheet.

![image](./images/switches_dasd_grephi.png)

Next, go to File -> Import Spreadsheet in Gephi, and load in the spreadsheet you just made. Make sure it is set to "Comma" and "Edge table" just like in Step 1, then press next.

Then, select "Append to existing workspace" in the Import report window:

![image](./images/append_to_data.png)

Press "OK". This should then take you to the main screen, with a bunch of lines and dots:

![image](./images/lines_and_Dots.png)

## Making it Look Good

Out of the box, the graph looks really bad. Gephi has tools to make a nice looking graph.

### Adding Node Colors

In the Window menu at the top, press "Data Table". This should open up a data table menu:

![image](./images/data_table.png)

Hold CTRL and select as many nodes as you want, then right click and select "Edit all nodes". This should open a small panel on the left with properties to edit:

![image](./images/edit_space.png)

Select the "null" next to Color, this provides some basic colors. You can also type in a particular RGB value in the form [#,#,#]. You can click back to the Graph tab on the top of the main window to see the change.

Repeat this for whatever nodes you want.

### Adding Labels and Edge Colors

On the bottom right of the main window, there is a small up arror on to expand a settings menu, click it to see the following menu choices:

![image](./images/label_colors.png)

Select the "Labels" tab, then select the "Node" checkbox. Finally, on the right side click "Configure" and choose "ID" instead of "Label" in the pop up window. It's recommended to change the color of the labels in the section below the "Node" checkbox.

### Expanding the Graph

Now you should have a graph with labels, some colors, but all jumbled together:

![image](./images/jumbled_graph.png)

The "Layout" menu on the bottom half of the left side has a list of algorithms to run to change the layout of the graph. Feel free to experiment, but here are a few recommendations. Each algorithm is selected from the drop down menu, has a small information blurb by hovering over the "I", and can be run by pressing "RUN".

![image](./images/layouts.png)

#### Manual Dragging

You can select any node and drag it around. This can be tedious, but feel free.

#### OpenOrd

Really good if you are looking at port-level data or entire-test floor style maps. Less good for smaller environments, though can be useful in combination with Yifan Hu.

#### Yifan Hu and Yifan Hu Proportional

Either (or one and then the other) are solid choices for most situations.  If you want your graph to be bigger, set the "Optimal Distance" to be larger, maybe 500 or 1000.

metadata.section_heading: Yifan Hu and Yifan Hu Proportional

content:
### Force Atlas and Force Atlas 2

Sometimes these are good, but they can create strange knots and things. It can be a helpful "reset" to run these if you want to bounce between algorithms. They run forever, so press "Run" again to stop. It's a bit buggy, and can be slow (up to a minute or two) to stop.

## Saving and Sending to Friends

By now, you might have a graph that looks OK. If not, keep monkeying with it. Go to Preview on the top. In the left window, select the "Node labels" check box and uncheck the "Curved" checkbox in the Edges menu. Then hit refresh to see the preview. You can change settings here, but this preview is what your export will be.

![image](./images/preview.png)

Then, go to File -> Export, and save the image to a location.

# Channel Insight & Actions

Channel Insights and Actions is a set of tools designed to run in [TOAD](/Automation/TOAD/README.md) to enhance your interaction with IO on the Z system.

Tools are designed to improve the speed and accuracy of your system health checks while also providing mechanisms to improve utilization and RAS in your config.

## Running CIA Tools

There are a variety of tools in CIA Tools, with more planned. Currently the commands implemented are fedcParser, bbrudumpparser, and cia_compare.

For all of these tools, their output is placed within the directory of ~/Documents/cia_tools/output. If a Documents folder does not exist on your local system it will be created as part of a tool being ran.

The following contains How tos on the tools.

### Channel State Compare

- fedcParser: This tool acquires the system's most recent iqzqfedc file generated(or you can trigger it's generation), parses through it, and then compares it to the previous file for differences and prints them out. This can be used used to compare your system state before and after you make changes.

Read the full guide [here](/Automation/CIA_Tools/fedcParser.md)

### IO Domain Visualization

- bbrudumpparser:This tool parsers through the system'sbbrudumpfile for several forms of data and generates multiple different files describing the layout of the system. It then creates a mermeaid file, which can be used to graphically represent the config of a given system(this currently only works on Metis)

Read the full guide [here](/Automation/CIA_Tools/bbrudumpParser.md)

### CIA Compare

- cia_compare: This can be used to compare any json file generated by CIA Tools. This way if you would like to compare config data from bbrudumps, or 2 older files from fedc, it can be done with ease.

This tool runs simply by giving it 2 json file names, the first being compared to the other. The primary functionality here allows you to compare fedc scripts from 2 specific points in time, as opposed to a point in time and the most recent file. In addition, you can use it to compare the files generated by bbrudumpparser, which generates multiple json files.

> ciatools cia_compare -f DCMDataB4020240926_16_06.json DCMDataB4020240926_17_20.json

> ciatools cia_compare --files DCMDataB4020240926_16_06.json DCMDataB4020240926_17_20.json

## Getting started

read the install instructions [here](/Automation/CIA_Tools/Setup_CIA_Tools.md) if you find that this isn't already setup in your TOAD Container

# Installing CIA Tools

Remember that pip is a requirement for installation of this tool. Once you have the most recent version of pip installed(as of the time of writing this it is 24.2), you may install this on your local machine with the following command:

> pip install CIA[LOCAL]@git+ssh://git@github.ibm.com/systemz/CIA_Tools.git

If you wish to update CIA tools, you may do so simply by adding --upgrade, like so:

> pip install --upgrade CIA[LOCAL]@git+ssh://git@github.ibm.com/systemz/CIA_Tools.git

If you are running CIA tools from within a TOAD container it should already be installed(assuming your TOAD container is up to date), if you wish to install it manually, here's what it looks like:

> pip install CIA[TOAD]@git+ssh://git@CIA/systemz/CIA_Tools.git

or for an update:

> pip install --upgrade CIA[TOAD]@git+ssh://git@CIA/systemz/CIA_Tools.git

## Running fedcParser

In order to start, you must first make sure the desired system is added in remoteZtoolset, so that the necessary file can be pulled from that system. In order to do this, simply run the following command(replacing the Ip address with the IP of the desired system):

> rz-add -i IPADDRESS

For the most basic functionality, all it takes is to type [ciatools fedcParser] and add the desired system name as a parameter(this is required)

> ciatools fedcParser --nametag A40

This will retrieve the most recent iqzqfedc file, and parse through it for the pertinent information for this script. It will then retrieve the next most recent file, and call a compare function which finds the differences between them, and prints it out.

Note that the first time this is run on a given system there will be no files to compare to, as there it will be generating  afile for the first time. To truly utilize this tool it must be run before and after you make changes, or even just run it every once in a while.

### Optional Parameters

there are a few parameters which can help you use this tool most efficiently, for one, if you would like to force a rebuild of the source file so you can compare the most recent data. In order to do this add the following options(replacing A40 with the desired system):

> ciatools fedcParser -N A40 -r

or

> ciatools fedcParser --nametag A40 --rebuild

By using this, you can make changes to the system and then easily compare how those changes just effected the PCHIDs, CHPIDs, CPs and more of that system.

Another parameter you could add would be reference, which sets a specific file to compare the system to. This allows you to check for differences between now and a certain date. You can do so by adding this option(replacing A40 with the desired system):

> ciatools fedcParser --nametag A40 --reference fedcA4020240819_13:36.json

or

> ciatools fedcParser --nametag A40 -R fedcA4020240819_13:36.json

m):

> ciatools fedcParser --nametag A40 --reference fedcA4020240819_13:36.json

or

> ciatools fedcParser --nametag A40 -R fedcA4020240819_13:36.json

This will compare the most recent file built on A40 with the file generated on august 19th at 1:36 (note: You need to have run this script before so that it has previously generated JSON files to compare itself to, since the source file it reads only overwrites itself.)

The 2 previously listed parameters can even be used together to compare a specififc file to the state of the system right now, instead of just when the fedc file was last rebuilt.

This function saves the last reference file you set, and continues to use this until you tell it otherwise. To set the script back to default behavior, set the reference file to be equal to None, like so.

> ciatools fedcParser --nametag A40 -R None

There are multiple settings which effect the verbosity of the output, giving you the ability to print more or less channel state changes that occur. By default it will only print the severity 1 defects, but can be adjusted to print severities 2 and 3, or just the return code.

if you run the command:

> ciatools fedcParser -N A40 -v

everity 1 defects, but can be adjusted to print severities 2 and 3, or just the return code.

if you run the command:

> ciatools fedcParser -N A40 -v

this will print out sev1 and 2 channel state changes, but will tell you if there are changes in sev3 to look at.

if you run the command:

> ciatools fedcParser -N A40 -V

This will print out the maximum output

Lastly, if you run:

> ciatools fedcParser -N A40 -g

This will minimize the output to the return code.

### Return Codes

The tool also prints out return codes based on the output it is printing

* RC=0: No changes
* RC=1: Changes in sev1 category(changes from operating to a negative state) are present
* RC=2 Changes in sev2(changes from negative to negative, and new data being added) are present and there isnt a sev higher present
* RC=3 Changes in sev3(changes from negative to Positive, other misc. changes) are present and there isnt a sev higher present

## Running pci_visualizer

Once again you must ensyure you have your desired system added to remoteZtoolset. You can do so by running this command(replacing IP Address with the desired system IP):

> rz-add -i IPADDRESS

once you have done this you can begin running the tool! You may do so simply by running the command:

> ciatools pci_visualizer --nametag A40

This command would run on system A40, and create 4 json files which detail system config information. It then creates a mermaid file which will graphically represent the systems layout.

In order to view this representation, you can use a vscode extension to your TOAD container, you may see guides on how to set that up [here](../TOAD/VSConnectTOAD.md) and [here](../TOAD/VSCodeExtensions.md).

![Alt Text](./images/mermaidExample.png)

# Jupitr Insights

Jupitr Insights is a CLI tool for managing and reporting on defects and test activities related to Z Systems driver testing. This tool helps report defect MCF details TPC sign off

## Contents

- [CLI Tool Help](./CLIToolHelp.md) - Command-line interface usage and available commands
- [Installing Jupitr Insights](./Installing_Jupitr_Insights.md) - Installation instructions and setup guide

## Overview

The JupitrInsights tool is automatically installed as part of TOAD Container creation and provides several key commands:
- **DriverTesterAction**: Supports pre-TPC defect management for driver testing
- **MetisESTDefects**: Shows all Metis EST defects in the current test bundle

# KVM Automation Tool (KAT)

KAT is an automation tool for managing KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) guests on Z Systems, including support for secure guests and various configuration options.

## Contents

- [KAT Documentation](./kat.md) - Complete guide to using the KVM Automation Tool, including setup, configuration, and usage examples

## Overview

The KVM Automation Tool simplifies the process of creating, configuring, and managing KVM guests on Z Systems. It provides automated workflows for common tasks and supports advanced features like secure guest configuration.

For questions or support, contact `@dawson.rosell` on Slack.

# KVM Automation Tool (KAT)

This documentation is a work in progress. If you have any questions, please reach out to `@dawson.rosell` on Slack.

## Table of Contents
* [Introduction](#introduction)
* [Required Setup](#required-setup)
* [Quickstart](#quickstart)
* [Configuration Options in `kat_config`](#configuration-options-in-kat_config)
* [Secure Guests](#secure-guests)
* [Functions of `kat_run`](#functions-of-kat_run)
* [`kat_commander`](#kat_commander)

## Intorduction
KAT is designed to automate the provisioning of KVM Guests at scale, as well as starting various workloads on all guests or a desired subset of guests. It does this by leveraging different Ansible playbooks and Python scripts and wrapping them up in an easy to navigate user interface.

There are three main scripts provided by KAT, `kat_config`, `kat_run`, and `kat_commander`.

## Required Setup

KAT requires the `python3-libvirt` package to be installed on your TOAD container. Automation of this step is being investigated.

Run `sudo apt-get install python3-libvirt` in your TOAD container.

By default, KAT will create a directory on each LPAR being used called `/guestimages`. This directory is where all the linux images and kvm qcow2 files live. If you intend to provision more than a handful of KVM's it is recommended to manually mount a second storage device, such as an NVME or a second DASD volume, and then create `/guestimages` and mount the new storage device to it.

* Currently (version 0.2.x) KAT does not ensure there is enough disk space on the LPAR before provisioning. It will attempt to provision however many KVM guests you defined in the configuration file, and keep provisioning until completed or until Ansible fails with errors related to storage space. This will be addressed in future updates.

## Quickstart

1. Create a configuration file by running `kat_config` and entering the required information
    * All created config files will be stored in `/home/tester/kvm_automation_tool/config_files`
2. Run your newly created configuration file with `kat_run -f [path_to_file]`
    * e.g `kat_run -f kvm_automation_tool/config_files/my_config.yaml`

## Configuration Options in `kat_config`

* Dual NIC Mode
    * Enabling Dual NIC Mode will set each KVM Guest to use two network interfaces. The first interface is the kvm_virtual_network running on the LPAR and is not able to communicate to Guests on different LPARs. The second NIC will be a physical device (OSD, ROCE, NETH, etc.) that gets bridged into the Guest with macvtap.
    * During the configuration file creation process, a list of all available network interfaces on the LPAR(s) will be presented for you to select from. The interface chosen is the interface that will be used with that KVM Guest.
* Virtiofs
    * Enabling Virtiofs will setup a directory on the LPAR and setup each KVM Guest to be able to mount to that directory, giving more storage space to the Guests.
    * This option is requried for running the Iperf3 workload as the Iperf3 logs are stored and processed from this directory.

## Secure Guests

* This section is a work in progress as the secure guest functionality is still in development.

## Functions of `kat_run`
Upon starting `kat_run` you will be presented with a list of options.
```
? Choose an option
  provision
  destory
  workload
  exit
```

### Provision
The `provision` command will attempt to provision all the KVM Guests defined in the configuration file.

### Destroy
The `destroy` command will shutdown and undefine each KGM guest in the config file, and then delete any files (including the qcow2 image) associated with the guest.

### Workload
In the `workload` menu you can select from predefined workloads to run on some or all of the KVM Guests in the configuration file.

* Lifecylce all/single
    * This will shutdown the guest(s), undefine them, redefine them, start them again, and then ensure they are in a running state.
* Iperf3
    * Create pairs of kvm guests to act as Iperf3 servers and clients, and then start running Iperf3. Once Iperf3 has finished running, a summary of the run is printed in the terminal.

## `kat_commander`

The `kat_commander` is a versitle script designed for executing a single command on multiple KVM Guests and returning the results to the TOAD contaienr terminal upon completion.

The three requried arguements are `--host`, `--guest_names`, and `--command`

`--host` - The ip address for the KVM Host LPAR

`--guest_names` - A list of KVM Guest names running on the `host` LPAR that you want to execute the `command` on.

he ip address for the KVM Host LPAR

`--guest_names` - A list of KVM Guest names running on the `host` LPAR that you want to execute the `command` on.

`--command` - A one line command with or without arguements that will be run on the KVM Guests.
Any existing command on the KVM Guests can be run with any number of arguments with a few exceptions.
* No Pipes
    * Commands like `"ps aux | grep 'some_text'"` are not supported in this release
* No `sudo`
    * Certain commands, like `stress-ng`, typically require you to run them with `sudo`. `kat_commander` uses the QEMU Guest Agent to execute commands on the guests and is able to execute these commands without needing `sudo` in the `command` parameter.
* No 'interactive' commands
    * Commands like `top` that open an interactive session or programs requiring user input will not work. Only commands that can be executed in one line and return a result can be run.
* No `apt install` or `yum install`
    * Testing has been limited with these and has not yielded successful results. Future releases will address this more definitively.

kat_commander --host 9.114.16.165 --guest_names '["ubuntu_guest1","ubuntu_guest2"]' --command "hostnamectl"

# Device Info Tool (DIT)

**Device Info Tool** provides a sortable and interactive list of all network interfaces available on a zLinux LPAR. The data in the table is not live. To check for configuration changes you will need to run the tool again.

## How to Use
You can run **Device Info Tool** by running:
```
lnts_dit
```
* Enter your LPAR information on the first screen. Either click or TAB between the text boxes. Press `ESC` and then `x` to continue to the next screen.
![](./images/dit1.png)

* A list of network interfaces will be displayed in a table. Naviagate the table with the **arrow keys**. Pressing `p` will sort the table by **PCHID**.
![](./images/dit2.png)

* Pressing `i` will display more detailed information for the currently highlighted row. Press `ESC` to close the pop up window.

# The Perfinator

___Automated Uperf and Iperf3 testing for OSA, OSD, RoCE, NETH, NETD, and Hipersockets in zLinux___

**If something is unclear or incorrect, please reach out to `@dawson.rosell` on Slack.**

---

## Table of Contents
* [Introduction](#introduction)
* [Options and Usage](#options-and-usage)
* [First Time Setup](#first-time-setup)
* [SSH Key Setup](#ssh-key-setup)
* [Configuration Files](#configuration-files)
* [Uperf Testing](#uperf-testing)
* [Iperf3 Testing](#iperf3-testing)
* [IP Address Assignment](#ip-address-assignment)

## Introduction

The **Perfinator** is a tool that automates **Uperf** and **Iperf3** regression on OSA, OSD, RoCE, NETH, NETD, and Hipersockets adapters.
It configures devices on Linux LPARs, assigns IP addresses, applies offload
options, and runs repeatable workloads defined in a YAML configuration file.

At a high level, the Perfinator:

1. Reads a workload configuration file
2. Configures devices on server and client LPARs
3. Assigns IP addresses per device
4. Executes the requested Uperf or Iperf3 workload
5. Collects logs and results on the TOAD container
6. Optionally removes all device configuration

### Key Concepts
- **Device Group (DG)**: The unit that receives one IP on each LPAR.
  - **Non‑bonded**: a single device (`dev0`)
  - **Bonded**: multiple devices (`dev0`, `dev1`, …), with `mode`
- **Per‑LPAR vs. per‑device settings**: `mtu`, offloads (`tso`, `tx_checksum`, `rx_checksum`), and `layer_2` can be set at:
  1. **workload** (required defaults)
  2. **LPAR** (overrides workload for that node)
  3. **device** (overrides LPAR/workload for that member)
- **Precedence**: `per‑device > per‑LPAR > workload defaults`

### Assumptions

This tool assumes:

- You have at least two Linux LPARs
- Network interfaces can communicate once IP addresses are assigned
- The chosen `starting_ip` allows subnet incrementation
  (see [IP Address Assignment](#ip-address-assignment))

## Options and Usage

The Perfinator is invoked by running the `lnts_perfinator` command.

### Command-Line Options
| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `-f <file>` | Path to workload YAML file |
| `-t <duration>` | Test duration (e.g. `100s`,`200m`,`24h`) |
| `--ping` | Configure the interfaces and run the ping test only. |
| `--noping` | Skip the ping test. |
| `--cleanup` | Remove existing interface configurations and exit. |
| `--nocleanup` | Leave interfaces configured after test (useful for manual debug) |
| `--verbose` | Starts Uperf in verbose mode and displays server and client outputs side by side in the terminal |
| `--debug` | Prints debug information from device configuration - For each interface it also compares desired configuration settings from the config file to what settings are actually applied to the interface after running the configuration. |
| `--on_error` | Options = `abort\|continue` Action to take on device configuration error, default=`abort`. If `continue`, the Perfinator will continue to configure remaining interfaces and attempt to test without the failed interfaces. If `abort` the Perfinator will log the error and exit at the first failed interface. |

content: ## First Time Setup

### TOAD Container Setup
* Create the following directories in the TOAD container home directory.
    ```
    /lnts/
    /lnts/perfinator_configs
    /lnts/perfinator_logs
    /lnts/perfinator_workloads
    ```
These directories are used to store user created configuration files, logs, and generated uperf workloads.

### LPAR Setup
* Uperf and Iperf setup is handled automatically by the tool.
  * Iperf3 on SLES/SUSE - This package is not automatically added and currently must be added manually.

## SSH Key Setup
Each LPAR being used needs its SSH keys added to the TOAD container for passwordless SSH.

From the TOAD container:
```bash
rz-add -u <LPAR_username> -i <LPAR_ip_address>
```

## Configuration Files
All tests are defined using YAML configuration files.
* Store files in `lnts/perfinator_configs`

---

### Configuration File Structure

* Every configuration file contains three top-level sections:
```yaml
servers:
clients:
workload:
```
* Devices/interfaces are defined in a list under the `servers:` and `clients:` top-level sections. Each item in the list is refered to as a **device group**. Each **device group** must include at least `dev0` with `id` and `type`. A **device group** is bonded if it also has `dev1` and `mode`.

* For OSA/OSD interfaces, only the first device number of the triplet should be entered. e.g. `0.0.0920,0.0.0921,0.0.0922` -> `0920`
```yaml

# non-bonded
devices:
    - dev0:
        id: "0920"
        type: "OSD"
    - dev0:
        id: "1a"
        type: "NETH"
```
```yaml

# bonded
    devices:
      - dev0:
          id: "0920"
          type: "OSD"
        dev1:
          id: "0923"
          type: "OSD"
        mode: "active-backup"
      - dev0:
          id: "1"
          type: "NETH"
        dev1:
          id: "2"
          type: "NETH"
        mode: "balance-rr"
```

### Normal (non-bonded) Example

```yaml

# example_config.yaml
servers:
  - lpar: "server_lpar_name"
    hostname: "9.114.16.150"
    username: "root"
    starting_ip: "10.10.1.150"
    persistent_devices: False
    devices:
      - dev0:
          id: "0920"
          type: "OSD"
      - dev0:
          id: "1"
          type: "NETH"

clients:
  - lpar: "client_lpar_name"
    hostname: "9.114.16.151"
    username: "root"
    starting_ip: "10.10.1.151"
    persistent_devices: False
    devices:
      - dev0:
          id: "0920"
          type: "OSD"
      - dev0:
          id: "1"
          type: "NETH"

workload:
  test_type: uperf
  test_name: netperf
  mtu: "9000"
  size: "8k"
  group: threads
  group_num: "400"
  protocol: tcp
  ipv6: False
  tso: "on"
  tx_checksum: "on"
  rx_checksum: "on"
  layer_2: "1"
```

### Bonded Interfaces Example
Below is an example of a config file that has been set up for bonded interfaces.

```yaml

# example_bonded_interfaces.yml
servers:
  - lpar: "server_lpar_name"
    hostname: "9.114.16.150"
    username: "root"
    starting_ip: "10.10.1.150"
    persistent_devices: False
    devices:
      - dev0:
          id: "0920"
          type: "OSD"
        dev1:
          id: "0923"
          type: "OSD"
        mode: "active-backup"
      - dev0:
          id: "1"
          type: "NETH"
        dev1:
          id: "2"
          type: "NETH"
        mode: "balance-rr"

clients:
  - lpar: "client_lpar_name"
    hostname: "9.114.16.151"
    username: "root"
    starting_ip: "10.10.1.151"
    persistent_devices: False
    devices:
      - dev0:
          id: "0920"
          type: "OSD"
        dev1:
          id: "0923"
          type: "OSD"
        mode: "active-backup"
      - dev0:
          id: "1"
          type: "NETH"
        dev1:
          id: "2"
          type: "NETH"
        mode: "balance-rr"

workload:
  test_type: uperf
  test_name: netperf
  mtu: "9000"
  size: "8k"
  group: threads
  group_num: "400"
  protocol: tcp
  ipv6: False
  tso: "on"
  tx_checksum: "on"
  rx_checksum: "on"
  layer_2: "1"
```

### Server and Client Configuration
`lpar` - The name of the LPAR.

`hostname` - The IP address of the LPAR

`username` - The username for the LPAR, typically `root`

`starting_ip` - The first IP address to assign to the first device in the device list. See [IP Address Assignment](#ip-address-assignment).

`persistent_devices` - [true | false] Enables or disables persistent devices on that LPAR. Currently this feature is only supported on LPARs running Ubuntu. RHEL and SLES support are planned for a future release.

`devices` - The list of device groups to run the defined workload on. The number of device groups must be the same for each LPAR being used.

`mtu` - The MTU is defined individually for each interface within the devices list.
* A note about `mtu` and bonds: The `mtu` of the bond is set to the `mtu` of the first interface in the bond (`dev0`). Precedence rules apply - if `mtu` is applied at the device level, then the bond will be configured with the `mtu` set for `dev0` in that bond.

`type` - The device type is defined for each item in the devices list. This allows for mixed-type tests. Valid types are: `OSA, OSD, Hipersockets, NETH, NETD, ROCE`

### Workload Configuration

`test_type` - [uperf | iperf]

`test_name` - See [Uperf Testing](#uperf-testing) and [Iperf3 Testing](#iperf3-testing) for available options

`size` - The transmission size, in bytes, for Iperf3 and Uperf to use when testing the devices. The `size` parameter supports the `k` and `M` suffixes. This allows one to use larger sizes without having to write out the full size in bytes, *e.g.* `size: 512k`

`group` - *Uperf Only* - [procs | threads] - Uperf supports running workloads as **processes** or **threads**.

`group_num` - *Uperf Only* - How many threads or procs to have Uperf run per device.

`parallel_connections` - *Iperf Only* - Number of sumultaneous connections each interface should make.

`bandwidth` - *Iperf Only* - Target bandwidth for the Iperf test in bits per second. If `parallel_connections` is greater than 1, the target bandwidth is applied to each connection. Supports `k` and `M` suffixes. *e.g* `bandwidth: "10000M"`

`protocol` - [tcp | udp]

eater than 1, the target bandwidth is applied to each connection. Supports `k` and `M` suffixes. *e.g* `bandwidth: "10000M"`

`protocol` - [tcp | udp]

`ipv6` - [true | false] - If using IPv6 (`ipv6: true`) then the `starting_ip` for each LPAR must be a valid IPv6 address of the following format: `xxxx:y::zzz`, where the second group in the address is the subnet being incremented for device assignment. *e.g.* `1234:1:150`

`tso` - [on | off] - TCP Segmentation Offload

`tx_checksum` - [on | off] - Tx Checksumming, off = offload

`rx_checksum` - [on | off] - Rx Checksumming, off = offload

`layer_2` - [0 | 1] - 0 = layer_2 mode disabled, 1 = layer_2 mode enabled.

### IP Address Assignment
* The Perfinator incrementally assigns IP addresses based on a defined `starting_ip` so that each device group is placed on a unique subnet.
* The Perfinator does not check if the IP addresses are in use by others.
    * Ensure that your chosen starting IP addresses, and the subsequent addresses are available for use in your tests and will not interfere with other tests.

#### IPv4 format:
* `a.b.c.d`
    * a.b are constant
    * c is incremented per device
    * d differentiates server and client

#### IPv6 format:
* `a:b::c`
    * a is constant
    * b is incremented per device
    * c differentiates server and client

#### Example
For two LPARs with IP addresses 9.x.x.150 and 9.x.x.120, the starting IP address chosen for each would look like `a.b.c.150` and `a.b.c.120`.

## Uperf Testing
Supported Uperf profiles - netperf (one to one), multicast (many to one)

### Netperf (unicast)

To use the Netperf (unicast) profile with Uperf, set the `test_name` to `netperf`

This profile requires one server LPAR and one client LPAR, each with the same number of devices to be tested.

#### Example:

Using 3 selected OSA devices on each LPAR and a starting IPv4 address of 10.10.1.195 and 10.10.1.196 (For Server and Client), the devices are assigned in the following way.

| Server LPAR | |Client LPAR | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Devices | IPs | Devices | IPs |
| 0330 | 10.10.1.195 | 0449 |  |
| 0333 | 10.10.2.195 | 045c | 10.10.2.196 |
| 0336 | 10.10.3.195 | 0450 | 10.10.3.196 |

This places each device on an LPAR on a subnet. Uperf will then start reading and writing between each device pair. 0330 and 0449, 0333 and 045c, and 0336 and 0450.

#### Example Uperf YAML
Below is an example configuration file that can be modified for your use.
``` yaml
servers:
  - lpar: "L13AOSA1"
    hostname: "9.114.16.150"
    username: "root"
    lnts_dir: "/root/lnts/"
    starting_ip: "10.10.1.150"
    persistent_devices: False
    # optional - per-LPAR settings
    # tso: 'on'
    # mtu: "1500"
    # tx_checksum: "off"
    # rx_checksum: "on"
    # layer_2: '1'
    devices:
      - dev0:
          id: "0923"
          type: "OSD"
          # optional - per-device settings
          # tso: 'on'
          # mtu: "1500"
          # tx_checksum: "off"
          # rx_checksum: "on"
          # layer_2: '1'
          tx_checksum: 'on'
          rx_checksum: 'on'
      - dev0:
          id: "1b"
          type: "NETH"

hecksum: "on"
          # layer_2: '1'
          tx_checksum: 'on'
          rx_checksum: 'on'
      - dev0:
          id: "1b"
          type: "NETH"

clients:
  - lpar: "L13AOSA2"
    hostname: "9.114.16.151"
    username: "root"
    lnts_dir: "/root/lnts/"
    starting_ip: "10.10.1.151"
    persistent_devices: False
    # optional - per-LPAR settings
    # tso: 'on'
    # mtu: "1500"
    # tx_checksum: "off"
    # rx_checksum: "on"
    # layer_2: '1'
    devices:
      - dev0:
          id: "0920"
          type: "OSD"
      - dev0:
          id: "1a"
          type: "NETH"
workload:
  group: threads
  group_num: '100'
  ipv6: false
  layer_2: '0'
  protocol: tcp
  rx_checksum: 'on'
  tx_checksum: 'on'
  size: '8k'
  test_name: netperf
  test_type: uperf
  tso: 'on'
```

### Multicast
To use the multicast profile with Uperf, set the `test_name` to `multicast`
Under the "servers" block in the configuration file, add a new server entry for each server being used in the multicast test.

Each LPAR being used (client and servers) must have the same number of devices in their list of devices to test.

Because of how Uperf works, multicast is one client to many servers, and is not capable of one server to many clients. However, after initial handshakes, Uperf runs bidirectional traffic - each device will read and write.

#### Example:
Each device defined in the client configuration will read and write to a device on each server LPAR.

| Server0 LPAR | | Server1 LPAR | |Client LPAR | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Devices | IPs | Devices | IPs | Devices | IPs |
| 0330 | 10.10.1.195 | 0926 | 10.10.1.151 | 0449 | 10.10.1.196 |
| 0333 | 10.10.2.195 | 0940 | 10.10.2.151 | 045c | 10.10.2.196 |
| 0336 | 10.10.3.195 | 0353 | 10.10.3.151 | 0450 | 10.10.3.196 |

In this example, each device on Client LPAR will read and write to two devices, one device on each Server LPAR. Each device on the Server LPARs will only read and write with one device on the Client LPAR. This means that the only devices that are being tested in multicast are those defined on the Client LPAR, and not the Server LPARs.

# Linux on Z Automation

Enclosed in this section you'll find user guides for a variety of tools intended to work with Linux on Z LPARs.

This includes tools that help install linux or complete some task by interacting with the resulting LPAR.  Workload tools may run either on the lpar or control it externally. External tools are often CLI based, but there are also more advanced frameworks like Rundeck or Jenkins used to help do this at scale.

## Installing Linux

[Rundeck](/Automation/LinuxOnZ/RundeckLinuxAutomation/) is our current automation tool to install the base linux distribution to a Z LPAR.

## Provisioning Guests

KAT Also known as [KVM Automation Tool](/Automation/LinuxOnZ/KVMAutomationTool/kat.md), is EST's lightweight tool capable of provisioning Kernel Virtual Machines at scale.  Currently the support is for SCSI Based QCOW Images only. The tool also is intended to support allocating any specific resources you may need to utilize inside your Linux Guests.

The scope of this tool does not include workloads.  To run automation workloads on KVM guests some specific application is needed.
## Workload

### Networking

Linux Networking Test Suite [(LNTS)](/Automation/LinuxOnZ/LinuxNetworkTestSuite/) is a tool included in TOAD which has automation in place to work with multiple lpars, configuring ethernet interfaces and driving traffic between end points.

### Generic Workload Execution

Linux Workload Execution is a package that can be found in systemz to run generic code inside a target linux lpar.

Rundeck is an open-source framework for deploying automation pipelines across Unix systems. In our lab, we use it to automate Linux installation on LPARs from a single control point. It provides a simple and repeatable service to deploy Linux as LPAR availability changes.

Please refer to the [EST Linux Installation via Rundeck](./rundeck.md) guide for an in-depth tutorial on how to setup Linux on your own LPAR.

## IOCDS Modification (Live Image)

## Should work with Team Lead/hardware owner on this step

What is the **“Live image”**? Short answer: Enables HMC netboot

The HMC in classic mode does not expose the FTP network boot capability through its API, so in order to circumvent this limitation, we make use of a linux live image to simulate the functionality.

This works by pre-allocating a DASD or FCP disk on each CPC, where LPARs are going to utilize netboot.  A network boot (or “netboot”) is a process where a computer starts up and loads an operating system or installation program directly from a central server over a local network, rather than from a local hard drive or USB stick.

A modification to the IOCDS is necessary on the machine in which Linux is to be installed. Below is a template that should be modified to adjust for your channel paths aka “chpids”

### **Phase 1** – Profile Information

Before installing Linux, you must gather the following information. This data is used to create a system profile, via Rundeck task “Initial LPAR Configuration or Update”, which serves as the backbone for the Linux installation.

#### Required System Information
- CPC/System name
- Test cell
- LPAR name (must be defined as a Linux LPAR in the activation profile on the SE (lowercase only))
- One IP Address per LPAR

#### Networking Requirements
- OSA device reachable to 9.x.x.x network
    - *Typical devices: 0900, 0901, 0902*
    - *Your team lead/hardware owner can help you if these device addresses are different*
- OSA port (default: 0)
    - *Default is usually 0 (The top port on the network card)*

#### If using NETH
- FID
- MAC address of the associated VCHID (Virtual Channel ID)
    - *To find the mac address: On the SE >> Select channels (Left sidebar) >> Select the VCHID on the panel that opens up >> Advanced Facilities… >> Card specific advanced facilities… >> View port parameters >> Ok >> At top of page/panel, copy entry for: Local MAC address (example: A088C26A71FF) (12 digit value)
    FYI: This value is entered in Rundeck as: A0:88:c2:6a:71:ff*

#### Storage Options
Determine which storage type will be used for the Linux installation:

- **FICON (DASD aka ECKD)**
    – *default: MOD-54 volumes minimum*
- **FCP (LUN/SCSI)**
    – *default: MOD-54 volumes minimum*
- **NVMe**

> Storage type determines which Rundeck job is used.

---

### Phase 1 Readiness Checklist

Before continuing, ensure you have:

- CPC and LPAR names
- Assigned IP address to LPAR
- Storage type selected (ECKD or SCSI)
- OSA/NETH information
- DNS configured on the SE

---

### **Phase 2** – Linux Installation

Once all prerequisite information is collected and the IOCDS is configured, Linux can be installed using Rundeck.

# Extending Support
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 02/29/2024

## How the Tool Supports Statements

The IOCDS build tool relies on three key files to perform converions. They all live in the config_files/ directory.

The first, iocds_conversions.yml, contains a YAML file with regular expressions for all statement types. Each new statement (RESOURCE, CHPID, etc.) is given a top-level key in the YAML file, and a 'regex_form' that determines how that code is defined.  Optional parameters, or parameters that can be listed in any order, are included in the 'optional' section. Repeated expressions can be parsed recursively with the 'repeats' section.

The second file, iocds_rebuild_examples.yml, gives example expressions that are used to generate regular expression match objects with the statements from iocds_conversions.yml.  These match objects are then used to substitute data from the IOCDS YAML file to convert it back to IOCDS statements.

The last file, iocds_rules.yml, includes various formatting and interpetation rules.  This includes defining when a new processor is created in YAML, the number of spaces and column lenghts in IOCDS, etc.

## Expanding Support

Changing these files are only necessary when there are new statements or new options in existing statements. Changes to possible choices in a particular statement, such as a new card type, do not require any support changes in this code.

It is highly recommended if you do need to extend support, to use an online regular expression checker to validate any changes you make, and to test your changes thoroughly.  The regular expressions must be as least greedy as possible to properly grab only the relevant data for the statement in question.

# Installing IOCDS Build Tools
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 02/29/2024

## Clone the Repository

Clone the repository to your laptop or TOAD container.

For a TOAD container, this should just be a quick set of commands:

cd ~
    git clone git@github.ibm.com:systemz/iocds_build_tools.git

For your laptop, it's recommended to clone it using Github Desktop.

## Install The Code

Navigate in a terminal to where iocds_build_tools was cloned, and do an editable pip install. For the TOAD containers, this would be:

cd ~/iocds_build_tools
    pip install -e .

In a UNIX-based environment (i.e. TOAD, Mac, Linux), you can check the version:

pip list |grep IOCDSBuilder

You should get a version number back.  On Windows, you can do a `pip list` and look through all your installed Python packages.
# M.A.G.I.C

## Manipulate, Automate, Graph I/O Configuration

Author: Eric Reid
Date: 02/28/2024

## MAGIC Version History

| Date       | Version | Update |
|------------|---------|--------|
| 2024.12.26 | 0.1.0   | Made it a distributable package |
| 2025.12.10 | 1.0.0   | [Put usage/description fields into each LPAR when converting to yaml](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/iocds_build_tools/pull/37) |

## IOCDS Basics

Every Z system has an IOCDS that defines the LPARs, CHPIDs, Control Units (CU's), Devices and PCIe Functions of the processor. This configuration is incredibly complex, requiring planning, coordination and expertise to work with, but is critical to the function of the Z. The parameters, statements and choices of IOCDS are written in the [IOCP User's Guide](https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/inputoutput-configuration-program-users-guide-icp-iocp).  IOCP has strict requirements on how to define all resources.

### IOCDS Methods

There are four methods to change your I/O configuration. In rough order of popularity in the test floor, they are:
 - z/OS Hardware Configuration Definition (HCD)
 - Standalone IOCDS in the zSE or zHMC or z/VM
 - Dynamic Partition Mode (DPM)
 - z/VM Dynamic

This tooling is most relevant for the first two methods of changing your IOCDS. Future integrations can take the YAML files this code generates and control the IOCDS through the last two methods.

## Tool Overview

This tool has two parts, convert_to_yaml.py and convert_to_iocds.py. These are just translation layers, converting from IOCDS statements to formatted YAML and back. These statements can come from HCD either manually or using Zowe-based HCD automation see [HCD Tools](../zOS%20Automation%20Suite/ZoweLab/Tools/HCD%20Tools/README.md). The statements can also come from stand-alone IOCDS files pulled from z/VM, the zSE or zHMC. The IOCDS statements are converted to YAML, where users or automation can edit an IOCDS. In theory, a brand new IOCDS can also be built in YAML, though this has limited practicality. The diagram below gives an overview of the processes:

![](./images/IOCDS_diagrams-Page-4.drawio.png)

The IOCDS build tools package is only responsible for performing this translation. Manipulating the YAML files and integrating it with anything else is outside of the scope of this tooling.   For HCD IODFs, each processors statements are seperated in the same YAML file and worked with sequentially in the ZoweLab code to bring the definitions in and out of HCD.

## Limitations and Usage Notes

The YAML file has particular formatting requirements, just like IOCDS, see [YAML Formatting](./YAML_Formatting.md) for more details. If you plan to use this with HCD, it is required to include HCD-specific details (notably, Partition Usage in the RESOURCE statement and TPATH in coupling CHPIDs) in your YAML to ensure a successful HCD migration. In the the same vein, if you want to send the IOCDS to a stand-alone system, it is recommended to _remove_ any HCD-specific IOCDS statements. HCD migrations are also subject to any restrictions in the HCD migration process at any particular point in time.

## Getting Started

Begin by cloning the repro and [installing the package](./Installing_IOCDS_Build_Tools.md).

# Running IOCDS Build Tools
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 02/29/2024

## Prerequisites

- Make sure you have [installed the package](./Installing_IOCDS_Build_Tools.md)
- In most cases, you should have an IOCDS text file from either HCD or stand-alone IOCDS on the same machine (laptop, TOAD container) as the IOCDS Build Tool package

## Convert to YAML

Navigate to the code: `cd ~/iocds_build_tools/src/IOCDSBuilder/`

Then, run the code to conver to YAML: `python3 convert_to_yaml.py`

This will open up a Finder (Mac), File Explorer (Windows), Open dialog (Linux) to find your IOCDS text file on your computer.

The code will run for a while, depending on the size of your IOCDS or IODF.  It will finish and print you where the output file is. The output file is the same file location and name as the IOCDS you provided, but with a .yaml extenstion.  Automation or manual users can now work with the YAML, see [YAML Format](./YAML_Formatting.md) for more details.

## Convert to IOCDS

You must have an IOCDS in YAML format to convert.

Navigate to the code: `cd ~/iocds_build_tools/src/IOCDSBuilder/`

Then, run the code to conver to YAML: `python3 convert_to_yaml.py`

This will open up a Finder (Mac), File Explorer (Windows), Open dialog (Linux) to find your IOCDS YAML file on your computer.

The code will run for a while, depending on the size of your IOCDS or IODF.  It will finish and print you where the output file is. The output file is the same file location and name as the IOCDS YAML you provided, but with a .dat extenstion.  This can be taken into systems for changing their IOCDS.

## Error Handling

This code has very minimal error handling at this time.  Please open a [Github issue](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/iocds_build_tools/issues) if you encounter any errors.

This is to allow for users, programmers and operators to understand their YAML files and find corresponding reference materials in the IOCP User's Guide or the HCD User's Guide Redbooks.

When applicable, restrictions on value inputs are also included. Each section of IOCP or HCD configuration is separated into its own table for easier navigation.

# How to Visualize your IOCDS or IODF with Gephi

Author: Eric Reid
Date: 09/27/2024

metadata.section_heading: How to Visualize your IOCDS or IODF with Gephi

content:
## Introduction

An application of M.A.G.I.C. is to visualize your IODF or IOCDS. This is an overview of how to do that using Gephi, an open source visualization tool. This can be a useful "map" of your environment to help plan changes in your I/O configuration.

## Installation and Setup

First, download and install the [iocds tools repository](./Installing_IOCDS_Build_Tools.md).

Then, download and install [Gephi](https://gephi.org/users/download/). Gephi works on Mac, Windows and Linux and is open source under the GNU license.

## Get Your IOCDS or IODF

If you use standalone IOCDS/IOCP, or have a standalone IOCP make sure you have a copy you want of the text you want to visualize on your workstation.

If you use HCD, you can use [zwe_hcd_standaloneIOCP](../ZoweLab/Tools/HCD%20Tools/getStandaloneIOCDS.md) in ZoweLab. The YAML and visualizer conversion script can handle the full IODF including OS and switch configurations.

## Convert to CSV for Visualization

Gephi can take a CSV file in to visualize. In the iocds_build_tools repository, there is a tool called `IODF_visualizer.py`.  Navigate to this directory, and run the code with: `python3 IODF_visualizer.py`.

This will open up a File Explorer, Finder, etc. on your workstation to navigate to your IOCDS file from the previous step, press "Open". The code will generate four CSV files that can be used in Gephi. These files will be put in whatever directory the code is run from.

The four CSV files are:
- All.csv - this has all CEC's, LPARs, CHPIDs, and control units (CUs) in the IOCDS
- Coupling.csv - this has all CEC's, LPARs, CL5, CS5, ICP channels and their associated csystem/cpath
- Storage.csv - this has all CEC's, LPARs, FC and FCP channels and all associated CU's
- Networking.csv - this has all CEC's, LPARs, OSA, OSD, OSC, OSM, OSE, IQD channels and all associated CU's

Each CSV needs to go through the visualization process below, though they can be saved in a Gephi file all together.

## Visualize the CSV

Start Gephi. It can be a little quirky depending on the operating system, and it takes a minute to start.

In Gephi, go to File -> Import spreadsheet. Navigate to one of the CSV's from the previous section.

![Open](images/import_spreadsheet.png)

Click "Next", then "Finish". This will open a new panel, then press "OK". This should leave you with a big ball of connections:

![Open](images/big_ball.png)

Gephi has many tools to help transform this into a usable image. The following steps can be performed in any order.

### Expand the Dots

On the bottom left panel with "Layout", choose a layout protocol from the dropdown.  The author of this document recommends Yifan Hu with an optimal distance of 200 for most IODF data. Press "Run" to expand the diagram.

![Open](images/yifan_hu.png)

### Add Edge Colors

The visualization automation adds data to the edges about what type of edge it is. In the top left "Appearance" box, select "Edges", then "Partition", then in the dropdown select "color". This should bring up a list of channel and control unit types. You can click the color boxes next to each to set a color, then press "Apply".

![Open](images/edge_nodes.png)

### Add Labels

In the bottom right hand corner of the main screen, there's a little up arrow. Click that to bring up the labels panel on the bottom. Then choose "Labels", and select "Node". You can set a font, color and size.

Then, on the right side, click "Configure" and select the "Id" box. This will go and add the labels to the diagram.

![Open](images/labels.png)

### Seperate Labels

The labels may be overlapping. You can choose the "Label Adjust" expansion in the "Layout" section to move nodes around to separate labels. It's recommended to set the speed as 5 or 10, and let it run.

## Conclusions

When you're done, you should have graphs you can send to others, print off and hang on your wall, or use the highligthing abilities of Gephi to help plan your next IODF configuration change. An example diagram:

![Open](images/banco_all.png)

# YAML Formatting
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 02/29/2024

## Overarching Format

Each processor is given as an element in a YAML file list, seperated by `---`.  This enables a single YAML file to have all the of the definitions from an HCD IODF. The list seperator is also used to seperate OS and Switch statements in HCD.

Each processor has sections for each type of statement (ID, RESOURCE, CHPID....). In manually written IOCDS, things are glued together unlike in the IOCDS.

Below is a list of examples of each statement. This is not the comphrensive list of all possible tags and configurations - that will be documented later.

### RESOURCE Example

RESOURCE:
    css_list:
    - css_num: '0'
        lpar_list:
        - partition_name: CF01
          mifid: C
          usage: CF
          desc: 'ZOS'
        - partition_name: CF5301
          mifid: '1'
          usage: CF
          desc: ''
        - partition_name: CF5302
          mifid: '2'
          usage: CF
          desc: ''
    - css_num: '1'
        lpar_list:
        - partition_name: CF11
          mifid: '1'
          usage: CF
          desc: ''
        - partition_name: CF5311
          mifid: '2'
          usage: CF
          desc: ''
        - partition_name: CF5312
          mifid: '3'
          usage: CF
          desc: ''
    - css_num: '2'
        lpar_list:
        - partition_name: CF21
          mifid: '1'
          usage: CF
          desc: ''
    - css_num: '3'
        lpar_list:
        - partition_name: CF31
          mifid: '1'
          usage: CF
          desc: ''
    - css_num: '4'
        lpar_list:
        - partition_name: CF41
          mifid: '1'
          usage: CF
          desc: ''
    - css_num: '5'
        lpar_list:
        - partition_name: ZOS1
          mifid: '1'
          usage: CF/OS
          desc: ''

### CHPID Statement

CHPID:
    css_list: '1'
    chpid: A3
    type: CS5
    part_access_list:
    - part_css_num: null
        part_partition_list: PL1CFM71
        part_candidate_list: '='
    cpath_css_id: '0'
    cpath: C3
    aid: '35'
    port: '1'
    csystem: LCST1

### Control Unit Statement

CNTLUNIT:
    - cntlunit: '0020'
    path_css_list:
    - path_css_num: '0'
        path_chpid_list: 02,1C
    - path_css_num: '1'
        path_chpid_list: 1C
    - path_css_num: '2'
        path_chpid_list: 1C
    - path_css_num: '3'
        path_chpid_list: 1C
    - path_css_num: '4'
        path_chpid_list: 1C
    - path_css_num: '5'
        path_chpid_list: 1C
    link_list:
    - link_css_num: '0'
        link_link_address_list: 20FE,20FE
    - link_css_num: '1'
        link_link_address_list: 20FE
    - link_css_num: '2'
        link_link_address_list: 20FE
    - link_css_num: '3'
        link_link_address_list: 20FE
    - link_css_num: '4'
        link_link_address_list: 20FE
    - link_css_num: '5'
        link_link_address_list: 20FE
    unit: '2032'
    unitadd_list:
    - address: null
        begin_add: '00'
        number: '001'

### IODEVICE

IODEVICE:
    - device_address: 61A0,032
    cu_number: 60C7
    part_access_list:
    - part_css_num: '0'
        part_partition_list: T14LVM1,T14LVM2,SAK14L1
    - part_css_num: '1'
        part_partition_list: T14LVM3,T14LVM4,SAK14L2
    - part_css_num: '2'
        part_partition_list: T14LVM5,T14LVM6,SAK14L3,S14LIOA4
    - part_css_num: '3'
        part_partition_list: T14LVM7,T14LVM8,SAK14L5,S14LIOA6
    - part_css_num: '4'
        part_partition_list: SAK14L7
    - part_css_num: '5'
        part_partition_list: SAK14L8
    stadet: N
    unit: XTV
    - device_address: 4800,128
    cu_number: '4801'
    part_access_list:
    - part_css_num: '0'
        part_partition_list: TC3EXZOS
    schset_single_ssid: '1'

# Automation

This section of the user guide contains instructions to help you get started with the most common automation tools relied on across the lab. You will find how to access or install different tools, how to get started, and where to find support.

## Using the right automation tool

As we work towards the goal of End-to-End Automation and total tool cohesion, it is important to become knowledgeable of the right tool for the job. Doing so will not only maximize your productivity, but also prepare you for the next stages of automation when they are made readily available.

Read on about the high level strategy you should be using to complete everyday tasks with the systems

## Installing Automation Tools

Many of the available automation tools can simply be installed from our [self-hosted Python package registry](https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/automation-packages/).

:::note
If running from TOAD, the steps below have been taken care of for you. More instructions on maintaining installs of automation tools in TOAD can be found [here](./TOAD/how-to-maintain/README.md#manage-automation-tool-packages).
:::

To be able to install from this registry in your local environment, please follow these steps:

1. Ensure you have `Python 3` and `pip` installed in your local environment
2. From a terminal, run:

```bash
    pip config set global.trusted-host vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com
    ```

3. Also run:

```bash
    pip config set global.index-url https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/automation-packages
    ```

After this, you will be able to install any of the packages available from the registry, by using this command syntax:

```bash
pip install -U <package_name>
```

For example:

```bash
pip install -U remoteztoolset
```

e from the registry, by using this command syntax:

```bash
pip install -U <package_name>
```

For example:

```bash

```

There are other tools that are not hosted in this registry, for which install instructions will be provided in their respective user guides under this `Automation` section and should be followed.

In the event those instructions don't work, please reach out to the listed tool owner. If there is no listed tool owner, please reach out in the [#test-floor-automation-guild](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C03JJCXNNJG) Slack channel for help.

## TOAD Containers - Your execution environment

The Test Operator's Automation Desktop is our delivery mechanism for a plethora of other tools. Using it places all the best tools at your fingertips and instills a commonality across different teams and the way they work.

Its purpose is to provide you an isolated environment where you can leverage the provided tools to conduct testing, system maintenance, and failure analysis

Read more in the [TOAD Section](./TOAD/README.md)

### Remote Z Toolset

[RZT](./remoteZtoolset/README.md) is how the TOAD Container interfaces with the Z systems you work on. It maintains a list of systems and their host information, allowing users and applications in your TOAD environment to target them with ssh and API requests, as well as offload files for post processing. It is a dependency used by many other tools within the environment.

### ZoweLab

Zowe is an open source set of software tools providing a modern way to interface with zOS. [This checklist](/Automation/ZoweLab/Setup/ZoweLab_checklist.md) will help you get your environment cleaned up and ready to run Zowe

ZoweLab is the collection of tools we built in house with our unique missions and lab nuances in mind.

When replacing legacy automation such as ditto scripts, it is important to understand the available tools and how they differ from the legacy tools they replace.

1. PCD | Python Channel Driver
2. PyThrash | CF Thrasher Procs
3. Ditto Killer | Everything Else

### 3270 Automation

[**mimic**](./mimic/README.md) offers powerful automation capability for any OS running in a 3270 console, while preserving your control of the console.

## STELAr

[STELAR](./STELA/README.md), formerly known as STELA is the Lab's backup repository where data from each system is routinely collected. The data is used for Jupitr tickets, anomaly analytics, and more.

### CARTES

[CARTES](./CARTES/README.md), or Connections And Records Tracking for Enterprise Systems is the smart database which replaces EPCT.  It utilizes much of STELA's data to help detect and correct documentation errors.

#### And much more

Those are just a few of the tools and resources available to help up your automation game. Be sure to be active in automation forums such as the guild meeting and office hours.

If a tool's documentation doesn't have links, the official bug and enhancement process may not be available  yet, if so please reach out to the Nova team. Github issues handle both bugs and feature requests.

Otherwise, make sure you can get into the systemz Github project, see this [procedure](AutomationBestPractices/DeveloperGuides/GithubHelp/SystemzSWAT.md)

# SAK Monitor
A companion application for 3270 operator environment manager 3270 consoles

SAK Monitor will periodically collect the SAK eyecatcher row from your 3270 consoles. The data is displayed on a Grafana dashboard. At a glance, you can keep track of all your SAK console status in one place.

## Requirements
SAK monitor runs from within the TOAD container, which is a Linux environment.

## Installation
The package should come pre-installed in your container. If `sak_monitor --help` works, then it's installed.

If that doesn't work, you can *pip* install the package. Run ` sh TOAD-MGMT/upgrade-tools.sh`

## Usage
1. Make sure 3270oe is running. `ps -A | grep run3270oe` This should return a reference. If it does not, you need to start `run3270oe` from a terminal window.
2. Start SAK monitor in a terminal window: `sak_monitor m`
3. Start your SAK consoles. If you do not know how to do this, reference: See the quick start guide [3270oe API Quick Start](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/3270OE/README3270oeApiQuickStart).

## Dashboard
To see your SAK partitions status see the dashboard at: [SAK Monitor Dashboard](http://9.114.114.214:3000/d/cejvzu322hurkf/sak-aggregation-test?orgId=1&from=1970-01-01T00:00:02.025Z&var-sak_session=A61_SAK01_SAK01_60@9.56.192.120:3270_0060&to=now&timezone=browser). You will need to login: `admin` *passw0rd*

## Troubleshooting
My data is not on the dashboard.
1. Is the 3270 operator environment managing your SAK partition 3270 session?
2. Is the sak_monitor running?

Do you see something like this from your SAK monitor session? You should.
```
[2025-05-09 08:45:49,702 INFO] CPC A61 LPAR SAK21 status is operating.
[2025-05-09 08:45:49,703 INFO] Reading file: /home/tester/Nova/sak_monitor/A61/A61_SAK21_SAK21_60@9.56.192.120:3270_0060.yaml
[2025-05-09 08:45:49,802 INFO] Performing analysis: /home/tester/Nova/sak_monitor/A61/A61_SAK21_SAK21_60@9.56.192.120:3270_0060.yaml
[2025-05-09 08:45:54,868 INFO] Writing to yaml output file: /home/tester/Nova/sak_monitor/A61/A61_SAK21_SAK21_60@9.56.192.120:3270_0060.yaml.
[2025-05-09 08:45:54,911 INFO] Writing to json output file:  /home/tester/Nova/sak_monitor/A61/A61_SAK21_SAK21_60@9.56.192.120:3270_0060.json.
[2025-05-09 08:45:54,943 INFO] Here is the SAK Aggregator response <Response [200]>
[2025-05-09 08:45:54,944 INFO] Output written, sleeping= 119.0. Counter=2.

```

# 3270 operator environment interface information
The sak_monitor module gets information from 3270oe. Specifically:
1. A list of `key:values` where **key** is a unique id for your 3270 session, e.g.
`A61_SAK21_SAK21_60@9.56.192.120:3270_0060` and **value** are the py3270_ibm and py3270_sak python objects to issue commands to the 3270 session.

For example:

```

sak_monitor l -p
[2025-05-09 08:38:45,498 INFO] Action L selected. Print is True
[2025-05-09 08:38:45,502 INFO] A61_SAK21_SAK21_60@9.56.192.120:3270_0060 : [<py3270_ibm.Emulator object at 0x7354e91a8eb0>, <oe3270.src.py3270_sak.SakEmulator object at 0x7354e9326470>]

**SATURN** is a telemetry platform developed by Engineering Systems Tests's Nova team to track automation and AI tool usage and impact across many teams and organizations within IBM.

content:
## Preparing data for SATURN

We have worked diligently to make sending your data as easy as possible.

Things to consider before you start:

-	At what point during your tool’s execution will you submit the data?  What if your tool run is interrupted early? Would the time savings data still be valid? If not, consider at what point in your code it makes the most sense to send the data submission.
-	Ensuring you are only sending “real” data to maintain SATURNs data integrity. This means being able to **justify EMTE values** and **excluding development runs** from submitting data (running a tool 25 times to fix a bug does NOT count as “real” tool uses).
-	To delete data from the database an admin must go in and manually delete it. So be careful and intentional about what data you are sending from the start. Check your data structure and test your code before submitting any data to SATURN.
### Data Structure

#### Here is a data example:

{
    'toolname': 'myToolName’,
    'toolowner': ['john.smith@ibm.com', 'amy.fisher@ibm.com’],
    ‘toolteam': [‘Nova’,’LCST’],
    ‘tags': [‘EST'],
    'emte’: 3.0,
    ‘toolversion’: “0.1.0”
    }

*TURN data must be in JSON format.*

- **Required**: toolname, toolowner, toolteam, emte (defaulted to zero if not passed in)
- All other keys are **optional**. **NOTE**: You can include any additional data you want. Future iterations of SATURN may include giving our tool owners the ability to make charts of their own. So, including any additional information you might want to use later is a good idea.

#### Key Definitions:
-	‘toolname’ (string) is the name of your tool.
-	‘toolowner’ (list) should include the IBM email of the owner of the tool, more than one email can be listed if there are multiple tool owners.
-	‘toolteam’ (list) should include team name (or names) the **toolowner belongs to** - this is NOT the team of the individual using the tool.
-	‘emte’ (float or integer) is the time in minutes your tool saves.
-	‘tags’ (list) key is optional. This should include any additional or unique tags you and/or your team would like to filter by.
-	‘toolversion’ (string) is optional. This should include the version of your tool as a string: “0.1.0”

> ⚠️ **Important:** If you must submit test data to SATURN include the value **"dummy"** in the **tags** key and that data will later be deleted.

### EMTE (Equivalent Manual Test Effort)

This is the time in minutes your tool saves per run.

The value can be determined by talking to your users about the manual/prior process that your tool replaces.
- How long did it take your users to perform the task your new tool automates?
- How long does it take a user to kick off your tool?

Use that information along with any additional manual time your tool does require to run (example: writing a yaml file to use for execution or configuring a tool between runs).

Calculate EMTE with this equation:

**EMTE = task_instances * (manual_time - automation_time)**

> ⚠️ **Note:** automation_time is hands-to-keyboard time; how long it takes the tool to run does not count toward your automation_time so long as the user does not have to be at the keyboard during execution.

how long it takes the tool to run does not count toward your automation_time so long as the user does not have to be at the keyboard during execution.

You can calculate this value in whatever way works for you. Maybe your tool performs one straight forward action that saves 2 minutes every time it is run. Maybe your tool is more complex, and the time savings is determined by several different factors related to that runs details (multiple systems or instances); in that case your tool might submit a different ‘emte’ value per run. Maybe your tool doesn’t save any manual time, but you want to track how often it is used, in that case you can set the ‘emte’ value as 0 (zero).

**The most important thing is that your emtes are valid and provable. Every tool owner must be able to justify their emtes.**

**Visit our [SATURN-Client](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/saturn-client) GitHub Repo for detailed instructions.**

## Reporting Bugs / Proposing Features

Found a bug? Want to suggest a new feature or improvement for SATURN? Visit our [SATURN Issues Page](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/SATURN/issues) to make a ticket!

## SATURN Origin & History

SATURN was originally developed within the Systems Assurance (SA) organization by the EST Nova team to address a need for better visibility into automation adoption and impact. At the time, the platform was named SATURN (Systems Assurance Tool Usage Report Node). The name intentionally incorporated the “TURN” (Tool Usage Report Node) concept, an industry-aligned pattern for collecting and reporting telemetry about tool usage and operational activity.

As the platform matured, its usefulness quickly extended beyond its original scope. Teams across multiple organizations at IBM began integrating with SATURN to track automation adoption, AI tool usage, and the measurable time savings these tools provide. What began as an internal reporting mechanism within Systems Assurance evolved into a cross-organizational telemetry platform supporting automation initiatives across IBM.

rnal reporting mechanism within Systems Assurance evolved into a cross-organizational telemetry platform supporting automation initiatives across IBM.

Because of this growth and broad adoption, SATURN is now treated primarily as the name of the platform rather than a strict acronym. While its origins remain an important part of its history, the platform’s mission has expanded to serve a much wider community. Today, SATURN acts as a shared telemetry framework that enables teams across IBM to measure automation impact, understand adoption trends, and make data-driven decisions that support the company’s broader automation strategy.

In this way, the SATURN name reflects both its origins and its evolution, growing from a Systems Assurance initiative into a unifying platform that helps track and advance automation efforts across IBM. 🚀

# BUP Tools

Bring UP Tools, better known as BUPTools is a community maintained collection of scripts.  They are specialized to help in the early stages of system bring up, but have many useful purposes in later stages of development and test. BUPTools often call lower level tools with meaningful intention for user convenience, the resulting function will help you query system conditions or apply changes to low level components.

Github Repo: [buptools](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/buptools)
Contact: Daniela Yaniv

## How to get BUP Tools

Bringup Tools are already installed with all tools drivers.  The latest version is usually obtained by running a zdnf tool update.

## Reporting an issue

1. If you know the maintainer of the tool, reach out to them directly
2. If you don't know the tool owner you can open a [github issue](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/buptools/issues/new)
3. If that hasn't gained traction you can reach out to Daniela for advice

## Contributing to BUPTools

Reach out to Daniela. You may also wish to start a dialogue in [#zmetf_buptools](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C0658FVSJBC) to see if a tool meeting your needs already exists.

# codes

```codes``` is a standalone script in BUP Tools which queries and displays various firmware code levels installed on a machine.

Its purpose is to take a snapshot of all the active code levels on the system for inspection by machine operators. The output file 'code.json' is convenient to include in test reports and failure analysis data,

`codes` was rewritten in Python for Metis and beyond. The legacy Perl version by the legendary Erv Con has been replaced with a python version for Metis which produces the same information in a json format.

## Where to get codes (D6X+)

codes *should* be included with buptools, but can also be downloaded from [Github](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/codes) and placed on the SE to run stand alone without any dependencies.

This file must be signed before it is executed or it will cause [TC errors](../../CommonProcedures/Z%20Configuration%20Help/TrustedComputing/TCErrors.md)!!

To install or update codes on an SE with tools:

```
gettool -file codes
fix -N -d /console/bin/tmp ./codes
```

Fix will move and sign the script for you.

## How to run codes

Running ```codes``` in any SE CLI with no arguments will take less than a couple seconds and then open the output in `less`

Three formats of the output are written to /tmp/ for your convenience:

```
/tmp/code.lvl
/tmp/code.yml
/tmp/code.json
```

### optional arguments

You can run `codes quiet` or `codes file` to prevent output from opening in less and holding thread. This is useful for running codes from another script or remote server.

### How to address bugs or enhancements

Open me a [Github Issue](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/codes/issues)
