# Console Log Basics

## What is the log and where do you find it
The iqyylog.log a.k.a SE/HMC Console Log, is the central log for system events across all firmware components. Many firmware areas also have their own ‘component log’ which contain additional detail that would clutter the iqyylog. You can produce a list of all log files by running `ll /console/data/iqyy*.log` on an SE command line.

The tasks to access these logs are shown below:

![image](./images/ConsoleLog1.png)

The view when opening a log is a high-level list of the events in chronological order. This is referred to as the **log directory**.

Each line in the *directory* links to the full content of that log event, which is organized by data blocks.

A description area may be blank or contain a short string describing the event

metadata.section_heading: What is the log and where do you find it

content:
### SRCs
Some log events use the description section to provide a one to three  8 Character hex words.
-	The first word is known as the System Reason Code, or SRC.  It will have a defined meaning which is always the same for all instances of that SRC.
-	The second and third optional word are called the trailer or extension refcodes and typically translate to identify the specific parts of the machine they relate to.

### A word about reading logs in the SE Tasks
It is important to know how to read the log using the default tasks. At times it is the only available or most convenient method.

However, once familiar with the tasks you are strongly advised to master the SE CLI tools. Doing so will step up your log reading game significantly.

metadata.section_heading: A word about reading logs in the SE Tasks

content: # CLI Tools for reading the log

metadata.section_heading: CLI Tools for reading the log

content:
## SE Log Reading Tools

:::note
These are not all BUP Tools as the enclose section might suggest. Its all relevent information so I have included extra context for completeness
:::

The CLI ways of reading a log is much faster than the tasks. These tools work in the VNC GUI, or in an ssh window. Using ssh provides the added luxury of being able to copy and paste log snippets when necessary.

## iqyx
 Every .log file is written in a proprietary binary format which requires a log reader to decipher

`iqyx` is such a tool and is used in the back end of all the tools described afterwards.

iqyx both lists the log directory and expands one or more logs based on your input arguments. You must specify the full path to the log file  and supply all arguments as it does not have any default values that the other tools tend to have.

### iqyx dir
This command will list the log directory in `less` so that it doesn’t flood your terminal

```
iqyx dir /console/data/iqyylog.log |less
```

![image](./images/ConsoleLog2.png)

When you are in the *less* viewer you can enter a search pattern by typing ‘/’ followed by what you are looking for.

In this example, /DrvStart is showing you when the SE rebooted:

![image](./images/ConsoleLog3.png)

Hit enter to finish the search pattern, then `n` will go to the next search match and so on.

Hit `q` to exit *less*

It can be very handy to combine `iqyx dir` with `grep` as shown in the examples below:

```

# Displays hardware messages, or “problems” in virtual retain
iqyx dir /console/data/iqyylog.log |grep PN

metadata.section_heading: Displays hardware messages, or “problems” in virtual retain

content: # |egrep lets you search multiple patterns

# Displays MCL Install events, hexpatch errors, and the ‘finished’ log
iqyx dir /console/data/iqyylog.log |egrep -I “MMC|hex|LIC_C”

```

metadata.section_heading: Displays MCL Install events, hexpatch errors, and the ‘finished’ log

content:
### iqyx expand
Once you have identified a log that you want to open, `iqyx expand` is how you can read the detailed information for the instance of that event.

You must supply a log index which is from the last section of the log in the directory listing.
For example, the SE reboot in the search above is index 450, so to ‘open’ that log event type:

```
iqyx expand /console/data/iqyylog.log 450 |less
```
![image](./images/ConsoleLog4.png)

## llog and elog
Now that you understand iqyx dir and iqyx expand, there are two basic tools that can do this a little faster *if installed* , `llog`  for listing the log directory, and `elog` for expanding the log of the provided index.

Both of these tools will pipe their output to less, unless you pipe to grep in which case your output goes to STDOUT unless you pipe to less!

|grep works great with llog + elog as demonstrated for plain iqyx.

Inspiration
```
[hmcmanager@UB40-/home/hmcmanager]llog |grep DrvStart |head -n 1
E015 07-07-23 10:43:23:17  DrvStart       E0150047 00000000          00         | 0x000359D9   450
[hmcmanager@UB40-/home/hmcmanager]elog 450 |tail
Standard Log Data:

Program Name................... logerror
Current Process ID............. 316F
Parent Process ID.............. 316C
Current Thread.Priority........ 0000
Current Thread................. 316F
Screen Group................... 0000
SubScreen Group................ 0000
Current Foreground Process..... 0000
[hmcmanager@LCST1A40-/home/hmcmanager]

```

## logloop
`logloop` is a constantly refreshing and color-coded view of the log directory.  Just type `logloop` and it will show you the iqyylog.log in your active terminal session.

#### logwin
`logwin` is logloop except it opens a popup window so you can keep your current terminal session for productive work. This only works in VNC unless you have xwindows setup for your terminal.

## plog.sh
Saving the best for last, `plog.sh` combines most of the best features of all the other CLI Log reader. This color-coded view of the log can be scrolled and searched through, your 'enter' key conveniently opens selected log entries to show its full content.

![image](./images/ConsoleLog5.png)

### Invoking plog.sh

There are three basic ways to run the tool

1. Simply type `plog.sh` to open the tool.
2. To open a specific log, provide the full path as an argument `plog.sh /console/data/iqyytccl.log`
3. **NEW** | Open TWO logs and merge chronologically

```
plog.sh /console/data/iqyylog.log -c /console/data/iqyycoeh.log
```

```
01D6 09-30-24 10:14:04:99  CEC_i390_FED   2CFEDC64 00000100 000D006C 90         | 0x000012F1      1 4     -> iqyycoeh
01D5 09-30-24 10:14:04:98  CEC_i390_FED   22FEDC50 0000FDC1 000A0000 90         | 0x00B0D1D4   0 1964     -> iqyylog
```

### Navigating plog.sh
Simply use Arrow keys, Page-Up, or Page-Down keys to scroll through the log. The highlighted log near the top is 'selected'.

![image](./images/ConsoleLog6.png)

You can **search** the log with /pattern  then *'ESC'* will return you to the log directory

hitting *'enter' (or 'return' on Mac)* will open the highlighted log file

### Monitor the log
Hitting `l` will enable logloop mode, and the log directory will start refreshing every couple of seconds.

:::note
Scrolling will cause plog.sh to exit logloop mode
:::

`plog.sh` defaults to /console/data/iqyylog.log but will also accept the name of any logfile you pass it.

# What now?

Log viewing proficiency will help you understand system behavior and problems more quickly, but finding the meaning of these events requires experience. Try incorporating some of these tools in your day to day tasks and you will notice improvements to your analytical skills when it comes to logs.

Do you know a better tools or some other log viewer tricks? Please contact Chris Hutton to get the details added to this user guide

# tc_fixer

```tc_fixer.py``` will list and fix trusted computing violations based on entries in iqyytccl.log. The fixing process will check each file that caused a violation for a valid signature, and sign it if an invalid or missing signature is found. This is done through calls to ```tcVerify.sh``` and ```tcsign.sh```.

## Use
To list the violations, run ```./tc_fixer.py``` with no options. Running with ```-f``` will list and fix any violations that are found.
Run with ```-h``` to display these options in the terminal.

The list of violations will print to the console ordered by newest to oldest.

![image](./images/tc_fixer_list.png)

The fixing process wil show each file being verified and highlight which already have valid signatures, and which have invalid signatures. At the end of the fixing process the script will delete ```/console/data/pa/bad_drive_file```

![image](./images/tc_fixer_fix.png)

# Unfixer
This tool can be used to run a mass unfix on your system in perparation for an mcl install, or if you just want to get rid of a bunch of fixes at once.
## Installation Instructions

### Installation Steps

Follow these steps if you would like to run this tool on either an HMC, or a pre-D61C Driver

1. **Download the script locally**
   ```bash

# Clone the repository or download unfixer.py directly
   git clone git@github.ibm.com:systemz/unfixer.git

metadata.section_heading: Clone the repository or download unfixer.py directly

content:
# OR download the file directly from the repository
   ```

2. **Transfer the file onto your support element**
   ```bash
   scp unfixer.py <username>@<support-element-hostname>:/ffdc/u/unfixer.py
   ```

3. **SSH into your support element**
   ```bash
   ssh <username>@<support-element-hostname>
   ```

4. **Sign the file using tcsign**
   ```bash
   tcsign.sh /ffdc/u/unfixer.py
   ```

5. **Make the file executable**
   ```bash
   sudo chmod +x /ffdc/u/unfixer.py
   ```

6. **Move the file to /usr/local/bin**
    ```bash
    sudo mv /ffdc/u/unfixer.py /usr/local/bin/unfixer.py

7. **Verify installation**
   ```bash
   unfixer.py --help
   ```

metadata.section_heading: OR download the file directly from the repository

content: ## How to use:

### Running the tool
The syntax for running the tool goes as follows:

unfixer.py

This will run the tool, checking if there are any files defined in the keeplist, and deleting any fixes that aren't. It will then print out which fixes are remaining on the system, and create a zip file of all the removed fixes.

In order to generate the keeplist, run this command:

unfixer.py -k or unfixer.py --keep

This will generate a file called keeplist.txt in /ffdc/unfixer, and wjile running, it will specifically look for this file in that location. in order to use this file, you must edit it, and place any fixes you wish to remain on the system after running the tool.

Example syntax for what the file should look like goes as follows:

example1.zip
    example2.zip
    example3.zip
    example*

a bad example of a keeplist would look like:

example1
    example2.zip example3.zip
    /path/to/example4.zip
    example5.*

Once the keeplist is set the program will refer to it going forward, no need to create a new one every time, deleting the file or emptying it will cause the program to run as default.

ram will refer to it going forward, no need to create a new one every time, deleting the file or emptying it will cause the program to run as default.

If you wanted to just list out the fixes currently present on the system, you can do so by running:

unfixer.py -l or unfixer.py --list

This will simply list out all currently installed fixes and do nothing more, another effective way to view this would be running codes.

Lastly, if you would like to not save the fixes in at all, you can run the following parameter:

unfixer.py -n or unfixer.py --nozip

When running the tool, it's important to note that many fixes may require a system reboot to be fully removed, and some will require a nondisruptive ucode apply on the specific area of code that the fix correlates to. It will say so when the reboot is required, but it is much less clear for the ucode apply, so please use some discretion.

# ECMDs

E Commands, better known as ECMDs are low level tools that talk to the hardware.  They can surface system status information or conduct powerful yet dangerous changes to low level components so should be used with caution.  The tools are available in CLI form, all prefixed with `zse`.  It is also possible to call them directly with Python and Perl classes.

## How to get ECMDs

ECMDs Tools are already installed with all tools drivers.  The latest version is usually obtained by running a zdnf tool update.

# Power Thermal Automation Suite
![ptSuite logo](./images/ptsuite_logo.png)

## About
The Power Thermal Automation Suite or "ptSuite" for short is a series of tools that test different elements of the power, cooling, and service network hardware/software for z17. Currently there are three different scripts within the suite that all test distinct functions within the subsystem.
***

### ptBmcRI.py
The **BMC** (Baseboard management controller) functions as a network interface adapter between the CEC/IO cages and the rest of the internal service network. This script triggers cascading resets on all of the controllers to ensure graceful shutdown, takeover, and recovery.

### ptPwrRI.py
The **Processer power controllers** (PPC) and **IO power controllers** (IPC) manage the internal power distrubution within the CEC and IO drawers respectively. This script triggers cascading resets on all of the controllers to ensure graceful shutdown, takeover, and recovery.

### ptAcdl.py
Certain components in the power thermal/service network subsystems have firmware that is upgradable via a process known as **Auto Code Download** (ACDL). These components include the **Cooling Control Assemblies** (CCA), PPCs, IPCs, **Power Distribution Units** (PDU), **Power Supply Units** (PSU), and the ethernet switches. ACDL occurs during repair and verify scenarios, following SE reboots, and during MCL updates. This script triggers ACDL to a chosen component type, first updating the components to an older level before updating them back to their original level. This can be ran once or over an extended period of time to test the efficacy and robustnesss of ACDL.
***

## How to use it
In order to install ptSuite simply open a terminal on your TOAD container and issue the following command:

`pip install ptSuite`

This will download the tool package onto your system. From here, you can simply issue the command

`ptScheduler`

from any directory to bring up the ptScheduler interface. This is a CLI that asks for a series of inputs, and uses said inputs to generate the command used to run your script of choice. See below for a comprehensive list of all possible input parameters

### General
- `-s` = Target System
- `-d` = Target drawer (options vary from script to script)
- "Duration" variables used for determining how long your script will run for (only one option per run)
  - `-c` = # of loops that will be performed
  - `-edt` = select an ending datetime (script will stop running on this day at this time)
  - `-ddt` = select the duration over which the script will run (30 minutes, 5 hours, etc.)
- `-sl` = choose the amount of time the script waits in between loops
- `-p` = choose whether or not to purge the iqyy log before your run (used to prevent pruning)

### BmcRI & PwrRI specific
- `-r` = reset type
  - PwrRI = Either `cold` or `warm`
  - BmcRI = Either `reboot` or `takeover`

### Scheduling
Once the command is composed, ptScheduler also provides the option to either run your automation immediately, or schedule it out for asynchronous testing. This scheduling can be done...

- Relative to the current time (now + 3 hours)
- targeting a specific day of the week (sunday at 15:00)
- targeting a particular datetime (12/12/12 at 01:23)

## Installing EST Tools (Any distro)

Note: only non production systems can install EST_Tools.

On a support element command line (ssh preferred)
 1. Browse the latest releases [here](http://9.56.193.90/EST-FTP/tools/?C=M;O=D)
 2. We must download the .tar file of the desired release into /ffdc/, then unpack and finally sign all of the files. This can be accomplished by copying all of the following commands and pasting them into the ssh window at once.

You may need to hit enter to execute the final command.

```console
cd /ffdc/
curl -O http://9.56.193.90/EST-FTP/tools/est_tools_zMeGA1-20260114.tar
tar -xvf est_tools_zMeGA1-20260114.tar
rm ./est_tools_zMeGA1-20260114.tar
find /ffdc/est_tools -type f -executable -exec /console/bin/test/tcsign.sh {} \;
cd est_tools
ls -l

```
If you need to install a different release, substitute the release name in the command above in the system slack log when you post that you installed this. :)

The legacy error_log_viewer script is used to help for the error_logs.pl program.

This utilization tool will scan through system logs for error entries and other informational high flying SRCs.

## How is the Error Log Viewer structured?

It contains an user defined error list file and additonal GREP user specified search parameters. It is recommended to include the filter in single quotes. This can be any Perl Regular Expression.  Whatever is specified will be included in the error list. This will not modify the default list.err file.
New Log enteries will read a file that stores the last time the program was run, and will only return the new data since that timestamp.  The file is located in ./html/last_time_scanned.txt. The iFrames default is to be maximized on the current SE version. The other option is to format the iframes for a W500 notebook at resolution setting of 1920/1200. It also contains an Offline Mode that will make HTML pages for all the expanded logs and allow the user to view the standard output plus all error data when not on the SE.

content: # My Format 3 For Ficon

## What is My Format Script?
myfmt3 is an iqyylog parsing tool which builds a report about channel events and gathers relevant data.
It is a convenient way to identify, classify, and enumerate the errors on your system.
The analysis is *ficon* focused, and does not replace the need to check the log for errors using traditional methods
The output files are launched in a web browser and viewable in html format
myfmt3 can zip up all the data to attach to defects.
## How to run myfmt3

### Basic
Myfmt3 can only run directly on the SE. It is recommended you VNC into the SE so that the final output can be displayed.
Obtain a command window and go to the myformat director
`cd /ffdc/est_tools/myformat/`

Now you just have to run `myfmt3`
```

```
Thousands of logs could take a couple minutes to sift through, then you what output files are created

Writing output to ./html_out/all_errors.html

Enter "myfmt3 -ze" to package the existing output data and associated logs (do not reprocess)

```

### Myfmt Options
1. `myfmt3 -n` | New runs only
    When you run myfmt3 it creates a timestamp file so that you can use this option to only process new logs since you last checked for errors.
2. `myfmt3 -z` | Process and zip the output
    If you already know there is reason to save the output for a defect, the -z option will create a .zip file of all the data and store it in ./archive/
3. `myfmt3 -ze <custom_name>` | Zip the existing output
    More often you will learn there were errors after myfmt3 ran. Go back to the command line and run with -ze to zip the output *without reprocessing*. You could also enter a custom name which will be added as a suffix to your output file.
4. `myfmt3 -t` | Don't store run timestamp
    If you wish to run myfmt out of your daily routine this option suppresses updating the last_time_scanned so the next -n run will still include the expected timeframe for daily checks.
5. `myfmt -h` | A full help menu covering additional options

## Errors Supported

These errors include the following:
* All 1F20 CCCs
* All other Ficon CCCs
* All FICON IFCCs
* EKM Logs
* Channel State Change Logs
* Some FCP Logs
* Some OSA Logs
* CTE Logs
* LIR Logs

## myfmt3 prereqs
1. The myfmt3 script must be run directly on the SE. Myfmt makes a local copy of the iqyylog to start finding channel problems, some events indicate that additional data of interest exists somewhere, myfmt grabs this data for the final output.
2. The SE Must have tools installed, especially iqyx. The iqyy*.log files on the SE are in a binary format which requires this DAISY tool to interpret

## Installing on the SE
- ### Cloning the Repo directly
  Instructions:
  - Set up ssh-agent by running 'ssh-agent -a username@ip' in a terminal.
  - Connect to the SE with the agent using the following command: 'ssh -A hmcmanager@ip'.
    - Doing these two steps will allow you to access github on the SE using the ssh key on your local machine.
  - Clone the repo by navigating to '/ffdc/u/' on the SE file system and running 'git clone git@github.ibm.com:systemz/ioinj_test.git'.
  - Sign the executables within the repo directory.
    - This can be done by navigating inside te project directory and running the following command: 'tcsign.sh ioinj_test.py; tcsign.sh utils.py; tcsign.sh chpidBreakDown.pl;'

navigating inside te project directory and running the following command: 'tcsign.sh ioinj_test.py; tcsign.sh utils.py; tcsign.sh chpidBreakDown.pl;'

- ### Using a ZIP file
  Instructions
  - Download a compressed ZIP file of the repo.
    - The option to download as a ZIP can be found on the github page for the repo in the menu that appears when clicking the code button.
    - Repo link: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/ioinj_test
  - Copy the zip file into the '/ffdc/u/' directory on the desired system.
    - The simplest way to do this is with an scp command: 'scp /path/to/zipfile.zip hmcmanager@ip:/ffdc/u/zipfile.zip'.
  - Connect to the SE via SSH and extract the copied zip file.
  - Sign the executables within the extracted directory.
    - This can be done by navigating inside the project directory and running the following command: 'tcsign.sh ioinj_test.py; tcsign.sh utils.py; tcsign.sh chpidBreakDown.pl;'

## Error Files
  In order to run the IOINJ inject tool, there needs to be a testcase file, a requirements file, and there needs to be an entry in error_data.json. The requirements file and the error_data.json entry(s) need to be referenced within the testcase file.

- ### Schema
  The schema outlining the format for each type of error file can be found in err_data/schema.

- ### Testcase File
  Contains errors referenced from the error data file, a reference to a requirements file, default settings for running the testcase, Paths of any log files to back up between injects, and any data to overwrite what's in the referenced error data. Testcase files can be in either YAML or JSON format.

```yaml

- ### Requirements File
  Contains hardware requirements for any IO cards being tested. Requirements files can be in either YAML or JSON format.
  ```yaml

# ./err_files/etu_spfw_einj_requirements.yml
  ATTDEV: DIANA
  CARDTYPE: PBU
  ```

```json
  > ./err_files/etu_spfw_einj_requirements.json
  {
    "$schema": "schema/requirements_schema.json",
    "CARDTYPE": "PBU",
    "ATTDEV": "DIANA"
  }
  ```
  - CARDTYPE property can be any of the following: PBU, ROCE, PEX8796, PEX8725, THUMPER2, PANTHER2, or KRAKEN.
  - ATTDEV property can be any of the following: DIANA, MENSA, FRAM, FICON, ROOSEVELT, CONNECTX, or MONTAUK.
  - See ./err_files/schema/requirements_schema.json for full list of properties.

- ### Error Data File
  Shared file containing catalog of error data to reference in individual testcase files. This error data includes the error type, the list commands to run when executing the error, custom variable definitions/sets to be referenced within the commands, and any defined custom threshold warnings.

Variables are referenced in the procedures using a '$' symbol and are populated with the values in the selected variable set(s) when running the tool. There are a few key variables that are filled using data pertaining to the target hardware instead of the variable sets. These being $hwa, $dev, and $vchid.

  etu_spfw_einj:
    Error Type: '1'
    Procedures:
    - '$dev $hwa etu_spfw_einj store $word0 $word1 # #'

        Time Interval: 600
      failure:
        Inject Count: 40
        Time Interval: 600
    Variable Sets:
      '1':
        Description: CBB_TIMEOUT_STATUS
        Variables:
          word0: '40000000'
          word1: '00000000'
      Default: '1'

    Error Type: '1'
    Procedures:
    - $dev $hwa.$port  Error_Check_Disable store 4
    - $dev $hwa.$port  Error_Check_Disable sense
    - $dev $hwa.$port  Uncorrectable_Error_Status sense
    - $dev $hwa.$port  Uncorrectable_Error_Status store $word0
    - $dev $hwa.$port  Error_Check_Disable store 0

## Functions

IOINJ is comprised of four main functions. These functions being print, query, inject, and file.

- ### Print
  The print function outputs content of an error file to the console. The user specifies the error file contents to be printed using the -f option. The outputted content of which includes populated requirements and error data from other files that correspond to the error file.

> python3 ioinj_test.py print -f etu_spfw_einj.yml

- ### Query
  The query function queries the system for connected hardware. This can be done as a general query or an error file can be provided by the user using the -f option to query for hardware that meets the requiements for an individual error.

> python3 ioinj_test.py query

> python3 ioinj_Test.py query -f etu_spfw_einj.yml

- ### Inject
  The inject function is used for executing error injects. Users provide an error file using the -f option and the tool will create a loop of injects to perform based on the data given within the testcase, requirements, and error_data corresponding to that error. Users can also provide one or more indexes using the -e option which determines what variable sets defined in the error data to use. These variable sets determine the values that are filled within the procedures when generating the inject loop. The inject loop will contain an inject for each combination of variable sets and hwa/pchid/vchid given.

The inject settings defined in the testcase file can also be overwritten in the command line by using the -n, -l, -d, and -ld options for inject count, loop count, inject delay, and loop delay respectfully. Some requirements parameters can also be overwritten in the command line, mainly DEV, HWA, PCHID, and VCHIDS using -dev, -hwa, -pchid, and -vchid.

> python3 ioinj_test.py inject -f etu_spfw_einj.yml

- ### File
  The file function is essentially a means of passing in cli arguments through a file as well as orchestrating mutliple IOINJ executions.
  This is done by passing in either a YAML or JSON file containing lists of arguments to pass into IOINJ.

  - - print

  ]

## Additional Notes

- This tool can also be used locally without installing on the SE with the restriction that the tool won't be able to get the VCHIDs when querying the system. This can be done using the -ssh option which accepts a username then an ip address. You can also pass into the name of an SSH key pair with the -k option if an SSH key is already being used to connect to a system.

> python3 ioinj_test.py query -ssh username ip

> python3 ioinj_test.py query -ssh username ip -k key

- ### Query

- Usage:

- Options:

    - -f error_file
      - Error file containing error(s) to inject.
    - -ssh
      - Username then hostname for remote execution via SSH.
    - -k KEY, --k KEY
      - Name of SSH key file for passwordless SSH connection.
    - -t timeout, --timeout timeout
      - Timeout for SSH connection.

# SE Tools

This section of the user guide contains instructions for some of the tools that are designed to run on the Z Support Elements.  There are many tools packages that are delivered as part of tools drivers or installed after the fact. Awareness of these tools and comfort using them is an important skill to develop if you wish to become proficient on the systems. It can also help save you from reinventing the wheel.

Do YOU have tools you made to run on the SE?

- Aren't sure where your tool fits in? Talk to your squad's Automation Rep, or start a discussion in [#test-floor-automation-guild](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C03JJCXNNJG)
 - Open up a new project idea as a github issue in our [Infrastructure Automation Pipeline](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/Infrastructure-Automation-Projects/issues)
 - Convert your tool to run in [TOAD Containers](/Automation/TOAD/README.md) using [Remote Z Toolset](/Automation/remoteZtoolset/README.md)
 - If the SE is the best place to run your tool, contribute them to a package to reach a wider audience
    - [EST Tools](/Automation/SE_Tools/EST_Tools/README.md) is best for intricate tools that have multiple parts or create output files and rely on running within a directory.
    - [BUP Tools](/Automation/SE_Tools/BUPTools/README.md) is a good choice if your tool is a standalone script that is path agnostic.
 - Instrument the tool to call [SATURN](/Automation/SATURN/README.md) and see how much use your tool gets!!
## SE Tool Packages

### BUP Tools

Bring UP Tools, better known as BUPTOOLs is a community maintained collection of scripts.  They are specialized to help in the early stages of system bring up, but have many useful purposes in later stages of development and test. BUPTools often call lower level tools with meaningful intention for user convenience, the resulting function will help you query system conditions or apply changes to low level components.

Github Repo: [buptools](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/buptools)

Contact: Daniela Yaniv

User Guide: [BUPTools](/Automation/SE_Tools/BUPTools/README.md)

### ECMDs

E Commands, aka ecmds, are low level tools that talk to the hardware.  They can surface system status information or conduct powerful yet dangerous changes to low level components so should be used with caution.  The tools are available in CLI form, all prefixed with `zse`.  It is also possible to call them directly with Python and Perl classes.

User Guide: [ECMDs](/Automation/SE_Tools/ECMDs/README.md)

Slack Channel: [#ecmd](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C560YSM1S)

### EST Tools

est_tools is a set of scripts developed to assist with EST Specific Workflows. Popular legacy tools include myformat, error_log_viewer, and REIT, a suite of Recovery Error Inject Tools.

User Guide: [EST_Tools](/Automation/SE_Tools/EST_Tools/README.md)

Github Repo: [EST Tools](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/EST_Tools)

Contact: Schayne Bellrose or Chris Hutton

usage: i390-trigger-fod [-h] [-v]

Fetch a new FOD record and install it on the CEC.

The command carries no data. Instead i390 will fetch the FOD file data/cec_configuration_data/fod.json.
The features will be installed on the CEC and will replace the existing FOD record, i.e. for proper functioning
it must be ensured that this file is present.
Features which are new will be installed, i.e. the according 'install' action will be triggered, if the feature is known to i390.
Features which are meant to be kept must be part of the new FOD record, i.e. they will be re-installed.
Features which are re-installed with unchanged data will not trigger any action, else they will also trigger the 'install' action.
Features which are no longer part of the new FOD record are erased and will trigger the 'erase' action.

On completion i390 sends an answer service word with a 32 bit return code.

# SKLM Log Cleanup

[Github Repo](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/sklm-log-cleanup)

[Github Issues](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/sklm-log-cleanup/issues)

## Usage:

This is a specialized tool which helps avoid full disk situations on ISKLMs running on s390 linux LPARs.  This is necessary because ECKD based linux is usually installed on a disk with relatively low capacity and the ISKLM Log files can grow quite large especially if the application is in debug mode.

## Setup and Invocation:

The script must be downloaded off github and transferred to the linux partition.

:::tip
you can use scp to transfer the file to an SKLM Server
:::

### Required:

example:
```bash
./log-cleanup.sh -c 50
```

* -c <storage_usage_percentage_cap>: The limit on storage usage percentage for the monitored directory

### Optional:

* -a <archive_dir>: Name of the logs zip file ( default="/tmp/log_archive" )
* -d <dir_to_monitor>: Name of the directory to be monitored ( default="/" )
* -o <outcome_value>: Value to check for outcome setting in SKLM config ( default="failure" )
* -t <types_value>: Value to check for types setting in SKLM config ( default="all" )

## Cronjob Config Example:

Proactively running the script to avoid a full disk is unlikely. There are much higher chances of success if you set it up in the crontab to be run periodically.

### Run Daily at Midnight and Write Output to Log File:

`crontab -e`
```text
* 0 0 * * * /path/to/script/log-cleanup.sh -c <storage_usage_percentage_cap> > /path/to/log/file
```

# STELA
System Test Error Log Analysis, better known as STELA is a tool which constantly backs up data from the systems around the lab.  The data is analyzed for errors and anomalies which might be harder to spot the significance of from the view of a singular system or defect.

STELA is the home of [JupOnDemand](/EngineeringManagement/EWM/JOD2.md)

Other applications which need this data are encouraged to get it from STELA rather than the systems themselves.  This is done over APIs and is made easy with out [STELA Software Development Kit](./STELA-SDK.md)

STELA Also contains the [CARTES](/Automation/CARTES/README.md) Front End, which reflects all passive connections constituting the Storage Area Network.

STELA can be accessed [here](https://prod.stela.dal.app.cirrus.ibm.com/)!

# Python SDK for STELA
A Software Development Kit or SDK is used to simplify interaction with a more complicated API set. This SDK for STELA APIs can be imported into python scripts, allowing you to gain access to some of STELA's data and help automate or guide input arguments.

## STELA-API Documentation
Here's a link to some of the STELA API [documentation](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/stela/zlab-api)

The documentation outlines supported API verbs and the data labels you are able to request using each of them. `curl` command examples are provided to individually exploit each supported API. Bottom line commands are not an efficient way to utilize the API's at scale, the STELA SDK is designed to ease the entrance and aid the scalability.

## Setting up the STELA SDK
Begin by downloading the zip or cloning [the github repo](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/STELA-SDK)

Once the code is in a desired location, Execute the following in the command line/terminal

pip install .

This will allow you to import STELASDK in python scripts that are running from any directory on this workstation.

The currently supported API queries in the SDK are enumerate, unregistered, lifelines, startstate, stopstate, fetch, checkcollection, enablecollection, disablecollection, prepare, and create.

## Using the STELA SDK
The STELA SDK is not meant to provide ready-to-go scripts to call stela API. Instead it is a module that you can import once installed.

`test.py` shows how to call some basic funtions, the code flow is shown below

1. You can call these APIs once installed by first importing different categories of API from STELASDK, for example,

from STELASDK import lifelines, datacollection, addingsystems, searchsystems, systemstate

Now you can write some basic python code to query STELA's records.

2. You must first gather your username and password, do so by creating an object for credentials

credentials = credentials.credentials()

3. You can call the credentials funtion with this code, once its called you just need to pass it into all other functions

userpass = credentials.getuserpass()

4. You must make a class for the category you wish to call such as:

searchsystems = searchsystems.searchsystems()

5. Now you can begin using the funcions as you see fit! All of the functions take in a dictionary as a parameter and reequire your w3 credentials to run.

searchsystems.enumerate({"name": "a40"})

refer to the stela API to find the data labels you need to query

Open a github issue [here[](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/STELA-SDK/issues)

# Migration to OneCloud

This is to detail the transition process from Fyre to the OneCloud environment. The general process is:

1. Preparation
2. Spinup
3. Transfer
4. Bringdown

## Preparation

Prior to planned migration, all VMs should be prepared with the correct environment.

### All VMs

Create the `cicd` and `cluster` directories. As root:
`mkdir -p /root/cicd/cluster`

Install `docker` and `docker-compose`. As root:
`apt install docker.io docker-compose`
Note: You may be asked to restart some services. You can say "OK" for the recommendations.

### Database VMs

Note: Database VMs include the Arbiter VMs.

Grab the docker-compose yaml and startup script for the DB you are replicating. The files are located at `/root/cicd/cluster/`. Once you have that file, place it in the new DB VM at the same location.

### Web VMs

The Web VM will need `machine_shift_web` pulled from GitHub. As root:
```
cd /root/cicd
git clone git@github.ibm.com:systemz/machine_shift_web.git
```

### API VM

Get the FTP api code. A copy can be found at `schedulemon-dev.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:/root/cicd/cluster/FTP-master/FTP-copy.tar`

Make sure that the python version used in `GithubStateService/Dockerfile` is `3.9.16`

Untar `FTP-copy` in `/root/cicd/cluster/`
## Spinup

### DB VMs

Note: Database VMs include the Arbiter VMs.

All done as root:
`cd /cicd/cluster`
`./start_dbrs.sh`

### API VM

All done as root:
`cd /cicd/cluster/FTP-Master`
`docker-compose -d`

Note: If this fails, you may not be in the right directory. Make sure you see something like this when you run `ls`:
```
FTP-master# ls
Docs  Elasticsearch  FTPService  GithubStateService  README.md  client-app  docker-compose.yml  ftp.code-workspace  mynginx
```
## Transfer

### Bring down Website

In schedulemon.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com as root:
```
cd /root/cicd/cluster
docker-compose -f webP01.yaml -f webP02.yaml -f nginx11_main.yaml -f nginx11_local.yaml down
```

### Update the Website info

You will need to update various locations to make sure the services all now know the new locations. The follwing files will need updating:

`/root/cluster/webP01` and `/root/cluster/webP02`: `GHE_API_URL_ROOT` will need to be updated to the new URL/IP for the API (FTP-master). `MONGO_URL` will need the new mongoDB IP addresses. You do not need to add the Arbiter addresses. Syntax is `mongodb://<hostname1>:<port>,<hostname2>:<port>,<hostnameN>:<port>/?replicaSet=rs&w=1`. You can have several comma-separated host:ports but `/?replicaSet=rs&w=1` is required.
### Bring down old Arbiters in Replica

metadata.section_heading: Bring down old Arbiters in Replica

content:
#### On Arbiter VMs

In the Arbiter DBs as root, bring down the Arbiters being decommissioned:
```
cd /root/cicd/cluster
docker-compose -f dbrs.yaml down
```

#### On Primary DB VM

On the Primary DB VM as root, remove the old arbiters as members of the set:
```
docker exec -it <mongoDB_container_name> bash
mongo
rs.remove("<mongoDBArbiter_IP:port")
```

### Add new DBs to Replica

While still logged into the Primary DB:
`rs.add("<mongoDB_IP:port>")`
Do this for both new hosts. Make sure to use the IP.
### Bring down old DBs in Replica

metadata.section_heading: Bring down old DBs in Replica

content:
#### On the DB VMs

In the DBs as root, bring down the DBs being decommissioned:
```
cd /root/cicd/cluster
docker-compose -f dbrs.yaml down
```

#### On Primary DB VM

On the Primary DB VM as root, remove the old arbiters as members of the set:
```
docker exec -it <mongoDB_container_name> bash
mongo
rs.remove("<mongoDB_IP:port")
```

### Add new Arbiters to Replica

While still logged into the Primary DB:
`rs.addArb("<mongoDBArbiter_IP:port>")`
Do this for the three new hosts. Make sure to use the IP.

### Bring up the Website

Back on schedulemon.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com as root:
```
cd /root/cicd/cluster
./start_webP01.sh
./start_webP02.sh
./nginx11_main_curr_start.sh
./nginx11_local_start.sh
```

## Bringdown

Once Transfer is complete, you are safe to shutdown and decommission the Fyre VMs.

# TOAD Administration

This section contains administrative documentation and procedures for maintaining and managing the TOAD (Test Operations Automation Dashboard) infrastructure. It really belongs in the docs folder inside the TOAD repository, but it's currently located here due to the way!
## Contents

### Infrastructure Components

- [Ansible](./ansible/) - Ansible playbooks and automation for TOAD deployment and configuration
- [API](./api/) - API server management and container operations
- [Blades](./blades/) - Blade server configuration and maintenance procedures
- [Database](./database/) - Database administration and maintenance
- [Podman Image](./podman-image/) - Container image management and updates

### Pipeline Management

- [Package Build Pipeline](./package-build-pipeline/) - Automated package building and testing
- [Package Deployment Pipeline](./package-deployment-pipeline/) - Package deployment automation

## Overview

These administrative resources are intended for TOAD system administrators and maintainers. Each subdirectory contains specific procedures, scripts, and documentation for managing different aspects of the TOAD infrastructure.

For general TOAD usage information, see the [main TOAD documentation](../).

# TOAD ansible Maintnenance

In an effort to easily maintain our collection of TOAD blades and containers, we have created the repo [`TOAD-playbooks`](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/TOAD-playbooks). `TOAD-playbooks` maintains our environment using a series of ansible plays.

## Management Environment and ansible venv

We manage our TOAD environment through the `nova-dev` server:

``` ssh-config
Host nova-dev
	HostName 9.114.114.192
	User toad-manager
	IdentitiesOnly yes
```

To have an up-to-date ansible framework, we leverage the Python installation of ansible in a virtual environment. You can access the environment with:

``` shell
source /home/toad-manager/ansible-venv/bin/activate
```

The `TOAD-playbooks` repo is located at `/home/toad-manager/TOAD-playbooks/`

## `generate_hosts.py`

This python script is your map to running maintenance and deployments in TOAD. This will create an ansible inventory that lists all the blades and current containers in the environment.

This script is located in the root of the `TOAD-playbooks` repo and located on `nova-dev` at `/home/toad-manager/TOAD-playbooks/generate_hosts.py`. With the virtual environment, you can run this script with `./generate_hosts.py` and it will output an inventory file titled `hosts` in your current working directory. This list is generated by accessing the TOAD api and finding a list of all blades and containers. For more information about the API, be sure to check [our documentation](../api/README.md).

The file will have a line that you will need to modify in the `[all:vars]` section, it should look like the following:

``` ini
[all:vars]
ansible_connection=ssh
ansible_password=<password>
```

The `ansible_password` line will need to be modified so that `<password>` matches the password for your targets. No ansible plays will work until this is done!

## Playbooks

There is a collection of playbooks that either serve an ongoing process or allow for simple one-off fixes/random maintenance jobs. All playbooks are found in `nova-dev` at `/home/toad-manager/TOAD-playbooks/playbooks/`. Below is a description of each play and how to use them.

### `add-eit-file.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/add-eit-file.yml
```

This play fixes an issue in legacy containers that do not have the `Execute in Terminal` desktop file.

#### Setup

You will need to point to the location of the eit desktop file in `nova-dev`. This is located in `/home/toad-manager/TOAD/essentials/`.

``` yaml
- name: Add Execute in Terminal Desktop File
  hosts: containers
  become: yes
  vars:
    password: passw0rd
    path_to_eit_file: <path_to_file>/eit.desktop
    toad_desktop_path: /home/tester/Desktop/

```

You will need to replace `<path_to_file>` with the location.

### `copy-tool-interactive.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/copy-tool-interactive.yml
```

This play is an interactive prompt that will allow administrators to deploy any named tools into the `TOAD-dist` directory. When prompted, you will be asked to give the toolname and the tool directory. Afterwards, this will go to each TOAD blade and add the specified tool to each blade.

If you wish to only send this to tool to a single blade, you always have the option to modify your hosts file prior to running `ansible-playbook`!

### `copy-tool.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook playbooks/copy-tool.yml --extra-vars "toolname=<absolute path of toolname> base_toolname=<just the name of the file you wish to copy basename of toolname)>" -i hosts
```

This is the non-interactive or scriptable version of the above tool. The codeblock shows that you effectively give the absolute path for the tool as well as the toolname itself and it will perform the same operations as above.

### `deploy-bash-profile.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/deploy-bash-profile.yml
```

This will deploy an instance of the bash profile found in your current working directory. There is an instance of a bash profile found in `/home/toad-manager/TOAD/essentials/.bash_profile`

### `deploy-file.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/deploy-file.yml
```

:::note
This is the recommended approach to sending data to the containers, as it leverages the use of the TOAD-MGMT mount point. This approach reduces the number of file transfers.
:::

This will deploy a file in all of the TOAD containers using a staged process of first deploying the source file into the TOAD-MGMT directory in the blades and seting permissions to `0777`. Then, it will take the file from there and place it in the target path in the containers, making sure the tester user can use said file. Afterwards, it will confirm the file is placed in the containers. If successful, it will remove the file from the blades, to clean up the intermediate step.

#### Setup

You will need to setup two variables found in the `vars` section:

``` yaml
  vars:
    blade_mgmt: /home/toad/TOAD-MGMT/
    container_mgmt: /home/tester/TOAD-MGMT/
    source_file: <file_name>
    source_path: "{{ playbook_dir }}{{ source_file }}"
    target_path: <target_path>

```

- `<file_name>`: This is the file you will be placing. Note that `playbook_dir` points to the underlying playbook directory (aka: `/home/TOAD-playbooks/playbooks/`) so it is recommended to place your file there when you run the play.
- `<target_path>`: This is the absolute path for the directory where you wish to place the file in the TOAD container. Be sure to include the trailing `/`!

### `deploy-history-timestamp.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/deploy-history-timestamp.yml
```

This play fixes an issue in legacy containers where the `history` command does not show a timestamp. It goes to all existing containers and adds `HISTTIMEFORMAT="%F %T "` to `.bashrc` if the line is not found.

### `direct-deploy-file.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/direct-deploy-file.yml
```

:::note
It is recommended to not use this approach to send files to the containers as this approach is being deprecated! Please reference [`deploy=file.yml`](#deployfileyml) for the correct approach!
:::

This is a slimmed down version of `deploy-file.yml`. It performs the same result, but it does not have the intermediate blade step, this also does not `chmod` the file.

#### Setup

This has the same exact setup as seen in [`deploy-file.yml`](#setup-1).

### `image-prune-cron.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/ansible-prune-cron.yml
```

This play creates a cron in all known TOAD blades that will run `/usr/bin/podman image prune -f`. Since all images on the blades should be the TOAD images, it will only remove unused images.

### `run-checker.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/run-checker.yml
```

This play runs the `tool-checker.py` script with the notification flag. For more information on `tool-checker.py`, be sure to check out [the documentation](/Automation/TOAD/how-to-maintain/toad-mgmt/#tool-checker).

`run-checker.yml` is run automatically every day at 12AM EST. Below is the cronjob on `nova-dev`:

``` shell
0 0 * * * cd /home/toad-manager/TOAD-playbooks && ./generate_hosts.py && /home/toad-manager/ansible-venv/bin/ansible-playbook -i hosts --extra-vars "password=passw0rd ansible_password=passw0rd" playbooks/run-checker.yml && rm /home/toad-manager/TOAD-playbooks/hosts
```

The cron goes into `/home/toad-manager/TOAD-playbooks`, generates a hosts file, runs `run-checker.yml` and then deletes the hosts file once done.

### `set-firefox-homepage.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/set-firefox-homepage.yml
```

This play sets the homepage for Firefox on all containers to the EST-User-Guide.

### `update-browser-tabs.yml`

This play will update the favicon for TOAD in the noVNC tab. We mostly ran this to update all older containers that did not have the icon, but this could be used if the icon changes in the future.

#### Setup

You will need to modify one variable:

``` yaml
  vars:
    noVNC_path: "/opt/noVNC/"
    ui_js_path: "{{ noVNC_path }}app/ui.js"
    load_html_path: "/root/vnc.html"
    logo_file_name: <image_name>
```

Set `<image_name>` to be the name of the new icon.

:::note
This does not add the icon file! Make sure to actually place the file in the containers at `/opt/noVNC/app/images/icons`!
:::

### `update-eit-icon.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/update-eit-icon.yml
```

This play updates legacy containers so that the `Execute in Terminal` icon more accurately represents it's purpose.

### `update-git-package.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/update-eit-icon.yml
```

This play will update an automation package using specifically the GitHub deploy key method.

#### Setup

You will need to modify three variables:

``` yaml
  vars:
    tool_name: <tool_name>
    repo_name: <repo_name>
    deploy_key: <deploy_key>
    git_package: "{{ tool_name }}@git+ssh://git@{{ deploy_key }}/systemz/{{ repo_name }}.git"
    expected_version: "<version>"

```

- `<tool_name>`: This is the name of the tool as it is packaged in TOAD. For example ZoweLab is packaged as `zowelab`, so the tool name is `zowelab`.
- `<repo_name>`: This is the name of the repo as it is in GitHub. For example ZoweLab's repository is at [https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation), so the repo name is `zOSAutomation`.
- `<deploy_key>`: This is the deploy key that is used by TOAD to reach private repos in GitHub. These are deployed on all containers and must be present in both `/home/tester/.ssh/` as well as have a config entry in `/home/tester/.ssh/config`. For example ZoweLab's deploy key is titled `ZoweLab`, so the deploy key is `ZoweLab`.

### `update-latest-toad-image.yml`

This play will update the TOAD image on all blades by specifically removing the previous image and tagging the new image ID with `latest`. The automation that handles the image being pushed to all the blades is here (Note: doesn't exist yet!)

#### Setup

You will need to modify two variables:

``` yaml
  vars:
    current_latest: <image_id>
    new_latest: <image_id>
    tag: vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:5000/toad:latest
```

- `current_latest`: This is the ID of the image that is currently being run on all blades for containers (the play will delete this one).
- `new_latest`: This is the ID of the image that will become the new latest.

### `update-package.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/update-package.yml
```

This play will update an automation package using the package tar.gz method.

#### Setup

You will need to modify three variables:

``` yaml
  vars:
    tool_name: <tool_name>
    package_path: <package_path>
    package_file: "{{ result.files|sort(attribute='ctime')|map(attribute='path')|last }}"
    expected_version: "<version>"
```

- `tool_name`: This will be the tool name that appears in the package distribution directory that ends with `.tar.gz`.
- `package_path`: This will be the directory where the package exists. Typically this will be `/home/tester/TOAD-MGMT/dist/`
- `expected_version`: This is the version of the package that should be seen once it is installed.

:::note
You will see there is a strange variable called `package_file`. This is generated in the play by looking for the specified package in the specified directory. It uses the results to grab the package name and run a pip install.
:::

### `update-x3270-version.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/update-x3270-version.yml
```

This is a play that will update and install x3270 to version 4.2ga6. This was done to resolve some issues with the apt installed version of x3270.

### `upgrade-blades.yml`

``` shell
ansible-playbook -i hosts playbooks/upgrade-blades.yml
```

This play will update the installed apt packages on all TOAD blades and let you know if there any that need an additional update afterwards.

## `Applying Code Changes`:
* `NOTE`: Schedule maintenance outage and notify users `BEFORE` proceeding!
1. **SSH** into **nova-dev** VM ( reach out for **SSH** info )
2. **Ensure** `main` branch is checked out and that latest changes have been pulled in **TOAD repository** at `/home/toad-manager/TOAD/`
3. **Navigate** to the **toad-manager directory**:
    ```
    cd /var/www/toad-manager/
    ```
4. **Stop** running process:
    ```
    sudo systemctl stop managecontainers.service
    ```
5. **Copy** `managecontainers.py` from **TOAD repository** over to **toad-manager directory**:
    ```
    cp /home/toad-manager/TOAD/api/managecontainers.py /var/www/toad-manager/
    ```
6. **Start** API process:
    ```
    sudo systemctl start managecontainers.service
    ```
# TOAD Blade Management

## `Get List of Blades`:
1. [Access database](../database/#access-database)
2. **View** records in **blades** table:
    ```
    select * from blades order by id;
    ```

## `TOAD Setup for New Blades`:
1. **Create** `toad` user:
    ```
    adduser toad
    usermod -aG sudo toad
    ```
2. **Switch** to `toad` user:
    ```
    su - toad
    ```
3. **Enable** linger for `toad` user:
    ```
    loginctl enable-linger $USER
    ```
4. **Install** `podman`:
    ```
    sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y podman
    ```
5. **Determine** `podman` socket:
    ```
    echo "${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR##*/}"
    ```
6. **Add** TOAD registry to `/etc/containers/registries.conf`:
    ```
    sudo echo "[[registry]]
    location = "vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:5000"
    insecure = true" >> /etc/containers/registries.conf
    ```
7. **Enable** `podman` socket for user:
    ```
    systemctl --user enable podman.socket
    ```
8. **Start** `podman` service for user:
    ```
    systemctl --user start podman
    ```
9. [Add record to blades table in database](../database/#add-record-to-blades)
10. **Setup** `Prometheus Node Exporter`:
    * `NOTE`: Check [here](https://prometheus.io/download/#node_exporter) for latest install link
    ```
    wget https://github.com/prometheus/node_exporter/releases/download/v1.8.1/node_exporter-1.8.1.linux-amd64.tar.gz
    tar xvfz node_exporter-*.*-amd64.tar.gz
    cd node_exporter-*.*-amd64
    nohup ./node_exporter > node_exporter.log 2>&1 &
    ```
11. **SSH** into **nova-dev** VM as **toad-manager** ( reach out for **SSH** info )
12. **Copy** SSH key to new blade:
    ```
    ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 toad@<new_blade_ip>
    ```
13. **Stop** **Prometheus** instance
    ```
    kill $(pgrep -f prometheus)
    ```
14. **Add** **Node Exporter** instance to list of **Prometheus** targets on **nova-dev VM**:
    ```
    cd /var/www/toad-manager/prometheus-2.52.0.linux-amd64
    vi prometheus.yml
    ```
    * `NOTE`: Append **blade IP** and port **9100** ( e.g. "9.56.197.227:9100" )
15. **Start** **Prometheus** instance:
    ```
    nohup ./prometheus --config.file=./prometheus.yml > prometheus.log 2>&1 &
    ```

# Automation Package Build Pipeline
The `toad-build-pipeline` GitHub app is used to validate code changes based on the standards required for deploying a package into the TOAD environment.
For any GitHub repository configured in the `toad-build-pipeline`, if a pull request is opened, the `TOAD Checks` automated process will run automatically.
This process includes the following steps:
* Verifies version in `TOML` file has been incremented by comparing what is in `main` branch
* Attempts a build of the package under `/var/www/toad-manager/build-pipeline` directory on the `TOAD manager VM`
* Runs `Pylint` for the files that have been changed
* If `unittests` directory is present, runs `pytest` for existing unit tests

## `GitHub App Info`:
[toad-build-pipeline](https://github.ibm.com/organizations/systemz/settings/apps/toad-build-pipeline)

[GitHub Repository](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/TOAD-build-pipeline)

Runs off of `nova-dev VM` as a `systemd service` named `toad-build-pipeline`

# Automation Package Deployment Pipeline
Automation packages are deployed to the TOAD containers via the `/package/build` endpoint of the [TOAD API](../api/README.md).

The GitHub repository for each automation package needs to be configured to use this endpoint as a webhook, which can be done by following these steps:

1. Navigate to the automation package's GitHub repository settings
2. Click `Hooks` from the left sidebar
3. Click `Add webhook`
4. For the `Payload URL`, enter `https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/package/build`
5. For the `Content type`, select `application/json`
6. For `Which events would you like to trigger this webhook?`, select `Let me select individual events`
7. Ensure only the `Pull requests` event is selected
8. Click `Add webhook`

Each GitHub repository also needs to be cloned on the `TOAD manager VM` under the `automation-repos` directory.

Once configured, the package deployment process will be kicked off automatically when changes are merged into the `main` branch.

This process includes the following:

the package deployment process will be kicked off automatically when changes are merged into the `main` branch.

This process includes the following:

1. Fetches the latest version of `main` from the corresponding GitHub repository clone
2. Builds the latest version of the package and stores it under the `automation-package-dist` directory on the `TOAD manager VM`
3. Removes any previous builds of the package from the `automation-package-dist` directory
4. Deploys package build to the [private registry](https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/automation-packages/) ( hosted at `/var/www/toad-manager/automation-packages/` on `TOAD manager VM` via `niginx` config at `/etc/nginx/sites-available/managecontainers` )
5. Deploys package build to the `dist` directory within the `TOAD-MGMT` mount point on all of the `TOAD blades`

## `Update Base Image`:
1. **SSH** into **nova-dev** VM as **toad-manager** ( reach out for **SSH** info )
2. **Pull** latest changes from `main` in **TOAD repository** at `/home/toad-manager/TOAD/`
3. **Build** New Image From **Dockerfile**:
    ```
    podman build -f /home/toad-manager/TOAD/Dockerfile -t toad:v$(grep -Po '^LABEL version="\K[^"]*' /home/toad-manager/TOAD/Dockerfile) --no-cache --squash /home/toad-manager
    ```
4. **Push** New Image to **Image Registry**:
    ```
    podman push toad:v$(grep -Po '^LABEL version="\K[^"]*' /home/toad-manager/TOAD/Dockerfile) vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:5000/toad:latest --tls-verify=false
    ```

## `Using Buildah`:
1. **Create** working container from latest **TOAD** image:
   ```
   ctr=$(buildah from toad:latest)
   ```
2. **Enter** working container:
   ```
   buildah run $ctr bash
   ```
3. **Make** desired changes to image
4. **Exit** working container:
   ```
   exit
   ```
5. **Commit** image:
   ```
   buildah commit $ctr toad:<new_version_number>
   ```
6. **Update** version number in **Dockerfile**
7. **Push** New Image to **Image Registry**:
    ```
    podman push toad:v$(grep -Po '^LABEL version="\K[^"]*' /home/toad-manager/TOAD/Dockerfile) vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:5000/toad:latest --tls-verify=false
    ```

# TOAD

![](./images/ScaleyToad.svg)

## Quick Links * [TOAD Dashboard](https://prod.toad-dashboard.wdc.app.cirrus.ibm.com/dashboard/) * [Slack](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C06JQ8Z8JJ0) * [GitHub Issues](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/TOAD/issues)

## What is the TOAD platform?
`TOAD` (Test Operator Automation Desktop) is the platform for executing test workloads in the `EST lab` and is where `automation tools` designed to augment those workloads are deployed!

`TOAD` allows users to create a fresh, `Ubuntu-based`, desktop environment `on-demand` and share it with other users.

These environments leverage [container technology](https://podman.io/) and are currently hosted on `10 blades` capable of supporting large numbers of `TOAD` containers.

In the past, teams have typically been responsible for obtaining and configuring their own execution environments which leads to silos of capability. These silos ultimately inhibit the advancement of coordinated innovation of the hands on automation tools which prove vital in conducting more workload, tests, and infrastructure management.

:::caution
We are not responsible for interruption of testing that results from `TOAD RAS` or performance deficit!
:::

and infrastructure management.

:::caution
We are not responsible for interruption of testing that results from `TOAD RAS` or performance deficit!
:::

:::note
If you have testing which is particularly important or client intensive, please <u>[contact the team](#contact)</u> who can assist you with installing the `TOAD` deployment dependencies on hardware you will own and maintain.
:::

<details>
<summary>TOAD Overview Diagram</summary>

![](./images/Revolution.png)

</details>

## What are the benefits of TOAD?
`TOAD` aims to provide testers with a common, shareable environment for executing test workflows that automation developers can reliably deploy their tools to.

This helps focus the `EST lab` testing strategy and allows automation developers to deliver better quality tools faster and with more consistent updates.

content: ## How do I access TOAD? Information for accessing `TOAD` can be found [here](./how-to-access/README.md).

## Getting Started With `TOAD`

:::warning
If you update or delete your container via the `TOAD Dashboard`, only data within your `TOAD` container's `mount point` will be recoverable!

Please keep all important data within your `mount point`!

Instructions for identifying your `mount point` can be found [here](./how-to-maintain/README.md#identifying-your-mount-point).

More information on managing your container can be found [here](./how-to-maintain/README.md).
:::

### Get a Container

Read how to **create a container** [here](./how-to-use/dashboard/README.md#creating-a-container).

### Access your Container

The dashboard provides a link directly to the `browser VNC interface`. This is one of a handful of ways to access each container.

You can also connect with `VS Code` or establish an `SSH tunnel` and use your preferred `VNC viewer` to access the desktop.

Read more about **container access methods** [here](./how-to-access/README.md#container).

### What to Do Next

Now that you have your new `TOAD` container you can get started running your workloads and using the [available automation tools](./how-to-maintain/README.md#list-of-available-automation-packages) to augment those workflows.

Further guidance on using TOAD can be found [here](./how-to-use/README.md).

:::tip
For more guides on how to use and make the most of your `TOAD` container, look [here](./how-to-use/container/README.md).
:::

:::tip
If you run into any issues while using your `TOAD` container, please refer to the [Common Issues page](./CommonIssues.md).

If none of those solutions resolve the issue, please reach out via the [Contact](#contact) section below!
:::

#### Adopt

Non-web-based tools can often be difficult to advertise, install, and keep up to date; `TOAD` containers solve many of these problems by providing tools right in the setting where you'll be conducting your tests.

The [remoteZtoolset](../remoteZtoolset/README.md) provides the `TOAD` container an interface into the `SEs`, `HMCs`, and `TKEs` you work with. You will want to add these systems to your `TOAD` container(s) before you get started using more sophisticated tools that will all work effortlessly with the systems you have added.

Instructions on adding systems to your container via `remoteZtoolset` can be found [here](../remoteZtoolset/sshToolHelp.md#adding-systems).

#### Integrate

All the tools delivered in the `TOAD` container are designed to work similarly and are usually capable of working together with minimal effort.

With modular tools referring to system targets in a common format you can start automating sequences and loops of any of these functions to create more autonomous workflows tailored to your exact needs.

This standardized test environment has many benefits to our organization. It is enabling you to rapidly develop tools that will have mobility and modulatory fundamental design values that will push the needle forward for automation.

## Container

:::tip
If you have difficulty finding your container, try the steps listed [here](../how-to-use/dashboard/README.md#searching-for-data).
:::

The sections below detail common methods of accessing your `TOAD` container.
### Credentials The credentials for accessing each container are as follows: * User: `tester` * Password: `passw0rd`

### Browser VNC Interface The `browser VNC interface` is great for running 3270 consoles, terminals to drive workload, and so on. But it can be difficult to perform certain tasks in this setting which is why you should learn all the ways to access your `TOAD` container to get the most out of it. To access this interface, find your container on the [dashboard](#dashboard) and click the `Container URL` under the `URL` column. :::tip Consider bookmarking this page for accessing your container directly in the the future! ::: :::tip If you observe that the desktop does not properly fit in your browser window, follow the steps [here](../CommonIssues.md#browser-access-resolution). :::

### Connect Using VS Code `Visual Studio Code` is capable of establishing and maintaining an SSH connection to your `TOAD` container. Doing so will provide an easy way to manipulate files on the host, transfer files to and from the host, edit files live on the host, and even run scripts directly in the host terminal. Follow the steps below for setup: 1. Find your container on the dashboard :::tip Steps can be found [here](../how-to-use/dashboard/README.md#searching-for-data). ::: 2. Click the name of your container under the `Name` column. 3. At the bottom of the [Container Management panel](../how-to-maintain/README.md#container-management-panel), copy the contents of the `VS Code Host Config` 4. Click the `Open a Remote Window` button in the bottom left corner. ![](../images/container-connect-vscode-2.png)
5. Prompts should appear at the top of `VS Code` to guide you through the connection process. - If this is your first time setting up SSH in VS Code, select the `SSH` option. ( `VS Code` you will now install the `Remote-SSH plugin` ) - Otherwise, select the option to `Connect to Host…`. ![](../images/container-connect-vscode-3.png)

now install the `Remote-SSH plugin` ) - Otherwise, select the option to `Connect to Host…`. ![](../images/container-connect-vscode-3.png)
6. Click `Configure SSH Hosts…`.
7. Select your `SSH config` file ![](../images/container-connect-vscode-6.png)
8. Paste the `VS Code Host Config` you copied into the `SSH config file` and save.
7. Connect to your container ![](../images/container-connect-vscode-8.png) - Hover over the entry in the `Remote Explorer` panel then click on either `Connect in Current Window` or `Connect in New Window`.

### VNC with SSH Tunnel You can access the desktop environment with your preferred `VNC viewer` if you establish an `SSH tunnel` similarly to how you can `VNC` into an `SE`. Native `VNC` will improve copy/paste experience and prevent the incidental character floods when a keyboard shortcut is used naively. You may experience improved resolution or scalability as well! Click the name of your container under the `Name` column. 3. At the bottom of the [Container Management panel](../how-to-maintain/README.md#container-management-panel), copy the contents of the `SSH Tunnel Command`. 4. In a terminal, paste the copied contents and execute. 5. Open a `VNC` session with your preferred `VNC viewer` by supplying the `loopback port` from the previous command: :::note For each `VNC` session, you will need to have a separate `SSH tunnel` open, if you have multiple `TOAD` containers for example. :::

# How to Contribute

For guides on how to contribute to `TOAD`, refer to the [As a Developer](../how-to-contribute/developers/README.md) section.

# Automation Tool Deployment Pipeline
The TOAD build pipeline is an automated CI/CD process that ensures supported TOAD automation tools can be successfully built and deployed in a pip installable format.

For each automation tool that has been officially added to the TOAD environment and formatted as a Python TOML package, an automated build process will be kicked off when pull requests are opened or updated. This build process will verify that the package can be built based on the changes being committed in the pull request. These checks can also be customized to run additional checks for that specific tool. ( e.g. Unit tests )

The status of the build process will be visible under the Checks tab of the pull request. If a failure occurs, the cause of that failure will be shown and should be corrected by a developer of that tool before merging. Otherwise the latest version of the tool will be deployed to the TOAD environment. If the process succeeds, the built package filename will be displayed.

:::note
All changes should include a change to the version in the TOML file to reflect the nature of the changes!
:::

The TOAD environment is based on `Ubuntu`, so your tool will need to be `Linux compatible`!
:::

You can refer to this [template repo](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/automation-tool-template) as an example.

### Add Source Code to Repository

:::note
There are several ways to interact with GitHub repositories once created.
You should find the method that best suits your needs.

Here are some of the common options:
* [command line interface](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/getting-started-with-git/set-up-git)

* [GitHub Desktop](https://desktop.github.com/download/)

* [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/sourcecontrol/overview)

The process below makes use of the `git CLI`.
:::

To make changes to your source code, follow this process:
1. First make sure you have an `SSH key` configured for your development environment on your GitHub profile, [instructions here](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/generating-a-new-ssh-key-and-adding-it-to-the-ssh-agent)

2. Open a terminal in your development environment and navigate to the directory that you want your repository to be cloned.

3. Clone your repository
    ```
    git clone git@github.ibm.com:systemz/<repository_name>.git

2. Try building a distribution package

3. Verify no errors occur, resolve all errors or reach out via the [Slack channel](../../README.md#slack)

4. Try `pip` installing your tool
    ```
    pip install dist/*

## Deploy Development Build to Users

There are many ways to do this, but this guide will focus on two.

### Transfer to TOAD Containers

You can transfer the development build directly one or more individual `TOAD` containers or even a team's mount point, which is accessible to any container created under that team.

For transferring to individual containers home directory, run this command:
```
scp -P <container_SSH_port> ./dist/<development_build> tester@<container_blade_IP>:~/
```

For transferring to a team's mount point, run this command:
```
scp -P <container_SSH_port> ./dist/<development_build> tester@<container_blade_IP>:<mount_point_path>
```

:::note
Follow [this guide](../../how-to-maintain/README.md#identifying-your-mount-point) for determining a the team mount point for a container.
:::

### Send Via Slack

You can simply send the development build to a user, group of users or a channel by uploading the build package under the `dist` directory in your tool's repository.
The user(s) can then install the development build in their desired environment(s).

:::note
If the user is NOT installing in a `TOAD container`, they must ensure they have `Python 3` and `pip` installed in that environment.
:::

## Have User(s) Install Development Build and Test

Now that your tool user(s) have access to your development build in their environment, they should execute the following command to install:
```
pip install <path_to_development_build>
```

Your tool user(s) will now be able to test your development build dependent on what the build is addressing ( bug fix, new feature, etc. ).
