# Structure Python for a TOAD Package

Author: Eric Reid
Date: 04/29/2024
Updated 05/01/2024

metadata.section_heading: Structure Python for a TOAD Package

content:
## Introduction

The TOAD v2 containers contain some important changes for a Python developer wanting to deploy their package at scale. These instructions are designed to help guide a developer to converting their Python into a package for TOAD v2.

## The TOAD v2 Package Requirements

1. All files that a package needs to read in and log or output need to exist in a directory managed by the tool in the user's home directory (~/), ideally under a directory of the tool's name.
2. If a package needs a subdirectory system inside of their user tool directory, the tool must dynamically create the needed file structure.
3. The Python code must be a full Python package that can do both `pip install` and `pip update`.
4. All functions must be able to be called anywhere inside of the TOAD container by making them shell commands.
5. Package owners must inform the NOVA team of their package's command prefix (i.e. 'rz' for remoteztoolset) to avoid duplication.

## Building a Python Package

There are many guides to building a Python package, this is a quick guide. Make sure you use the more modern pyproject.toml format, as it has better support for requirement (4).

### Structuring your code

The easiest structure for your code library is:

MyTool/
    |
    ->    pyproject.toml
    ->    src/
        ->    mytool1/
        ->    mytool2/

Obviously the folder names can change. This structure allows for a clean single package installation for a lot of tooling. There are other options, refer to Python Package documentation [here](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/overview/)

### Build a pyproject.toml

The pyproject.toml file tells the Python package manager, `pip` how to install your package.  It has a few key sections:

#### build-system
This configures what package builder `pip` will use, I recommended the default setuptools.

[build-system]
    requires = ["setuptools",
                "setuptools-scm"] #SCM is for packages, see:
                # https://stackoverflow.com/questions/69647590/specifying-package-data-in-pyproject-toml
    build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

#### project

This includes a lot of project metadata, such as version, authors, and dependencies.  See the example below:

[project]
    name = "ZoweLab"
    version = "3.0.0"
    authors = [
        {name = "Eric Reid", email = "eric.reid@ibm.com"},
        {name = "Savannah Portilla", email = "Savannah.Portilla@ibm.com"},
        {name = "Chris Hutton", email = "Christopher.Hutton1@ibm.com"}
    ]
    description = "Zowe tools for the Z Test Floor lab"
    readme = "README.md"
    requires-python = ">=3.6"
    classifiers = [
        "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
        "Operating SYstem :: OS Independent"
    ]
    dependencies = [
        'pandas',
        'numpy',
        'xmltodict',
        'argparse_prompt',
        'pyyaml',
        'progress',
        'colorlog',
        'inputimeout',
        'zowe-core-for-zowe-sdk',
        'zowe-zos-console-for-zowe-sdk',
        'zowe-zos-files-for-zowe-sdk',
        'zowe-zos-jobs-for-zowe-sdk',
        'zowe-zos-tso-for-zowe-sdk',
        'zowe-zosmf-for-zowe-sdk'
    ]

#### project.urls
This provides metadata about useful links for the package, like the Github repo:

[project.urls]
    Homepage = "https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation"
    Issues = "https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/issues"

#### project.scripts
This tells `pip` to build shell command aliases to run particular components of your package. Each line is in the format mycommand = "upperdirectory.lowerdirectory.scriptfilename:method". This points to a method inside of your code base. It is not recommended that the method is part of a class.

Example:

[project.scripts]
    zwe = "ZoweHelperScripts.zowe_main:main"
    zwe_dittokiller = "ZoweLab.DittoKiller.dittokiller:main"
    # HCD
    zwe_hcd_activateSWandHW = "ZoweLab.HCD_Dynamic.activateSWandHW:main"

### Github

Make sure your Python package is in the [systemz Github](https://github.ibm.com/systemz).

## Working with Files

These are some tips and tricks for working in the TOAD file system in your Python code.

### Creating a File Structure

The easiest thing to do is to have your code mirror the directory structure of the repository itself. That allows each tool to "find itself" in the users' home directories and expect files and output files there with  minimal effort. It also more easily allows for adopting new tools, they can create a new directory in `MyTools/src/` and work with all their files their automatically.

This code builds a mirror file system in the users' home directory, without deleting any files that exist in that directory structure as it stands:

import os
    from pathlib import Path
    import shutil

def build_file_systems():
        home = Path.home() # home directory
        source = Path(os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))).parent.parent  #add parents to get the top directory of your package
        dest = home
        shutil.copytree(source,dest,ignore = shutil.ignore_patterns('*.*')\
                        ,dirs_exist_ok=True)
        return home

st = home
        shutil.copytree(source,dest,ignore = shutil.ignore_patterns('*.*')\
                        ,dirs_exist_ok=True)
        return home

I recommend that the users' home directory is set to a variable that can be referenced later. In ZoweLab, as an example, the core ZoweLab Helper class has the following set to a class variable during the class initialization:

class Zowehelper():
        def __init__(self,toolpath = None):
            '''
            Provide a toolpath at initialization to organize output files and logs
            '''
            self.get_sysplexfile()
            self.home = self.build_file_systems() / 'ZoweLab' # prepare file systems, ZoweLab v3.3.0
            if toolpath is not None:
                self.toolpath = self.home / toolpath
            else:
                self.toolpath = self.home # we'll default to this and not like it
            self.wait_count = 0

### Working with files in Tools

Tools can pass in their owning directory, and automatically glue that into the home path of the overall package. This enables tools to use the `Zowehelper.toolpath` variable to use files in that tools file directory. An example from zOSDittoKiller:

import os
    from pathlib import PurePath

tool_directory = PurePath(os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))).name  # get the directory, DittoKiller, that it is run from.
    zwe_help = Zowehelper(tool_directory)
    with open(zwe_helper.toolpath / 'dittorunfiles' / sys.argv[1],encoding='utf-8') as ditto_file:
        interpeted_ditto = list(yaml.safe_load_all(ditto_file))

A tool can make a new directory in a similar way:

tool_directory = PurePath(os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))).name
    zwe_help = Zowehelper(tool_directory)
    zowe_connection = zwe_help.make_connection(args.sysplex)

if not os.path.exists(zwe_help.toolpath / "IODF_Compare_Outputs"):
        os.mkdir(zwe_help.toolpath / "IODF_Compare_Outputs")
        os.chmod(zwe_help.toolpath / "IODF_Compare_Outputs",755)
# How to Maintain

## Container Management Panel

Each container has a separate view that displays further details and controls. This is accessible by clicking on the `name` of the container on the dashboard.

The available controls are listed below:

* Start

* This starts the container if it is in an exited state

* Restart

* This restarts the container

* Stop

* This stops the container if it is in a running state

* Update

* This brings your container to the latest image version, which gives you a fresh slate.

:::warning
    This is a `disruptive process` that takes about 5 minutes to complete!! Please ensure that all of your workloads have completed before proceeding!
    :::

:::warning
    All data stored outside of the mount point will be lost!
    Refer to the guide on identifying your mount point [here](#identifying-your-mount-point).
    :::

* Delete

* This will delete the container permanently.

:::warning
    All data stored outside of the mount point will be lost!

Refer to the guide on identifying your mount point [here](#identifying-your-mount-point).
    :::

:::note
    Only the user that created the container is permitted to delete it.
    :::

## Container Management Tools

Within the container, there is a `TOAD-MGMT` directory containing various tools that help with maintaining your container.

More details can be found [here](./toad-mgmt/README.md).

## Identifying Your Mount Point

Within your container, you can run the following command to identify the `mount point`:
```
echo $TOAD_MP
```

From the dashboard, you can also find your`mount point` under the `Mounts` column.

## Manage Automation Tool Packages

:::caution
Installing the latest version of a tool while a process is still running for that tool is known to cause abnormalities.

It is recommended to wait until automated processes are complete before updating tools.
:::

The automation packages within `TOAD` have the latest version automatically deployed to all of the containers, under the `~/TOAD-MGMT/dist/` directory, so that you may easily install them individually or by running the `upgrade-tools` script when you're ready to update them.

### Automated Tool Upgrade

There is a script within the `TOAD-MGMT` directory that assists with keeping all of the automation packages up-to-date. View [this guide](./toad-mgmt/README.md#upgrade-tools) to learn more.

### Manually Maintain Packages

Below is a list of steps of how to manage the automation packages via `pip` inside `TOAD`:

:::note
If you have issues when any of the commands, make sure you check the `~/TOAD-MGMT/dist/` directory for how the package is named.

If the issue persists, please reach out via the [Slack channel](../../../README.md#slack)!
:::

-   Installing

:::note
    There is a new method for installing automation tools packages. This method leverages our new `self-hosted registry`.
    This install method also works outside of `TOAD` once you've [configured registry in pip](#configure-pip-for-our-self-hosted-registry).
    Below you will find instructions for installing from the new registry and the legacy method.
    :::

`New Method`:

```
    pip install -U <package_name>
    ```
    -   `Example`:
        ```
        pip install -U remoteztoolset
        ```

:::note
    Specifying the registry index ensures you're getting the correct tool version.
    :::

`Legacy Method`:

```
    pip install ~/TOAD-MGMT/dist/<package_name>*
    ```
    -   `Example`:
        ```
        pip install ~/TOAD-MGMT/dist/remoteztoolset*
        ```

-   Uninstalling

AD-MGMT/dist/<package_name>*
    ```
    -   `Example`:
        ```
        pip install ~/TOAD-MGMT/dist/remoteztoolset*
        ```

-   Uninstalling

```
    pip uninstall <package_name>
    ```
    -   `Example`:
        ```
        pip uninstall remoteztoolset
        ```

If you have followed the [GitHub Setup guide](../how-to-use/container/README.md#github-setup), you can use the following commands to install specific versions directly from the repository.

:::note
This is usually done when working with tool developers to test new features/fixes before official release.
:::

-   Installing From a Branch

```
    pip install <package_name>@git+ssh://git@<git_repo_path>@<branch_name>
    ```
    -   `Example`:
        ```
        pip install remoteztoolset@git+ssh://git@github.ibm.com/systemz/remoteZtoolset.git@1.1.0
        ```

# TOAD-MGMT

Within the `TOAD` containers there is a directory, `/home/tester/TOAD-MGMT/`, which holds various tools that assist in maintaining them. View the following to learn more about each tool.

## fetch-deploy-keys

This script fetches the latest deploy keys from the `TOAD Management server` and makes sure they are added to the SSH agent within your container.

## install-extensions

This script installs the `VS Code` extensions provided with every `TOAD` container, which are stored in `/home/tester/extensions/`.

1. Setup a [connection in VS Code](../../how-to-access/README.md#connect-using-vs-code) for your container

2. After connecting via `VS Code`, navigate to the `Extensions` tab

3. Open a terminal within `VS Code`

4. Run the following script to install the default extensions
    ```
    ~/TOAD-MGMT/install-extensions.sh
    ```

5. You will then see the installed extensions under the `SSH Installed` list

## upgrade-tools

:::caution
Installing the latest version of a tool while a process is still running for that tool is known to cause abnormalities.

It is recommended to wait until automated processes are complete before updating tools.
:::

This script will ensure that `ALL` automation packages are on the latest version.

Manual upgrades for individual tools are also possible, for which more information can be found [here](../../how-to-maintain/README.md#manually-maintain-packages).

## tool-checker

This script will check the status of your installed tools and compares them to currently available tools in `~/TOAD-MGMT/dist`. There are three flags:

- `-o`: This sets the output for the package logs. This log details when the script is run and the output of the results. By default, the logs for output are placed in `~/package.log` if this flag is not set.
 - `-v`: This enables the verbose option. This will change the log output to give detailed info about all packages installed instead of just showing what packages are out of date.
 - `-n`: This will send a notification if there are packages out of date. The notification is sent using the package `notify-send`.

:::note
**Developer tip**: Administrators may notice that there is a declaration of `DISPLAY=99.0` at the beginning of the notification call. This is the default display identifier for all TOAD containers. Administrators can leverage this for other application development in the future.

# How to Use

Refer to the following sections on how to use the [TOAD dashboard](./dashboard/README.md) and [TOAD containers](./container/README.md).

## TOAD Best Practices

:::warning
While using TOAD, keep in mind that you are sharing resources with other developers on each respective TOAD server. There are several tools and applications that are available on our containers that we want users to leverage, but we must warn users that you should *stop any processes that you are not utilizing*. The following processes have been found to cause trouble for users in TOAD:

- Mozilla Firefox: This web browser tends to use up memory even while idle. We recommend that if you are using TOAD with Firefox, restrict your usage to actions with tools in TOAD that require Firefox. As an example, you may need to acces the EST-User-Guide. After you're done with your task, please make sure to close your Firefox session!
- IBM Bob/VSCode: We do not recommend installing these applications into TOAD at this time.
:::

### Common TOAD Cleanup Tasks

As Nova developers, we try to write code that is memory safe and performant. That being said with processes being run on shared resources, there are some times where TOAD will be bogged down by processes. A common cause for this is forking processes that spin up new processes. With this situation, sometimes the parent process will close, but the underlying child processes will still remain. This causes a Memory and CPU utilization issue, especially around Python. Below are some suggestions for handling this.

#### Close any Duplicate Tasks

If you're running multiple sessions that are utilizing the same test case, or maybe have a session that is running idle with no jobs, it's a good idea to close those out.

#### Killing Rogue Processes

You will sometimes have to kill processes that you may not be aware are running. First, to see if there is something wrong, familiarize yourself with the command `top`. This is similar to `Task Manager` for those familiar with Windows. After running this command, you should get a good understanding of what is running on your system. Typically, you will want to look at the columns labelled `%CPU` and `%MEM`. This will be how much CPU and Memory processes on your container are utilizing for the whole server!

If you find some processes taking up a lot of resources, the next thing would be is to check what `COMMAND` is causing this utilization. If the command looks like something you are actively using, then let it stay running. However, if the `COMMAND` looks unfamiliar or it's something you know should have closed by now, then you should kill that process.

To start, you may notice that the process keeps jumping around. To stop this (and close `top`), you can press `q` on the terminal. Then if you note on the left column called `PID`, that is the `Process ID`. We can use this ID to kill the process by typing `kill -9 <PID>`.

erminal. Then if you note on the left column called `PID`, that is the `Process ID`. We can use this ID to kill the process by typing `kill -9 <PID>`.

Sometimes, you may need to kill a group of processes. You can do this with `pkill`. This is done with:

```
pkill -9 "<name of command>"
```
Note: Make sure to keep the name of the command in quotes, as to capture the full output, otherwise it may kill too many processes! The name of the command will be the full string of the command under the `COMMAND` column in the `top` output.

##### If the Process Name is Long

Sometimes, your command may be too long to even see in the `top` command. To fix this, there's a couple of approaches. One is to leverage `ps`. You can do something like so:

```
ps -ef | grep "<partial name of process/process ID>"
```

What this will do is get you all the known processes in a static format. We then pipe the output to grep so we can filter for the info we are looking for. A good start is part of the command or the process ID. For example, if I was looking for something related to `mimic`, I could do:
```
ps -aux | grep "mimic"
```

What I will see next is something that looks like this:

```
tester@OSA_Networking_SAK_Stuff_Plus:~ $ ps -aux | grep mimic
tester   1458145  0.0  0.0   4088  2048 pts/22   S+   21:24   0:00 grep --color=auto mimic
tester   2957953 21.0  0.0  40124 13516 pts/5    R    May22 1532:01 /usr/bin/python3 /home/tester/.local/bin/mimic-session-manager -o Networking/Grayson1/sak-automation/b231-sak-sessions.yml
tester   2960532  0.0  0.0   3156  1920 pts/21   S+   May22   0:06 tail -f Networking/mimic/OSA_Networking_SAK_Stuff_Plus/b231-sak-sessions.log
```

The output is like this:

content:
0.0 3156 1920 pts/21 S+ May22 0:06 tail -f Networking/mimic/OSA_Networking_SAK_Stuff_Plus/b231-sak-sessions.log ``` The output is like this: ``` <%CPU> <%MEM> ``` This output will give you the full command so that you may track and kill the affected process. At that point if the process name is too long, you may get an error from pkill about the length of the command. If that is the case, run the command again but with the `-f` flag: ``` pkill -9 "" ```
For more info on how to use `top`, check out [Boolean World's article](https://www.booleanworld.com/guide-linux-top-command/).
For more info on `ps`, check the [Unix Tutorial article](https://www.unixtutorial.org/commands/ps/).

## Copy/Paste via VNC Browser Interface

You can highlight the desired content and use native copy shortcuts to add it to your local system clipboard.

## GitHub Setup

This guide covers how to setup your `TOAD` container(s) to be able to `clone GitHub repositories` and `other git capabilities`.

:::note
This procedure needs to be followed for each container that needs `git` capability!
:::

### Generate an SSH Key

From a terminal within your TOAD container(s), follow these steps:

1. Run this `ssh-keygen` command, replacing the `example email` with your `w3 email`:
    ```
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
    ```
    * You will be asked to specify the file path and name or use the default

:::note
    Keep note of the file path and name, as you will need to know this for following steps!
    :::

:::caution
    Ensure that your generated keys have the proper permissions!
    Your public key (ending with `.pub`) needs to have the permission of `644`.
    Your private key need to have the permission of `600`.

If you modify this, you will run into unexpected warnings about unprotected key files!
    :::

2. Ensure the `SSH agent` is running with this command:
    ```
    eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
    ```

3. Add the `SSH private key` you just generated to the `SSH agent` with this command:
    ```
    ssh-add path/to/the/private/key/from/step/1
    ```

3. Add the `SSH private key` you just generated to the `SSH agent` with this command:
    ```
    ssh-add path/to/the/private/key/from/step/1
    ```

4. Output the contents if the `SSH public key` you just generated with this command:
    ```
    cat path/to/the/public/key/from/step/1
    ```
    * The public key has the same file path and name, but has the `.pub` file extension
    * For example: `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`

5. Copy the output from the following step
    * This will be used in the next section

### Add Your SSH Key to Your GitHub Enterprise Account

From a web browser, follow these steps:

1. Navigate to [https://github.ibm.com/](https://github.ibm.com/)

2. In the `top right corner` of the page, click your `profile icon`:

![](../../images/github-setup-add-key-2.png)

3. Click `Settings` from the drop down menu that appears

4. On the `next page`, click `SSH and GPG keys` on the `left side panel`:

![](../../images/github-setup-add-key-4.png)

5. At the `top middle` of `next page`, click `New SSH Key`:

![](../../images/github-setup-add-key-5.png)

6. On the `next page`, enter a `title` for your container's SSH key
    :::note
    It is recommended that you use the `name of your TOAD container` as the title!
    :::

![](../../images/github-setup-add-key-6.png)

7. In the `textbox under` the `Key` section, `paste` the content of your `SSH public key` that you `copied` on `Step 5` of [Generate an SSH Key](#generate-an-ssh-key)

8. Click `Add SSH Key`

* You will now be able to use `git` within your TOAD container!

:::warning
    It is advised that you `delete your SSH key from your GitHub account` when you no longer need to use git in your TOAD container!!

## Execute in Terminal In `TOAD`, there is an `Execute in Terminal` icon on the `Desktop`. To execute any scripts that you may have in a terminal, this tool will accept multiple files and execute them in separate terminals simultaneously. Simply drag and drop the scripts that you wish to execute onto the `Execute in Terminal` icon.

## Data Migration

This is a guide on how to transfer data between TOAD containers.

1. Start by visiting the [TOAD Dashboard](../../how-to-access/#dashboard)

2. Find the `URL` of the container you want to transfer data from, as it contains information needed for this process

- For `v2 containers`, this can be found on the `dashboard` under the `URL` column
   - For `v1 containers`, the old dashboard was deprecated, so you will need to do one of the following:
     - If you have the `URL` saved ( `bookmarked in browser`, `written down`, etc. ), retrieve it from where it is saved
     - Post a message in the [toad-discussions](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C06JQ8Z8JJ0) channel and we can get that `URL` for you.

3. In the `URL`, identify the `host blade IP address` and the `VNC port`

- The `host blade IP address` is the address preceding the colon
   - The `VNC port` is the `4 digit number` following the colon

4. Using your `VNC port`, determine your `SSH port`

- For `v2 containers`, `subtract 1000` from the `VNC port` number
   - For `v1 containers`, `add 1000` to the `VNC port` number

rmine your `SSH port`

- For `v2 containers`, `subtract 1000` from the `VNC port` number
   - For `v1 containers`, `add 1000` to the `VNC port` number

5. Hold onto the `host blade IP address` and `SSH port`, as they will both be used in a later step

6. Access the container that you're transferring data from

7. Create a directory called `transfer-data`

8. Copy all the data you wish to transfer into the newly created `transfer-data` directory

9. Run the following command to package the `transfer-data` directory

```
   tar -czvf transfer-data.tar.gz <path_to_transfer-data_directory>
   ```

:::note
   Make note of the path of the `transfer-data` package
   :::

10. Access the `v2 container` that you wish to transfer data to

11. Run the following command to fetch the packaged `transfer-data` directory

```
    scp -P <SSH_port_from_Step_4> tester@<host_blade_ip_from_Step_3>:<path_to_transfer-data_package>/transfer-data.tar.gz $TOAD_MP
    ```

12. Run the following command to unpack the `transfer-data` package

```
    tar -xf $TOAD_MP/transfer-data.tar.gz -C $TOAD_MP
    ```

13. Verify data was transferred successfully

to unpack the `transfer-data` package ``` tar -xf $TOAD_MP/transfer-data.tar.gz -C $TOAD_MP ``` 13. Verify data was transferred successfully 14. Run the following command to remove the `transfer-data` package ``` rm $TOAD_MP/transfer-data.tar.gz ```

content:
## Purpose and Goals
This automation is designed to provide a set of classes and methods, as well as functional scripts, to automate HCD operations and testing. HCD is a large part of teams like Mixplex, but many teams use it across the floor to manage, change and test their I/O configurations. HCD has no Zowe equivalent, these scripts are designed to bridge that gap.

Due to the large scale of functionality of HCD, this code base is relatively large. Different classes are designed to simplify building the larger pieces of automation. Classes also exist to work with z/OS resources (channels, PFIDs, devices, etc), as this is critical for end-to-end I/O automation.

content:
## Major Components
There are three major types of files in the main directory:
1. User scripts, these start with a lower case letter and will accept user input. These will also call ZoweLab helper scripts to import sysplex_credentials.txt, etc.
2. Classes, start with either 'HCD' or 'zOS', depending on what the class is designed to do. Each file has one class
3. JCL jobs for HCD operations, ending in .txt. These, by default, are also accessible from the ZoweLab package due to the *.txt inclusion of the package

content:
## Operation Flow
To make a dynamic I/O change, the user has three main steps:
1. Build an IODF in HCD, and convert it from a work to a production IODF
2. Vary off any resources that are getting deleted, comparing to their currently activated IODF
3. Perform a software (SW) and hardware (HW) activate, keeping track of one LPAR per CEC to reserve for HW activates.

Users will likely then vary on anything that is new in their new IODF, though this isn't strictly required.

content:
## Association with the Classes
The classes are built to handle specific operations. There are three main classes, each with their own documentation in this repository:
1. HCD_operations is for operations working with HCD, through JCL and master console
2. zOSResource_helper is for varying off and on z/OS resources, and eventually for validating that. This will work with HCD classes to find the resources to vary based on IODF changes, though there are methods to target any particular resource.
3. HCD_commpare_interpet is a custom-build parsing class of the HCD IODF compare report.

# HCD_operations Class
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 07/26/2023

## Goal
This class contains operations dealing with HCD and activation.

## Starting Operation
To start, import the class using a Zowe connections dictionary, which should be acquired using the ZoweHelper make_connection [method](../ZoweHelper%20class.md#make_connection)

Example code block:
    from ZoweLab.ZoweHelperScripts.ZoweHelper import Zowehelper
    from ZoweLab.HCD_Dynamic.HCD_operations import HCD_helper

zwe = Zowehelper()
    (zowe_connection, debugstring) = zwe.make_connection("Plexnamehere")
    hcd = HCD_helper(zowe_connection)

## Methods
HCD_operations has a lot of different methods

### activateIODF
    HCD_operations.activateIODF(IODF:str,LPARSTRING:str="",FORCE:bool=True,PROC:str=None,SOFT:bool=False,TEST:bool = False):

This method has all different methods of performing activate sequences, depending on what parameters are put in. The function returns a bool if the activate was successful or not.

#### Parameters:
    IODF:str
This is the IODF number, and is required. Example would be "4F".

LPARSTRING:str
This is the LPAR route string, which isn't strictly required. Default is to route to wherever Zowe is running, which is normally ineffective. An example LPAR route command would be:
"ro *all,"
OR:
"ro (S01,S07,S08),"

NOTE: All LPARSTRING entries MUST end in a ','

FORCE

This is to set the force parameter for hardware activates. This is default true, and can only be set to False if there are _only adds in the new IODF_.

PROC

This is a rarely used parameter to target a particular processor ID.

SOFT

This is to enable software IODF changes

TEST

This runs a test IODF change for validating, but the automation suite does HCD IODF compare instead of this as the default architecture.

### SWthenHWactivateIODF
    HCD_operations.SWthenHWactivateIODF(IODF:str,:LPARlist:list,FORCE:bool=True):

This method finds the CECs in the sysplex, then walks through all LPARs in the sysplex, reserving the first one found on each CEC through d ios,config for a SW/HW activate.

The program then goes one at a time through the other LPARs and perform SW activates, verifying afterwards with a d ios,config. After all SW moves, we perform HW activations one CEC at a time. Future improvements are possible to parallelize the operations.

The method returns if the entire process is completed as a bool.

#### Parameters
    IODF:str
This is the IODF number, and is required. Example would be "4F".

LPARSTRING:str
This is the LPAR route string, which isn't strictly required. Default is to route to wherever Zowe is running, which is normally ineffective. An example LPAR route command would be:
"ro *all,"
OR:
"ro (S01,S07,S08),"

NOTE: All LPARSTRING entries MUST end in a ','

FORCE

This is to set the force parameter for hardware activates. This is default true, and can only be set to False if there are _only adds in the new IODF_.

### queryIOCONFIG
    HCD_operations.queryIOCONFIG(LPAR:str,retrycount:int=100):

This method queries the I/O config of an LPAR using the d ios,config command. It returns an I/O config dictionary with key data.

The output dictionary has the format:

ioConfigDict = {
        "SW IODF":
        "LPAR":
        "Source Image":
        "HW Token":
        "CSS":
    }

#### Parameters
    LPAR

This is the name of an LPAR, only a single LPAR.

retrycount

This is how many times to retry asking d ios,config when waiting for config changes. The method uses the ZoweLab.getStaggeredWaitTimes [method](../ZoweHelper%20class.md#getstaggeredwaittimes)

### validateIODF
    HCD_operations.validateIODF(LPAR:str,targetIODFuser:str,SOFTWARE:bool:True):

This method validates that an LPAR is on the correct either HW or SW IODF, using the query IODF.

The method returns a bool if the LPAR is on the desired IODF.

#### Parameters
    LPAR

This is the name of an LPAR, only a single LPAR.

targetIODFusuer

This is the user-defined IODF name, which is interpeted using the targetIODF method.

SOFTWARE

# ZoweHelper Class
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 07/26/2023
Updated: 09/15/2023

## Goal:
The ZoweHelper class includes a few functions that are frequently using in ZoweLab operations.

## Starting:
In your code, initiate the ZoweHelper class, and then you can use the methods inside of it.

Example:
    from ZoweLab.ZoweHelperScripts.ZoweHelper import Zowehelper
    from zowe.zos_console_for_zowe_sdk import Console

zoweHelperinstance = Zowehelper()
    (zowe_connection, debugstring) = zoweHelperinstance.make_connection("Plexnamehere")

zosConsole = Console(zowe_connection)
## Methods:

### get_sysplexfile:
    Zowehelper.get_sysplexfile():

This method is mostly internal use, called during __init__. It loads in the sysplex_credentials file, which is where all Zowe connection information should be pulled from as the user.

### make_connection:
    Zowehelper.make_connection(_plexname_:str,_logoutput_:list=[]):

This method uses the class-read in sysplex credentials file, interpets it and returns either errors to the user if the file doesn't exist, or if the file is improperly formatted. If everything is correct, it returns to the code the Zowe connection dictonary for the sysplex name that is passed in. The developer must have a user-inputted sysplex name to pass to this definition. Optionally for PCD legacy, you can pass in a list to append log data to.

### getStaggeredWaitTimes:
    Zowehelper.getStaggeredWaitTimes(expectedTimeinSec:int=120,maxWaitTimeinSec:int=3600,speedUpTuning:int=4):

Frequently when working with z/OS, we have to wait for things to be done and query them again. A developer can choose to wait a static amount of time, i.e. time.sleep(1) for re-checking every second. However, many operations will either complete in a short time, or a very long time, depending on the configuration. Checking every second for hours is excessive and can bog the system down.

This method implements a sigmoid (S-curve, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmoid_function) function of wait times that can be passed to time.sleep(). A counter is started when the Zowehelper class instance is created, and incremented every time that getStaggeredWaitTimes is called. This counter serves as the "x" axis, with some additional math to shift the curve to the +x axis and tune how fast the counter moves up the curve. The return value of the function is passed back as the time to wait in seconds to time.sleep(), and the y-axis is scaled to the maxWaitTimeinSec, which is the upper horizontal asymptote of the $(S(x))$ curve.

Full equation utilized:

ime.sleep(), and the y-axis is scaled to the maxWaitTimeinSec, which is the upper horizontal asymptote of the $(S(x))$ curve.

Full equation utilized:

$$ returnedTime = 1+ { maxWaitTimeinSeconds \over( 1+ \exp(-waitCounter-expectedTime/speedUpTuning))} $$

You can utilize this very simply:
    from ZoweLab.ZoweHelperScripts.ZoweHelper import Zowehelper

i = 0
    zwe = Zowehelper()
    while i < 0:
        time.sleep(zwe.getStaggeredWaitTimes())
        i += 1

# Release Procedures
Author: Eric Reid
Date:  09/15/2023

## Preparing for a Release
Zowelab releases should be coordinated across developers working in the same development branches. Multiple development branches are supported, but must be taken with care.

Checklist for release:

1. All developers on branch to be release agree on their code(s) readiness
2. EST User Guide Documentation is created. Make sure beta flags are put at the top of procedures on beta-tested products.
3. New (or edited code) should strive to achieve pylint values over 7.

## Creating a Release

Releases are done through Github. Release notes should adhere to the [EST Lab Release Guidelines](/Automation/AutomationBestPractices/DeveloperGuides/GithubHelp/GithubReleases/README.md).

Example Update procedure:

cd ~/zOSAutomation
    git pull
    pip install -e ~/zOSAutomation/.

Have users verify successful updates with [Verifying ZoweLab Version](../../ZoweLab/Setup/Checking%20ZoweLab%20Version.md)

Make sure users know the update path from the last major release.

# ZoweLab
Github: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/tree/main

"Zowe offers modern interfaces to interact with z/OS and allows you to work with z/OS in a way that is similar to what you experience on cloud platforms today. You can use these interfaces as delivered or through plug-ins and extensions that are created by clients or third-party vendors. " https://www.zowe.org/

**ZoweLab** is a suite of built for purpose tools which interact with zOS via the APIs Zowe provides. The tools are very useful for completing common tasks and tests in your zOS environment, it completely removed your need for a 3270 console with these tasks.   It is just one way to interact with Zowe, you can also use ZoweExplorer in VSCode or the web browser UI.

![](./images/ZoweNetworkDiagram.png)

## Prerequisite

Zowe was added to the OSS zOS distribution for the test floor in Fall 2022 and requires some initial one-time setup.
A direct link the these instructions is [here](https://github.ibm.com/Operating-Systems-Support/STAKEHOLDERS-PORTAL-POK-ESTFTP-ZOS/wiki/How-to-Set-Up-Zowe-Local-Environment).

## Education

Eric Reid has written a work doc to help you get logged in and oriented in Zowe. It is intended to show you how to find some of the same panels you are familiar with in ISPF and perform some basic actions which can replace some aspects of console interaction -
[Beginner Zowe User's Guide](/Automation/ZoweLab/Setup/README.md)

## Getting Started

If you want to use ZoweLab Suite in TOAD review our [Update Guide](/Automation/ZoweLab/Setup/UpdatingZoweLab.md)

If you know ZoweLab is installed, get started by running `zwe -i` then setting up a sysplex_credentials.txt file, following the [procedure](./Tools/Sysplex%20Credentials%20File.md).

# Checking ZoweLab Version
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 09/15/2023

## Procedure
In your container, to see your ZoweLab version, perform the following command:

`pip list |grep ZoweLab`

This should return something like this:

`ZoweLab                       1.0.0                /root/zOSAutomation`

The ZoweLab version is the number in the middle.

# EST Zowe User’s Guide

Author: Eric T Reid

Date: 11/15/2022
Github: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/tree/main

## Introduction: What is Zowe?

Zowe is an open-source, modern platform for interfacing with z/OS, including a GUI-based Zowe
Desktop, a Zowe CLI installable on any platform (Windows, Mac, Linux....), a VSCode Zowe Explorer
extension, a rich API catalog, and much more. Due to the open-source nature of Zowe, it is continuously
improving to meet the needs of the Zowe community, which includes many of IBM’s biggest mainframe
clients. You can learn more about Zowe at their website: [http://www.zowe.org](http://www.zowe.org)

This guide is designed as an active introduction for IBM Z Engineering Systems Test, written by
an early adopter and advocate of the technology. Not all parts of the guide will be useful to all users, but
the hope is you can work through relevant sections to you. In as many places as possible, comparisons
from standard 3270 console interactions are drawn, to aid the adoption process.

**ZoweLab tools must be used within TOAD containers to receive support.**

_Special thanks to this guide to Barb Weglinski, Bob Simmons, Liam Hogan, Chris Hutton and
Andrew Hicks who were critical in delivering this technology to EST._
# Part 1: Installation, First Steps

## Installation

You should refer to Operating System Supports installation instructions located here: [How to Setup Zowe Local Environment](https://github.ibm.com/Operating-Systems-Support/STAKEHOLDERS-PORTAL-POK-ESTFTP-ZOS/wiki/How-to-Set-Up-Zowe-Local-Environment)

Notes:

EST should have address 4855 free in general to install Zowe on. You can check this by going to 3.4 and
verifying there is only a VTOC on it:

2. This should likely return volser SC
3. You can put that into the “VOLSER” line of ISPF 3.4 and verify there is only a VTOC.

_If you need help with this, reach out to Barb or Eric_

You’ll want to know your z/OS hostname, this procedure gives details about finding that: Configuring
TCPIP on zOS · Operating-Systems-Support/STAKEHOLDERS-PORTAL-POK-ESTFTP-ZOS Wiki (ibm.com)

## First Login

First, verify that your browser is pointing to:
```https:// _yourhostnamehere_ :7554/zlux/ui/v1/ZLUX/plugins/org.zowe.zlux.bootstrap/web/```

If you go into the 7556 port things won’t work.

Logon with your z/OS login (typically TESTFLR...):

![](../images/Picture1.png)

![](../images/Picture2.png)

You’ve logged into Zowe!

## Personalization

Just like your personal desktop, you can customize different parts of your desktop. In the lower right-
hand corner, click the wrench and screwdriver, then press the personalization button:

From here, you can upload a wallpaper (note maximum size of photo is 3MB....). It’ll take a second to

# Update ZoweLab

ZoweLab comes ready to use out of the bo in TOAD. Like most tools in TOAD, you are responsible to periodically update it between workloads to pick up function and fixes.  You are also able to install directly to a personal work station, it should work in Mac, Windows, and Linux environments.

## How to Update ZoweLab
First, check your version of ZoweLab. In the TOAD container terminal, you can do:

`pip list |grep ZoweLab`

:::note
Some environments will need to substitute commands with `pip3`
:::

This should return something like this:

```bash
tester@TOAD $ pip list |grep ZoweLab
ZoweLab                       3.7.7
 ```

If nothing is returned, you either made a typo or you are not in TOAD and you need to do a fresh install.

Now, read about [using ZoweLab for the first time](#using-zowelab-for-the-first-time) for your next steps

## TOAD Update Instructions

You should take this moment to pick up the latest release of all tool packages in your container.  Simply run the script in `~/TOAD-MGMT` directory.

```bash
~/TOAD-MGMT/upgrade_tools.py
```

```bash
tester@ThrasherStation:PyThrash $ ~/TOAD-MGMT/upgrade_tools.py
...
pip install text
...
Installing collected packages: zowelab
  Attempting uninstall: zowelab
    Found existing installation: ZoweLab 3.7.7
    Uninstalling ZoweLab-3.7.7:
      Successfully uninstalled ZoweLab-3.7.7
Successfully installed zowelab-3.7.8
Successfully upgraded: zowelab

All outdated packages have been updated.

```

## Non-TOAD Installation

If you are not using TOAD, you will need to install ZoweLab by pointing pip to our self hosted PyPi Registry.  You can do this by running the following commands:

### Set pip config

```bash
pip config set global.trusted-host vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com
pip config set global.index-url https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/automation-packages
```

If you ever need to revert this pip config, run:

```bash
pip config unset global.trusted-host
pip config unset global.index-url
```

### Install ZoweLab

Now you can use pip or pip3 to install ZoweLab!

```bash
pip install ZoweLab
```

Thats it. Read about [using ZoweLab for the first time](#using-zowelab-for-the-first-time) for your next steps

## ZoweLab Update Instructions

This update can be down in TOAD or on your local machine if pip is configured.

### Latest Version

If you would like to update ZoweLab package run the command:
```bash
pip install --upgrade ZoweLab
```

### Specific Version

If you would like to update ZoweLab package to a specific version run the command:

```bash
pip install ZoweLab==<version>
```

The available versions may be viewed in our private PyPi Registry: [here](https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/automation-packages/zowelab/)

## Using ZoweLab for the first time

If its your first time using ZoweLab you need to run the following command which will setup your ZoweLab working directories.  On TOAD, this will be in your team mount point which will be `/home/tester/<TOAD_MP>`

```bash
zwe -i
```

Now it is time to setup your `sysplex credentials file` so ZoweLab will know how to talk to your Plexes.  [How to setup sysplex Credentials](/Automation/ZoweLab/Tools/Sysplex%20Credentials%20File.md)

# ZoweLab Preliminary Checklist

Authors: Savannah Portilla, Eric Reid

## Overview

Bellow is the step-by-step checklist of what your system needs in order for you to utilize these tools. Be sure to follow these steps in order to ensure proper setup. These steps also include helpful links and people you can contact who are knowledgeable on these topics.

# Channel Driver Dataset Cleanup
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 04/10/2024

## Introduction

For the past few years, Channel Driver has been leaving datasets out on DASD as it runs. In theory, things like `%setup,init=yes` should clean these up, but not everyone runs that all the time, and it can be destructive to a plex. Eventually, when the datasets get full, you can't run any jobs to the volumes at all. Because the datasets are uncatalogued, this also involves a volume-by-volume cleanup. This automation is designed to clean this up for you.

## How to Run

First, make sure you have ZoweLab setup. Then, from your TOAD container, go to `cd zOSAutomation/ZoweLab/PCD`.  Then, start the script with `python3 .\dataset_cleaner.py -sp A54 3000 4000`.

Parameters:

-sp: Sysplex, as specified in your sysplex_credentials.txt

-v: Volser prefix, optional. Default is `SH`.

startDevice: mandatory, positional. Starting device in range

endDevice: mandatory, positional. Ending device in range

This code checks that the volser is available to the LPAR with Zowe and z/OSMF. It then runs a bunch of API calls to go and find what datasets meet the format `SYS*.T*` and delete them all. This can take quite a while to run.

# z/OS Ditto Killer
Author: Eric Reid
ZoweLab v1.1.0
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0

## Introduction
The z/OS Ditto Killer is designed to handle a lot of basic automation requests for z/OS using Zowe. In the past, many of these would have been handled by Ditto, which is not stable and deprecated. Users will now build YAML's with commands to run.

:::note

This is limited to z/OS, no other operating systems are supported. When possible, we encourage you to investigate any other z/OS automation first: this is very dumb automation.

:::

## How to use it?
You'll build a YAML (.yaml) file in ZoweLab/DittoKiller/dittorunfiles/. You can copy the example.yaml next to the dittorunfiles directory into the dittorunfiles direcotry as a start.

Make sure you've defined your sysplex definition in the sysplex_credentials.txt file, follow this [procedure](./ZoweLab/Setup/Sysplex Credentials File.md)

Basic YAML format:

#This is an example yaml of how to do the ditto killer
    zosCommandBlock:
    sysplex: your_sysplex #from sysplex_credentials, in quotes
    loop: 3 #how many iterations of the commands in commands
    lparString: 'ro S33' #route string, exact
    wait: 5 #how long to wait in seconds between submitting commands
    commands:
    - "d xcf"
    - 'd iplinfo'
    waitFor: 'COMMAND' #be careful!

--- #put three dashes inbetween command blocks, add as many as you need
    zosCommandBlock:
    sysplex: your_sysplex
    commands:
    - "d xcf"
    - 'd iplinfo'

Save the YAML file, with extension .yaml.  Make sure your sysplex name is in quotes!

Run: `zwe_dittokiller __yourfile__`.  Example: `zwe_dittokiller example.yaml`

We'll then go through the automation, one block at a time.

in quotes!

Run: `zwe_dittokiller __yourfile__`.  Example: `zwe_dittokiller example.yaml`

We'll then go through the automation, one block at a time.

Things to note:
1. The automation runs through each zosCommandBlock in order
2. The sysplex can be any in your sysplex_credentials file, and you can combine many sysplexes in a single file with different command blocks
3. Wait specification is between every command in the command list
4. waitFor is slow and ultra sensitive to case, spelling, etc. Be careful! We can end up in an infinite loop
5. Make sure your lparString includes an ro at the beginning

## What does this do under the covers?
This is basically the fanciest Zowe PythonSDK console command automation ever. Most of this script is dedicated to interpeting what is put in the YAML and gluing it together to send over Zowe to z/OS.

# Activate IODF Sysplex Wide
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 08/09/2023
Github: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/tree/main
Release: ZoweLab v1.1.0
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0

## Objective
This automation is designed to replace the process of the HCD 2.7 panel, which is to activate a production IODF sysplex-wide.

## Prerequisites
1. Zowe up and running
2. A production IODF ready to go. This automation doesn't verify anything about your IODF, be careful!

:::caution
This script does not check to see if all required z/OS resources are offline beforehand. See other HCD automation tools that perform those tasks.  The hardware activate will fail if z/OS detects things online when they should be offline.
:::

## What to Do
Start the script: `zwe_hcd_activateSWandHW [options]`.If you specify no options, the script will prompt for what it needs, taking any defaults listed below. If you specify `zwe_hcd_activateSWandHW -h`, you'll get a help display.

Parameters:
-s: Sysplex name, as defined in your sysplex_credentials.txt file

-n: New IODF name, the one you want move to

-f: Optional, defaults to "True". Specify "False" if you are ONLY adding z/OS resources

-w: Optional, defaults to software then hardware (SWHW). Specify HWSW if you want to do hardware and then software activates

When specifying an IODF, you can specify in one of two ways. Work IODFs are not supported.
1. If your IODF has the form 'IODF.IODF##', you can just put in the ## (see Example 1)
2. If your IODF doesn't have the form above, specify your entire IODF dataset name (see Example 2).

:::note
As of 08/09/2023, IODF's of not IODF.IODF## have not been tried using this automation, but is expected to work based on z/OS documentation.
:::

Examples:
1. zwe_hcd_activateSWandHW -s A50 -n 4F
2. zwe_hcd_activateSWandHW -s LCST3 -n LCSTALL.IODFF3

## Logging
This script produces run logs in a directory in HCD_Dynamic called ZoweLabRunLog. Run logs are by date and time.

## What is it doing under the covers?
The automation will determine what LPARs exist in your sysplex, and what CPC's they are associated with. Then, it will reserve the first LPAR of each CPC for hardware activation, and perform software activations on all other LPARs, going one at a time and checking if any didn't activate. Then, it will activate each CPC one at a time.  The script will error out if any activation results in the LPAR not being on the expected IODF.

To do this work, ZoweLab uses the `d xcf`, `d ios,config` and `activate IODF=##` commands.

# Build Production IODF
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 03/06/2024
ZoweLab v1.6.0
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0

## Introduction

This script provides the ability to take a work IODF and convert it to a production IODF by invoking the HCD JCL.

## How to Use It

You need to have a work IODF in z/OS, you can use the [migrate IOCDS](./Migrate_IOCDS.md) to help with this if you have an IOCDS on your laptop. Then, invoke this script:
`zwe_hcd_buildProduction -s _sysplex_ -i _IODFname_` .

Parameters:

-s: Sysplex, as defined in the sysplex_credentials.txt file.

-i: IODF, either a 2 digit hex value (i.e. `E4`) in the case of IODF.IODF##, or the fully qualified DSN name (i.e. `LCSTALL.IODF3B`)

-d: Delete automatically, optional. Specify this flag (just add `-d`) if you want to automatically delete an existing production IODF of the same name. If not specified, the script will ask you to confirm deletion.

-v: Volser (optiona). Specify the volser to build the production IODF on.

-a: Allocate size (optional). Specify the size in 4K blocks you want the IODF to be.

-w: Work IODF DSN (optional). Specify the work IODF DSN if it isn't the same as your production IODF DSN suffixed by ".WORK".

## What is this doing?

This invokes VSAM JCL to initialize an IODF VSAM, then the HCD JCL to initalize it as a production IODF, then convert it to production IODF.

## The CC 0004

The code may come back and say the job fails with a CC 0004. This likely means that there are warnings. Later versions of this code will display these.

# Copy IODF
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 03/06/2025
ZoweLab v3.4.0

## Introduction

This script provides the ability to take a copy from one IODF to another. This includes initializing the new IODF.

## How to Use It

You need to have an existing IODF in z/OS. In general, this should be a work IODF, but the code has a flag for production IODF copy.

Command: `zwe_hcd_copyIODF -s <myplex> -n <IODF> -o <IODF>`

Parameters:

-s: Sysplex, as defined in the sysplex_credentials.txt file.

-n: IODF, either a 2 digit hex value (i.e. `E4`) in the case of IODF.IODF##, or the fully qualified DSN name of the new (target) IODF (i.e. `LCSTALL.IODF3B`)

-o: IODF, either a 2 digit hex value (i.e. `E4`) in the case of IODF.IODF##, or the fully qualified DSN name of the old (source) IODF (i.e. `LCSTALL.IODF3B`)

-d: Delete automatically, optional. Specify this flag (just add `-d`) if you want to automatically delete an existing production IODF of the same name. If not specified, the script will ask you to confirm deletion.

-v: Volser (optional). Specify the volser to build the production IODF on. Default is IODFPK

-sz: Allocate size (optional). Specify the size in 4K blocks you want the IODF to be.

-p: Flag if you want to copy production IODFs. Otherwises, ".WORK" will be appended to all IODFs involved.

## What is this doing?

This invokes VSAM JCL to initialize an IODF VSAM, then the HCD JCL to copy it to a new IODF.

# HCD Compare

Developer: Eric Reid

Documentation date: 07/11/2023
Github: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/tree/main
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0

## What is HCD Compare?

HCD offers the ability through a JCL exec to compare two IODFs in z/OS to see what changes between them. This produces a compare report that can be useful to figure out what is changing in the IODF that you move to.

HCD Compare is a Python script using Zowe that runs this JCL exec and prints the output into a directory where the script runs. This can be SFTP'ed off the 3270, investigated in the OE, etc.

This requires the sysplex_credentials.txt file to exist in the ESTZowe directory as part of version 1.0.0 of EST zOSAutomation tools, and for running the install. Please see relevant procedures on setting this up.

## How do I run HCD Compare?

Start the script: `zwe_hcd_compareIODF -s _yoursysplex_ -n _yournewIODF_ -o _youroldIODF_`

If you specify no options, the script will prompt for what it needs, taking any defaults listed below. If you specify python3 loopDynamicChanges.py -h, you'll get a help display.

Parameters:

-s: Sysplex name as defined in sysplex_credentials.txt

-n: New IODF, or the one you want to move to

-o: Old IODF, or the one you are currently on

When specifying an IODF, you can specify in one of two ways. Work IODFs are not supported.
1. If your IODF has the form 'IODF.IODF##', you can just put in the ## (see Example 1)
2. If your IODF doesn't have the form above, specify your entire IODF dataset name (see Example 2)

The script will automatically determine which you have and act accordingly.

Examples:
1. zwe_hcd_compareIODF -s A50 -n 4F -o 41
2. zwe_hcd_compareIODF -s LCST3 -n LCSTALL.IODFF3 -o LCSTALL.IODFF0

# Loop Dynamic Changes
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 08/09/2023
Github: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/tree/main
ZoweLab v1.1.0
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0

## Prerequisites
1. Zowe up and running
2. A production IODF ready to go. This automation doesn't verify anything about your IODF, be careful!

## Objective
This nearly end-to-end automation is the glue of [Activate sysplex wide](/Automation/zOS%20Automation%20Suite/ZoweLab/HCD%20Tools/Activate%20Sysplex%20Wide.md) and [Vary z/OS Resources](/Automation/zOS%20Automation%20Suite/ZoweLab/HCD%20Tools/Loop%20Dynamic%20Changes.md). The idea is a user can specify a list of IODFs and a number of loops to run through that list. This uses the test activate method to vary resources both offline and online through interpeting the test activate.

:::caution
This automation does not check for iqyylog or call to errors in the SE as part of these actions. It also doesn't verify resources are coming online or offline throughout the process.
:::

:::note
As of ZoweLab v1.1.0, this automation cannot perform any varies that require SE/HMC deactivates or activates (such as SACF, LPAR removals and adds, etc.). It also doens't perform SE error checking. As ov ZoweLab v1.1.0, we only verify that activates performed successfully, not resource varies.
:::

## Automation Flow

At a high level, this is the process performed in each IODF change in loopDynamicChanges.py. This is performed for each IODF in your IODF list, and is looped through the number of times specified by the loop parameter. The purpose of outlining this flow is so users know how the various options will work inside the test. If any errors are found druing the sequence, error logs are written out for later analysis.

1. Perform a test activate on the LPAR that Zowe is on. If "no_condition" is set, resources to vary off and online will be found even if the test activate shows no condition that would cause an activate to fail.
2. If compare is set, perform a [compare IODF](./HCD%20IODF%20Compare.md) and add the resources found there to those from the test activate
3. Vary commands will be issued to z/OS based on what is found in steps (1) and (2) [vary resources](./Vary%20zOS%20Resources.md)
4. If you have defined before commands in your YAML, these will be issued
5. If you have specified a user-defined wait time, it will now wait.
6. We will wait for all LPARs to have no message codes indicating vary operations are occuring within the last 5 minutes. [wait for resources](#waiting-for-vary-resources)
7. If you have specified hotplug, the automation will pause for user confirmation to continue
8. Activation will occur, see [activate sysplex wide](./Activate%20Sysplex%20Wide.md)
9. If activation fails, vary commands are issued for known REASON codes in the activate output. A retry going through steps (1), (3) and (8) is performed. If this fail, automation stops.
10. Assuming 8 or 9 are successful, automation will continue
11. If you have specified hotplug, the automation will pause for user confirmation to continue
12. Vary commands will be issued based on the results of (1) and (2) [vary resources](./Vary%20zOS%20Resources.md)
13. If you have defined after commands in your YAML, these will be issued
14. If you have defined a user-defined wait time, it will now wait
15. We will wait for all LPARs to have no message codes indicating vary operations are occuring within the last 5 minutes. [wait for resources](#waiting-for-vary-resources)
16. If you have specified hotplug, the automation will pause for user confirmation to continue
17. If all succesful, the next move in your IODF list will be starting, restarting at step 1.

### Special use case - a single loop, single IODF
There is a special use case of this automation when you use the default loop number of 1, and only put one IODF in the IODF list. In this case, the automation will simply move your sysplex to the new IODF, varying resources offline then online with that activation. This is a full path to move your sysplex to a new IODF using HCD as a tool in your environment without running a full test.

Example:
zwe_hcd_loopDynamicChanges -s A54 -i 35 -l 1

## YAML Inputs
New in ZoweLab v1.1.6!

A new directory exists in HCD_Dynamic: `HCD_Dynamic/execution_yamls/`. ZoweLab comes with an example.yaml, which can be copied to form run YAMLs of different test cases and scenarios. It's recommended to do this through VSCode and an SSH connection to it, follow this [procedure](../../../TOAD/how-to-access/README.md#connect-using-vs-code)

The example.yaml has all the fields that are needed for the YAML. Unlike the CLI option, as of ZoweLab v1.1.13, not specifying a value will take the default in the program, only sysplex and IODF list are required.  The easiest way to do this is copying the YAML file, which contains some defaults, to a new file and changing any values needed.

For repetition, here is the example.yaml:

For repetition, here is the example.yaml:

sysplex: example_plex #sysplex from sysplex_credentials.txt
    IODFlist: 1,2,3,5 #IODF list
    waittime: 0 #waittime in seconds
    loop: 1 #number of loops through IODF list
    FORCE: True #only specify False if you are only adding resources, rare
    whichorder: SWHW #which order, SWHW (software then hardware) or HWSW (hardware then software)
    bugFix: False #only set if directed to
    hotplug: False #enable hotplug mode
    nocondition: False #vary resources even if z/OS detects no conditions that would fail activate
    compare: False #vary resources based on compare as well as test activate
    before:
    - "d xcf"
    after:
    - "ro *all,d xcf"
    - "d iplinfo"
    se_slot: A1,A2   #must be a list of two IOCDS slots to avoid hitting write protection errors on loops

YAML allows for the user to specify z/OS commands to run before and after the activate sequence [see Automation Flow](#automation-flow). Each command is seperated by 1 second, and is fired blindly. Users are responsible for having correct commands.

To run a YAML, specify the file name (including .yaml or .yml) as the only parameter in the run command: `python3 loopDynamicChanges.py example.yaml`

## Logging
This script produces run logs in a directory in HCD_Dynamic called ZoweLabRunLog. Run logs are by date and time.

## What is it doing under the covers?
This automation really calls the two tools it is built on in a loop. Please refer to those pages for more details on each of the sub-steps of the automation [Activate sysplex wide](/Automation/zOS%20Automation%20Suite/ZoweLab/HCD%20Tools/Activate%20Sysplex%20Wide.md) and [Vary z/OS Resources](/Automation/zOS%20Automation%20Suite/ZoweLab/HCD%20Tools/Loop%20Dynamic%20Changes.md).

# Migrate IOCDS
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 02/20/2024
ZoweLab v1.5.0
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0, v3.4.1

## Introduction
This automation is designed to invoke the extended migration in HCD to migrate IOCDS statements into HCD from an IOCDS file on your computer. The full path is to use the [standaloneIOCDS process](./getStandaloneIOCDS.md) to pull an IODF to your computer as IOCDS, use the IOCDS tools package to convert it to YAML, change your IODF there, use the IOCDS tools package to convert it back to IOCDS, then use this tool to bring it back to HCD.  This process builds a work IODF, another tool will convert to production, and then you can use tools like [Loop Dynamic Changes](./Loop%20Dynamic%20Changes.md) to dynamically change your configuration.

## How to Run the Automation
Make sure you have setup your [sysplex_credentials.txt](./ZoweLab/Setup/Sysplex Credentials File.md) file and have pip installed ZoweLab as per the Release Notes. Make sure you have a valid IOCDS on your computer to point to to migrate into z/OS HCD.

Start the script: `zwe_hcd_migrateIOCDS -s _yoursysplex_ -i _IODFnumber_`.  Available options:

-s: Sysplex as specified in sysplex_credentials.txt

-i: The IODF name or number you want to build a work IODF of in z/OS.

-d: Optional, Enable autodeletion of existing IODF's. Otherwise, users must respond to prompts to agree to delete existing IODF's.  Defaults to not autodeletion.

-v: Optional, enter the volser where you want the IODF to be built. Default is IODFPK

-f: Optional, full path to IOCDS file. If you don't specify this, the program will open up a Finder or File Explorer window to choose your IOCDS file and specify it to the program.

-a: Optional, specify how large of an IODF to specify in 4K blocks (known to VSAM as records). Default is 10000

S file and specify it to the program.

-p: Optional, specify to do a partial IODF migration to an existing work IODF. Specify the PROCESSOR ID in HCD (NOT THE LSYSTEM!!!). Note that there are many restrictions on partial migrations in HCD.

## About IODF deletion
If you select the `-d` option, the code will delete the existing IODF of the specified name or number if there is one automatically. Otherwise, users will be prompted to delete the existing IODF if there is one. There is no recovery for deleted IODF's.

## What is going on under the covers
This code invokes an extended migration from HCD. This migrates all statements from an IOCDS with a particular format into HCD. This first builds a dataset in z/OS (USERNAME.AUTO.IOCDS) where your IOCDS is copied into z/OS.  There are some restrictions on this process. It is important to note that this automation _does not_ use incremental migration, instead building the entire IODF from scratch to ensure maximum compatibility across all IOCDS definitions.

# HCD Tools
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 12/06/2023

## About HCD Tools
HCD tools are designed to better manage dynamic I/O testing in z/OS, and work with HCD. Many of these functions require JCL to be run, or many z/OS console commands.

## Prerequisites
In order to use any HCD tool, you need to install, configure, and start Zowe in your z/OS sysplex.  See more on this in the [EST Zowe User Guide](../README.md)

Next, any username specified in your sysplex_credentials.txt [file](./ZoweLab/Setup/Sysplex Credentials File.md) must manually start HCD in z/OS TSO at some point. This generates profile, message log, and other datasets for that user. If you have used HCD before, this likely isn't a problem.

# Rebuild IODF's
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 12/06/2023
Github: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/tree/main
ZoweLab v1.3.0
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0

## Purpose

This is mostly test code for HCD, though the key technical achievements introduced to achieve this will later be used by automated IODF build processeses.  ZoweLab v1.3.0 HCD_Dynamic has a new structure for JCL jobs in its directory due to the number of JCL jobs that are now run in rebuild_IODFs.py.

This automation generates IOCP statements from all the processors in an IODF, extracting them all from HCD and putting them in a file in `ZoweLab/HCD_Dynamic/IODF_Migration_Testing/filename`. These can be saved for later use, and were uploaded to Github from test runs, see the [tf_iodf repository](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/tf_iodf_repo).  This data is then migrated back into a new WORK IODF that is specified. The work IODF is then pushed into a production IODF, and the original production IODF and new production IODF are compared using the [HCD IODF Compare](./HCD%20IODF%20Compare.md) job. If errors are found in the migration or the comparison, error files are generated in `ZoweLab/HCD_Dynamic/IODF_Migration_Error_Logs/`. These error files include the HCD MSGLOG, LISTING file and IOCP Assembly output.

## How to Run rebuildIODFs.py

Run rebuildIODFs.py from either your desktop off of a cloned ZoweLab installation, or in the TOAD containers.  Run with `zwe_hcd_rebuildIODFs [options]`.  If you specify no options, the script will prompt for what it needs, taking any defaults listed below. If you specify `zwe_hcd_rebuildIODFs -h`, you'll get a help display.

-s: Required, specify sysplex from sysplex_credentials.txt

-o: Optional, old IODF. Specify if you only want to test rebuilding one IODF. If you want to rebuild all of the IODFs in the sysplex, leave this out.

-n: Required, new IODF. Specify the IODF name or number (assuming standard IODF.IODF## format) of a new IODF to rebuild into. This IODF will be deleted and rebuilt, make sure it is a free slot in your IODFPK. This automation also defaults to building on IODFPK with 10,000 cylinders of space, make sure you have 20,000 cylinders (WORK and PRODUCTION)

IODFPK. This automation also defaults to building on IODFPK with 10,000 cylinders of space, make sure you have 20,000 cylinders (WORK and PRODUCTION)

-p: Optional, prefix. Specify if your IODF prefix is not `IODF` (i.e. LCST). This likely should also be defined in your LOADEx member of your z/OS Load, see [Automating your z/OS IPL](<../../../../CommonProcedures/OperatingSystemsOnZ/zOS/Automated IPL Setup.md>) with more details.

## About HCD Errors, JCL and Warnings

This automation runs many HCD JCL jobs to achieve each action. These jobnames are in the format `HCD*`, with the suffix hinting at what step of the process is being performed.

Note that HCD returns JCL CC's based on what the IOCP migration assembly finds. A CC 0004 indicates warning messages, but no errors. CC 0008 means errors, and CC 0012 means something is missing in either the JCL or the system (i.e., missing datasets).  This automation builds error logs on anything that isn't a CC 0000 or CC 0004.

# Vary z/OS Resources
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 08/09/2023
Github: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/tree/main
ZoweLab v1.1.0
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0

## Prerequisites
1. Zowe up and running
2. A production IODF ready to go. This automation doesn't verify anything about your IODF, be careful!

## Objective
The goal of this automation is to vary resources offline and online before or after a dynamic IODF change.  This is a complex process, and can be incredibly time consuming. The automation comes equipped with two operating modes, the default "Test Activate" mode and the "IODF Compare" mode.

### The Test Activate Mode
The test activate mode performs a test activate to a specified target IODF. It then waits and interpets the SYSLOG output of that test, parsing it to determine what resources need to be varied offline. This is the preferred method when turning things offline before an IODF activate, as it finds edge cases where your IODF changes all the channels to a set of devices, making those devices go offline even though that change isn't explicit in the IODF's.

### IODF Compare Mode
The IODF Compare mode performs an IODF compare (like compareIODFs.py) and interpets the results to figure out what has changed. This is the preferred method for varying resources online, as it includes resources on systems without LPARs such as stand-alone coupling facilities (SACF's).

:::note
As of ZoweLab v1.1.0, this automation cannot perform any varies that require SE/HMC deactivates or activates (such as SACF, LPAR removals and adds, etc.)
:::

## What to Do
Start the script: `zwe_hcd_varyResources [options]`. If you specify no options, the script will prompt for what it needs, taking any defaults listed below. If you specify python3 varyResources.py -h, you'll get a help display.

Parameters:
-s: Sysplex name, as defined in your sysplex_credentials.txt file

-n: New IODF name, the one you want move to

-m: Optional, method. Defaults to "TestActivate", specify "IODFCompare" if you want to vary based on IODF compare.

-d: Optional, direction. Defaults to "OFFLINE". specify "ONLINE" (caps important!) if you want to vary resources online

-f: Optional, force. Defaults to "True". Specify "False" if you are ONLY adding z/OS resources. See the Appendix on the use of force in vary.

-o: Optional, old IODF name. Defaults to None. Used only if performaing an IODFCompare based vary

-c: Optional, Control Unit option. Defaults to False. Specify True if you want to vary control units. See appendix on control unit varies.

-b: Optional, bugfix. Defaults to False. Do not use unless directed

-g: Optional, GONOGO. Defaults to True, meaning "go". Setting to False will return what commands would be submitted, but not actually submitted.

When specifying an IODF, you can specify in one of two ways. Work IODFs are not supported.
1. If your IODF has the form 'IODF.IODF##', you can just put in the ## (see Example 1)
2. If your IODF doesn't have the form above, specify your entire IODF dataset name (see Example 2).

:::note
As of 08/09/2023, IODF's of not IODF.IODF## have not been tried using this automation, but is expected to work based on z/OS documentation.
:::

Examples:
1. zwe_hcd_varyResources -s A50 -n 4F
2. zwe_hcd_varyResources -s A50 -n 4F -m IODFCompare -d ONLINE -f False -o 41

## What is it doing under the covers?
This tool will perform one of the two methods to figure out what to vary offline or online, parse it, and then perform all of the vary commands. At this time, this script doesn't verify the status of the resources after submitting the commands. Depending on how many resources you are varying, z/OS may take a while to actually complete all of the commands. This is a 'surgical vary', only varying off the required resources from the specific LPARs needed for a particular IODF change.

From a z/OS command perspective, see the table below for what is supported and how it is done.

| z/OS Resource  | Command used to vary |  Force statement |
|----------------|----------------------|------------------|
| Channel        | cf chp(##-##,##-##)  |  ,UNCOND         |
| Device         | v (####-####)        |  Unsupported     |
| PFIDs          | cf pfid(####-####)   |  ,FORCE          |
| Control Units  | vary CU(####)        |  Unsupported     |

## Appendix 1: The use of Force in vary operations
Force is a dangerous, but sometimes required when performing vary operations. The code cannot perform a force if it will require manual confirmation, even if the user specifies True on Force. This preventative work enables the default to be to perform a force when required.

metadata.section_heading: Appendix 1: The use of Force in vary operations

content:
## Appendix 2: Control Unit Vary Operations
Control units are displayed as part of both methods of determining what has to be varied, but z/OS will vary them offline once all devices and paths connnected to a particular control unit is varied offline. In practice, control unit varies take significantly longer to perform, as they must be performed a single control unit at a time. This automation defaults to not varying control units, relying on varying all required devices and channels. This has been successful in beta testing, but the control unit code still exists in the code with the '-c' flag to enable varying these off if required.

# Get Standalone IOCP

Author: Eric Reid
Date: 10/20/2023
Github: https://github.ibm.com/systemz/zOSAutomation/tree/main
ZoweLab v1.2.0 -> Introduced
ZoweLab v1.3.0 -> Updates
ZoweLab v1.7.0 -> Updates
Update: ZoweLab v3.0.0

## Purpose
The HCD IOCP build tool builds an IOCP file and prints it to a .txt file in the environment you run ZoweLab from. This can be useful for sharing with others, and for IML'ing if HCD isn't available during a test cycle.

There are two ways HCD can do this (technically, one is build a Stand-Alone IOCP (HCD option 2.3) or Build I/O configuration data (HCD option 2.10)). The first is of only a single CEC in the IODF, and is designed to be taken directly into an SE's IOCP for IML (see note below). The second glues together the IOCP's of every processor in your IODF. Note that this option can take 10-15 minutes to run depending on how busy your system is and how big your IODF is. This script does put a dataset out on IODFPK.

## How to run HCD Standalone IOCP

Start the script: `zwe_hcd_standaloneIOCP -s A50 -i _youriodf_`

If you specify no options, the script will prompt for what it needs, taking any defaults listed below. If you specify python3 standaloneIOCP.py -h, you'll get a help display.

Parameters:

-s: Sysplex name as defined in sysplex_credentials.txt

-i: The IODF you want to get a standalone IOCP from

-p: Optional, specify to run the 2.3 option and get an IOCP from a specified processor in your IODF. Default is to run 2.10 and get all of the configuration statements from the IODF

-o: Optional, specify if you want HCD operating system configuration statements, such as z/OS esoterics

-sw: Optional, specify if you want HCD switch system configuration statements

-sa: Optional, specify if you want HCD to produce stand alone statements for a particular processor. You must specify '-p'

When specifying an IODF, you can specify in one of two ways. Work IODFs are not supported.
1. If your IODF has the form 'IODF.IODF##', you can just put in the ## (see Example 1)
2. If your IODF doesn't have the form above, specify your entire IODF dataset name (see Example 2)
