content:
### Get-CPC
Usage:
> rz-api get-cpc [OPTIONS] [NAMETAG]

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| nametag           | string | Enter CPC nametag to return status of the CPC given or HMC nametag to return list of cpcs under that HMC [default: None] |

Options:

| Options | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| -ip|  Enter IP to return list of cpc associated with that IP. |

### Activate

To see the arguments required use:
> rz-api activate --help

Usage:
> rz api activate [OPTIONS] CPC LPARS...

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| cpc           | string | Enter your CPC nametag to get the lpars. [default: None] [required] |
| lpars   | string | Enter your lpar/s to activate. [default: None] [required] |

Options:

| Options | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| -f| Use -f to override SE in service mode. |

### Decativate
To see the arguments required use:
> rz api deactivate --help

Usage:
> rz api deactivate [OPTIONS] CPC LPARS...

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| cpc           | string | Enter your CPC nametag to get the lpars. [default: None] [required] |
| lpars   | string | Enter your lpar/s to activate. [default: None] [required] |

Options:

| Options | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| -f| Use -f to override SE in service mode. |

### Get Lpars
To see the arguments required use:
> rz api get-lpars --help

Usage:
> rz api deactivate [OPTIONS] CPC LPARS...

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| cpc           | string | Enter your CPC nametag to get the lpars. [default: None] [required] |
| ip   | string | Enter IP if you want to user override [Optional] |
| user | string | Enter user id  if you want to user override [Optional] |
| pswd | string | Enter password  if you want to user override [Optional] |

Options:

| Options | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| -f| Use -f to override SE in service mode. |
| -s| Use to get status of the lpars.|
| --lpar -l| Use -l or --lpar to get status of specific lpar.|

***NOTE** `-s` should only be used when getting a list. When using --lpar or -l the status will automatically given.

Example:
To use information from rz-sys table:
> rz api get-lpars cpc_nametage

If providing user override for ip, username and password:
> rz api get-lpars [OPTIONS] CPC [IP] [USER] [PSWD]

### Load
To see the arguments required use:
> rz-api load --help

Usage:
 > rz api load [OPTIONS] CPC LPARS... [ADDR] [PARAM]

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| cpc           | string | Enter your CPC nametag to get the lpars. [default: None] [required] |
| lpars   | string | Enter your lpar/s to activate. [required] |
| addr | string | Input lpar load Address [Optional] |
| param | string | Input lpar load Parameter [Optional] |

Options:

| Options | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| -f| Use -f to override SE in service mode.|

### View Activation Profile

Usage:
> rz api profile [OPTIONS] CPC LPARS...

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| cpc           | string | Enter your CPC nametag to get the lpars. [default: None] [required] |
| lpars   | string | Enter your lpar/s to activation profile. [required] |

Options:

| Options | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| -f| Use -f to override SE in service mode.|

### Update Activation Profile

Usage:
> rz api update-profile [OPTIONS] CPC LPARS... PROPS

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| cpc           | string | Enter your CPC nametag to get the lpars. [default: None] [required] |
| lpars   | string | Enter your lpar/s to activation profile. [required] |
| props | json | Required, JSON format, Ex: "{\"load-at-activation\": true}"|

Options:

| Options | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| -f| Use -f to override SE in service mode.|

### Send OS message

Usage:
> rz api send-message [OPTIONS] CPC LPARS... MESSAGE

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| cpc           | string | Enter your CPC nametag to get the lpars. [default: None] [required] |
| lpars   | string | Enter your lpar/s to activation profile. [required] |
| message | string | Input your message. [required]|

Options:

| Options | Description |
| ------- | ----------- |
| -f| Use -f to override SE in service mode.|

### Set Credentials

Usage:
> rz api set-cred

| Command      |  Argument Type| Description |
| ----------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| username           | string |  Enter your username to change for HMC login. [required] |
| password   | string | Enter your password to used as default for HMC login. [required] |

## How to use rz-api functions
When installed, the remoteztoolset is importable through a simple import statement.
> import remoteztoolset

Beyond the top level package, to access the api tools functions import System class.
> from remoteztoolset import System

## Instantiating system objects

A system object can be populated using data from a csv file through the use of the get_one/get_many base class functions.
System data loaded using class functions will load from systems.csv found within the .rzt_data will by default unless otherwise specified.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")
```
### Running rz api functions

#### Get CPCS

- get_cpcs
    - **Parameters**: None
    - **Description**: Get CPCs and their full properties in json format
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_cpcs()

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```

- **Returns**: JSON format list of cpcs and their properties
-  get_cpcs_status_list
    - **Parameters**: cpc(set to NONE, but can be overried by the user)
    - **Description**: Get CPCs and their full properties in json format
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_cpcs_status_list()

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```

- **Returns**: List format list of cpcs and their status

While Getting a status of specific CPC.
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_cpcs_status_list(cpc=<CPC_NAMETAG>)

print(res)

rt System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_cpcs_status_list(cpc=<CPC_NAMETAG>)

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Returns**: JOSN format of cpc given and its status.

#### Get Lpars

- get_lpars
    - **Parameters** : None
    - **Description** : Get lpars and their full properties in JOSN format.
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_lpars()

print(res)
        except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```

- **Returns**: JSON format list of lpars and their full properties.

- get_single_lpar_status
    - **Parameters** : Lpar Name
    - **Description** : Returns status of lpar give..
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_single_lpar_status(lpar_name='<LPAR_NAME>')

print(res)
        except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```

- **Returns**: JSON format of lpar given and its properties.

- get_lpars_list
    - **Parameters**: None
    - **Description** : Gets a list of lpars from a CPC provided
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_lpars_list()

on

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_lpars_list()

print(res)
        except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Returns**: List of Lpars

- get_lpars_status_list
    - **Parameters** : None
    - **Description** :Get a list of lpars and their status
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.get_lpars_status_list()

print(res)
        except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Return**: List of lpars and their status

#### Activate Lpars
- activate
    - **Parameters** :
        - lpar name
        - load - default: None
    - **Description**: Activate the lpar provided, Load Parameter is set to None resulting in the load-at-activation value bing used is default value from the activation profile, set load value to True or False to get more control and will override when using the activate api and will set back to what is was prior in the profile.

```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.activate(lpar_name)

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Return**: ```{"success": True, "msg": f"{job_message}"}```

- lpar_batch_activate
    - **Parameters** :
        - List of lpar names
    - **Description**: Activate the lpar provided from the list
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.lpar_batch_activate([lpar_name1,lpar_name2])

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Return**: ```{"success": True, "msg": f"{job_message}"}```

#### Deactivate Lpars

- deactivate
    - **Parameters** :
        - lpar name
    - **Description**: Deactivate the lpar provided
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.deactivate('lpar_name1')

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Return**: ```{"success": True, "msg": f"{Deactivated}"}```

- lpar_batch_dectivate
    - **Parameters** :
        - List of lpar names
    - **Description**: Deactivate the lpar provided from the list

        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.lpar_batch_deactivate([lpar_name1,lpar_name2])

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Return**: ```{"success": True, "msg": f"{Deactivated}"}```

#### Load Lpars

- lpar_load
    - **Parameters** :
        - lpar name
        - load address(Optional)
        - load parameter(Optional)
    - **Description**: Load the lpar with the lpar name provided in the parameters, Load address and Load parameters are optional and are fetched automatically when the function is called, but can be overridden by the user.
    ```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.lpar_load(lpar_name)

print(res)

If providing a load address and load parameter use the example below:

print(res)

    - **Return**: job completion message

- lpar_list_load
    - **Parameters** :
        - List lpar name
        - load address(Optional) - default set to None
        - load parameter(Optional) - default set to None

#### Update/View Activation Profiles
- lpar_activation_profile_get_properties_list
    - **Parameters** :
        - Lpar name - string
    - **Description**: View activation profiles

```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

try:
            myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

res = myZ.lpar_activation_profile_get_properties_list(lpar_name)

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Return**: JSON format of Activation Profile Properties

- lpar_activation_profile_update
    - **Parameters** :
        - Lpar name - string
        - update_props: dict

- **Description**: Update activation profiles based on user input JSON

```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.lpar_activation_profile_update(lpar_name1,update_props={"properties_name": properties_value"})

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```
    - **Return**: Activation Profile JSON with user updated properties

#### Send OS messages
- send_os_messages
    - **Parameters** :
        - Lpar name - string
        - message - string
        - is_priority - default set to False, if you want you message to get priority and get executed first set to True
        - hide_output - default set to False, if you don't want a return of screen grab form the console set to True
        - load - default to None, uses the load-at-actiavtion on the profile, users can set

- **Description**: Send message to the os and get a return conformation of the sent message

```python
        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.send_os_messages(lpar_name1,message)

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e

Function call method if making the message priority is set too true:

        from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "cpc_nametag")

try:
            myZ.logon()

res = myZ.send_os_messages(lpar_name1, message, is_priority=True)

print(res)

except Exception as e:
            raise e
    ```

Call method if you are hiding output:

messages(lpar_name1, message, is_priority=True)

print(res)

except Exception as e:

```python

            myZ.logon()

## Archive

This documentation is running remoteztoolset below 1.0 version.

### Running the CLI Interface

The scripts can be ran on a single lpar or on multiple lpars

### Passing `-h` or `--help` argument

To view all arguments for a script use the `-h` or `--help` flag to view all required
arguments.

```text
% rz-api -h
usage: rz-api [-h] [-i I] [-u U] [-p P] [-n N] [-c {login,get-cpc,get-lpars,activate,deactivate,lpar-load,profile,send-message,update-profile}] [-l [L ...]] [-s [S]]
              [-param PARAM] [-addr ADDR] [-cpc CPC] [-m M] [-sm SM] [-up UP]

zHMC api tools

file,send-message,update-profile}] [-l [L ...]] [-s [S]]
              [-param PARAM] [-addr ADDR] [-cpc CPC] [-m M] [-sm SM] [-up UP]

zHMC api tools

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -i I                  IP of the system you want to login too.
  -u U                  Username of the host ip.
  -p P
  -n N                  Input your system name for login
  -c {login,get-cpc,get-lpars,activate,deactivate,lpar-load,profile,send-message,update-profile}
                        Input the command based on the list of commands.
  -l [L ...]            Input the choice of Lpar
  -s [S]                Get Status of Machines
  -param PARAM          Input your load parameter
  -addr ADDR            Input your load address
  -cpc CPC              Input your CPC.
  -m M                  Input your message for the send message os.
  -sm SM                Input your os message you want to send
  -up UP                Required, JSON format, Ex: -up '{"load-at-activation": true}'
```

### Input Arguments

The user can also enter the necessary fields for a Python script via arguements. Please
refer to [help argument](#passing--h-or---help-argument) section for specific arguments for each script.

The `-c` argument can be seen in [help argument](#passing--h-or---help-argument) that allows the user to run the specific function of the api tools.

```commandline
"login","get-cpc", "get-lpars","activate",'deactivate', 'lpar-load','profile','send-message','update-profile'
```

The `-cpc` argument will be your CPC name or should come from the nametag that is provided by running the [ssh tools](sshToolHelp.md)

The `-s` tag can only be used with the choices of get-cpc and get-lpars to get status of the lpars and cpcs. You can run the two choices without the `-s` tag as well.

```commandline
% rz-api -cpc A40 -c get-lpars -s
You have sucssefully logged in.
[['SAK13A1', 'not-operating'], ['S13AOSA1', 'not-activated'], ['T13AHP11', 'operating']]
```
The `-l` argument should be used to execute your `-c` tag command on specific lpar. The tag should be used with:
activate, deactivate, lpar-load, profile, send-message, update-profile.

o execute your `-c` tag command on specific lpar. The tag should be used with:
activate, deactivate, lpar-load, profile, send-message, update-profile.

```commandline
% rz-api -cpc A40 -c activate -l SAKCF13A
You have sucssefully logged in.
{'success': True, 'msg': 'None'}
```

The `-param` and `-addr` tag should be used with lpar-load choice. These two tags are generated automatically if you from activation profile if you don't have specific values.

```commandline
rz-api -cpc A40 -c lpar-load -l SAKCF13A -param 0000  -addr 00000
```

The `-sm` tag is used with the choice of send-message. After the -sm tag write you message you want to send to the lpar.

```commandline
rz-api -cpc A40 -c send-message -l T13AHP71 -sm "vary cn(*),activate"
```

The `-up` is the profile properties you want to update. The -up tag needs to be in dict format for the profile to get updated. ex: '```{"workload-manager-enabled": true}'```

```commandline
rz-api -cpc A40 -c update-profile -l PL4CF13A -up '{"workload-manager-enabled": true}'
```

### Running Multiple Lpars

To run the cli commands on multiple lpars you need to add the lpars after `-l` tag.

Look at the example below.

```commandline
% rz-api -cpc A40 -c send-message -l T13AHP71 PL4CF13A -sm "vary cn(*),activate"
```
### Examples

### Activate Lpar

```commandline
% rz-api -cpc A40 -c activate -l SAKCF13A
You have sucssefully logged in.
{'success': True, 'msg': 'None'}
```

### Deactivate Lpar

```commandline
% rz-api -cpc A40 -c deactivate -l SAKCF13A
You have sucssefully logged in.
{'success': True, 'msg': ''}
```

### Error Handling

The zhmcclient api now handles a check case for HMC not have a SE added to the rz-sys table.
Support Element not communicating and if the SE is in service mode. There will a check for all these cases before program runs for ease of use.

```commandline
% rz-api -cpc T4 -c get-lpars -s
You have sucssefully logged in.
SE in service Mode.
```
# remoteZtoolset Devloper Guide

## Imports
When installed, the remoteztoolset is importable through a simple import statement.
import remoteztoolset

Beyond the top level package is src, then utils/classes.
- import remoteztoolset.src.utils
- import remoteztoolset.src.classes

All top level imports from utils/classes/src including the modules themselves are all importable directly through the remoteztoolset module.
All the following import statements are valid.

- from remoteztoolset import classes
- from remoteztoolset import System
- from remoteztoolset import utils
- from remoteztoolset import file
- from remoteztoolset import src
- from remoteztoolset import rz_con

## System class
The system class can be imported with the following statement:
> from remoteztoolset import System

The system class contains the vast majority of functionality that involves performing actions on individual systems.
This includes creating SSH connections, transferring files, syncing system data,
loading/exporting data to/from a file, executing comments, etc.

### Instantiating system objects
A blank system object can be instantiated through the system class.
> myZ = System()

A system object can be populated using data from a csv file through the use of the get_one/get_many base class functions.
System data loaded using class functions will load from systems.csv found within the .rzt_data will by default unless otherwise specified.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")
```

System objects have the username set to "hmcmanager" and the default key location set as the SSH key by default.
This means that the system data can also be populated through setting the IP
(and optionally the username/ssh_key if not using the default values) and utilizing the sync_info function
(the sync_info function returns the object calling the function).

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System(ip="9.56.193.21").sync_info()
```

### Accessing System object properties
All columns in the rz-sys table are properties within the system class that can be accessed through the system.get function.
All properties have a base class property referencing each column name. These properties can be used as a more standardized means of refererencing the columns but the column names can be referenced manually as well.
```python
System.IP = System.PRIMARY_KEY = "ip"
System.HOSTNAME = "hostname"
System.USERNAME = "username"
System.TIMESTAMP = "ssh_timestamp"
System.SYSTYPE = "system_type"
System.SERIAL = "serial"
System.MODEL = "model"
System.OS_LEVEL = "os_level"
System.NAMETAG = "nametag"
System.MACHTYPE = "machine_type"
System.SSHKEY = "ssh_key"
System.PRIMARY_HMC = "primary_hmc"
System.PROD_MODE = "prod_mode"
System.ALT = "alternate"
```

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

ip = myZ.get(System.IP)
ip = myZ.get("ip")
```

The base system class also contains standardized options for referencing the potential options for the system_type column.
```python
System.SE = "SE"
System.HMC = "HMC"
System.OTHER = "OTHER"
```

zed options for referencing the potential options for the system_type column.
```python
System.SE = "SE"
System.HMC = "HMC"
System.OTHER = "OTHER"
```

As an example, this is a means of determining if a system is an HMC:
```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

# System.SYSTYPE = "system_type", System.HMC = "HMC"
is_hmc = (myZ.get(System.SYSTYPE) == System.HMC)
```

### Programmatically adding systems.
Systems can be programmatically connected/added to the systems table through three different python methods.
These methods being add_system, add_system_ip, and add_systems_stela. Each methods adds system(s) through a different input.
The add_system method will add system objects, the add_system_ip method will add a system based on an IP input,
and the add_systems_stela method will add systems by name using the Stela API.
Each of these methods goes through the process of establishing/verifying the SSH connection and syncing the system information.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System, add_systems_stela, add_system_ip, add_system

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

add_system(myZ)
add_system_ip("9.56.193.21")
add_systems_stela("B40")
```

### Running remote commands
As long as a System class object is instantiated and is populated with enough data to start an SSH session,
terminal commands can be programmatically executed on the remote system via SSH using the run_command function.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

output = myZ.run_command("ls -al")
```

The run_command function returns the output of the terminal command executed on the remote system.
By default, the remote shell runs in the background and doesn't get outputted to the console running remoteztoolset.
In order to have the remote command execution output on the console as it runs,
simply invoke the run_command function with verbose set to True.
A timeout can also be set in seconds to have the function timeout if in case it hangs.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

myZ.run_command("ls -al", verbose=True, timeout=10)
```

### Transfering files

Files can be transferred to/from remote systems programmatically using the get_files and the put_file methods.
The get_files method accepts any number of file inputs and will transfer files from the specified paths into
the zfilepulls directory for that system under the same path.
The put_file method takes a path for a local file and a destination path on remote system to copy the file to.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

# files to download off the system.
myZ.get_files("/console/data/iqyvpd.xml", "/console/data/iqyvpdc.xml", "/console/data/iqzqfedc.trm")

metadata.section_heading: files to download off the system.

content:
# local path and destination path.
myZ.put_file("~/Desktop/test.txt", "/ffdc/u/example/test.txt")
```

The system class also has an instance method called get_pull_dir which essentially returns the base path to the zfilepulls directory
for that system, where all the files pulled from a remote system are stored.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

zfp_path = myZ.get_pull_dir()
```

### Runstatic operations

The system class also has a number of instance functions meant for running runstatic commands on remote SEs.
These functions being se_ready, se_reboot, se_query_ss, se_enable_ss, se_disable_ss, se_toggle_ss.
The se_ready function checks the system to see if the boot process is finished.
The se_reboot function reboots the se. The se_query_ss function checks to see if system service status is enabled.
The se_enable_ss and se_disable_ss functions enable/disable system service status respectfully.
Lastly the se_toggle_ss function will toggle the system service status to the opposite state.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

myZ.se_ready()
myZ.se_query_ss()
myZ.se_disable_ss()
myZ.se_enable_ss()
myZ.se_toggle_ss()
myZ.se_reboot()
```

### Sending data to TURN server

The system class has a built in function for sending data to the TURN server. The function takes a JSON data payload as an input.
The system data needed to be sent to the TURN server is automatically appended to the payload and doesn't need to be included.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

### Using the SSH Client
The System object has an SSH client subclass built using paramiko for handling SSH sessions with remote systems.
Any System class instance function that needs to connect to a system is designed to either create a new SSH session/logout once finished,
or use an existing SSH client/keep the session open. This means that while individual functions will handle the SSH session on their own,
multiple functions can be used in succession with the same SSH session instead of having to create/logout of multiple SSH sessions if the client is manualy invoked beforehand. SSH sessions for a system can be created using the start_ssh_session function within the system class. This function returns the SSH client itself and is designed to be used as a context manager.

```python
from remoteztoolset import System

myZ = System.get_one("nametag", "B40")

with myZ.start_ssh_session() as client:
    myZ.run_command("pwd")
    myZ.run_command("ls -al")
```

# remoteZtoolset
Remote Z Toolset is **the** SDK for interacting with z systems via ssh and WSAPIs. An instance of RZT maintains a list of systems to work with.  It offers a powerful set of commandline tools to do basic functions and can be imported into python scripts.  It is tailored for TOAD environments but can also run on MAC, Windows, and Linux.

Read *installation steps* for your platform [here](/Automation/remoteZtoolset/installRZT.md)

You can find the repository [here](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/remoteZtoolset)

![](./images/RZT.png)

## [Summary of SSH Abilities](/Automation/remoteZtoolset/sshToolHelp.md):
 - Add public ssh key to system, enabling password-free ssh and file get/push
 - Establish ssh connection with:
    - Loopback for VNC Tunnelling
    - Loopback for Browser Connection on Metis and Beyond
 - Retrieve and store basic system info in local system table
 - Collect and store files in programmatically generated file tree
 - Post-process common files for use as documentation and script consumption
 - Run non-interactive scripts with stdout/err passthrough and collect output files

## [Summary of API Abilities](/Automation/remoteZtoolset/APIToolHelp.md):
 - View CPC and LPAR status via targeted HMC.
 - Perform Activation, load, deactivation to one or more LPARs
 - Retrieve specific or all activation profile properties
 - Send commands to Operating System Messages
 - Parse and react to OSM response

# How to Install RZT

Remote Z toolset is supported on Mac, Windows, and Linux, enabling you to interface with HMC/SE Consoles from any of these environments. It comes pre-configured in TOAD but should still be updated periodically there.

Installing remoteZtoolset varies by platform but in all cases, you will need to install python 3.6 or higher.

[Setting up Python on Windows](https://docs.python.org/3/using/windows.html)

[Setting up Python on Mac](https://docs.python.org/3/using/mac.html)

[Setting up Python on Linux](https://docs.python.org/3/using/unix.html)

## Installing remoteZtoolset using pip via our package repository:

Using pip or pip3, it is recommended you install remoteZtoolset from our [package repository](/Automation/README.md) . This way you will easily pick up any dependencies of ours.

```
pip config set global.trusted-host vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com
pip config set global.index-url https://vm-192.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com/automation-packages
```

Now you may pip install remoteZtoolset:

```
pip install remoteZtoolset
```

try to run `rz -h`

# remoteZtoolset
The remoteZtoolset is a suite of command line tools for remotely interacting with Z systems. This toolset provides functionality for quickly establishing passwordless SSH connections, locally mimicking remote file systems, and obtaining/saving data for the 3270OE and all your other automation needs.

Read *installation/update steps* for your platform [here](/Automation/remoteZtoolset/installRZT.md)

## Adding Systems:
- ### Adding a system
    In this context, adding a system is a means of quickly establishing a passwordless SSH connection to a remote host, saving the connection/general system information, and creating a subdirectory for storing local copies of remote files from that system. This is all done through the use of the rz-add command. Adding a new system requires the use of the -i/-ip/--ip flag, which accepts an IP address as an input. The username is assumed to be 'hmcmanager' by default, however a different username can be specified using the -u/--user/--username flag. For example, the following command would attempt to add a system using 9.56.56.1 as the IP address and' exampleuser' as the username:

> rz-add -i 9.56.56.1 -u exampleuser

This will add the same system using the default username of 'hmcmanager':

> rz-add -i 9.56.56.1

This runs through the process of generating(if needed) and copying an SSH key(~/.ssh/rzt by default) to the server with the given IP address.
    This also saves an entry for the system into a csv file and performs a basic system file pull, both of which are expanded upon in other sections.

## Saved Systems:
- ### System Data
    Upon adding a system, an entry for the system is added/updated into a local csv file(/path/to/remoteZtoolset/systems.csv by default). Each entry contains the following data fields:

> hostname,username,ip,ssh_timestamp,system_type,serial,model,os_level,nametag,machine_type,ssh_key

This allows for quick reference to general data for multiple systems through the use of the rz-sys command. Using the rz-sys command will quickly display stored system information. The rz-sys command can also perform basic queries as well as filter the data fields of the output. The following command will display all system information stored in the csv file:

> rz-sys

This will display system information for system(s) that have a hostname of "test":

> rz-sys -q hostname test

This will display the hostname and serial of all stored systems:

> rz-sys -s hostname 'machine serial'

This will display the username and os level of systems that have an ip of 9.56.56.1:

> rz-sys -q ip 9.56.56.1 -s username 'machine os level'

serial'

This will display the username and os level of systems that have an ip of 9.56.56.1:

> rz-sys -q ip 9.56.56.1 -s username 'machine os level'

- ### Nametags
    There's also functionality for giving machines a unique custom identifier. Each system entry has a datafield called "nametag" which essentially serves as a unique label for each system that can be set by the user. For example, the following will display information for a system with the value 'test' in the nametag datafield:

> rz-sys -n test

This will set the nametag of the system with the ip of 9.56.56.1 as "test2":

> rz-sys -q ip 9.56.56.1 --set-nametag test2

These nametags are the primary means for identifying target systems when using other tools in remoteztoolset. For example, the following command will start an ssh connection with a system assigned the nametag of "test2":

> rz-con -n test2

## Pulling Remote Files:
- ### zfilepulls

Each system that has been added or pulled from has its own directory created under ~/.rzt_data/zfilepulls. Each of these directories are named as the system's hostname. For example, if a machine has a hostname of "test", then that system's pull directory would be:

> ~/.rzt_data/zfilepulls/test/

This essentially acts as the system's root directory. When files are pulled from the system, the complete path to that file is replicated within the pull directory and saved at that location. For instance, if a file was pulled from the same system at /console/data/example.txt then the contents of the file would be saved locally as:

> ~/.rzt_data/zfilepulls/test/console/data/example.txt

- ### Performing Pulls

Pulling remote files can be done using the rz-get command. Assuming rz-add was previously used to save the connection, the file used in the previous example would be saved locally by running the following command:

> rz-get -q hostname test -f /console/data/example.txt

If rz-add was not used to add this system, then the -u/--user option could be used to input the username and ip address instead of -q/--query.

## Consoles
- ### Parsing Configs
    Consoles are obtained by pulling, then parsing, /console/data/iqzc*.trm files from a system.
    This parsing operation can be done through using the rz-parse-icc command. This command takes a system input through the use of -n/--nametag. The following will pull and parse all files that match the path /console/data/iqzc*.trm on the machine with a nametag of test:

> rz-parse-icc -n test

The output is written to a json file with the same naming convention as the zfilepulls directores. This json file is saved into a subdirectory named osc_sessions. If this tool is used to parse consoles from a system with a hostname of test, that output would be saved to this location:

> ~/.rzt_data/systems/osc_sessions/test.json

NOTE: This uses a script in EST_Tools called chpidbreakdown.pl to filter out outdated config files. It is reccomended that the target system is IML complete and has EST_Tools installed when running this tool.

n.pl to filter out outdated config files. It is reccomended that the target system is IML complete and has EST_Tools installed when running this tool.

- ### Selecting Consoles/Systems
    Specific consoles can be selected from session data files and saved as a new file. This is done through the rz-sel command. This can be used by specifying the files to select data from using -f/--files. If no files are specified, you will be prompted to select from the available system/session files. This is done through a selection interface and it is the same interface used for selecting consoles/systems.

The way this interface works is the items to select from are displayed in an indexed list. The user is then prompted to enter the indexes of the items to select. The input accepts both numbers and ranges using a hyphen('-'). The following input would indicate the selection of items 12, 13, 14, 15, and 18:

> 12-15 18

put accepts both numbers and ranges using a hyphen('-'). The following input would indicate the selection of items 12, 13, 14, 15, and 18:

> 12-15 18

There are two ways to write the selections to a file. The output path can be given beforehand using the -o/--output option when running the command.  If the -o/--output option is not used, the user will be prompted if and where they want to save their selections after they are made. The following command will launch the selection interface using consoles from the system with the nametag test2 and write the selections to an output file called test2.json:

> rz-sel -n test2 -o test2.json

The output file of the previous command would be written to this path:

> ~/.rzt_data/systems/osc_sessions/test2.json

This would open the selection interface for all session data between two files:

> rz-sel -f test3.json -f /users/exampleuser/documents/test4.json

These files being located on the local system at:

>~/.rzt_data/systems/osc_sessions/test3.json
    >/users/exampleuser/documents/test4.json

st4.json

These files being located on the local system at:

>~/.rzt_data/systems/osc_sessions/test3.json
    >/users/exampleuser/documents/test4.json

- ### Session Files.
    By default, files created using rz-parse-icc will be in a JSON format. That being said, session files can also be in a csv format. Outputting session data in these formats is as simple as defining the output file as a file with a txt or csv extension when using rz-parse-icc (-o/--output filename.csv) or rz-sel in the ways described previously.

## Command Reference:
- ### rz-add:
    Establishes a passwordless SSH connection with a remote server and saves the system/connection data.

# CEC Interaction

This directory contains utilities for interacting with Central Electronic Complex (CEC) systems, including environment checking and system operations.

## Contents

- [IML Utility](./rz-mcl.md) - A tool to run IML remotely, select IOCDS and power cycle
- [Environment Check (envcheck)](./README_envcheck.md) - Tool for checking CEC environment configuration and status
- [System Operations (sysops)](./README_sysops.md) - System operations utilities for CEC management

## Overview

These utilities provide programmatic access to CEC systems for automation and monitoring purposes. They enable checking system configurations, performing operations, and integrating CEC management into automated workflows.

# Environment Check
Using `rz-envcheck`, we can learn pertinent info about the state of a system while working on it.
## Running on the command line

### Check status of CEC
The following command options allow you query the status of your CEC:
```
rz-envcheck B24 -status iml
rz-envcheck B24 -status power
rz-envcheck B24 -status clocks
rz-envcheck B24 -status xstop
```

### Find PBUs for scom commands
This will return a list of PBUs that have Pavo or Felis cards plugged.
```
rz-envcheck B24 -pbu
```

### Find last used IOCDS
This will return the ID of the last used IOCDS or none of one cannot be found.
```
rz-envcheck B24 -iocds
```

### List the cores on the system
Running the following command will list the cores present on the system:
```
rz-envcheck B24 -cores
```

metadata.section_heading: List the cores on the system

content:
### List the logical cores on the system
Running the following command will list the logical cores present on the system:
```
rz-envcheck B24 -lcores
```

content: ## Importing and calling from python

### status functions
thing_to_check is one of: iml, power, clocks, xstop
Result is boolean, True - iml complete, powered on, clocks running, not checkstopped
```
from rzutilities.modules.environment_checker import z_system_power_iml_check

# Set Arguments
z_system = "B24"
thing_to_check = "iml"

# check IML state
status = self.environment_checker.z_system_power_iml_check(
                z_system=z_system,
                thing_to_check
                )

print(f"IML is complete: {status}")
```

### pbu
Return a list of lists. List entries per plugged PBU have form: `[fru_type, enclosure_id, slot_id]`
```
from rzutilities.modules.environment_checker import find_pbu

# set argment
z_system = "B24"

pbus = self.environment_checker.find_pbu(
                z_system=z_system
                )

print(f"PBUs with plugged hub cards: {pbus}")
```

### iocds
```
from rzutilities.modules.environment_checker import get_previous_iml_iocds

# set argument
z_system = "B24"

iocds_id = self.environment_checker.get_previous_iml_iocds(
                z_system=z_system
                )

print(f"Last IOCDS used: {iocds_id}")
```

### cores
Return a list of lists. List entries per plugged core have form: `
zme.core -e0x13 -s0x10F4 -p1 -c6`
```
from rzutilities.modules.environment_checker import find_cores

# set argument
z_system = "B24"

cores = self.environment_checker.find_cores(
                z_system=z_system
                )

print(f"Cores available in config: {cores}")
```

### machine_type
Return the machine type as "zme" or "za". Format suitable for scom commands.
```
from rzutilities.modules.environment_checker import find_machine_type

# set argument
z_system = "B24"

machine_type = self.environment_checker.find_machine_type(
                z_system=z_system
                )

print(f"machine type: {machine_type}")
```

### rzt_connect_test
Attempt to use remoteZtoolset rz-ex function to issue `pwd` to target system. Returns True, connect test worked or False.
```
from rzutilities.modules.environment_checker import rzt_connect_test

# set argument
z_system = "B24"

result = self.environment_checker.rzt_connect_test(
                z_system=z_system
                )

print(f"result: {result}")
```
# System Operations Utility - IML, Power off/on

metadata.section_heading: System Operations Utility - IML, Power off/on

content:
## Kick off an IML from the command line
The following command will run an A0 IML on the target system. This will only perform an IML if the system is not already IML complete.
```
rz-sysops B24 -iml A0
```

To perform an IML even if the system is IML complete. Use the `force` flag.
```
rz-sysops B24 -iml A0 -force
```

metadata.section_heading: Kick off an IML from the command line

content:
### Power On, Off, or do both
This will Power off the machine. Use the `force` flag to force the power off:
```
rz-sysops B24 -power off -force
```

Or to power on:

```
rz-sysops B24 -power on
```

This will power off the system and then power it back on. Note the `force` option to force the power off:

```
rz-sysops B24 -power both -force
```

from rzutilities.modules.system_operations_utility import iml_controls

## IML Utility

### Passing `-h` or `--help` argument

To view all arguments for a script use the `-h` or `--help` flag to view all required
arguments.

```text

usage: rz-iml [-h] [-u] [-p] [-r] [--force] [--viewIOCDS] tagName [IOCDS]

IML Utility

positional arguments:
  tagName      The system TAG name for the operation
  IOCDS        The IOCDS identifier for the operation

options:
  -h, --help   show this help message and exit
  -u           This will undo IML for a system

  -r           This will retain last IML'ed IOCDS and IML the system
  --force      Force the IML operation

'

# Installing IML Utility Tools
Author: Naga Revathi Peri
Date: 04/02/2025

## Clone the Repository

For your laptop, it's recommended to clone it using Github Desktop.

OR

Clone the repository to your laptop using following command

cd ~
    git clone git@github.ibm.com:systemz/IMLUtility.git

## Install The Code

Navigate in a terminal to where IMLUtility was cloned, and do a pip install. For the TOAD containers, this would be:

cd ~/IMLUtility
    pip install .

In a UNIX-based environment (i.e. TOAD, Mac, Linux), you can check the version:

pip list |grep imlutility

You should get a version number back.  On Windows, you can do a `pip list` and look through all your installed Python packages.

# IML

## Initial Machine Load

Author: Naga Revathi Peri
Date: 04/02/2025

## What is IML

In the context of IBM z/VM and IOCDS (I/O Configuration Dataset), “IML” stands for
“Initial Machine Load,” which refers to the process of booting up a central processor complex (CPC) and loading the current I/O configuration stored within the IOCDS, essentially initializing the system’s input/output connections based on the defined settings.

### What is IOCDS

The IOCDS defines the hardware configuration to the physical CPC (central processor complex).The IOCDS allows the various devices, channels, etc. to understand what is attached to the box.One IOCDS can serve multiple LPAR’s
## Current Active Process

### Through Support Element:

Navigate to SE Console Application via web browser or VNC.
 Open Power on Reset task
 Select desired IOCDS (A0,A1,A2,A3, or D0)
 Perform IML.

### Through SE CLI:

SSH to SE.
 Execute command “zseiml LPAR A<#>.”With desired IOCDS (A0,A1,A2,A3, or D0)
 Perform IML.

Most of the comforts the Support Element GUI offers could be replicated in a TOAD CLI way that could actually improve the IML experience while positioning us to integrate this step into much more E2E and semi manual process flows.

This solution would provide a CLI way and python class functions that supply amenity to the IML CLI tool which is already included with tools systems

## Importing and calling from python
The real power of check_for_refcodes is when you use the functions from your automation code.

Basic idea:
1. Define a list of analysis rules in a configuration file to decide what events in the iqyylog to analyze and whether to treat those matching events as errors (designated failures), whitelist (acceptable errors), or required (must be present)
2. The result of analysis is pass or fail plus a return code from 0-4 and your code can make decisions based on that return, i.e. `[return_code, return_text]`.
3. Supporting evidence for the analysis result is provided.
4. The tool keeps track of what it's doing in `check_for_refcodes.log`.

## How to define the rules config file
The default config file is `default_analysis.xml` and is in the python lib packages path. A user specified config file, if used, must be in the TOAD mount point directory.

There is also a `sample_analysis.yaml` config file. By running, `setup_cfr_samples.py` you can copy the sample yaml file to your TOAD mount point directory.

```

metadata.section_heading: How to define the rules config file

content: # Rule file

# Can have multiple rule nodes in the file to cover all test cases
rule:
  key: default  # Default key is used if no key is specified

prefilter:  # Specify the grep patterns to use
    pattern:
      - "\\+"

iqyyfiles: # Specify a list of iqyy*.logs to use, default is iqyylog only
    pattern: []

strict_checking:  # Strict checking True or False
    pattern: "True"

errors:  # Specify what to search for in the log that would indicate the test failed
    pattern:
      - "^.{26}\\+"

whitelist:  # Specify errors found above that should not be flagged as failed
    pattern: []

required:  # Specify what SHOULD be found in the log (e.g., system events), otherwise rule failed
    pattern: []
```

content: ## Calling check_for_refcodes from your code

### Sample programmatic useage sequence
1. your_script does some stuff, and calls *check for refcodes* with arguments:
   - **system** and **init**. This establishes datetime pointers for *check for refcodes*.
2. your_script runs some tests then calls *check for refcodes* with arguments:
    - **System**, **analyze**. Analysis uses `default` behavior that finds all **“+”** events in iqyx output.
    - No events found: Return code 0, Pass
    - At least one event found: Return code 1, Fail
3. your_script handles the return code and text:
    - If RC=0, Pass, then *go back to 2.*
    - Else, RC=1, Fail, perform some exit handling
4. your_script does some end of run processing including call *check for refcodes* with arguments:
    - **System** and **history**. This causes history print of all **“+”** error events.

# rz-get-osc-sessions

[GitHub Repository](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/rz-get-osc-sessions)

## Purpose

For any list of `z systems`, fetch and parse OSA-ICC (Open Systems Adapter - Integrated Console Controller) session data. This tool retrieves console session configurations including LU names, IP addresses, ports, device addresses, and console types for all configured OSC sessions on target systems.

## Install

`rz-get-osc-sessions` is included as part of the `rzUtilities` package, which is available in `TOAD` and our `self-hosted Python package registry`. Instructions for installing from that registry can be found [here](../../README.md#installing-automation-tools).

If you want to install `rz-get-osc-sessions` as a `standalone` package, you can get the latest package file [here](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/rz-get-osc-sessions/releases/latest). Once you download either the `zip` or `tar ball`, you can simply run the following:

```bash
pip install /path/to/package/rz-get-osc-sessions*
```

## Usage

:::note
This tool requires that you have entries in the [remoteztoolset](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/remoteZtoolset/) systems table for your target systems. Only `SE` (Support Element) type systems are supported.
:::

### Help Menu

```bash
rz-get-osc-sessions -h
```

### Basic Usage

Fetch OSC session data for one or more systems:

```bash
rz-get-osc-sessions nametag1 nametag2...
```

Or using the `-n` option:

```bash
rz-get-osc-sessions -n nametag1 nametag2...
```

### Filtering Fetched Data

:::note
The following filter options can be combined. Each filter option supports an `--exclude` flag to exclude the passed values from the final output instead of including them.

For **multi-system requests**, filters must include the nametag prefix (format: `nametag:field:values`).
For **single-system requests**, the nametag prefix is optional.
:::

#### Filter by LPAR

```bash

# Single system (implicit nametag)
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 --lpar SAK13A1,SAK13A2

# Multiple systems (explicit nametag required)
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 B40 --lpar A40:SAK13A1,SAK13A2 B40:SAK13B1

# With exclude flag
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 --lpar SAK13A1,SAK13A2 --exclude
```

#### Filter by CSS (Channel Subsystem)

```bash

# Single system
rz-get-osc-sessions B40 --css 0,1

# Multiple systems
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 B40 --css A40:0,2 B40:1,3

# Exclude specific CSS
rz-get-osc-sessions B40 --css 0,1 --exclude
```

#### Filter by PCHID

```bash

# Single system
rz-get-osc-sessions B40 --pchid 01C8,0310

# Multiple systems
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 B40 --pchid A40:03EC B40:0310
```

#### Filter by LU Name

```bash

# Single system
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 --lu_name T13BHP14M,T13BHP51M

# Multiple systems
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 B40 --lu_name A40:SAK13B3 B40:T13BHP14M
```

#### Filter by Device Address

```bash

# Single system
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 --device 5400,5409

# Multiple systems
rz-get-osc-sessions A40 B40 --device A40:0060 B40:5400
```

#### Filter by Console Type

Valid console types: `Operator Console`, `System Console`, `TN3270`, `TN3270E`

```bash

`rz-get-partition-ids` is included as part of the `rzUtilities` package, which is available in `TOAD` and our `self-hosted Python package registry`. Instructions for installing from that registry can be found [here](../../README.md#installing-automation-tools).

If you want to install `rz-get-partition-ids` as a `standalone` package, you can get the latest package file [here](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/rz-get-partition-ids/releases/latest). Once you download either the `zip` or `tar ball`, you can simply run the following:

pip install /path/to/package/rz-get-partition-ids*

## Trusted Computing Violations

### What are Trusted Computing Violations?

When certain hardware issues occur on the SE, a marker file is created at `/console/data/pa/bad_drive_file`. When this file exists, it causes three serious problems:

1. **Mirroring is suppressed** - The primary SE stops copying data to the alternate SE
2. **Periodic refcodes are logged** - System keeps reporting errors
3. **New MCLs can't mirror** - Any new MCL you install won't copy to the alternate SE

### How rz-mcl Handles This

**Automatic Detection:** Before applying MCLs, `rz-mcl` automatically checks for trusted computing violations (even in `--dry-run` mode).

**Default Behavior:** If violations are detected, the tool will stop and display a warning:

```
⚠️  WARNING: Trusted computing violations detected!
   File /console/data/pa/bad_drive_file exists on the SE.
   This suppresses mirroring and inhibits new MCLs from mirroring to alternate SE.
   Periodic refcodes are being logged.

❌ MCL apply cannot proceed with trusted computing violations.
   To fix this issue, use the --force flag:
   rz-mcl S03 B99 --force
```

**Using --force Flag:** To automatically fix violations before applying MCLs, add the `--force` flag:

```bash
rz-mcl tst B01 --force
```

This will:
1. Detect the violations
2. Run `tc_fixer.py -f` to clean up the violations
3. Verify the fix was successful
4. Proceed with MCL apply

**Note:** The `--force` flag will NOT fix violations in `--dry-run` mode. It will only report what would happen.

**Important:** MCL applies targeting the HMC are not currently supported by the tool. This tool is designed for zSystem CPC MCL installations only.

Author: Eric Reid

## Introduction

This automation has three parts designed to help automate bringing up and down z/OS. Originally designed for use with daily driver testing, it is broadly applicable.

## Setup

1. In an HMC where your system(s) you are trying to IPL z/OS are defined, you must setup an automation user. Right now, this is:
User: `automate`
Password: `abc123`

This user must be authenticated to activate LPARs, receive API calls, and work with Operating System Messages.

2. Your z/OS sysplex must already be able to auto-IPL using the z/OS Automated IPL procedure, outlined [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/CommonProcedures/Operating%20Systems%20On%20Z/zOS/Automated%20IPL%20Setup).  Both your cold and warmstart LPARs must use this method to IPL from activation. This automation only uses the partition activation commands from the HMC.

## Creating Your YAML

In your TOAD container, (recommended in your mount point), set up a z/OS IPL YAML file. An example is included in the rzUtilities repository, and outlined below:

D container, (recommended in your mount point), set up a z/OS IPL YAML file. An example is included in the rzUtilities repository, and outlined below:

zOSIPL: # required, sets IPL block for zOS
        testcell_1: # need some user-defined key per system, arbitrary
            timeout: 3600 # max time to wait for things, in seconds. default is 3600 seconds (1 hour)
            cecname: 'mycec' #cecname as shown in HMC/SE
            hmcip : 'myip' # HMC to use for API calls
            cf_partitions : #List of CF partitions on this CEC to activate
                - "CF01"
                - "CF02"
            cold_lpar_list: #List of LPARs on this CEC to cold start
                - "TC4R01"
            warm_lpar_list: #List of LPARs on this CEC to warm start
                - "TC4R02"
                - "TC4R03"
        testcell_2: # need some user-defined key per system, arbitrary
            timeout: 3600 # max time to wait for things, in seconds. default is 3600 seconds (1 hour)
            cecname: 'mycec' #cecname as shown in HMC/SE
            hmcip : 'myip' # HMC to use for API calls
            cf_partitions : #List of CF partitions on this CEC to activate
                - "CF01"
                - "CF02"
            warm_lpar_list: #List of LPARs on this CEC to warm start
                - "TC4R02"
                - "TC4R03"

                - "TC4R02"

Requirements:
1. You must start with a `zOSIPL` block. This is to enable future integration with other operating systems.
2. You must seperate each CEC in your plex into a unique block within `zOSIPL`.
3. Your `cecname` must be what is displayed in your HMC as your CEC.
4. You must specify the IP address of the HMC to use.

### On partition lists

You can have multiple partitions in each of the `cf_partitions`, `cold_lpar_list` and `warm_lpar_list` parts of the YAML. This enables a user to specify multiple sysplexes worth of cold starts, CF's, etc. The code will skip any LPARs that are `Operational`.

## Running the Automation

Ideally, run the automation from TOAD, though the package can be cloned anywhere, all the dependencies exist in TOAD already.

Run the script with: `zosipl _options_ _yamlfile_ `

Options:

-sd, --shutdown,  Specify to shutdown z/OS. Runs `ro *other,%shutdown` in each cold LPAR, waits for the partitions to be `Not-Operating`, issues `%shutdown`, and then waits for the cold LPARs to be shutdown.

-cf, --cfactivate, Specify to activate CF partitions. Activates the CF partitions in `cf_partitions` in the YAML file.

-ipl, --iplzos, Specify to IPL z/OS. Activates all cold partitions in `cold_lpar_list`, checks each are in the JES-PLEX with `$D MEMBER(1)`, then activates all the warmstart partitions and waits for them to be `Operating`. Note the last few warm IPL LPARs may need another couple of minutes to enter the JES-PLEX and be ready to run workload. Future ZoweLab code can help figure this out.

Yamlfile, required. Specify the file path to your YAML file. If you run the script from a directory with the YAML file, you can just specify the YAML file. Otherwise, specify the full path to the file in the filename.

## What can go wrong

This automation will fail if you have problems, especially during the IPL sequence. In the case of these failures, manually recover the IPL with Operator Messages or a 3270 console. In the event of any other errors, please open a Github in the rzUtilities [repo](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/rzUtilities).

With ZOA Utilities, you can run traditional MVS™ commands, such as IEBCOPY, IDCAMS, and IKJEFT01, as well as perform several data set operations in the scripting language of your choice.

ZOA Utilities is useful for z/OS developers who want to automate tasks that access MVS resources.

# D61C Bundle Regression Recommendations

This section of the user guide contains the bundle regression recommendations that are generated by Bob for each bundle.  Bob passes the output of [Jupitr Insight's](/Automation/JupitrInsights/README.md) into a script that reformats the excel file into a format more easily ingested by an LLM.  A skill was adapted to describe the desired report structure and details as well as what to avoid. Using the skill, bob is able to read the test procedure for hundreds of fixes and summarize the areas with the most changes which should therefore receive the most attention during that bundle's regression test efforts.

:::info Important!
  When any bundle breakage is discovered that can be attributed to tests motivated by this report we would like to ask EST teams to mark defects with tag #bobregression
:::

:::note
This initiative started on bundle S26 and was first attempted during S24 so reports since then are included.
:::

## Testing Methodology Recommendations

### 1. **Prioritization Strategy**
- **Tier 1 (Critical)**: I/O Topology, FICON/FCP, Partition Management
- **Tier 2 (High)**: Crypto, HMC/SE, MCL/MCF
- **Tier 3 (Medium)**: Network, Hardware, Storage Groups, Logging
- **Tier 4 (Low)**: LICCC, GUI/UX

### 2. **Test Environment Requirements**
- **Hardware**: Petra, Pegasus, Musica cards
- **Switches**: Cisco and Brocade configurations
- **Systems**: z17, Metis, pre-Metis systems
- **Browsers**: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge
- **Users**: Multiple concurrent users with different roles

### 3. **Automation Opportunities**
- API call monitoring and validation
- Property change event verification (STOMP clients)
- RPM version queries
- Log file parsing and validation
- CSV export data integrity checks

### 4. **Common Code Transparency**
Many test procedures note "common code" or "driver transparency" requirements. These should be validated through:
- Standard regression test suites
- No new errors in logs
- Consistent behavior across code updates
- Successful MCL activation/deactivation cycles

---
## Risk Areas Requiring Extra Attention

### High-Risk Areas:
1. **Concurrent Operations**: Multiple partition updates, bulk volume operations
2. **Timing Windows**: SE removal, alert expiration, cache cleanup
3. **Permission Boundaries**: Crypto operations, dual control workflows
4. **API Efficiency**: Redundant calls, thread management
5. **Data Consistency**: Property change events, STOMP notifications

### Known Defect Patterns:
- NullPointerException during bulk operations
- Timer-USER events in logs
- Incorrect connection counts (>100 connections)
- Missing end nodes in topology views
- Case sensitivity issues (uppercase requirements)

---

## Conclusion

This regression test summary identifies **12 major functional areas** requiring emphasis beyond the specific test procedures documented. The highest priority areas are:

1. **I/O Topology & Storage Management** - Most frequently tested, highest complexity
2. **FICON & FCP Adapter Management** - Critical for I/O operations
3. **Partition Management & Processor Configuration** - Core system functionality

Testing should focus on:
- **Multi-component interactions** (topology views, concurrent operations)
- **Permission and security boundaries** (crypto, dual control)
- **Performance and efficiency** (API calls, connection counts)
- **Data consistency** (property changes, event notifications)
- **Browser and platform compatibility**

Regular regression testing should cover all areas, with increased depth in Tier 1 and Tier 2 categories, especially when common code changes are introduced.

# DASD

For more information on DASD and DASD-related procedures & automation, please contact Katherine Reid (katherine.porfirio@ibm.com) on the SLT Team.

## Introduction

This document serves a foundation of understanding of the different components and functionality inside of the DS8K, specifically the DS8900 series DASD, along with some of the key features. The objective at the end of understanding this document is for the reader to be able name each of the parts of the DS8K, identify their location in the system, as well as understand where the DS8K sits in a enterprise computing and storage ecosystem.  In addition, the information in this document will be referenced in other informational documents, conversations with the POK SLT team, and in storage procedures.

This document is not a replacement of a similarly named section in the DS8K Redbook, however the point of this document is to compress that information into a more easily digested form, that is more readily useful for the test team. Important terms are highlighted throughout the document, so that they can be readily found and remembered.

## What is Storage? What is DS8K?

In enterprise computer systems, there are three main pieces that interact to be able to process transactions and other user requests. The first is the **processing unit**, in IBM enterprise systems, that is the z-series (z15, z14, etc.). This is where the main transactions take place. Once transactions take place, they need to be transmitted through a **network** to **storage**, where the data, logs and other information is stored for later processing, analysis or archiving. These three main components, the processing unit, network and storage, each have many layers of complexity beneath them. The goal of this document is to discuss one of IBM’s storage products, the **DS8000 series**.

![alt text](images/Storage%20Picture%201.png)

The DS8000, often abbreviated DS8K, is one of IBM’s storage products. Enterprise data storage is a diverse and complex field, where a customer must balance cost, speed, reliability and redundancy with each new component in their data storage ecosystem. Each storage technology has a variety of advantages and disadvantages in each of these categories. The DS8K is typically used as the high speed-high availability counterpart to the IBM z-series; designed to be fast, readily accessible storage for processing and analytics. As such, the DS8K is an expensive piece of hardware in terms of storage space per dollar and is a poor choice for long-term archival storage, for which IBM has tape storage products. The difference between the three main modern storage technologies as well as some perspectives to other storage technologies will be discussed later in this document. The focus for Z testing will be on DS8K, due to their close cooperation and similar purpose. Because it historically has been directly attached to the mainframe and remains the storage unit most closely connected to the mainframe, the DS8K is frequently called the **DASD** (pronounced dæzdi), which stands for Direct Access Storage Device.

most closely connected to the mainframe, the DS8K is frequently called the **DASD** (pronounced dæzdi), which stands for Direct Access Storage Device.

The DS8K is designed around this high-speed, high-availability goal. The heart of the DS8K is where the data is actual stored, called **drives**. You may hear them called “disk drives” for historical reasons, however the more accurate term for the newest DS8900 is to just say drives due to how the data is now stored. The difference in wording will be explained later. In order to efficiently get data into and out of the DS8K, there are other pieces of technology such as input/output bays, and computation drawers, as well as two monitoring and management computers. Each of these components will be explained in this document. However, to get a better understanding of where the DS8K fits into the modern enterprise storage environment, we’ll first talk about the different methods of digital data storage.

## Different Digital Storage Technologies

There are three primary methods that are used in modern computers and enterprise systems for digital data storage, each of which have their advantages and disadvantages. It is important to acknowledge the existence of the three main technologies, as you may encounter them especially with older hardware, or if you interact with customers. Each storage option is best suited for a different application.

### Flash Storage

Flash storage is by far the newest type of storage, having initially been invented only in the 1980’s. Due to this recent history, as well as how flash storage is built, it is the most expensive of the three main storage technologies in bits/$. However, this cost has been drastically decreasing as the technology has matured and can now be found all over the world. Flash storage is used in USB sticks, your phone, and now the new **DS8950F is entirely flash-based storage**. Flash storage has the best resilience of the three technologies to vibration and mechanical problems, as well as some of the fastest read and write times due to the lack of moving parts. Flash storage is relatively complicated to explain the inner workings of, and therefore more detailed descriptions require their own document (see the LVL 2 document on this technology). The key take-away is that flash is relatively expensive, fast and reliable storage.

### Spinning/Hard Disk

This technology has its roots back to the 1950’s and the IBM RAMAC storage. This technology relies on magnetic domains being flipped back and forth between North and South to represent 1’s and 0’s in a spinning platter, or disk. This spinning disk is the origin of the term “disk drive”. The technology has greatly matured over the past 70 years, and is still used in many enterprise environments, as well as older DS8K models. **IBM no longer manufactures an enterprise-grade storage system with spinning disk drives**. Hard disks have a cheaper bit/$ ratio compared to flash storage but is generally slower than flash storage. Due to the mechanical nature of the spinning disk, the drives are more susceptible to mechanical failure, especially in large arrays like in enterprise storage, where they must be specially engineered to combat these types of failures. Hard disk storage is still popular as a relatively fast storage method that is more economical than flash storage.

### Tape Storage

Tape storage also began in the 1950’s, though the technology is slightly older. In tape storage, magnetic stripes are flipped back and forth similarly to hard disks, but the tape is wound around a central spool. Tape storage has very low write speeds due to the need to move to each point in the tape, and very poor random read due to the same reason. Sequential reads are slightly faster, but still very slow. However, **tape is the cheapest storage by nearly an order of magnitude in terms of bits/$** compared to hard disk, and has excellent data retention over time, making it excellent for archival storage that may need to be accessed occasionally. IBM continues to make tape storage which incorporates advanced robotics to sort and utilize a vast library of tapes without needing all of them to be powered on.

## Components of the DS8900

The DS8900 is based around the flash storage, which are arrayed in a **High-Performance Flash Enclosure (HPFE)**. For redundancy, these enclosures always come in pairs and are mirrored to each other, so that if one enclosure encounters an error the data can be preserved in the other enclosure. Inside the HPFE there are an array of 2.5” flash drives, which are vertically aligned and have a flashing LED at the top indicating they are processing data. Due to the nature of flash storage, **they will typically be flashing even if new data is not being processed**. The number of HPFE’s depends on how much storage the customer wants to pay for. In addition, each HPFE pair can be filled with different types of flash storage that has different capacities and speeds, each of which has its own cost. Each HPFE pair must have the same disks however, for RAID to work. RAID will be explained later in this document.

The **storage servers, also referred to as CEC’s or P9 (POWER 9 processor) servers**, process the incoming data from the I/O bays and passes it to the HPFE’s for storage. The CEC’s have internal memory that can operate as another faster layer of storage for data that is accessed frequently enough, however this is transparent to users. All DS8900’s that are shipped to customers include a special type of memory called NVDIMMs (Non-volatile Dual-In-line Memory Module) is able to retain data in flight even if the CEC power is cut, which reduces data loss in disaster situations. The CEC’s communicate with the I/O bays and the HPFE’s through PCIe Gen3 interfaces. There are two CEC’s in the DS8900, which are redundant, and workload can dynamically be passed between them. Each CEC has a separate LPAR, labelled ESS01 and ESS11 which can be talked to by other programs and the HMC’s.

The **I/O bays** use optical (FICON, FCP) and sometimes copper interfaces to take data from the network, and have two ports on each bay for zHyperlink, which a direct high-speed link between a z-series and the DS8K that bypasses the network link for small, data-logging jobs. Each bay is accessible by each CEC, though they have a primary assignment that they prefer if everything is operating properly to spread workload evenly. Each I/O bay has a set of different cards (such as Plaquemine, Portage) that connects through the back plane to an interface card (known as the Sturgeon card) to the CEC. zHyperlink is directly connected to the Sturgeon card. The I/O bays also have two **device adapter** (DA) cards that process the data coming over PCIe from the CEC’s and transmit them onto the HPFE’s. The DA’s are also responsible for data encryption and RAID management.

The **management enclosure** contains two **Hardware Management Consoles (HMC’s)** which are used to manage the different components of the DS8K, and are what are typically used by field technicians, service personnel and customers to monitor the state of the DS8K, as well as to service the machine. For those familiar with the z-series, this is akin to the Service Elements (SE’s), though it has many of the same functionality for the DS8K as the z-series HMC. Try not to confuse the two HMC’s here between the z-series and the DS8K. Other documents in this library will discuss how to login to the different interfaces of the DS8K HMC’s and there are several procedures using these components. The HMC’s are redundant.

The **KVM unit** is a laptop that can be used to interact with the HMC’s directly on the DS8K, and a set of cables at the bottom of the backside of the DS8K can be used to switch between the two. In practice, it is typically easier to do day-to-day operations from a remote computer.

In addition, the DS8K has redundant power through two sets of **iPDU’s** (intelligent Power Distribution Units). These units can monitor power, and switch to the internal backup batteries on the NVDIMMs if needed. The DS8K is entirely air cooled, including for the processors in the CEC.

The DS8K can be extended to have a second extension frame with more I/O bays and HPFE’s, this is used to have even more storage in a single DS8K.

## Reliability, Redundancy and Accessibility

As mentioned in the previous section, many of the components inside of the DS8K are redundant so that the system can continue to function even if individual parts fail. However, in the modern enterprise environment data integrity is so essential that IBM has implemented a suite of different products to ensure that data is protected in a variety of different failures. Different clients will use different combinations of these products depending on their needs, and how much money they have to spend on data reliability and integrity.

### RAID

**RAID** is a method invented in the late 1970’s and implemented in the early 1980’s to address single-drive failures. There are a variety of different RAID levels, which balance speed or performance, data redundancy and cost in different ways. RAID was originally called Redundant Array of Inexpensive Disks, though this was changed to Redundant Array of Independent Disks as the disk drives became more and more expensive.

RAID has three methods of ensuring data redundancy in case of a drive failure: **mirroring, striping and parity**. Mirroring is the process of having two identical, up-to-date, copies of a dataset on two different drives. Therefore, if one drive fails, the data is preserved on the mirrored drive. In addition, because each drive can be accessed individually and don’t really need to talk to each other to ensure data redundancy, mirroring typically gives higher performance to the system. However, this means that each byte of storage available to the system really requires two bytes of space, doubling the cost of the storage system without increasing the system space.

Striping involves placing a single volume of data across multiple disk drives. Therefore, when a user puts data into a logical volume, the data is spread across all of the disks in an array. This doesn’t provide any data redundancy but does enable the workload to be spread across all of the disks evenly, instead of having heavily accessed volumes stored on a single disk that wears faster than all others.

Parity is a mathematical operation that can be performed across disks to increase data redundancy. Although the actual Boolean math isn’t too difficult to understand, it is unnecessary to know for most users. The best way to think about Parity is as a simple addition problem. If I have data A on Drive 1, B on Drive 2 and C on Drive 3, I could calculate a “parity” number by saying that P = A + B + C. The P “parity” number is stored on either a different drive or on a different section of each of the drives in the array (Drives 1,2,3 and P are in an array). Then, if one of the drives (say Drive 2) fails, I could just use math from the other three drives to calculate the data lost: B = A + C – P. Again, the actual math is a Boolean statement, but the principle is the same.

Parity increases redundancy and enables fewer backup drives than mirroring. In the example above, for the price of four disks, I get three disks of usable space, whereas I would get two from a mirroring operation. However, calculating parity for each of the bits on the disk takes additional computation that slows down the system compared to mirroring. Additional problems arise during reconstruction, where data is rebuilt using the parity math after a drive failure. On large drives (2TB +) this process can take hours or days, and on large arrays with large drives this can take a full week. During this time, the entire array is under extreme strain performing this math, and it is highly likely that another disk will fail, at which point all the data in the array is lost.

Different RAID levels combine parity and mirroring in different ways to try and get the best of both functions. There are two primary RAID levels used in enterprise storage, RAID 6 and RAID 10.

#### RAID 6

RAID 6 uses two different parity calculations, with volumes striped across the array, and the parity information striped across the disks as well. The advantage of RAID 6 is that due to the dual parity, two drives can fail before all the data is lost. This enables a drive to fail even during long reconstructions without a complete loss of data. RAID 6 requires the overhead of calculating two parity bits, which is typically performed in enterprise systems by an Application-Specific integrated Circuit (ASIC) specially engineered to perform the calculations as fast as possible. Even with ASIC’s, RAID 6 does relatively poorly with random reads and writes to the array.

#### RAID 10

RAID 10, also known as RAID 1 + 0, is where data is striped across two sets of disks, and then mirrored between the two sets. This means that for each write or read, only the two pools are involved, and there is no need for any additional calculation. Data redundancy is provided by the mirroring to the second pool. This method can provide much faster read and write speeds compared to RAID 6, however doubles the cost per bit, as each array of disks takes is only half used, the rest is mirrored.

### Copy Services

Although RAID provides protection against a single drive failure, it doesn’t prevent a disaster from wiping out an entire DS8K system and all the data inside. To prevent against data loss in these disaster scenarios, IBM has a variety of features collectively known as **Copy Services**. Copy Services can create a complex, interconnected network of storage for a variety of redundancies at various levels, and with different types of storage and equipment. Copy Services is an additional cost for customers and depending on which features they have enabled can be very costly.  However, for customers who can’t afford to lose data, Copy Services is a method to make sure data is protected in all situations.

There are many Redbooks and a plethora of other documentation on various Copy Services features, however much of this is beyond what someone starting out needs to know right away. This document will just introduce a few of the key services, where they are used, and various limitations involved.
