#### Flash Copy

**Flash Copy (FC)** is a method of instantly creating a point-in-time copy of a storage volume to another volume inside of a DS8K, or between two DS8K’s. This can then be used for remote copying without interrupting primary workload volumes or can be used to perform separate analytics on this point-in-time data set, or to copy data from DS8K to another once.

#### Metro Mirror

**Metro Mirror (MM)** is a method of data mirroring between two DS8K systems. The nominal specification is for MM DS8K’s to be less than 300km apart from each other, though in practice many are located at the same site, possibly in different buildings. MM is a synchronous system, where the data needs to be written to both DS8K’s before they report back to the mainframe that a write has completed, and the short distance between them ensures that this shouldn’t take too long. MM typically has a primary DS8K that directly talks to a mainframe, and a second DS8K used as the mirroring, backup system that talks to the primary DS8K. Metro Mirror is sometimes referred to as PPRC (Peer-to-Peer Remote Copy), a legacy term.

In some MM configurations, specifically in zHyperswap configurations, if a primary DS8K becomes non-functional during operation, data can be automatically re-routed to the secondary DS8K in the MM. This requires many different features and FICON connections between the mainframe and each of the DS8K’s involved but can provide a high-level of availability to customers that need it.

#### Global Mirror

**Global Mirror (GM)** is a method of data mirroring to remote sites through a global network. Since the global network is of unknown speed and quality, this is an asynchronous system, where reads and writes are performed to a primary DS8K on site first, then sent separately to the secondary DS8K at the remote, global site without the mainframe’s knowledge. GM can be performed off a MM secondary box, which is called an MGM (Metro-Global Mirror) configuration. GM is useful for situations when an entire region may be compromised, such as in floods, hurricanes, or mass power outages, that the data can be preserved at offsite, and typically off-continent locations.  GM also typically performs the mirroring operation with regularity, for some clients as frequently as every second to ensure that most of the data is preserved.

## Conclusion and Further Reading

This information is designed to get a reader familiar with the basic concepts in IBM storage, as well as more specific details of the DS8K. Feel free to ask people in the Storage test team (SLT) any questions you may have.

# EST Daily Driver Acceptance Tests
Documentation for the tests related to daily driver acceptance.

## Daily Driver Acceptance
EST daily driver (DD) acceptance testing is accomplished by automated, self-checking code that can be initiated by the zFW development continuous integration process. The tests rely on a TOAD runtime environment.  This runtime is called by the zFW CI Jenkins process after the daily driver is loaded onto the target EST primary and alternate SEs.  In the language of DD testing, EST tests are tier three, of three tiers.  Tier one is subsystem integration testing and tier two are system integration tests that automatically cause the DD snapshot to be declared status red, i.e. failed, on the [DD dashboard](https://dd-dashboard.dal1a.cirrus.ibm.com/#/driver-status/D6X_HEAD).

In practice, anything that can be automated via TOAD can be part of this automated pipeline.

## Reporting failures and reaching the right help
Please use the [dailydriver_est](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C06CP1CQ3UK) slack channel and [@schaufle](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/DAEBG30E6) and [@wojciak](https://ibm.enterprise.slack.com/archives/D8AE789AT) to get our attention.

content:
## Debug steps
1. Check the slack channel entries and the dashboard entry.  By clicking on the red `est_tests` dashboard entry you are taken to the Jenkins pipeline results and from there can get the console output.
2. Look into the console output to see how far along the pipeline got.

aken to the Jenkins pipeline results and from there can get the console output.
2. Look into the console output to see how far along the pipeline got.

* Sometimes the pipeline fails checking the primary and alternate SE driver levels.
* Sometimes the pipeline fails trying to load the primary or the alternate snapshot.
* Sometimes the pipeline fails launching the `start_dd_tests` script.  When this happens, the problem is almost always an issue with the ssh keys we need to talk from the TOAD to the SE.  We use remoteZtoolset for this.  By doing the `rz-con -n B24` command from inside the TOAD container, you will see if the connection is made or there is an issue with ssh keys.  In the later case, you need to run `rz-add -i 9.56.192.91` for `B24` to fix the keys.  The next time through this shouldn't be the problem.
* There has been a hang of the target SE under ticket `1072861`.  This is still under debug as of `20240815`.
* There are cases were a pipeline run fails.  Then the next pipeline run also fails because a lock on the Jenkins side needed to be cleared by the system integration team.

# Preventing the automatic Jenkins pipeline from running
To prevent your machine from being disrupted from a Jenkins pipeline process, on your primary SE touch the file: `/home/hmcmanager/no_est_test`.  This flag is good for one night suspension of snapshot install.

In order to prevent snapshot installs for more than one night, on your primary SE touch the file: `/home/tester/no_est_test_persist`.

- This option is available in the AROM for HMC, TKE, and SE.

# How to Load an AROM

An AROM load is a fundamental task here on the EST testfloor. It is our main way of loading the Drivers we test, once we start our EC mode test phase and test cycle. The following procedures are a guide of the various ways we load AROMs here on the EST testfloor

## Below are a few things to keep in mind while loading an AROM.

- Before loading an AROM you may need to install or change your trusted computing keys. More information and procedures for trusted computing keys can be found [here](/CommonProcedures/Z%20Configuration%20Help/TrustedComputing/Trusted%20Computing%20Key%20Setup.md)

- instances where you may need to reload Trusted computing keys:
        - New System install without knowledge of what is installed
        - switching from Production to Hybrid keys or vice versa
        - Bad or corrupted Trusted computing Keys

- #### Always save a copy of your Upgrade data to a USB before an AROM load

- HMC: HMC manager -> Save Upgrade data task
        - the Upgrade data file should be saved as UpgradeDataAllTower.zip

- SE: SE manager -> save Upgrade data task
        - the Upgrade data file should be saved as SEUpgradeDataAllTower.zip

## HMA-SE: Alt SE Preload
The following procedure is a guide on Alt SE preload. this method of code load Uses the HMC to drive a SE code load on the Alternate SE that is defined on the HMC. The Alt SE Preload includes the following task in order.

- save upgrade data
- Alt SE code load (via EC upgrade)

### Procedure

1) For the target Alternate SE to be preloaded, ensure that Service Status has been enabled on the Pri SE.

2) Ensure the HMC being used has the correct USB AROM inserted and is NOT the HMA HMC that is
hosting the Alternate SE. (Use either the HMA HMC that is hosting the Pri SE, or a Traditional HMC)

3) On the HMC, Systems Management → select the system → Alternate Support Element EC Changes (ECs)
under the Change Management task list.

4) Select ‘Upgrade Alternate SE (Preload)’ and press OK.

5) Press option ‘Removable Media’.

6) Select the correct image from the displayed list and press OK. Then press OK again on the next panel that
shows the EC Streams being upgraded.

7) Select the system from the displayed list and press OK.

8) Let the preload run until completion.

9) Login the Alt SE and review the iqyylog for any errors or problems.

10) If no errors, then perform a SE switchover to make the preloaded Alt SE the new Primary SE.

11) Login the Pri SE and review the iqyylog for any errors or problems.

12) If no errors, install any delta MCLs and make a new backup critical data for use to Restore the new Alt SE.
# AROM

## What is an AROM
An AROM is media with the combination of MCP, driver application, and active MCFs, used to load code for SEs,HMCs, and TKEs. Each AROM is built with a 'Control' level which includes all the released MCL bundles at that time the AROM was built. We typically start using AROMs when we enter EC mode test phase.  Besides base code loads, an AROM can be used for recovery or reload of a system, if a hard fail occurs or if your system is stuck in a bad state. Keep in mind the AROM load procedure is a disruptive task.

- There are 2 types of AROMS. "Tools"(development) and "no tools"(production or customer) AROMS
- AROMs are available at the EST HMC/SE corner on collum K-11, 012-2. Please return the AROM after you are done, someone else may need them.
- We keep AROM for the last 3 drivers familys. Curently these are Z15(Themis), z16(Aretemis), z17(metis)

# ssh to SE or HMC

Connecting to a system via ssh is essential to working on the machines. It is the most efficient way to peruse the file system, diagnose certain problems, run [SE tools](/Automation/SE_Tools/README.md), and more.

It is also necessary for accessing VNC on all drivers D41C and on.  Starting on D61C, tools systems require ssh to access the console application via web browsers.

This guide covers the basic distinctions you need to know for each driver model, covers manual commands. Lastly it talks about [RemoteZToolset](/Automation/remoteZtoolset/README.md), the preferred automation to connect to systems as efficiently as possible.

## Pre-requisites

Before you can ssh into a system, you need to be on the Poughkeepsie site VPN, have a terminal capable of ssh, information about the system, and BlueGroup authorization.

1. **Poughkeepsie Site VPN**: You must be connected to the Poughkeepsie site VPN to access the systems. If you are not connected, you will not be able to SSH into the systems.
    2. **Terminal**: Any terminal emulator that supports SSH (Terminal.app mac/linux, WindowsSubsystem for Linux on Windows, or the terminal in VS Code)
    3. **System Information**: You need to know the IP address of the system you want to connect to. This information can be found in the system's slack log
    4. **Authorization**: You must be in [zSystemHardware](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2/requests/new?element=9967&authorities=603) bluegroup on SWAT:

:::warning[IN CASE YOU LIVE UNDER A ROCK]
D61C Tools systems REQUIRE you to register an ssh key in SWAT and zAUTH.  We will tell you how to do this.
:::

## Basic SSH Syntax
The way you authenticate will differ for each driver version and for tools vs production systems, but the basic syntax is the same.  Certain environments support Loopback Ports which help you access the console GUI via either VNC or Browser.

The standard command to SSH into lab systems is:

```bash
ssh hmcmanager@<SE or HMC_IP_ADDRESS>
```

:::tip
If you don't like typing hmcmanager 10x a day or remembering IPs, the RZT Command is simply: `rz con <SE or HMC NAME>`
Read about installing remoteztoolset [here](/Automation/remoteZtoolset/installRZT.md)
:::

## The SSH Key

For all cases, you will benefit from having an ssh key.  If you know you have one already, ensure it has been added to SWAT and zAUTH. If you don't have one, follow the steps below to generate and register an SSH key.

### Generating an SSH Key

1. Open your terminal
2. Run: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"`
3. Press Enter to accept the default file location
4. You will be prompted for a passphrase - you can press Enter twice to leave it blank (recommended)
5. The public key will be saved in `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`

You can now view your public key with `cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` and copy it to your clipboard.

### What to Do with your ssh key

This key should be used by default for all ssh connections unless you made prior environment changes.

You are going to want to add the key to SWAT and zAuth to reach any D61C or beyond systems.  The command `ssh-copy-id` will exchange the key with legacy. You can also copy this key pair to be used by remote z toolset.

## Troubleshooting

### Enable ssh on production

Most production systems have SSH disabled by default. To enable you must create what is known as a marker file which will tell the system to enable ssh after the next SE/HMC Reboot.  This marker file is named `/console/data/noopcallpasswd`

1. Get a command window by any means possible.  This could probably be done in a web browser connection to the SE/HMC, searching for 'command' in the task search.
2. Enter command `touch /console/data/noopcallpasswd` and press enter.  This will create the marker file.
3. Reboot the SE/HMC.  This should be done with the task in SE or HMC Management.

When the SE comes online, retry your ssh activity.  D61C currently removes ssh access after the *next reboot* :(

### "Host key verification failed"

**Cause**: System was reinstalled or SSH host key changed

**Solution**:
```bash
ssh-keygen -R <SE_IP>
```
Then try connecting again and accept the new host key.

### "Connection refused" or "Connection timed out"

**Causes**:
- Not connected to VPN
- System is powered off or not network accessible
- SSH Is nt Enabled or Firewall blocking SSH port (22)
- Incorrect IP address or username typo

**Solutions**:
1. Verify IP address is correct, no other typos like `hmcamnger`
2. Ping the IP address: `ping <SE_IP>`
3. Check if SSH port is open: `telnet <SE_IP> 22`
4. Check if you are on VPN

### "Permission denied (publickey)"

**Cause**: SSH key not registered or not distributed to system

**Solutions**:
1. Verify key is registered in [SWAT](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2/)
2. Ensure description includes `server:hmcse`
3. Wait 5 minutes for key distribution
4. Try connecting again to trigger key refresh
5. Check that you're using the correct private key:
   ```bash
   ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 hmcmanager@<SE_IP>
   ```

### LDAP Authentication Failures (D41C/D51C)

**Cause**: LDAP server not configured for secure ports

**Solution**: See [fix_ssh_ldap](/CommonProcedures/Z%20Configuration%20Help/fix_ssh_ldap.md) for driver-specific fixes

### "Too many authentication failures"

**Cause**: SSH trying multiple keys before finding the right one

**Solution**: Specify the correct key explicitly:
```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 hmcmanager@<SE_IP>
```

Or configure SSH config file (`~/.ssh/config`):
```
Host <SE_IP>
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    IdentitiesOnly yes
```

1.	Plug in Trusted computing key USB.

6.	At the end of trysted computing key install type reboot and press enter to continue
7.	Break into bios and confirm secure boot is enabled.

content:
### Updating Daily Driver on HMC

- If you reload a HMA-HMC you will need to load the virtual SE after the HMC is loaded.

1.	Save upgrade data of HMC and SE to hard drive and USB
2.	Enable "Service status" on Primary SE
3.	Shutdown virtual SE
4.	Stop HMC application from starting using the following command:
```mv /console/data/actzdesk.dat /console/data/actzdesk.bak```
5.	Reboot HMC. It should come up to blue screen.
6.	sudo startx to open gray background GUI
7.	right click on gray screen GUI and open a terminal
8.	sudo zdnf
9.	enter your jfrog artifactory token.
10.	Select option 4 (to uninstall current driver)
11.	Then select option 1 (to install driver)
12.	Verify driver stream is "D6X_HEAD_HMC", then press Enter
13.	Press Enter for next two options
14.	At advisiory prompt, type in daily driver (e.g.: hmc-D6X_HEAD-20241003_1100)
15.	Type "y" to install
16.	Selection: X (to Exit, after driver is successfully installed)
17.	Verify ```/mnt/upgrade/restore/restore.lst``` file is present
18.	If not then, ```cp /mnt/upgrade/restore/restore.stf /mnt/upgrade/restore/restore.lst```
19.	Ensure restore.lst states to retrieve tower data from “HARDDRIVE”
20.	Type "reboot" to reboot HMC
21.	Allow HMC to come up, restore will complete (upgrade data will be restored from hard drive)

### Updating Daily Driver on SE

1.	If not already done, then save upgrade data from Primary SE to hard drive and USB
2.	Same upgrade data must be used to restored Alt SE
3.	Mount USB with upgrade data on Alt SE
4.	On USB, copy SEUpgradeDataAllTowers.zip to UpgradeDataAllTowers.zip
5.	From USB copy UpgradeDataAllTowers.zip to Alt SE subdirectory ```/mnt/upgrade/uplinux```
6.	Unmount USB
7.	If not already done, then enable "Service status" on Primary SE
8.	Deactivate CEC
9.	Stop SE application from starting
10.	```mv /console/data/actzdesk.dat /console/data/actzdesk.bak```
11.	Reboot SE. It should come up to blue screen.
12.	sudo startx to open gray background GUI
13.	right click on gray screen GUI and open a terminal
14.	sudo zdnf
15.	enter your jfrog artifactory token.
16.	Select option 4 (to uninstall current driver)
17.	Then select option 1 (to install driver)
18.	Verify driver stream is "D6X_HEAD", then press Enter
19.	Press Enter for next two options
20.	At advisiory prompt, type in daily driver (e.g.: se-D6X_HEAD-20240926_0141)
21.	Type "y" to install
22.	Selection: X (to Exit, after driver is successfully installed)
23.	Verify ```/mnt/upgrade/restore/restore.lst``` file is present
24.	If not then, ```cp /mnt/upgrade/restore/restore.stf /mnt/upgrade/restore/restore.lst```
25.	Ensure restore.lst states to retrieve tower data from “HARDDRIVE”
26.	Type "reboot" to reboot HMC
27.	Bring down system (shutdown both SE and HMCs)
28.	Turn OFF breakers if possible
29.	Turning breakers ON
30.	Allow system to come up, restore will complete (upgrade data will be restored from hard drive)
31.	Power ON and IML with D0 first

# HMC & SE Procedures

This section contains procedures for Hardware Management Console (HMC) and Support Element (SE) operations.  Including accessing the machines, driver loading, updates, configuration, and more.

## Contents

- [RSF Call Home Setup](./RSF%20Call%20home%20Setup.md) - Configuration procedures for Remote Support Facility (RSF) call home functionality
- [AROM](./AROM/) - AROM (Active Release of Microcode) procedures for loading and updating system code
- [IBM Z HMC HOWTO videos](./hmc_howto_videos/README.md)

## Overview

These procedures cover essential HMC and SE operations including:
- Initial system setup and configuration
- Daily driver installation and updates
- Remote support facility configuration
- AROM media usage for code loads and recovery

### Understanding System Types

These procedures cover essential HMC and SE operations including:
- Initial system setup and configuration
- Daily driver installation and updates
- Remote support facility configuration
- AROM media usage for code loads and recovery

#### Support Element (SE)
The SE is the primary management interface for IBM Z mainframe systems. It provides:
- Hardware management capabilities
- System configuration and monitoring
- Access to the Hardware Management Console (HMC) interface
- Direct control of the CPC (Central Processor Complex)

#### Hardware Management Console (HMC)
The HMC manages multiple systems and provides:
- Centralized management of multiple CPCs
- Workload management
- System monitoring and reporting
- Remote management capabilities

#### Trusted Key Entry (TKE)
The TKE workstation provides:
- Cryptographic key management
- Secure key loading operations
- Crypto configuration management

## Contacts

For questions or procedure updates, contact:
- James Burke
- Hiten Gandhi
- Yu Li

# RSF Call Home Setup HMC SE

Information and utilities for setting up RSF (aka callhome) on the HMC and SE.

Enabling RSF is required for the following:

Problem reporting (to IBM*)
    TSAD
    VPD Transmit
    Firmware downloads (excluding from FTP servers)
    Mobile notifications
    LICCC Downloads (CoD, SAR, BvP, R&V)
    Attestation reports
    Remote Code Load

*Test systems are no longer capable of opening “real” tickets on the IBM side (now CSP)
Registration

All development and EST systems must be registered in zRSF, otherwise all RSF requests will fail.

Registering these systems in zRSF allows the system to access all of the remote support capability, while also bypassing any attempts to open cases in CSP. Instead, for problem reports from dev/test systems, zRSF returns a mock response and completes the transaction. No data is upload to ECuRep. If needed, for details on how to test with CSP see est-csp-overview

See here for a (probably) current list of dev/test systems registered in zRSF:
zrsf-temp-entitlements

Reach out to the zfw-rsf-test slack channel to request a system be added.

RSF (callhome) setup

All Remote Support Facility (RSF) requests are handled by an HMC. The HMC is the only component within zFW that communicates directly with IBM. In order to submit RSF requests (such as Report a Problem, Transmit Service Data, Mobile Notifications, etc) some setup is required on the HMC.
Manual RSF setup on the HMC:

Open Customize Customer Information, fill out the required fields.
        Please use real contact names, and email
    Open Customize Outbound Connectivity -> Configure ... -> select Enable the local console ...
    Optional: Perform the Test ... under Customize Outbound Connectivity -> Configure ...
    Optional: If you want to esure only this HMC will handle RSF requests it submits, de-select Use discovered ...
    Optional: In order for the HMC to callhome for itself:
        Open Customize Remote Service
        Enable all options, use any dummy phone #.

# HMC VPD

RSF requires that the HMC have valid VPD, including a valid MTM/SN of the 'owning CPC’. Its the owning CPC SN which is used to check entitlement for RSF requests that originate from the HMC, including the new Test Transaction in D40.

If you want to change the MTM or SN of the HMC’s owning CPC, you can use the Update HMC Configuration Data task on the HMC (as PEMODE or equivalent) to update the HMC VPD.

For real HMC hardware, VPD is typically already in place, but on zFOCS HMCs you will need to set VPD from scratch using the tqyvvpdc commandm which will prompt for information on the associated CPC. You can also copy over an existing VPD file and reboot the HMC.

Its recommended you use the SN of an actual CPC in the lab or EST, or a system listed in the zrsf-temp-entitlements list above, as those should be entitled for service.
Manual RSF setup on the (CPC) SE:

he lab or EST, or a system listed in the zrsf-temp-entitlements list above, as those should be entitled for service.
Manual RSF setup on the (CPC) SE:

Open the Remote Service task.
        Enable all options, use any dummy phone #.
    Open Customer Information, fill out the required fields.
        Please use real contact names, and email
        NOTE: If you do this from an HMC, it will copy the HMC’s customer info the SE, if the SE data is not set.
    Open the Manage Remote Support Requests task
        Go to Options -> View All Call Home Servers
        Verify at least one HMC is in the list. If so, the CPC setup is complete.
    If no HMCs are listed, or the expected HMC is not listed, go to that HMC and:
        Verify the CPC is defined to the HMC and communicating. Add the CPC if not defined.

        Verify that Act as call-home server is enabled.

By default, the config for new driver builds points to the production environments.

D50C and newer

Starting in Artemis, RSF uses the new hmrs-client for all HTTP requests to IBM. The hmrs-client config can be found at /console/data/hmrs-client/hmrs-client.properties

To switch between different zRSF environments, run:

`hmrs-client -m switch -n <env>`

To see the current environment and hmrs-client version:

Use the callhome-switch command to change target zRSF environment.

For this will need the tools package, or the callhome-setup-pfix (for D41C or older).
Installing the callhome-setup pfix

For D41C and older the callhome-setup-pfix.zip can be install to provide the callhome-switch command and some other utilities.

Install via:

fix -p callhome-setup-pfix.zip
export PATH=$PATH:/console/bin/test/

To switch between different zRSF environments, run:

`callhome-switch <env>`

The supported environments are:

- prod
- prd
- prd-direct
- pre
- pre-direct
- cdt
- cdt-direct

If the callhome-switch command is not available (i.e. tools cannot be installed), or if there are other settings you wish to change, there are config files that can be edited, which differ dependin on the driver.
callhome config

On D41C and older, RSF used the callhome component to drive all HTTP requests to IBM.

I’t primary config file is /console/data/callhome/config.xml.

The default file in the driver does include entries for CDT and PREPROD, both EDGE and Direct. To use
those you can simply uncomment those lines. If another environment is needed see an RSF developer for further guidance.

## What is a BMC?
Baseboard Management Controllers (BMCs) are the network interface cards that facilitate communication between the CPC/IO drawers and the SE. BMCs operate in Master-Secondary pairs with one BMC able to go fully offline while the other compensates for this by picking up its workload. This happens during normal system proceses such as PSCN MCL updates, manage power service state activation, switch auto reboot scheduled operations, etc. Occasionally, our testing requires us to reboot BMCs ourselves. Below are instructions on how this operation can be performed.
## How to reboot a BMC

### Finding your BMC
Most commands targeting the BMCs address them by the control domain ID (CDID) of the drawer that they are in. The easiest way to view this information is with the command `bbqpscnmon.se` via the SE command line. The result should be similar to the image seen below
![Alt Text](./images/bbqpsnmon_readout.png)

This data can be used to target any BMC in the system. In order to determine what drawer a BMC belongs to, simply refer to the second digit of the cdid. For example, the BMC with cdid 0x51 resides in CPC1. The BMC with cdid 0x6C resides in IO12.

### Issuing the reboot command
Once a BMC has been selected, rebooting it is as simple as issuing the command `bbqssh-bmc.sh cdid[XX]-[role] /sbin/reboot` where **xx** is the CDID of the target BMC , and **role** would be either "master" or "slave" depending on which BMC is being targeted. For example, to reboot the master BMC in CPC3, the command would be `bbqssh-bmc.sh cdid53-master /sbin/reboot`.

An alternative command that can be used is `bbqcli.se hostman cdid[XX]-[role] [reboot/takeover]`. This has the same functionality as the previous command with the added utility of being able to trigger a takeover. This option prompts the secondary BMC to issue a command to the master BMC telling it to reboot itself. This causes the secondary BMC to take over as the Master which in turn causes the previous master to become the secondary upon completing it's reboot.

This causes the secondary BMC to take over as the Master which in turn causes the previous master to become the secondary upon completing it's reboot.

The [Power thermal automation Suite](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/SE_Tools/EST_Tools/Power/) also contains a tool, namely ptBmcRI (power thermal BMC reset inject), that autonomously triggers system-wide BMC reboots in a loop over a user-designated interval. See the linked page for more information on that tool.

# How to Perform a JEMT Roll

This procedure is a guide on how to switch out your JEMT consoles/systems. These procedures include what to do with your current HMA-SE/ Traditional SE in preparation for JEMT roll, and Procedures on how to setup and load code on your New JEMT, wether it be a Traditional SE or a HMA-SE.

- JEMTs will come either as HMA or a Traditional SE depending on how the corner orders them.
- Both top and bottom 1Us will be loaded with Production Keys and the current driver(s) that MFG is shipping with.

## Pre JEMT-Roll Procedures:

Before powering off and disconnecting the existing system, do the following:

1.	Zeroize all configured Crypto’s.
    - target CPC > Configuration > Cryptographic Configuration > select ALL > Zeroize

2.	Do an Update HOM & VPD  (z15 only) or Rebuild VPD (z16 and up)

3.	Save Upgrade data from both HMA-HMCs (lable them to identify each HMC) and the Primary SE to USBs and FTP server.
    - For traditional SEs, save upgrade data from the primary SE to USB and FTP server.

4.	Makes Sure you remove all lab owned parts that was installd to the system and move all cards back to thire original location.

## Removeing TER records before returning a JMET
For instances where you have added a TER record to you SE confiuration, you must remove the TER record before returning your JMET. Follow this procedure to remove the TER record.

1. On your SE, navigate to Configuration > Perform modle conversion

2. navigate to Temporary Upgrades > Manage. If you have any TER file they will be listed here. If you do not have a TER record a message stating no file will be dispalyed.

3.  Any TER records listed will be in either an active or installed state. If there is a TER listed, ensure that it is not in an active state.

- If the Ter record is active, you must put it into an intalled state. To do this, select the record and use the Remove Processors button. Use the Undo radio button, press OK. A panel indicating the removal of the commodity should be displayed. Press OK. This should change the record to the installed state.

- If the Ter Record is in the installed state proceed to step 4

4. If the TER record is in the installed state you can delete it using the radio button

content: # Configuring a Dump Volume

## Dump Volume Background
The dump volume is an additional storage volume that can be used to dump the memory content of a linux LPAR onto DASD for later failure analysis. The size of this volume must be greater than the amount of memory in the LPAR for the dump to succeed. To trigger the dump, the "Load a dump program" option should be selected in the LOAD task when targeting the configured partition. This will of course be disruptive to the linux partition.

## ECKD Set up the linux LPAR
The following instructions were tested on RHEL 8.6 but should be similar on other linux versions.

[The IBM instructions](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/linux-on-systems?topic=dadd-installing-tool) lacked some details but provides a nice outline which is elaborated upon below.

0. Bring the volume online
    `lscss` command will show you the online devices in your lpar.
    ```console
    lscss
    Device   Subchan.  DevType CU Type Use  PIM PAM POM  CHPIDs
    ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    0.0.0930 0.0.0260  1732/01 1731/01 yes  80  80  ff   be000000 00000000
    ```

# Linux On Z

IBM Z has been able to run linux since 2000, but there has been recent emphasis on these capabilities in Z's marketing strategy on recent models in the form of the LinuxOne mainframe server.

A Linux One system is using the same hardware and firmware as the equivalent classic Z model, but feature codes dictate that all the processors in the system are set as IFLs (Integrated Facility for Linux) thus making it so only Linux runs on servers with this feature.

In the lab we run Redhat, SLES, and Ubuntu. Generally we focus on the two latest stable releases for each Linux version unless there is an explicit need for some test.

Installations are currently automated using Rundeck. You can learn more about Rundeck [here](/Automation/LinuxOnZ/RundeckLinuxAutomation/rundeck.md)

Contact Sarath Muddana or Jeff Martin for help with your linux environment requirements
# Operating Systems on Z

## Testing with LPARs

The Z platform is renowned for blazing the trail to virtualization well before other architectures were running Virtual MAchines (VMs).  LPARs (Logical Partitions) provide isolated environments for testing underlying firmware functionality on Z Systems. Each operating system offers different abilities for exercising specific firmware areas, making it essential to use multiple operating systems for thorough test coverage.

A high-end Z System can run up to 85 Logical Partitions simultaneously, sharing the underlying processor, memory, and channel subsystem resources. An LPAR performs an IPL (Initial Program Load) to boot up an OS, this is the equivalent of the "start" task on partition objects in DPM Mode.
## Operating Systems

### z/OS

z/OS is IBM's flagship enterprise operating system for Z Systems, providing robust transaction processing, security, and workload management capabilities. From a testing perspective, z/OS excels at exercising complex I/O subsystems, cryptographic operations, and multi-workload scenarios that stress system resources under realistic enterprise conditions. Its comprehensive system management facilities make it ideal for validating firmware behavior under production-like workloads.

[Learn more about z/OS procedures](./zOS/README.md)

### Linux on Z

Linux on Z (including distributions like Red Hat, SLES, and Ubuntu) provides an open-source environment that is particularly effective for testing modern cloud-native workloads and containerized applications. Linux excels at validating IFL (Integrated Facility for Linux) processor functionality, network I/O performance, and KVM virtualization features. Its flexibility and extensive tooling make it valuable for automated testing and continuous integration scenarios.

[Learn more about Linux on Z procedures](./LinuxOnZ/README.md)

### SAK (System Assurance Kernel)

SAK is a specialized operating system developed internally at IBM specifically for hardware and z/Architecture verification. It provides the most comprehensive framework for low-level hardware testing, executing pseudorandom test sequences that rigorously evaluate CPUs, I/O cards, cryptographic cards, and their interactions. SAK's ability to autonomously cycle through configurations makes it unparalleled for uncovering hardware anomalies and validating processor instruction sets, cache coherency, and serialization behavior.

[Learn more about SAK procedures](./SAK/README.md)

### z/VM

z/VM is IBM's hypervisor for Z Systems, enabling multiple operating system instances to run simultaneously on a single LPAR. From a testing perspective, z/VM is invaluable for validating virtualization features, testing multiple operating systems concurrently, and simulating complex multi-tenant environments. It excels at exercising memory management, virtual I/O operations, and resource sharing mechanisms that are critical to modern mainframe deployments.

[Learn more about z/VM procedures](./zVM/README.md)
# System Assurance Kernel (SAK)

## What is `SAK`?
The `System Assurance Kernel` (`SAK`) is a specialized operating system developed for internal use at IBM. Its primary purpose is to provide a robust framework for hardware and z/Architecture verification through a comprehensive suite of diagnostic and stress tests.

`SAK` enables users to rigorously evaluate mainframe components- including CPUs, I/O cards, cryptographic cards, and various combinations of them. SAK operates by executing pseduorandom test sequences. Once a test program is initiated with user-defined parameters, SAK autonomously cycles through a wide range of configurations to maximize test coverage and uncover potentional hardware anomalies.

## Test Coverage Areas
SAK supports a broad spectrum of hardware validation scenarios, including:
* Processor Achitectures
    - Single-Processor (UNI)
    - Multiple-Processor (MP)
* Instruction Sets
    - General and Control Instructions
    - Branching Instructions
    - Floating-Point Operations (HPF, BFP, and DFP)
    - SIMD Instructions
* System Behaviours
    - Cache Coherency
    - Serialization
    - Memory Access Ordering
* I/O Subsystem
    - I/O Devies and Subsystem

## Primary Users
Sak is utilized across multiple engineering and testing domains within IBM, including:
* z/Series Processor Hardware System Testing
* z/Series New Machine Bringup
* z/Series Processor Engineering Validation
* z/Series EC Level and Machine Driver Testing
* DASD/Control Unit Engineering Test
* z/VM Regression Testing
* Z/Series I/O Attachment Testing

## SAK/PCX Hardware Requirement
`SAK` can be `IPLed` (Initial Program Loaded - I.e. Booted) in two different ways: `PCX` and `SAK`

### `PCX` Mode ("Sak in the Box")
* Pre-installed on the Support Element (SE) hard disk of each z/Series machine.
* Utilized the SE disk for both SAK execution and spooling.
* Interaction Occurs via Operator Console Mesages.
* Does not require an I/O cage.

### `SAK` Mode
* Requires three dedicated disks:
    - SAK IPL Disk
    - SAK Spool Disk
    - SAK Dump Disk
* Interaction can be performed via:
    - A dedicated SAK Console (e.g., OSC session)
    - The Operatror Messsage Console.

## SAK User Guide
For more general information, please consult the [SAK Userguide](https://ibm.ent.box.com/s/ijdzetb4bvrbajfjfv5g4zzddjj9kf4i), or reach out to a SAK developer.

# Automated z/OS IPL Setup
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 08/09/2023

## Introduction
This procedure outlines how to setup your z/OS LOADxx and USER.PARMLIB to enable an automated, 3270 console-free IPL. Depending on how many sysplexes and LPARs you have, this can take anywhere from an afternoon to a few days to setup, but is a fully customer-supported method to IPL z/OS.

Additional reference links will be provided for more details from IBM, and details about what is happening and why will be included. The goal is to be a straightforward, comprehensive guide to automating your z/OS IPL. Some of these steps are also required for the 3270 OE-controlled IPL sequence, such as AUTORxx.

ward, comprehensive guide to automating your z/OS IPL. Some of these steps are also required for the 3270 OE-controlled IPL sequence, such as AUTORxx.

Your IPL is likely already customized to you, and different teams have different levels of automation during z/OS IPL. This guide assumes you have nearly no automation at all, so you can go check through your configuration. IBM also provides a few different places that some of these parameters (such as SYSPARM) can be defined. This is but one implementation, but the underlying IPL process follows the same flow. If you already have parts of your z/OS IPL sequence automated in different ways, make sure you learn and understand that before continuing.  Reading this guide can help you find some of the key areas where your current automation exists.

## Step 1: Understanding your Activate and IPL
Likely, your IPL starts from activating partitions in your HMC or SE. A few customizations here can make this process much faster. In your HMC (or SE), navigate to selecting your z/OS partitions, then select Operational Customization -> Customize/Delete Activation Profiles. Select whichever profile you use (if you use multiple, you'll have to go one at a time), and select Customize Profile.

Select the Load option from the left hand side, and it should bring you to this ![screen](images/activationloadscreen.png)

If you have nothing in the "Load" and "Load parameter" boxes, this means that you have either memorized or written down somewhere what those parameters are for your sysplex (see later in this procedure for what these parameters mean). If this is the case, put whatever values you use into these boxes. If you use multiple values (say for different z/OS versions) you'll need different activation profiles with different load parameters. This guide is designed only for "normal" ECKD, CCW, z/OS loads. Other types of loads will need SME input.

The other major thing to enable here is the "Load during activation" button, which will automatically perform the "Load" operation after a partition is activated. This makes bringing z/OS up after an IML much faster.

### Explanation 1: Load Address and Parameters
The load address is a DASD device address where the z/OS bootstrap data is stored. In EST, these are standardized at address 4800-4802, with the different addresses corresponding to different z/OS versions (i.e. 2.4, 2.5, 3.1). This address is set in your IOCP that you IML'ed the Z with, or with the latest one dynamically applied and in hardware token. These devices live on EST "Infrastructure DASD", managed by Chris Moretti in coordination with the OSS team.

ynamically applied and in hardware token. These devices live on EST "Infrastructure DASD", managed by Chris Moretti in coordination with the OSS team.

The load parameter is composed of four parts (see the official IBM documentation for even more [details](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.5.0?topic=software-explanation-ainitialize-system-control-program-a2-field)). See IBM's parameter ![breakout](images/loadparameter.png).
The first two are strictly required. The first four characters are the DASD device address where your LOADxx parmlib member is located. The LOADxx member should be part of SYS#.IPLPARM. You may have multiple different SYS#.IPLPARMs on different DASD devices, this points to which one is the correct one for this load.  EST has standardized these volumes somewhere in the 4800,98 range, likely an IODFP# volser addresses 4840-4843. The LOADxx member conceptually takes the IPL further once the z/OS bootstrap is complete off of the load address.

:::note

:::note

The SYS#.IPLPARM may or may not be cataloged. If it is not cataloged, it cannot be accessed by Zowe or z/OSMF, and must be found specifying a volser through the ISPF 3.4 panel. You can find what volser this is by issuing the command `d u,dasd,,####` where #### is the first four digits of your load parameter. The device number can also be found in the output of `d iplinfo`.

:::

The next part of the load parameter is the two-digit pointer to your LOADxx member in SYS#.IPLPARM. This will be more important later, but for now write down this number.

The last two parts of the load parameter are optional. The third is the prompt feature, which is a set of characters that break out of automated IPL sequences and force operator responses to override settings set in this procedure. See the IBM help page listed above for more details, but the key table is copied here for ![conveinence](images/promptvalues.png).

The final parameter is for an alternate nucleus parameter. At this time the author knows very little about this parameter, please reach out to OSS for more details, or refer to the IBM documentation.

Tune all of these settings in every activation profile you use to IPL z/OS before proceeding to Step 2.

## Step 2: Configure your LOADxx
__The next steps require z/OS to be IPL'ed and operational. It is recommended to use Zowe or Zowe Explorer [see the guide here](/Automation/ZoweLab/README.md) to perform these steps, though uncataloged datasets won't appear in these interfaces. Cataloging datasets is outside of the scope of this procedure, but the author is willing to explain that if needed.__

Navigate to your SYS#.IPLPARM dataset in z/OS (see Step 1 Explanation for more details). You may have many LOADxx statements, or you may have very few. Either way, find the LOADxx where xx matches the character set in your load parameter.

:::note
If you want to have multiple IPL configurations (CF configs, system names, etc), this can be acheived by having different activation profiles point to different LOADxx members in the same SYS#.IPLPARM.
:::

:::

:::note
The LOADxx member has a lot of detail, this guide will go over key pieces of details, but the IBM documentation contains the definitive reference for all statements [reference](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.5.0?topic=sys1parmlib-loadxx-system-configuration-data-sets).  Details of each of the parameters can be found [here](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.5.0?topic=sets-statements-parameters-loadxx)
:::

Your LOADxx member may have some or none of the following pieces of automation. Here is an example of a "completed" ![LOADxx:](images/loadxx.png).

Note that the column position of these character is very important. OSS provides a header that specifies where user-specified changes must occur past (the "1" column")

### IODF
The first line points to your IODF dataset name to load the software IODF configuration. Normally, you should run with matched hardware and software IODF configurations.  An easy way to achieve this is to set the IODF number as **, where z/OS will read the IODF name from your hardware token and use that as its software configuration.  The HLEV section of the line specifies the High Level Qualifier (HLQ) for your IODF files. Default is to name IODF files as IODF.IODF##, and this parameter is set to "IODF".

:::warning
If you delete your IODF file or write over it, this can cause problems in this configuration because the IODF in the HW token may not match what is read in from the IODF file. Don't do this. See the HCD tools automation that can help you with HCD operations and IODFs.
:::

### SYSCAT
This specifies system catalog information. This shouldn't be changed without contacting the OSS team.

### IEASYM
This specifies a list of IEASYMxx members to use during IPL to configure system symbols and parameters.  You must include 00, which is provided by the OSS team and includes many "default" parameters.  Other members should exist in USER.PARMLIB  (see PARMLIB). IEASYM can be used to perform per-LPAR customization (see Step 3), however this guide takes the route of customizing the LOADxx instead. IBM has an entire document about the [decision](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.1.0?topic=parmlib-step-3-determine-where-specify-system-name#symnam__tabnamn).

### PARMLIB
This should at least include USER.PARMLIB.  Contact OSS procedures or consult IBM documentation if you need to use other or additional PARMLIBs. This specifies where other parameters can be specified.

### Other parameters
Your team may have a number of other parameters, depending on what you are doing and how you are doing it.

### LPARNAME and SYSPARM
This guide decides to specify sysparm members in the LOADxx member. Again, there are other places to do this.  This is done in LOADxx by a combination of two commands:
First, put the parameter LPARNAME, and specify your partition name as specified in your IOCP or as displayed in your HMC.
On the line after, put the parameter SYSPARM and point to a two digit hex number ##, which will correspond to a IEASYS## member in your USER.PARMLIB dedicated to this LPAR. This provides a clean association between partition and LPAR configuration. If you have the same partition names on different Z systems, you can specify HWNAME with your CPC name as defined in HCD before specifying LPARNAME for each of the partitions in that CEC. Again, see IBM's parameter [documentation](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.5.0?topic=sets-statements-parameters-loadxx).

:::caution
DO NOT SPECIFY 00 as an IEASYS## member. This will cause a LOGREC failure during IPL. 00 is reserved for OSS-provided defaults.
:::

Here is an example of an LPARNAME definition:

LPARNAME TC4R52
    SYSPARM  0F
    LPARNAME TC4R51
    SYSPARM  0E
    LPARNAME TC4R42
    SYSPARM  0D

extracted_errors: DO NOT SPECIFY 00 as an IEASYS## member. This will cause a LOGREC failure during IPL. 00 is reserved for OSS-provided defaults.

content:
Here is an example of an LPARNAME definition:

LPARNAME TC4R52
    SYSPARM  0F
    LPARNAME TC4R51
    SYSPARM  0E
    LPARNAME TC4R42
    SYSPARM  0D

You need to specify one pair of LPARNAME and SYSPARM for each LPAR you have in your configuration.

## Step 3: Configure IEASYM##
Your IEASYM## should live in USER.PARMLIB, which should likely be cataloged. This includes many sysplex-wide symbols, settings and details. You can choose to specify (or may already have specified)  your partition to LPAR association here, this would look like:

SYSDEF LPARNAME(TC4R52)
      SYSPARM(0F)

Again, the LPARNAME is the name of the partition as specified in HCD and shown in the HMC, and SYSPARM is the IEASYS## member in USER.PARMLIB for that particular LPAR.

## Step 4: Configure IEASYS##
Each LPAR needs its own IEASYS## member, though it is helpful to build one for one LPAR, test it out, then copy and paste and make LPAR-specific edits.  It's suggested (for clarity) that each IEASYS## number matches the S## number of your LPAR, but this is not strictly required. Make note of the warning below:

:::caution
Do not specify an IEASYS00 member, 00 is reserved for OSS-specified defaults. This will cause your IPL to fail.
:::

Your IEASYS## member has what you would normally respond to `IEA101A SPECIFY SYSTEM PARAMETERS FOR z/OS`, seperated by line and comma. It also includes extra parameters. Here is a simple example for LPAR S02:

SYSNAME=S02,
    COUPLE=C1,
    GRS=STAR,
    AUTOR=01,
    CMD=(XX,DR,01)

The full parameter list is given by IBM [here](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.5.0?topic=list-overview-ieasysxx-parameters).

### AUTOR##
The AUTOR## parameter specifies which AUTOR## member in USER.PARMLIB contains automatic responses to system requests (see Step 5). You can specify multiple LPARs to use the same AUTOR policy, or specify individual per LPAR. This is useful for specifying different responses for the first LPAR coming up in a sysplex (see Special Considerations for Cold Starts).

:::note
It is not recommended to build an AUTOR00 member. 00 is generally reserved for defaults provided by OSS.
:::

### CMD
The CMD parameter specifies which COMMND## members in USER.PARMLIB should be run during the IPL sequence.  This can be useful for running %setup, and starting Zowe (see Step 6). You can specify multiple LPARs to use the same CMD member, or specify individual per LPAR. This is useful for specifying different responses for the first LPAR coming up in a sysplex (see Special Considerations for Cold Starts).

The CMD members you add should be specified instead of (or in addition to) 01 above. The XX an DR cover OSS-provided defaults, in the format: `CMD=(XX,DR,##,##,...)`.

:::note
It is not recommended to build an COMMNDXX member. XX is generally reserved for defaults provided by OSS.
:::

## Step 5: Configure AUTOR##
The AUTOR## member specifies an autoresponse policy to system requests, where a user normally responds `r ####,response` during IPL. Critically, this is used in things like JES warm and cold start, etc.  The AUTOR## member should be placed (if it doesn't already exist) in USER.PARMLIB.

:::note
It is not recommended to build an AUTOR00 member. 00 is generally reserved for defaults provided by OSS.
:::

An AUTOR## statement consists of three parts:
1. MSGID - what message ID, normally specified for a specific request number (i.e. HASP426)
2. Delay - how long to wait before responding. It's recommended to not wait more than 5 seconds to avoid timing issues with the COMMND commands.
3. Reply - what to reply to the message, which is normally what you put in as a response.

Here is an example for a JES warmstart IPL:

Msgid(?HASP426)   Delay(3S) Reply('WARM,HASPPARM=CFDASD')
    Msgid(?HASP870)   Delay(5) Reply('Y')
    Msgid(?HASP417)   Delay(5S) Reply('Y')

And a JES cold start IPL:

elay(3S) Reply('WARM,HASPPARM=CFDASD')
    Msgid(?HASP870)   Delay(5) Reply('Y')
    Msgid(?HASP417)   Delay(5S) Reply('Y')

And a JES cold start IPL:

Msgid(?HASP426)   Delay(3S) Reply('COLD,HASPPARM=CFDASD')
    Msgid(?HASP441)   Delay(3S) Reply('Y')
    Msgid(?HASP870)   Delay(5S) Reply('Y')
    Msgid(?HASP417)   Delay(5S) Reply('Y')

You can include automation to respond to ANY messages generated at any point in the lifecycle of the LPAR.

:::note
If you see the commands in your COMMND member not executing during your testing of this process, lower your delay timers in your AUTOR member.
:::

## Step 6: Configure COMMND##
The COMMND## member includes command statements to run as part of the IPL sequence. IBM lists some restrictrions and recommendations [here](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.5.0?topic=sys1parmlib-commndxx-commands-automatically-issued-initialization).

:::note
It is not recommended to build an COMMND00 member. 00 is generally reserved for defaults provided by OSS.
:::

:::warning
IBM recommends against placing large numbers of commands in the COMMND## member, it can cause problems in the IPL sequence. An example would be to NOT vary many devices using this method.
:::

Command statements need to be preceded by a COM= and be wrapped in single quotes ''.  Here is an example to run %SETUP and start Zowe:

COM='%SETUP '
    COM='S ZWESISTC,REUSASID=YES  '
    COM='S ZWESLSTC,JOBNAME=ZWE1SV '

## Step 7: Testing and Deploying
It's recommended to build the sequence of members and statements for one LPAR, shut it down and test everything, then work your way from there. That way, you can test against any typo's, misconfigurations, etc. Cold start from no LPARs then becomes the last major hurdle.  Some teams may determine they prefer to manually cold start if they don't do it frequently, and only automate all the other LPARs.

## Step 8: Using your new IPL Configuration
If you've automated the entire process, you still have to wait for the first LPAR to make it past cold start before activating all of the other partitions. Eric plans to write container-native automation for this in the future, but for now, wait a minute or two after the first partiton shows as "Operating" in the HMC before activating all the other LPARs in the sysplex.

Otherwise, you should be able to activate the partitions, wait and have z/OS ready to go in a short time.

metadata.section_heading: Step 8: Using your new IPL Configuration

# Other Information and Considerations
This section contains other helpful hints and notes.

## Considerations for Cold Starts

A sysplex cold start occurs when there are no LPARs in the sysplex already. This requires additional work compared to a warm start. It is recommended to pick one LPAR to be the LPAR you _always_ cold start from, and configure the members accordingly.  Special note should be given to AUTOR## and COMMND##, where the first LPAR likely has additional steps compared to other LPARs in the sysplex.

## Multiple Sysplex Configurations

There are many 'break points' in the process where you can change the configuration of what IPL's.  You can specify a different LOADxx parameter in your load parameter in the activation profile, you can IPL a different partition name and associate that in the same LOADxx to a different IEASYSP## member, and different IEASYSP## members can have different AUTOR## and COMMND## members associated with them. The idea is you can build a set of members and activation profiles to automatically navigate your IPL sequence to its destination.

## Debugging, if Things Go Wrong

If you end up stuck, you can IPL M0 and fix anything you need to and try again.  You can also force operator response on the load parameter by adding a 'P.' to the end of it.  This will force asking for just about everything in the IPL sequence.

## Integration with the Test Containers

Right now, this doesn't integrate with the test containers, but we'll work on that.

# BCPii

BCPii = **B**ase **C**ontrol **P**rogram **i**nternal **i**nterface : An API service built within zOS which can target partitions (and more) to query and modify resources and their settings.

BCPii is one of zOS's core services which predates modern RESTful API protocols.  The legacy SNMP based protocols are still supported, Artemis GA2 introduced BCPii V2 which is adhering to modern HTTP standards and is exclusively where all new support is to be implemented.

## Setup and usage

In order to use BCPii, configuration work must be done on the SE, read about how [here](./Enable_BCPii.md).

The function is exercised by running jobs on zOS which consist of REXX or ZTT scripts that are controlled by basic JCL.

The generally available test scripts are provided by zOS SVT and delivered in our image by OSS.

The latest function added by BCPii allows customers to set up an HMC user which has security and administrative benefits. This is commonly referred to as JWT authentication, for which the HMC setup steps can be found [here](./HMC_JWT_user_setup.md)

Additional work is planned to create automation tools to compliment the test scripts via ZoweLab.

# How to Check APARs on z/OS

Barb Weglinski and the OSS team deliver z/OS to many test teams. If your z/OS is from Barb, you can follow this procedure to check what APARs are in your z/OS installation. This procedure is much easier with Zowe. Typically, you'll want to have an APAR number.

:::note
Definition: A z/OS APAR is a z/OS patch.
:::

Either in 3.4 or in Zowe, find the dataset: `$$OSS.DRIVER.INFO`.

Your APAR number will be in the form of: `OA####`.  Drop the first character and search in the file. As an example, for APAR `OA64114`, search for `A64114`.

If the APAR is applied, you'll find it in the file in a block like:

EA64114   TYPE            = APAR
            STATUS          = REC  APP
            FMID            = HCS77E0
            REWORK          = 2024292
                        INS   = 24.299  09:50:57

The rework date is the latest update of that APAR, in Julian year and day. For the example above, the APAR (patch) was updated in 2024 on the 292'nd day. Use a calendar like this: [Julian Calendar](https://www.fs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2019-04/julian-calendar.pdf) to conver the day of the year to a month and day.

# How to Get to and Login to z/OS

Author: Eric Reid

metadata.section_heading: How to Get to and Login to z/OS

content:
## Introduction

There are many ways to get to z/OS. This procedure attempts to explain each of them, and the benefits and drawbacks of each.

For system operators, this guide WILL NOT RECOMMEND OSC 3270 CONNECTIVITY. The default connection to z/OS should be OSD.

You need the OSD IP address of a z/OS Sysplex to perform these steps, as well as a z/OS login. Contact your team lead or test environment owner for these details.

## Connection via TOAD

TOAD is good for Mac or Linux users, and for shared z/OS environments with tight coordination.

See TOAD documentation for how to connect to [TOAD](../../../Automation/TOAD/ContainerAccessMethods.md)

In TOAD, open a terminal.

Then, start x3720 pointing to the IP address: `x3270 <IPADDRESS> &`

![Open](./images/toad_3270.png)

This should start a TSO 3270 Console and come up with the z/OS login screen. Continue the procedure [here](#login-to-zos)

## Connection via PCOMM (Windows Only)

PCOMM is good only for Windows users.

Install PCOMM from w3: [Install PCOMM](https://w3.ibm.com/#/apps/ibm-pc)

Once installed, click the "Start and Configure Sessions" .exe.

Then, click "New Session":

![Open](./images/PCOMM_welcome.png)

In the window that opens, go to Communication -> Configure. Then, go to "Link Parameters":

![Open](./images/link_parameters.png)

In this window, put in the OSD IP address. Press "OK", then "OK". This should bring you to the z/OS login screen. Continue [here](#login-to-zos).

## Connection via VSCode and Zowe CLI

Connecting via VSCode is great for working with datasets, jobs, and programming. Especially favored if your workflows already take you into VSCode.

Install VSCode from w3: [Install VSCode](https://w3.ibm.com/#/apps/visual-studio-code)

Open VSCode once installed. Then, go to Extensions on the left sidebar:

![Open](./images/vscode_extensions.png)

Search the marketplace for "Zowe Explorer". Click it, and in the main window press "Install".

![Open](./images/VSCode_install.png)

You can then follow the procedures about using it in [Zowe Introduction](../../../Automation/ZoweLab/README.md) or advanced setup in the [Zowe CLI](../../../Automation/ZoweLab/Tools/Zowe%20CLI%20Setup.md).

metadata.section_heading: Connection via VSCode and Zowe CLI

content:
## Connection via Zowe GUI

If your environment has Zowe installed, you can follow the guide [here](../../../Automation/ZoweLab/README.md) to connect via Zowe.

## Connection via OSC 3270

This is not recommended for most operators!!!!

You'll need the LUName from your 3270 configuration of device 060, and your OSC IP address. If you don't know this, talk to your team z/OS expert.

Repeat either the [Connection via TOAD](#connection-via-toad) with `x3270 <LUName>@<OSCIpaddress>:<port>`

Or the [Connect via PCOMM](#connection-via-pcomm-windows-only) and add the port and LUName next to the IP address in the "Link Parameters" screen.

## Login to z/OS

If you end up at a z/OS Login screen (i.e. not Zowe), follow this procedure to login. The login screen looks like this:

![Open](./images/zos_login.png)

It is very important in z/OS TSO that your cursor is in the right location. For new users, it is recommended to use the "TAB" key to go between entry points and avoid using the mouse.

If you can no longer type, there may be a red "--x--" in the bottom corner, this indicates you are typing in the wrong place and the keyboard is locked:

![Open](./images/keyboard_lock.png)

Depending on the environment, you may need to disconnect/reconnect to get out of keyboard lock, or press F3, F12, or reset. In x3270, there is a keyboard button with these keys available.

Type in the following in the line below the login text: `logon <youruser>`

![Open](./images/logon_userid.png)

Depending on your environment, press "Enter" by pressing your right control key or by pressing "Enter". This can be configured in the keyboard settings of your 3270 console.

onment, press "Enter" by pressing your right control key or by pressing "Enter". This can be configured in the keyboard settings of your 3270 console.

Type your password into the "password" field. If you have never logged into z/OS with the login you have, the password will be set to be 'newpass0'. z/OS will then ask you to change your password. It must be 8 characters or less and include a number and a letter. Otherwise, put in the password the system adiminstrator gave you.

Press "Enter" (remember, it may be right control!).

This should take you to some red text:

![Open](./images/logon_success.png)

If the text ends with '***', press enter. If the text ends with "READY", type:  `ISPF` then press enter.

You are into z/OS when you get to ISPF:

![Open](./images/ispf_done.png)

# How to Take an HCD Trace
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 08/02/2024

metadata.section_heading: How to Take an HCD Trace

content:
## Why?

Take an HCD trace if there is an ABEND or other problem in HCD. The goal is to get the data for a Jup.

## How?

1. Login to z/OS TSO
2. Start HCD
3. Start trace by putting command: `TRACE RESET ON,ALL,LEVEL=255` on the COMMAND line of HCD
4. Perform the set of actions that trigger an ABEND or other error. If the error causes you to end up outside of HCD, skip steps 5 and 6.
5. Go back to HCD
6. End the trace with command: `TRACE OFF,CLOSE`

The trace exists in USERNAME.HCD.TRACE. The easiest way to get this text out is with Zowe. Either copy/paste the data straight into a Jup comment, or attach it in a seperate text file.

# Brand New z/OS Procedure

Author: Eric Reid
Date: 11/24/2025

## Decide if you need a new z/OS IPL Pack

A z/OS IPL pack is an logical control unit (LCU, known as CUAdd in the IOCDS) that has all the data for a standard z/OS IPL, workloads, features, etc. delivered by the Operating System Support team (OSS).

A single z/OS IPL pack has the ability to IPL multiple sysplexes, as long as there are fewer than 32 total LPARs in all combined sysplexes.

You may need a new IPL pack if you fall into one of the following categories:

1. You have a brand new machine or test cell that has never IPL'ed z/OS
2. You have an existing machine or test cell that may or may not have IPL'ed z/OS in the past, but nobody on your team know anymore.
3. You have an z/OS IPL pack, but it has been overwritten, corrupted, or otherwise compromised.
4. Chris Moretti or the OSS team told you to get a new IPL pack.

metadata.section_heading: Decide if you need a new z/OS IPL Pack

content:
## Requesting a New IPL Pack

Gather the following information:
1. Your name, your team's name, and any members from your team you want to be able to update z/OS in the future. You can always add new people later, but will require another ticket.
2. Your machine's test cell and/or red/blue coordinates.
3. If you IPL another operating system today (SAK, z/VM, Linux), it's helpful to add their IPL PCHIDs if you know them.
4. Why you need a new z/OS IPL pack. Please refer to the list above as primary causes for a new IPL pack.

Open a ticket with all the information above to the Test Floor Infrastructure team to request a new IPL pack. Follow the general procedure here: https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/ibm-z-test-development-floor-ewm-guide/opening-an-issue

Author: Eric Reid

## Prerequisite steps
Make sure you have completed the [Setup Procedure](/CommonProcedures/Operating%20Systems%20On%20Z/zOS/New%20zOS%20Update%20Procedures/Setup%20Procedure.md), and received a ticket complete on your EWM ticket.

:::

## Login to Copy Services Manager (CSM)
Point your browser to the [EST CSM](https://9.114.114.90:9559/CSM/) and accept the self-signed certificate.

Login with your w3 credentials. You should get to a page that looks like ![CSM homepage](images/csm%20homepage.png)

## Find your session
Go to the "Sessions" button on the top ribbon, this should load a table with sessions. Depending on how many z/OS packs you update, you will see a different number of rows in the table. Each row is a copy session (specifically Flash Copy), and are named by the Z test cell. Find the test cell you are updating in the table. ![CSM session table](images/session%20table.png)

Click on the text of the session, this should bring you to a new page with information about your session ![CSM Session](images/csm%20session.png)

:::warning
Make sure z/OS is shutdown!!!!!
:::

## Start your session
Click the "Session Actions" button, and then select "Commands" then "Flash" ![Flash](images/flash%20session.png)

This should open up a confirmation window, press "Yes" to continue.

This should process for a minute or so, then you should get a loading bar in the table of the flash session. A green checkmark should show up at the top of your screen, this indicates that the copy has started.  Wait for the bar in the "Progress" column of the table to reach 100%. After the session has reached 100% in the progress bar, go to "Session Actions", then select "Commands" then "Terminate". Wait for the session to return to "Status" = Inactive.   This entire process should take around 5 minutes.

:::warning

On older DS8K's, there is a known bug that CSM doesn't update the progress bar, even though the data is being copied successfully. If your progress bar doesn't move from 0% after a minute or so, wait 10 minutes, and assume the data has moved successfully, and go to "Session Actions", then select "Commands" and "Terminate".  You will check this later in the procedure regardless. As we migrate to newer DS8K's, this should become less of a problem.

# How to Setup and Start a z/OS dump
Author: Eric Reid

Date: 11/25/2025

Credit for this goes to Rick Stearns.

metadata.section_heading: How to Setup and Start a z/OS dump

content:
## Why take a z/OS Dump?

Most z/OS problems are handled by SVC dumps automatically generated by z/OS on the fly, or with GTF traces which trace address spaces around a problem. Both of these data collection methods can be found here: https://github.ibm.com/Operating-Systems-Support/STAKEHOLDERS-PORTAL-POK-ESTFTP-ZOS/wiki

An operator can manually trigger a z/OS dump of particular addresses when needed by development, this is covered in this procedure.

## Setup the IEADMCxx member

In `USER.PARMLIB`, make a new member of the format IEADMCxx, or copy a member from `USER.PARMLIB` and change the member name. An example may be `USER.PARMLIB(IEADMCRD)`

In the new member `USER.PARMLIB(IEADMCxx)`, set the dump paramemters. A useful example for a pretty broad set of common addresses spaces is here:

JOBNAME=(*MASTER*,IOSAS,PCIE,VTAM*,TCPIP*,OMVS,JES2),
    DSPNAME=('*MASTER*'.*,'XCFAS'.*,'IOSAS'.*),
    SDATA=(CSA,GRSQ,LPA,LSQA,PSA,RGN,SQA,SUM,SWA,TRT,
    ALLNUC,COUPLE,XESDATA),
    END

Save this member, and make a note of the two characters at the end of IEADMCxx.

## Run the dump

Run whatever test(s) you need to, and then trigger the dump. It is ideal to get the dump pretty close to when the problem occurs in z/OS.

To run the dump, use the command:

`dump comm=(description),parmlib=xx`

Where `description` is 8 characters to describe the dump, and the `xx` is the characters at the end of your member name.

An example of this command for the example member `USER.PARMLIB(IEADMCRD)` (Note it is important to include the paranthesis!):

`dump comm=(mydump),parmlib=RD`

This will cause the z/OS dump. It is offloaded the same as an SVC dump, follow the guide here:
https://github.ibm.com/Operating-Systems-Support/STAKEHOLDERS-PORTAL-POK-ESTFTP-ZOS/wiki/SVC-Dump-Collection and/or use the z/OS Dump tool here: https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/ZoweLab/Tools/Dumps

## Introduction
The new z/VM dumps process requires access to shared DASD with z/VM development were dumps can be written to. To get access to this, you need to open a ticket to the EST Test Infrastructure team.  As part of this process, a few things will happen:

1. Standardizing the z/VM installation to 32 devices, if not already done.
2. Migrating your z/VM IPL packs to a new DS8K if necessary, which may require coordinated IOCDS updates.
3. Giving you IOCDS definitions to shared dump volumes.
4. Preparing for new Copy Services based z/VM Updates.

This will be coordinated with the EST Test Infrastructure team through EWM tickets, including coordinating any migration activities.

## Step 1: Open up an EWM ticket with the required information

:::note

This procedure must be performed once per z/VM installation pack you run on. For most people, this is once per z/VM partition.

:::+

In z/VM, issue the following commands:

`q dasd details 4E00`

Where 4E00 is replaced by the load address you IPL z/VM from. This should return an output that looks something like:

Save the output of both of these commands. Now, follow the guide here to open up a ticket: https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/ibm-z-test-development-floor-ewm-guide/opening-an-issue.

If you get an error that says you don't have access or the project isn't specified, please request access to EWM [with this procedure](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/ibm-z-test-development-floor-ewm-guide/getting-access-to-ewm).

Open the ticket with the following parameters and information:

1. Summary should say: "z/VM Dump Request" and your team name
2. Open up the ticket against Z Test and Development Lab -> Z I/O, and either EST for EST and bringup or SWT for all others
3. Put this as a severity 3 item
4. Include the following information in the ticket description:
    a. Your name and team or squad, and the names and emails of any other team members you want to be able to update your z/VM in the future

b. The Z system names and test cells that are part of your team that run z/VM.

c. The output of the two commands in step 1.

The Test Infrastructure team will respond to your ticket with details, and coordinate with you if required.

# Major z/VM Updates and Installs
Author: Eric Reid
Date: 04/29/2024

## Prerequisite steps
Make sure you have completed the [Setup Procedure](./Dumps/zVM_dump_ticket.md), and received a ticket complete on your EWM ticket.

:::warning
Shutdown your z/VM LPARs!
:::

## Login to Copy Services Manager (CSM)
Point your browser to the [EST CSM](https://9.114.114.90:9559/CSM/) and accept the self-signed certificate.

Login with your w3 credentials. You should get to a page that looks like ![CSM homepage](./../zOS/New%20zOS%20Update%20Procedures/images/csm%20homepage.png)

## Find your session
Go to the "Sessions" button on the top ribbon, this should load a table with sessions. Depending on how many z/VM packs you update, you will see a different number of rows in the table. Each row is a copy session (specifically Flash Copy), and are named by the Z test cell. Find the test cell you are updating in the table. ![CSM session table](./../zOS/New%20zOS%20Update%20Procedures/images/session%20table.png)

Click on the text of the session, this should bring you to a new page with information about your session ![CSM Session](./../zOS/New%20zOS%20Update%20Procedures/images/csm%20session.png)

:::warning
Make sure z/VM is shutdown!!!!!
:::

## Start your session
Click the "Session Actions" button, and then select "Commands" then "Flash" ![Flash](./../zOS/New%20zOS%20Update%20Procedures/images/flash%20session.png)

This should open up a confirmation window, press "Yes" to continue.

This should process for a minute or so, then you should get a loading bar in the table of the flash session. A green checkmark should show up at the top of your screen, this indicates that the copy has started.  Wait for the bar in the "Progress" column of the table to reach 100%. After the session has reached 100% in the progress bar, go to "Session Actions", then select "Commands" then "Terminate". Wait for the session to return to "Status" = Inactive.   This entire process should take around 5 minutes.

:::warning

ct "Commands" then "Terminate". Wait for the session to return to "Status" = Inactive.   This entire process should take around 5 minutes.

:::warning

On older DS8K's, there is a known bug that CSM doesn't update the progress bar, even though the data is being copied successfully. If your progress bar doesn't move from 0% after a minute or so, wait 10 minutes, and assume the data has moved successfully, and go to "Session Actions", then select "Commands" and "Terminate".  You will check this later in the procedure regardless. As we migrate to newer DS8K's, this should become less of a problem.

:::

:::note

Only 12 flash copy sessions can be active at the same time in a single DS8K. If you get an error (it'll show a red "x" after you submit the flash), wait 5 minutes and try again. If this fails, open up a support ticket to the EWM team [EWM Site](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/ibm-z-test-development-floor-ewm-guide)

:::

:::note

If you don't terminate the session, you will not be able to IPL z/VM, it will come back with a load failure because the DASD is still locked.

:::

# Setting Up SSH access with Step CA

*Note: This is essentially following the [Workstation Setup Guide](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/ciso-operations/team-hub/stepca/workstation)*

1. Make sure you have [Step CA installed](https://smallstep.com/docs/step-cli/installation/).

2. Bootstrap Step CA with the following:

```
step ca bootstrap --context ciso --ca-url=https://step.ciso.ibm.com:443/ --fingerprint=343b62c35729b55a39d3902833ca3d74414fb8676c1384d5a7b9c0769d984d78
```

3. You are now able to generate an SSH Key backed with your W3 ID:

```
step ssh login --context=ciso
```
:::caution If you are running Windows and the above command fails, try enabling ssh. Run the following as Administrator in Powershell:
```
Start-Process powershell.exe -Verb RunAs -ArgumentList "-Command", "Get-Service ssh-agent | Set-Service -StartupType Automatic"
Start-Service ssh-agent
```
You only need Powershell to enable ssh, you can use Windows CMD for all other commands.
:::

4. To confirm that your SSH agent has a valid configuration, run:
```
ssh-add -L | step ssh inspect -
```

You should see something similar to the following:

# Using 1Password with Step CA

To use 1Password, you need to set up an SSH agent for 1Password. That requires the installation of the [1Password CLI tool](https://1password.com/downloads/command-line). To install the CLI tool, please visit the [Get Started page.](https://developer.1password.com/docs/cli/get-started) Afterwards, you will need to follow the steps for your OS to integrate SSH with 1Password. The steps are located [here.](https://developer.1password.com/docs/ssh/get-started/)

With 1Password, you can add your Step CA ssh key into your 1Password vault. NOTE: 1Password requires that you use a set of specific encryption methods. Ed25519 is recommended. You also need to include an email address once you use this method.

The new command will look as follows: `step ssh certificate --crv=Ed25519 --kty=OKP <EMAIL>@ibm.com ~/.ssh/step-key`

Once done, you will be able to authenticate using 1Password.

## Resetting your Key

You will find that after 24 hours, your key will stop working. That means that your key has expired. To fix this, run `step ssh certificate --crv=Ed25519 --kty=OKP <EMAIL>@ibm.com ~/.ssh/step-key` (or wherever you placed your key) to "reset" the key. Afterwards, edit your Step SSH key by clicking "Edit", followed by "Replace Private Key" and basically update with the same key.

### Simple script to automate the reset
```
#!/bin/bash

step ssh certificate --crv=Ed25519 --kty=OKP <EMAIL>@ibm.com ~/.ssh/step-key
```

content: # System Triage Instructions

### Background

Our main role as testers is to recognize, identify, and report upon problems as efficiently as possible.

This section of the EST User Guide is dedicated to resources pertaining to the first two steps of this workflow (see [EWM](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/EngineeringManagement/EWM/) for more info on reporting problems)

While recognizing and identifying may seem synonymous, they are very different steps from a test perspective. Recognizing is the initial determination that a problem exists, whereas identifying is discovering the root cause of that problem. See below a brief summary of tools and methodologies used to accomplish each of these steps

### Service Required State

This is a status viewable via the "service required state query" task on the SE that identifies both the presence of a persisting problem as well as the nature of said problem. There are numerous states the system can be in, with the most common being N-mode Power, N-mode service network, and N-mode IO domain.

### Hardware Messages

The Hardware Messages task on the SE contains an index of previous and current problems on the system. Each problem as two numbers associated with them. Each problem as a unique 8-digit hexadecimal number associated with it that is specific to type of problem that it represents. For example, the refcode 32C20710 is specific to a single ethernet link failure. The other number, known as the Problem Number (often abbreviated as PN) is a non-unique identifier used to index all past and current problems on the system. When a problem is erased within hardware messages its PN will become available again and will be assigned to the next new problem identified by the system. Both of these numbers can also be seen within the iqyy log.
