### System Logs

The main log on the system is the iqyy log. This can be viewed from either the "view console log" task on the SE, or from either plog.sh or logloop on the SE command line. The logs contain information related to numerous processes running on the system such as HOM, PSCN, and Problem Analysis.

Each log entry contains a timestamp, a series of data blocks, and a unique refcode.

All errors in the log are prefixed with a "+". +PA_Result is the log representation of a hardware message. Its log entry will contain the same refcode and PN seen within the

Hardware Messages task with additional information available such as the primary and secondary data blocks.

Within the "view component logs" task on the SE, a multitude of logs can be found all pertaining to different areas and subsystems. Once a problem has been identified, this can be a good resource for seeking out additional information.

# Apply a Private Fix (PFIX)

:::warning
This is a generalized instruction. If your PFIX requires different installaiton steps from your developer, always follow their instructions.
:::

# Introduction

Private fixes, or PFIXES, are binaries code packages from development that they want you to apply to your machine and test to verify a fix works before releasing it into hte main driver, or to experiment with different settings. Your system typically cannot be in production mode for these.

# Procedure to Install a PFIX
1. VNC into your Z SE, or go out onto the floor. You'll need access to the standalone browser on the SE
2.	Minimize the GUI page, so that you see the blue background of the SE
3.	Right click, and select “Command Window” to open up a terminal session
4.	Go to the ffdc/u directory: cd /ffdc/u
5.	If you’ve already had a PFIX for the Jup, skip to step 6. Otherwise, create a directory with the Jup number: mkdir jup#######
    a.	Replace the number signs with the Jup number with the PFIX. If this is a PFIX for a problem you’ve already received a PFIX for, you can skip this
6.	Go to the folder you just made: cd jup#######
7.	Right click the blue background again, and go to “Standalone Browser”
8.	You should be able to login to Jupiter from the Firefox browser, do so
9.	Find your Jup and select the file, and using the GUI navigate to the /ffdc/u/jup### folder you just made, download the PFIX file to that folder
10.	In command window, go back to the Jup folder: cd /ffdc/u/jup#######
11.	Fix on the PFIX: fix PFIXFILENAME, **NOTE**: if the pfix is packaged as a .zip file, the -x argument should be used when issuing the fix command
12. This should look like:
 ![](

LENAME, **NOTE**: if the pfix is packaged as a .zip file, the -x argument should be used when issuing the fix command

 ![](images/applypfix.png)

14.	Power on Reset (POR) the Z.

# Procedure to Uninstall a PFIX

1.	To remove a PFIX, go back into the Command Window in the SE
2.	Then move to the PFIX directory: cd /ffdc/u/jup#######
3.	Unfix the PFIX: unfix PFIXFILENAME
4.	Then do a POR

# Notes

1.	For some SE PFIX’es, at the end of the FIX and UNFIX scripts (after the COPYING line), the system will ask you to reboot the SE to apply the fix. You’ll need to do so to continue
2.	You can apply a PFIX on top of another PFIX. They will stack and add a number to the file in /console/fix/pucode, i.e. the first will be i390.bin.000, second will be i390.bin.001…etc

# How to generate and use Artifactory Token

Beginning June 13th 2023, interacting with artifactory will not be possible with your w3ID. Artifactory, aka JFrog, is the code repository for driver snapshots, tools packages, and other related RPMs. This is what DAISY and zdnf are using behind the scenes, so if you load code on D51C or later, you will need to complete the process below.

metadata.section_heading: How to generate and use Artifactory Token

content:
## Process Summary
The in depth instructions from TaaS can be accessed [here](https://taas.cloud.ibm.com/guides/artifactory-authentication-access-tokens.md)

If you don't enjoy sifting through convoluted word vomit, read on for simplified instructions.
1. You will generate a shortened 64 character "Reference Token" in your [JFrog User Profile](https://na.artifactory.swg-devops.com/ui/user_profile) which is valid for 90 days
2. When using `zdnf` you will be prompted for a "jfrog identity token" which is where you will paste in the Reference Token

Complete these steps in an SSH connection to your SE or HMC. Copy/paste is required so you will **not** be able to do it inside of VNC.

### Generate your Reference Token
Go to your [JFrog User Profile](https://na.artifactory.swg-devops.com/ui/user_profile)

If the link doesn't take you right to the user profile, get there by clicking on your name in the top right

Log in if prompted. If you are not directed to your user profile, you can get there by clicking on your name in the top right corner of the screen.

You should see the Authentication Settings section at the top of the page with a button to *`Generate an Identity Token`*
Enter a description if you'd like and click next.
**DO NOT** close the next page without copying your Reference Token and pasting it somewhere you can reference it later. This is the only time the full reference token will be viewable in JFROG

Once saved in a text file, or slacked to yourself for example, you can close the window

### Using your Reference Token
When you run `zdnf` or the [zdnfToolUpdate.sh script](./D51CToolUpdate.md) now you have to provide a Reference Token or a full length access token *instead* of using w3 user and password.

The new `zdnf` prompt looks like below
When you paste a token, the hash is **NOT** shown. If you paste multiple times you will fail authentication. Just paste once and hit enter
```console
[hmcmanager@Axx-/home/hmcmanager]sudo zdnf
Enter your jfrog identity token (audience=jfac@* or audience=*@*), or skip for credentials :
```

If you followed the steps correctly, you will get authenticated and can continue your code install per usual

# Automatic MCP Update

You can now update MCP level automatically without doing a hard disk
restore. This method works to update MCP within a "family" i.e.
MCP8xxx-\>MCP8xxx or MCP9xxx-\>MCP9xxx. You **cannot** use this method to
move from 8-\>9 or install initial MCP on a brand new SE.
## Procedure:

### Get Access
0. Request access to DAISY API [here](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2/requests/new?element=16937&authorities=5083)

This seems to be different access than DAISY itself

## Prepare you system

1. Take save upgrade data, save on the hard drive. It is a good
precaution to save this externally

2. In a command line issue:

```mv /console/data/actzdesk.dat /console/data/actzdesk.bak```

3. restart driver cleanly via ```startdriver -neit```

### Install the tool

4. Using the standalone browser in the right click menu, go to
<https://github.ibm.com/tseeger/AutomaticMCPUpdate> and using the 'code' drop down download the repository as a .zip. save in /ffdc/u/

5. Back in the command line, unzip the file then go into the directory

```cd /ffdc/u/```
```unzip AutomaticMCPUpdate-master.zip```
```cd AutomaticMCPUpdate-master```

6. Sign the directory to avoid TC violations

```find /ffdc/u/AutomaticMCPUpdate-master -type f -exec /console/bin/test/tcsign.sh {} \;```

### Run tool to install MCP

7. The following command will now update MCP to the specified level

```
sudo ./updateMcpIfNeeded.sh -m <TARGET MCP LEVEL> -u <your W3 email>
```

You will be prompted for the root password (passw0rd) and your w3 password. You may not see anything print to the console after it says your login worked. While you wait, you can check if you have access using the link above.

The installation can take a half hour or longer. Reboots will occur.

### What's Next

Once finished it should return to a blue screen, your driver will not boot until you restore actzdesk.

However it might be better to install a new daily driver while the system and SE are down.

New MCP and new snapshots work better together.

```
mv /console/data/actzdesk.bak/console/data/actzdesk.dat
```

and reboot. Before doing this, you can update your snapshot level.

# Hit a snag?

If anything goes wrong, collect the following files and alert Tim Seeger
```
/mnt/upgrade/root/autoupdate-\*
/ffdc/AutomaticMCPUpdate-master/logs/\*
```
# SE or HMC Network Setup

## When to use Command Line Network Setup for SE/HMC
After a hard disk restore of MCP and prior to loading a driver, some manual configuration of the network interface must be performed so you can access the remote servers containing code and restore data.
When network settings are configured this way they do not persist past reboots, so if a restore does not take place, or you haven’t used the panel driven task to configure the network (once your driver is loaded) you will have to repeat these steps after every reboot until either of those steps are completed.

        TX errors 0  dropped 0 overruns 0  carrier 0  collisions 0
        device memory 0x92720000-9273ffff
```
For almost all systems on the floor, this will be a 9.56.19x.xxx but many test cells intentionally use an IP on a different subnet.

If this is configured, you can try to ping your gatewateway
`ping 9.xxx.xxx.1`

If you can ping your gateway on your subnet, but can't ping a gateway on another subnet, you are probably missing the `route` for this interface.

If you can ping your gateway on your subnet, but can't ping a gateway on another subnet, you are probably missing the `route` for this interface.

If you can ping IPs but still can't get to websites in the browser, you are probably missing resolv.conf for the SE.

## Configuring an IP for a specific ethernet device.
Remember to replace 'em3' with 'eth0' in the following commands if you are on an HMC

Enter this command, filling in the full IP designated for the Primary SE of your test cell.
`ifconfig em3 9.xxx.xxx.xxx/24 up netmask 255.255.255.0`
Now retry ```ifconfig em3``` to make sure it was accepted
If this command didn't work for some reason, try the next two which inexplicably work when ifconfig fails, but fails if ifconfig would have worked
`ip addr add 9.xxx.xxx.xxx dev em3`
`ip link set dev em3 up`

## Setting up resolv.conf
resolv.conf is what contains your domain name servers which resolve a URL into an IP address. These servers are internal to the lab and therefor all fresh linux installs must be made aware of them
```

hit 'i' to insert, type the following

search pok.stglabs.ibm.com ibm.com
nameserver 9.0.0.1

nameserver 9.12.16.2
nameserver 9.12.18.2
```
'esc' to exit insert mode.
Holding 'shift' and hiting 'z z' will save and exit vi like a pro.

Now `ping google.com ` to prove you can get out.

The network is now able to reach internal code servers and you can use the appropriate method to install the driver.
D50 and up uses zdnf to install driver snapshots
D41 and below uses DAISY via remote code install

You may be trying to configure an IP which is taken, have physical connection issues, or be attempting to use a subnet not valid for your ethernet connection's VLAN.

# D51C Tool update with zDNF

This guide outlines how to use zdnfToolUpdate.sh to update your systems tools to the latest snapshot tool without having to go to daisy or enter prompts. It will request your artifactory token, which you can generate following [these steps](./ArtifactoryTokenCheatSheet.md)

## Setting up the tool for first use
The `zdnfToolUpdate.sh` script is a slimmed down version of `zdnf` which queries the [advisory listing](https://daisy.boeblingen.de.ibm.com/repositories/sys-zfw-fwd-team/browseadvisories.html?snapshotDriver=D51C)  and auto-fills the default options you (usually) need when making a tool update.

The script is available [here](http://9.56.193.90/EST-FTP/tools/?C=M;O=D)

:::note
You can open this link in the SE browser, or download to your workstation and transfer to the SE hard drive.
:::

1. **Check** that zdnf is installed and your driver level variable is set correctly

if running `zdnf` returns command not found run the following rpm command:

`sudo rpm -U https://daisy.boeblingen.de.ibm.com/zdnf.noarch.rpm   `

Then check your driver variable by reading file:

`>cat /etc/dnf/vars/driver`

```D51C```

This file must be D51C! *Not* D5X_HEAD or anything else

2. **Sign** the script and make it executable with these two commands:

`chmod +x ./zdnfToolUpdate.sh`

`tcsign.sh zdnfToolUpdate.sh`

**Run** the tool as root. This will require the ./ even when you are in the same directory as the tool.

Running the script with no arguments picks up the latest 'tst' tools package - typical use
:::

If you are running release level mcls, be aware that the snapshot with the base flag is usually behind one bundle. Install this level by passing argument 'base' in as shown

`sudo ./zdnfToolUpdate.sh base`

# How to determine your OSD (TCPIP) IP

metadata.section_heading: How to determine your OSD (TCPIP) IP

content:
## What is an OSD Channel?
The two most common OSA flavors are OSC and OSD. Some Operating systems like Linux will exclusivley use OSD channels, while zOS has valuable interfaces to offer from both protocols.

An OSD channel is configured in the IOCDS with three devices, *read, write, and data*, which can be spanned into all CSS's and shared by all LPARs. Each Operating System with access to these devices may use them to establish an ethernet interface with a unique IP address. Many IP addresses for many partitions live on one card which can typically only access *one subnet*.  Specific IPs are reserved and intended for each LPAR. Unlike OSC, where all network parameters are defined in OSA Advanced Facilities, each Operating system establishes the IP definition and attempts to connect to the network over it at IPL time. It is important to know your IP and ensure it is set correctly to avoid collision, and allow access to the resource it beholds.

## How to determine the OSD IP used by zOS
 Most of the time in the lab we use the OSC adapter to connect and interact with zOS TSO and Master Console. If you run zOS, your test cell and system should have at least one OSD card and an IP which can be configured for zOS OSD.

From either a Master Console or Operating System Message, Issue the following command to see the address
 `d tcpip,tcpip,netstat,home`
 ```
 HOME ADDRESS LIST:
LINKNAME:   LOOPBACK
  ADDRESS:  127.0.0.1
    FLAGS:
INTFNAME:   OSA2900
  ADDRESS:  9.xx.xx.xx
    FLAGS:  PRIMARY
INTFNAME:   LOOPBACK6
  ADDRESS:  ::1
    TYPE:   LOOPBACK
    FLAGS:
3 OF 3 RECORDS DISPLAYED
END OF THE REPORT
```

content:
# How do I know I have a hardware dump?

A hardware dump can occur for a number of reasons, but many lead to hardware system checkstops. In this case, they may have hardware dump data.

You can see the hardware dumps with the command: `ls -all /ffdc/dumps/hwdump*`

This data needs to be sent to bughouse, which has tools for analyzing hardware dumps.

metadata.section_heading: How do I know I have a hardware dump?

content:
# How do I send the hardware dump to bughouse?

From your SE, run the command `xdump`. You can do `xdump -h` to see the help menu.

An example command format:
`xdump -d /ffdc/dumps/__yourhwdumphere__ -u __yourusername__ -t __titleofdump__`

content:
## About This Page

After one or more DCM replacement on a Z system, you will need to update your secure execution keys, otherwise, your system will enter a service required state.

## Procedure
1. Your first step will be to retrieve the vpd file, or at the very least denote its location, which will be: /console/data/iqyvpd.xml. Ensure your vpd file is dated after the DCMs were replaced. As you will need their serial numbers for the key generation.
2. Next you will navigate to this link: https://gemserv6.pok.ibm.com/debugkeys2. This is the page in which you will generate new keys. If you have trouble with access for some reason, reach out to Brian Stocker for more information.

5. You can now hit the Create button at the end of the page, which will download the file to your system.
6. From there, you will need to either upload the zip file to an FTP server, or a USB. Whichever your preference is.
7. Now, on your SE, navigate to the System Details panel, and hit manage, next to the Secure Execution for Linux info.

# Setting up your PCHID seeding File
If you are IML complete and the system has no channels, you have probably come to the right place.

metadata.section_heading: Setting up your PCHID seeding File

content:
## What is a PCHID seed
The PCHID seed is what assigns the order of your Hemlock IO drawers. PCHIDS, or Physical Channel Identifiers count in hexadecimal starting at 0x100, reserving 4 PCHIDs per slot and counting up to reach a maximum possible value of 37F on a 4 frame system with 12 IO cages.
The number of MES frame layouts make the variety of hemlock drawer placement change in most configurations and models, therefore you must declare the IO drawer order per the plan of record's definition for all IO configuration and serviceability tasks to work appropriately.

## What is required
In order for the system to use and display channels ```/console/data/enclosureId2pchid.json``` must be present when you power on and IML the system. The correct definition within this file is vital to sane operations of the system.

If you find that this file does not exist in a new config, or modification is necessary due to a model conversion, it is recommended you create a ```iqyvmpchid.xml``` file and run ```tqyvsePchidSeed``` to generate the required json format. This is because it is easier to identify the required information for the .xml file and assures the .json file has no formatting issues.

Read on to see an example and how to determine the correct seed for your frame layout
## How to create iqyvmpchid.xml

## How to create iqyvmpchid.xml

cd /ffdc/u/
touch iqyvmpchid.xml
vi iqyvmpchid.xml
```
hit 'i' to insert, copy and paste the following.
```

<enclosure type="IO" location="Z01B" basePchid="0x100">
</enclosure>

</enclosure>

</enclosure>

</enclosure>
<enclosure type="IO" location="A23B" basePchid="0x280">
</enclosure>

</enclosure>
<enclosure type="IO" location="C09B" basePchid="0x300">
</enclosure>

</enclosure>

```

</enclosure>

This example xml was updated for Metis to reflect fixed PCHID numbering. You should only have to remove the drawers you DON'T have in your system and proceed with the remaining steps

## Running tqyvsePchidSeed to generate enclosureId2pchid.json
Run ```tqyvsePchidSeed```
```
Using default seeding file at: /console/data/iqyvmpchid.xml

# Converting a Machine to z/OS Dynamic I/O

Author: Eric Reid

metadata.section_heading: Converting a Machine to z/OS Dynamic I/O

content:
## Introduction

This procedure is designed to guide testers from using standalone IOCDS to manage their machine to classic dynamic I/O managed by z/OS, using the latest tools and technology to drastically simplify the process. There are potentially alternate methods of doing things (DPM, remote dynamic, etc.), but this is by far the most straightforward way to begin performing dynamic I/O.

## Prerequistes

1. z/OS must be IPL'ed on the machine that dynamic I/O will performed on.
2. z/OSMF must be setup with an IP address. The best way to do this is as part of the Zowe setup [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/ZoweLab/Setup/ZoweLab_checklist).
3. You need a text, human readable version of your IOCDS.
4. You need a TOAD container in which to run the ZoweLab tools, see TOAD docs [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/TOAD/).

## Verify the ID Statement
Many manually written IOCDS files do not have a full ID statement, and the automation looks for key values in the ID block to fill in the requirements of the JCL jobs to do the HCD migrate. Here is an example of a good ID block for this task:

```
         ID    MSG2='IODF.IODF0C - 2026-02-05 13:57',SYSTEM=(3931,1),  *
               LSYSTEM=A53,                                            *
               TOK=('A53',00800006BB489175135719450126036F00000000,0000*
               0000,'26-02-05','13:57:19','IODF','IODF0C')
*$HCDC$        SNAADDR=(IBM390PS,A53)
```

The key data here is the `SYSTEM=(3931,1)`, and the `TOK=('cecname')`. This data is needed for HCD to define the processor type and the Processor ID (cecname).

Make sure your IOCDS starts with an ID block with this data for your CEC, then put your IOCDS into TOAD.

## Grab a Software Configuration

Download the `OSS.IODF01` base software configuration from Github, [here](https://github.ibm.com/systemz/tf_iodf_repo/blob/main/IOCP_OSS.IODF01%20ALL_2026-04-02%2014-03-53.605732.txt).

Copy the entirety of this text to the bottom of your IOCDS.

## Migrate the IOCDS

From TOAD, run a `zwe_hcd_migrateIOCDS`, see the full documentation [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/ZoweLab/Tools/HCD%20Tools/Migrate_IOCDS). If you have no IODF, it is recommended to build IODF 01, `IODF.IODF01`.

It is best to run this in the TOAD GUI, so the File Explorer can be opened to find your IOCDS. You can also past the `-f` parameter and point to the full path of the IOCDS in TOAD.

If the CC > 4, the migrate failed, and an error log will be generated in TOAD. This can include IOCDS failures, JCL failures, etc. Debug as required.

When successful, you will now have a work IODF in HCD, `IODF.IODF##.WORK`.

extracted_errors: If the CC > 4, the migrate failed, and an error log will be generated in TOAD. This can include IOCDS failures, JCL failures, etc. Debug as required.

content:
## Build a Production IODF

We now need to build a production IODF for the system to use. From TOAD, run a `zwe_hcd_buildProduction`, see the full documentation [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/ZoweLab/Tools/HCD%20Tools/BuildProd).

This, especially for coupling, can create other problems. If the CC > 4, the build failed, and an error log should be generated in TOAD. Debug as required.

This will turn the work IODF into a production IODF that the machine can use, `IODF.IODF##`.

:::warning

If your configuration includes coupling, you will need to go into HCD's panels and attach the coupling for the first time, and you will need to run a partial migrate (see `zwe_hcd_migrateIOCDS` for more details) of each of the processors in the environment. In future IODFs, be sure to use the `zwe_hcd_standaloneIOCDS` code to get the `TPATH` paramemters required to avoid this in the future. Talk to Eric Reid for more details about how HCD works with coupling.

:::

extracted_errors: This, especially for coupling, can create other problems. If the CC > 4, the build failed, and an error log should be generated in TOAD. Debug as required.

content:
## Write the IOCDS to the SE

The IODF (HCD version of IOCDS) needs to now be written to the SE, this can be done with `zwe_hcd_wiocds`, full documentation [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/ZoweLab/Tools/HCD%20Tools/writeIOCDS).

This will overwrite one of your IOCDS slots (A0, A1, A2 or A3). Go into the I/O Configuration panel in the SE to verify that the IOCDS is now written to that slot. Use the `-p` of your `cecname` in the Token of the `ID` statement.

metadata.section_heading: Write the IOCDS to the SE

content:
## Configure Your LOADxx

Now, we need to prepare z/OS to use this IODF during IPL, more details of this process can be found [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/CommonProcedures/Operating%20Systems%20On%20Z/zOS/Automated%20IPL%20Setup/).

In the LOADxx, it is recommended to use `**` for the IODF specification in this case, and then to change the LOADPARM address to IODFPK's device address, normally at device address 4813. This would necessitate changes to the LPAR's activation profiles.

:::note

The operator will have to decide how committed to dynamic I/O they would like to be. It can make sense to have a set of LPARs or activation profiles for dynamic I/O, pointing to the LOADxx with the `**` set, pointing to device 4813 to establish token match when IML'ed onto the correct configuration. This could be a "unique case". Or - commit to dynamic I/O, and use this process every time to make I/O configuration changes forever, and build the environment to use these dynamic configurations on all valid LPARs.

:::

## Establish Token Match

Now, shutdown z/OS and whatever else you need to on the CEC, and IML the IODF written to the SE earlier. Then, IPL z/OS with the activation profile, load parameters, and LOADxx member set above.

After z/OS is IPL'ed, verify that the hardware token (set by IML) and the software token (set by IPL with the LOADxx parameter) are the same. The easiest way to do this in most environments is with the `d ios,config` command:

```
d ios,config (A50.zosmf)
 IOS506I 14.21.36 I/O CONFIG DATA 526
 ACTIVE IODF DATA SET = IODF.IODF90
 CONFIGURATION ID = TC4SYSR        EDT ID = 00
 TOKEN:  PROCESSOR DATE     TIME     DESCRIPTION
  SOURCE: TC4SYSR  25-11-04 11:26:32 IODF     IODF90
 ACTIVE CSS:  0    SUBCHANNEL SETS CONFIGURED: 0, 1, 2, 3
 CHANNEL MEASUREMENT BLOCK FACILITY IS ACTIVE
 SUBCHANNEL SET FOR PPRC PRIMARY: INITIAL = 0   ACTIVE = 0
 HYPERSWAP FAILOVER HAS OCCURRED: NO
 LOCAL SYSTEM NAME (LSYSTEM): B50

```

The software configuration is specified with `ACTIVE IODF DATA SET =`, and the hardware configuration is specified is specified with `SOURCE:### Date TIME...`. In the example above, both the hardware and software tokens are IODF90, and therefore match.

:::note

There are conditions that can exist where `d ios,config` does not show the level of detailed required to validate token match, but they are rare.

:::

## Build the Target IODF

A dynamic I/O moves the CEC's configuration from one IODF to another. It is recommended to build all further configurations from the IODF that is built above. You can use `zwe_hcd_standaloneIOCDS`, full documentation [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/ZoweLab/Tools/HCD%20Tools/getStandaloneIOCDS) to pull out a full IODF (hardware and software combined).

Edit the configuration to a new configuration, different from the first, to run a test. Dynamic I/O is very broad, and many possible test scenarios.

Once you are done, run the `zwe_hcd_migrateIOCDS` again, but point to a new IODF, normally incrementing the number by one, i.e. `IODF.IODF01` goes to `IODF.IODF02` as the next IODF.

Once the migrate completes, then run `zwe_hcd_buildProduction` again to build the new IODF into a production IODF.

## Run a Dynamic I/O

You're finally ready to do dynamic I/O! Run the `zwe_hcd_loopDynamic` script, full documentation [here](https://csl-dev3.onecloud.stglabs.ibm.com:3001/Automation/ZoweLab/Tools/HCD%20Tools/Loop%20Dynamic%20Changes).

This will use the z/OSMF API's to dynamically move the CEC's configuration from the first IODF to the second IODF. You can put both IODFs in a list and loop back and forth between them if you'd like as well. You can build more IODFs with more tests and add them into the list as well.

## Trusted Computing on Z Support Elements

Put simply, Trusted Computing is the technology used to ensure all firmware and software running on the Z system is authentic. Doing this involves a few components which are worth having basic understanding of, so that issues involving them can be resolved without an excess of time or pain.

Additional articles in this section will help explain the moving parts and get you out of some jams.

## Trusted Computing Lingo

1. TPM = Trusted Platform Module

The TPM is a physical chip on the motherboard of our SEs and HMCs. It contains the registers to which the Trusted Computing Keys are written and is also responsible for monitoring the hardware for suspicious activity, like excessive reboots, which may indicate nefarious activity. When a threshold for reboots in 24 hours is exceeded for example, the TPM will brick the SE until one of like 3 people on the planet can reset the TPM chip using heavily guarded secret procedures

# TC Errors
This guide helps explain some of the common misunderstandings about Trusted computing errors (also called TC violations) and should help you handle situations involving signing code and cleaning up after unsigned code if it is run by mistake.

## Why you should care about TC Errors
TC Errors are the result of some unsigned code being executed or from immutable files/directories being modified.

All modern physical SEs **will** have Trusted Computing enabled. Violating TC policy will put the SE in a condition where mirroring fails until the "bad_drive_file" is removed. Hardware messages will log for the initial violation and for each subsequent failing mirror attempt.

The above is true for SEs in "Monitor" mode. *Some* SEs will be in "Monitor & Protect" mode which is quite obvious since any violation of TC Policy will blue screen the SE until authorized personnel can gain physical access to unbrick the hardware.

metadata.section_heading: Why you should care about TC Errors

content:
## How do I run my code then?
"Hybrid mode" systems are most common in the lab and can run your own scripts and executables without violating TC policies, so long as you properly sign files prior to execution.

metadata.section_heading: How do I run my code then?

content:
### Sign one script
When in the directory containing your script, run `tcsign.sh <YourScriptNameHere>`

This is required ANY time the script is modified. Even whitespace appended to the file changes the checksum which is used to validate the signature hash at runtime.

If you are debugging and changing your script in great frequency, it can help to get one command in your 'up arrow' that signs and executes your script in one go. This saves you time and reduces the chance of you forgetting to sign.

### Sign and run your script in a single command
`tcsign.sh <YourScriptNameHere> ; ./<YourScriptNameHere>`

metadata.section_heading: Sign and run your script in a single command

content:
### Recursively sign an entire directory
If you have many scripts to sign that are in nested directories, you may wish to sign them all at once.  This command is most easily copied and pasted into an ssh connection.

`find <ThePathToDir4Signing> -type f -exec /console/bin/test/tcsign.sh {} \; `

replace `<ThePathToDir4Signing>` with the full path to the directory

## Shoot! I ran some unsigned code!
Worry not young Padawon, you can clean up after yourself and post in the system slack channel to ignore the instance of TC Hardware message....
1. Properly sign your executable scripts using the steps above
2. issue `rm /console/data/pa/bad_drive_file` on the CLI
    - pa stands for "problem analysis"
    - bad_drive_file is created by firmware when the violation occurs, logging an SRC.
    - if that file exists when its time for a routine mirror, it fails and logs more SRCs
3. Determine the problem number you generated to report.
    - by now your mistake has surely created a problem number. Run `llog |grep PN` to quickly determine what the most recent number is. The timestamp should match the time you executed the unsigned script. If in doubt do an SRC search of the PN to ensure it is TC related and not some other issue requiring attention.
    - Do the right thing and post in the system log what occurred.

metadata.section_heading: Shoot! I ran some unsigned code!

content:
## How do I know what file caused the TC Errors
The answer is inside the trusted computing component log; /console/data/iqyytccl.log

One entry is posted per execution of an unsigned script. Modified files in immutable directories are routinely checked for checksum and will also eventually log TC errors.

The SRC Trailer will be distinct for each file that caused a violation. Opening the primary data block will reveal the filename, but tooling exists to build a list which counts all the occurrences of each distinct file requiring some attention.

## Advice for assessing violations
Some basic deductive reasoning will guise determining if this TC violation is something to clean up and move on from, educate the freelance scripting culprit, or open a defect to the appropriate FW development team.

1. If you recognize the tool and know it was recently installed, or developed on the SE, signing the executable was likely missed as we are only human. Sign the file, remove the bad_drive_file, and have a good rest of your day
2. If this seems to be a repeat occurrence, or you think you have a first time offender, send them this article.  1. and 2. of course apply to TOOLS, not firmware
3. If the violating files don't look like scripts or tools, they are most likely part of firmware. In rare cases some code makes it into a daily driver build or tools package that is not properly signed.  If this is the case, it is appropriate to [Open a ticket in EWM](/EngineeringManagement/EWM/README.md)

# Trusted Computing Key Info

## What are Trusted Computing Keys?
The SE/HMC hardware comes equipped with a "Trusted Platform Module" or TPM which is a physical chip capable of imposing security policies across all other code executing on the machine. The TPM tracks reboots, code signatures, and much more.
To operate securely, the TPM is loaded with Trusted Computing Keys often referred to as TC Keys. Loading the keys are often necessary when setting up a system, and occasionally after some firmware updates that require a newer version of the keys.
The TC Keys are loaded via the BIOS using a bootable USB disk provided by the HMC team.

## How do I know what keys are necessary?

The level of TC keys you will use depends on your hardware, the SB level of your hardware and the Driver you are trying to load and if you want to load a Production or Tools console.

content: # Fix SSL issues on SE/HMC/TKE

## Why perform these steps?

Should your certificate expire, you will be unable to run zdnf commands, or communicate with external sites like DAISY. The certificates shipped with drivers must be updated to reinstate communication with these sites. You will know if you run into this issue when you see errors like this:

`url: (60) SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired
   More details here: https://curl.haxx.se/docs/sslcerts.html`

## Steps to perform the update manually
1. Download latest pem certificate [here](https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/certhub/ibm-internal-ca-application/root-intermediate)
   - If a browser on SE/HMC/TKE is available, the .pem file can be downlaoded directly to your /home/hmcmanager/Downloads directory.
   - Otherwise, download to your work station and use `scp` or some other ftp client to transfer the certificate.

Example Command:
   ```
   scp ./CA\ Intermediate\ certificate.pem hmcmanager@9.xxx.xxx.xxx:.
   ```

2. On the SE/HMC commandline, find the .pem file and copy it to the following directory

```
   sudo cp CA\ Intermediate\ certificate.pem /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/
   ```

3. Update trusted CAs:

```
   sudo update-ca-trust
   ```

# Fix ssh LDAP Login

Author: Chris Hutton
Date: 2/27/24

## Why are ssh logins broken?

At the end of February 2024, changes were made to IBM's LDAP authentication server which is used to authenticate our w3 ID when logging into SE, HMC, or TKE via ssh.  The server now only authenticates over secure ports, but the driver firmware still defaults to the non secure ports.

## How can I fix it?

See [Defect 1072722](https://jupitr.boeblingen.de.ibm.com/ccm/web/projects/System%20z%20Defects#action=com.ibm.team.workitem.viewWorkItem&id=1072722) for more background on the change.

### Method 1 |  `zdnf` tool update

The zdnf tools package for later D51 snapshots *should* include the fix and you will be good to go. [Follow these instructions](./D51CToolUpdate.md) to update your tools.

### Method 2 |  standalone pfix

Jup 1072722 has fixes attached for driver D41 and D51, however without ssh access, you can't VNC in, so you can't open the browser, so you can't download and install the fix.

I took the liberty of downloading these pfixes to a midas box so they can easily be scp'd to the desired cpc via the browser login.

1. Access your SE via a browser, http://<SE|HMC|TKE_IP>/preloginmonitor/index.jsp

4. **Enter `cd` to go to /home/hmcmanager**

D41C:

D51C:

`scp hmcmanager@9.56.192.113:pfix-artemis-all.zip .`

type `yes` when asked to trust the M71 SE.

7. Reboot your SE. You can do this with the task under SE Management or using command `startdriver -neit`

Reach out to Chris if you experience any issues. A D36 fix is also available, but I don't see a need for it since D36 accepts generic ssh credentials, no need for LDAP.

# Why aren't I seeing this?

If you previously used copy-ssh-id, the ldap server is not engaged when you login so you probably haven't noticed any disruption. If you type your password every time, chances are this issue is affecting you, but if not, someone already did one of the two steps above.  If you are reading this further in the future, the ssh login rules have likely changed.

# CECSIM

In addition to downloading SSH public keys to the SE the **z-auth-webapp** also downloads the key to be used when using *CECSIM*. When CECSIM uses this key it needs the W3 ID of the user that is using CECSIM. In order for things to work with this key the **INTRANET_ID** environment variable needs to be set for the process trying to communicate with CECSIM.  There are several modes that CECSIM can be run in.

RANET_ID** environment variable needs to be set for the process trying to communicate with CECSIM.  There are several modes that CECSIM can be run in.

* CECSIM standalone
    * In this mode the user defines the INTRANET_ID in the environment.
  * zFOCS SE
    * If the SE driver is invoked from a SSH session authenticated with a SWAT registered public key then the INTRANET_ID is set to the W3 ID associated with the SSH public key and this value is defined in the environment for all SE driver related processes.
    * If not defined as described above the INTRANET_ID is set to the user that owns the zFOCS instance (the user that created the instance) and this value is defined in the environment for all SE driver related processes.
  * Real hardware SE
    * If the SE driver is invoked from a SSH session authenticated with a SWAT registered public key then the INTRANET_ID is set to the W3 ID associated with the SSH public key and this value is defined in the environment for all SE driver related processes.
    * If not defined as described above and the */ffdc/intranetid* file exists, the INTRANET_ID is set to the value specified in this file  and this value is defined in the environment for all SE driver related processes.

# General Login Support

In the past any console (i.e. HMC, SE, or TKE) with *tools* installed provided an "out of the box" solution for being able to login to these consoles using a valid W3 ID and password.  This was accomplished with the built-in LDAP server support, with Bluepages being used as the LDAP server. The problem with this approach is that the firmware on these consoles actually has access to the password in the clear when performing the authentication and this is a vulnerability that allows a *bad actor* to steal these credentials. This was true when using a W3 ID and password to log on via SSH, with a remote browser, or on the local console.

The approach to eliminate this vulnerability is to make it easy for each potential user's SSH public key to be automatically loaded onto these consoles and to base all authentications on the use of this SSH public key. The general idea is the following.

y to be automatically loaded onto these consoles and to base all authentications on the use of this SSH public key. The general idea is the following.

* Each of these consoles is registered with a central server using the IP address(es) of the console (IP address ranges will be used to cover things like zFOCS, etc.).
  * Each user registers their SSH public key with this central server as well.
  * The development MCP will contain support that periodically gets the list of registered SSH public keys from the central server. The list also maintains the W3 ID associated with each SSH public key.
  * For SSH connections, the user no longer needs to specify a password when authenticating since they will automatically be authenticated using their public key. In fact, password based authentication for SSH will eventually be disabled.
  * For remote browser logins there are 2 methods for authenticating.
    * Using a short lived One Time Password (OTP).
    * Automatic login using a SSH tunnel connection (similar to what is done for VNC use already).
  * For local logins there are 2 methods for authenticating.
    * Using the same one time password method as for remote logins.  This requires the use of an ssh session to request the one time password.
    * Creation of local users on the HMC/SE/TKE.

**Note:** All of the W3 ID support described in this document require the *tools* package to be installed with the driver along with the development MCP.

# Local Login

Local logins are supported via 2 different methods.

* Using the the same one time password support that is available for remote logins.
  * Defining real HMC/SE users on the console.

## One Time Password Support

Refer to the **Remote Login** section for details on using a one time password.  The one time password can only be generated using an ssh session, but once created it can be used to login to the console locally.

## Defining Real Users

Real HMC/SE users can be defined with the same permissions as the previous Bluepages authenticated template users.  To do so login as a user with access administator access and use the **User Management** task.  When creating the local user it is important to select the following roles for the user to get the same level of permissions as the previous Bluepages authenticated template users.

* Access Administrator Tasks
  * All Resources
  * All System Managed Objects
  * Product Engineering Tasks
    * Note: This role is not exposed when viewing the roles available on the HMC/SE, but it is available when selecting the roles for a user.

Some settings you might want to consider altering for the user being created are listed below.

* Session timeout
  * Verify timeout
  * Idle timeout (this should really be enabled to make sure a locally logged in user gets disconnected if the session is idle for too long)
  * Remote access (you probably want to enable this so the user can be used from a remote browser)

# Login Support

This section provides guidance on various login methods and support options for accessing Z Systems through the Z Authorization Webapp.

## Contents

- [General Support](./General%20Support.md) - General login support and troubleshooting
- [Local Login](./Local%20Login.md) - Local login procedures and configuration
- [Remote Login](./Remote%20Login.md) - Remote login access methods
- [VNC](./VNC.md) - VNC (Virtual Network Computing) access setup
- [Web Services API](./Web%20Services%20API.md) - Web services API authentication and usage

## Overview

The Z Authorization Webapp supports multiple login methods to accommodate different access scenarios and user preferences. This section covers configuration and usage for each supported login method.

# Remote Login

Remote logins are supported using 2 different methods.

* Use of a short lived one time password.
  * Automatic login using an ssh tunnel connection.

## One Time Password Support

Once a user has established a SSH session with the console, they can request a short lived one time password.  This password can be used with their W3 ID when logging onto the console from a remote browser or on the local console.  Once used the one time password is no longer valid and it will expire in 3 minutes if it is never used. If the user gets prompted for a password, the user can simply request another one time password and use it. Example of when a user might be promoted for their password are when a user's verification timeout has elapsed or when the user is presented with a disruptive confirmation.

It is important to remember that the user never specified their W3 ID when establishing the SSH connection or when requesting the one time password. The W3 ID is determined automatically based on the public key that was used to authenticate the SSH connection.

If you frequently need a one time password when creating an SSH session to the console, then you could run the necessary command (described below) automatically when connecting.  For example:

```
     ssh -t hmcmanager@9.47.77.205 'w3idtool getpw; bash -i'
```

necessary command (described below) automatically when connecting.  For example:

```
     ssh -t hmcmanager@9.47.77.205 'w3idtool getpw; bash -i'
```

This will create an SSH shell session and obtain a one time password that can be used for logins to the console.

## SSH Tunnel Connection Support

SSH tunnels are currently used quite often for using VNC.  It is the same idea except instead of creating a SSH tunnel to the VNC port (5900), the user creates a SSH tunnel to a new port for the console's web server, which is 7443. For example, if a HMC or SE console had an IP address of 9.47.77.205, the user could use the following command on Linux to establish a SSH tunnel to the new web server port 7443 through local port 8001.

```
     ssh hmcmanager@9.47.77.205 -L 8001:127.0.0.1:7443
```

The user could then use the URL `https://127.0.0.1:8001` in their remote browser and they would see the welcome page for the console.  The cool part is that when the user clicks on the "logon" link of the welcome page, they are not presented with the logon window, instead they are automatically logged on with their W3 ID. Just like for one time passwords, the user's W3 ID is determined automatically based on the SSH session associated with the SSH tunnel. When logged on in this manner the user will need to request and use a one time password if ever promoted for a password.

sociated with the SSH tunnel. When logged on in this manner the user will need to request and use a one time password if ever promoted for a password.

**Note:** In order for the automatic logon capabilities to work correctly the `-N` option of the *ssh* command or the putty *Don't start a command or shell at all* option cannot be used for the ssh tunnel.

### SSH Tunnel Limitations

There are a couple of things that would not work correctly when using an SSH tunnel with a remote browser to an HMC as described above.  Specifically, the *Single Object Operation (SOO)" task or any *SE task on the HMC* will not work with this type connection. This is due to the fact that the HMC really thinks the remote browser is at IP address 127.0.0.1, when in fact it is not. This is important because the SOO traffic uses a different port on the HMC (ports 9950-9959) so that the data can be easily proxied to the SE.  The addition of a few extra command line arguments on the *ssh* command can solve this issue.

```
      ssh hmcmanager@9.47.77.205 -L 8001:127.0.0.1:7443 -L 9950:127.0.0.1:9950 -L 9951:127.0.0.1:9951 -L -L 9952:127.0.0.1:9952 ....
```

This would only need to be done for HMC sessions since that is the only place this issue exists and it would have the restriction that this can only be done to a single HMC at a time.

## W3 ID User

When logging on with a one time password or automatically via a SSH tunnel, a W3 ID based user is created on the console. This user has a user name of the W3 ID and initially has the same settings as the template based users previously used. Unlike the previous template based users, these new W3 ID users allow for all characteristics and user settings for the user to be persisted and included in upgrade data. The previous template based users only allowed for user settings to be persisted. Since a W3 ID based user has *Access Administrator* authority the *User Management* task can be used to change most of the attributes of the user (except for the password).

Note: W3 ID based users do not show up in the *User Management* task until they are used at least once after driver startup.

## w3idtool Script

The **w3idtool** script, which is part of the "tools" package, provides several different operations that can be performed for W3 ID users. This script can only be used from the command shell associated with a SSH session that was authenticated with a registered public key.

* getpw
  * This operation will generate a one time password for the W3 ID associated with the command shell of a SSH session.  The one time password is only valid for a single use and will go away after 3 minutes if it is not used.
* exists
  * This operation will determine if a W3 ID based user exists for the W3 ID associated with the command shell of a SSH session. A W3 ID based user is created when a one time password is requested for it or if it is used to automatically logon via a SSH tunnel connection.
* remove
  * This operation will remove an existing W3 ID based user from memory if it is not currently in use for a session with the console.

The usage information for the **w3idtool** script is as follows.

```

W3 ID logon support utility program.

positional arguments:
  command     Command to perform. See command descriptions below.

W3 ID logon support utility program.

positional arguments:
  command     Command to perform. See command descriptions below.

optional arguments:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

Supported commands are:

nd     Command to perform. See command descriptions below.

optional arguments:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

Supported commands are:

getpw  - Gets a short lived, one time password for logging on; currently 3 minutes.
           This creates a W3 ID based user on the console that can be logged into
           using the returned password. An exit status of 0 indicates success and
           any other value indicates a failure.
  remove - Removes a previously used W3 ID based user from the console.
           An exit status of 0 indicates the user was successfully removed or
           no user associated with the W3 ID exists. An exit status of 1 indicates
           the user exists, but cannot be removed because it is in use. Any other
           exit status value indicates a failure.
  exists - Checks to see if a W3 ID based user currently exists on the console.
           An exit status of 0 indicates no user associated with the W3 ID exists.
           An exit status of 1 indicates the user exists and is in use. An exit
           status of 2 indicates the user exists and is not in use. Any other
           exit status indicates a failure.

```

## Potential User Conflicts

The W3 ID based users can conflict with regular or template based users defined on the console.  For example, consider the W3 ID *ibmer@ibm.com*, a user with that user name can be created in several different ways.

* W3 ID based user
  * A user that was created by requesting a one time password or used to automatically logon via a SSH tunnel connection.
  * A user of this type can only be created if no other type of user exists with the same user name.
  * A user of this type can be removed using the **w3idtool** script using the *remove* operation.
* Regular user
  * A user was created using the *User Management* task with the user name of *ibmer@ibm.com*.
  * This type of user is created during driver startup and can only be removed by deleting the user definition using the *User Management* task.
* Pattern/template based user
  * A user was created by logging on the console with a user name of *ibmer@ibm.com*, which matched a configured user pattern.
  * This type of user is created the first time it is used for logging on the console and will remain until the driver is restarted.

# VNC Access

Nothing has really changed with regard to VNC access; specifically:

* VNC should continue to be used over SSH tunnel connections.  For example, *ssh hmcmanager@9.47.76.222 -L "5900:127.0.0.1:5900"* to establish the SSH tunnel and then using *127.0.0.1:5900* in your VNC viewer.
  * Login to the console in a VNC session will need to use the one time password support described in the *Remote Login* section.

# Web Services API

A few enhancements have been made to help Web Services API (WSAPI) applications authenticate using the new **z-auth-webapp** support.

## SSH Tunnel Connection Support

WSAPI login requests (POST to /api/sessions) flowing over an authenticated SSH tunnel connection allow for *automatic login* support similar to that provided for remote browser connections using an authenticated SSH tunnel connection.  The SSH tunnel connection needs to go to the standard WSAPI TLS port of 6794, for example using the following command the */api/session* request would be sent to IP address 127.0.0.1 at port 12345.

```
     ssh hmcmanager@9.47.77.205 -L 12345:127.0.0.1:6794
```

Assuming a W3 ID of `someuser@ibm.com` the request body for the request would look like:

```
      { "userid":"someuser@ibm.com", "password":"SSH_TUNNEL" }
```

The fact that the login request came in over an authenticated SSH connection and the special password of `SSH_TUNNEL` is used causes the login processing to lookup the W3 ID associated with the SSH public key used for the connection and if this W3 ID matches the `userid` in the request the login succeeds.

lookup the W3 ID associated with the SSH public key used for the connection and if this W3 ID matches the `userid` in the request the login succeeds.

While the SSH tunnel connection could be used to send all WSAPI requests to the HMC/SE, it is only necessary for the login, `/api/session`, request flow over this connection.  Once successfully logged in the returned API session can be used over any connection, such as a direct connection to port 6794.

## WSAPI Test Framework

This framework is available for driving WSAPI requests for automated testing.  This framework provides command line options and configuration file options for specifying things like target IP address/port, and userid/password to use for logins. If the IP address/port of an SSH tunnel connection and a userid/password as described above is used then the automatic login support will be used to authenticate any login requests sent by this framework.

The framework also provides support for using One Time Passwords (OTP) as well. The following steps can be used to tell the framework that it should obtain an OTP using SSH for any login operation.

* The password must be specified as `use_w3idtool` via a configuration file or command line option. This is what causes the framework to try and obtain an OTP for each login request.
* Optionally an SSH private key file can be specified using the `sshIdentityFile` directive in a config file or the `--ssh-identity-file` command line option. This file is used when the framework establishes an SSH connection to the target machine to obtain an OTP.

## Potential User Conflicts

The same potential user conflicts that can occur for remote browser logins to the UI also exist for logging in via WSAPIs (see the *Remote Login* section for more details).

# Z Authorization Webapp The **Z Authorization Webapp**, or **z-auth-webapp** for short, is an application that distributes public SSH keys of users across HMC/SE/CECSIM/zFOCS systems. The public SSH keys are used for granting SSH and browser login on the target systems. z-auth-webapp also provides key material for downloading packages from Artifcatory, running Cecsim sessions and other external services.

# Motivation This application was created to address security concerns regarding secret handling of the SE/HMC/TKE. These concerns include: - remove secret handling off the SE/HMC/TKE - store secrets - process secrets The z-auth-webapp is one of the building blocks needed to achieve better handling of secrets.

# Usage

The z-auth-webapp is used for password-less authentication to System Z Support Elements and Hardware Management Consoles

## Scenarios There are 5 scenarios which are z-auth-webapp addresses: - [Remote login](./Login%20Support/Remote%20Login.md) via SSH to a SE/HMC/TKE using SSH. - Start a [CECSIM session](CECSIM%20session/cecsim.md). - Start [external services](Use%20external%20services/external_services.md) like Jupitr on SE/HMC/TKE. - Use a token for DNF to [download RPMs](Token%20for%20DNF/artifactory.md). - [Login via browser](./Login%20Support/Remote%20Login.md) to a SE/HMC/TKE via SSH. See the picture below for those scenarios ![Scenarios](./images/se_csirt.drawio.png)
# Initial setup for each user

## Request Access to Bluegroups

In order to gain access to z-auth-webapp and it's functionalities, you must be a member of at least one of the following bluegroups:

- [afaas-sys-zfw-fwd-team-read](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2/requests/new?element=11184&authorities=603)
- [zfocs_users](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2/requests/new?element=11553&authorities=603)
- [zSystemsHardware](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2/requests/new?element=9967&authorities=603)

## Generate SSH Key

**Every** user must generate a SSH Key pair before they can submit their public key to SWAT.
See [here](generatesshkey) for details.

## Register public SSH Key(s)

**Every** user must register a public SSH key in their user profile in [SWAT](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2).
See [here](./UI%20Guide/fetchSwatKey.md) for details.

# Authentication

In the past SSH authentication was available to users *hmcmanager* and *root* using a stylized password of the form `w3id:w3password`. The long term goal is to have all SSH authentication to be done using public keys that can be mapped to the W3 ID associated with the key. This transition will be staged in during the *Metis* program.

The key (no pun intended) is to have a master list of SSH public keys always available on the HMC/SE so that any registered user can SSH into any registered HMC/SE using their SSH public key. To accomplish this a new service is being added to the development MCP called the *zFW Authorized Keys Service*. This service, which is part of the development MCP, will periodically download the master list of registered SSH public keys.

## zFW Authorized Keys Service

The **zFW Authorized Keys Service** is a component of the development MCP for HMC/SE/TKE that provides the following capabilities.

1. Periodic download from a central server of a master set of authorized SSH public keys.
  2. Periodic download of a read only Artifactory identity user name and token, which can be used for things such as *dnf*.
  3. Periodic download of the CECSIM private key.
  4. Automatic refreshing of the master set of authorized keys when an SSH connection is being authenticated.
  5. General purpose script that allow for items 1-3 above to be performed at any time.

The intent of this package is to allow system owners to easily provide SSH access to their internal systems with minimal effort.

### sysz-authorized-keys.py

The *sysz-authorized-keys.py* script provides the majority of the support for this package.  It can be run in 2 modes:

* service mode
    * Runs as a systemd service that performs the periodic retrievals listed above as well providing as a UNIX domain socket interface for requesting any of these retrievals at any time. This service is automatically started each time MCP is started on the HMC/SE/TKE.
  * utility mode
    * Runs as a stand alone script to allow for real time requests to retrieve the supported information at any time.

### service mode

Service mode is provided via 2 systemd units and an associated configuration file.

* sysz-authorized-keys.socket
    * A systemd *socket* unit file that defines the UNIX domain socket that will be used.
  * sysz-authorized-keys.service
    * A systemd *service* unit file that describes how the *sysz-authorized-keys.py* should be run for service mode.
  * sysz-authorized-keys.env
    * A configuration file (found in /etc/sysconfig) that defines the arguments to be provided to the *sysz-authorized-keys.py* script.

The arguments for the *sysz-authorized-keys.py* script in service mode are as follows (all are required).

The systemd socket and service are started during normal boot up and will continue to run to perform the periodic updates and to service real time requests for retrieval.

#### utility mode

The same *sysz-authorized-keys.py* script when executed not as a systemd service provides the ability to request real time updates for the following:

* SSH authorized keys,
  * Artifactory user name and token, and
  * CECSIM key.

The arguments for the *sysz-authorized-keys.py* script in utility mode are as follows.

```
usage: sysz-authorized-keys.py [-h] --request {auth-keys,artifactory-token,cecsim-key}

The sysz-authorized-keys systemd service handler.

optional arguments:

  --request {auth-keys,artifactory-token,cecsim-key}
                        Send request to service to get authorized keys, Artifactory user name and token, or CECSIM key.
```

When run in utility mode the script simply connects to the UNIX domain socket and asks the systemd service to do the work.

### sshd integration

By default, the systemd service downloads the ssh authorized key data into 2 places:

* /home/hmcmanager/.ssh/zfw_authorized_keys
  * /root/.ssh/zfw_authorized_keys

The *sshd* configuration needs to be updated for this information to be used.  This is accomplished by added a configuration file to the */etc/ssh/sshd_config.d* directory that overrides some of the default systemd settings.  The following settings are overridden.

figuration file to the */etc/ssh/sshd_config.d* directory that overrides some of the default systemd settings.  The following settings are overridden.

* AuthorizedKeysFile
    * This is changed from the default of `AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys` to `AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys2`.
  * AuthorizedKeysCommand and AuthorizedKeysCommandUser
    * The *AuthorizedKeysCommand* is added to point at the */usr/bin/sysz-authorized-keys.sh* script, which does the following.
      1. Calls the *sysz-authorized-keys.py* script to request an update of the *zfw_authorized_keys* files noted above.
        * Note: By default the *zfw_authorized_keys* file is updated at most once every 5 minutes. This is to reduce request load on the central server, but it does mean that a user may need to wait up to 5 minutes before a newly registered SSH public key is available on a system.
      2. Dumps the contents of the *.ssh/authorized_keys* and *.ssh/zfw_authorized_keys* files for the user to standard output for sshd to use.
    * The *AuthorizedKeysCommandUser* is defined as *root*.
  * ExposeAuthInfo
    * This is changed from the default of `no` to `yes` so a temporary file is created that contains the public key used for an SSH session, which will then be used to figure out the W3 ID associated with that public key.
      * Note: There is no need to worry about password information getting written to this temporary file during the transition period. If password based authentication is used this file simply contains the word *password* indicating that a password was used for authentication.
  * PasswordAuthentication
    * Overridden with the value of `no` so that password based authentication is not allowed for ssh connections.
    * Note: This will start being the case after the transition period for migrating to this new support is over.

is not allowed for ssh connections.
    * Note: This will start being the case after the transition period for migrating to this new support is over.

This setup provides the following behavior.

* If no *.ssh/authorized_keys2* file exists for a user (the default), then the contents of the user's *.ssh/authorized_keys* and *.ssh/zfw_authorized_keys* files are used for SSH public key lookup.
    * Note: The *.ssh/authorized_keys file is only intended to be used during the transition to getting all of the necessary SSH public keys registered with the central server. At some point the expectation is that this file becomes empty and can eventually no longer be used.
  * If a *.ssh/authorized_keys2* file does exist for a user, only that file will be used for SSH public key lookups.  In this case the system owner has decided they want to completely manage the SSH public keys for their system.

# Tokens for DNF

So far the user needed to call the utility `setupAccessToken.sh` to get a token for artifactory which is
needed for any DNF download actions. Like installing a full snapshot or upgrading individual RPMs.

That utility is being sunset. Instead a systemd service is introduced to MCP which downloads an
artifactory token from the Z authorization webapp. This token only grants read access to locations in
artifactory which a Z bringup user has anyway.

All of this is done transparently for the user. The user can directly use DNF on any SE/HMC/TKE without any
preceeding setup!

# Rollout and required user actions

During the feeback and test phase the `setupAccessToken.sh` utility will only print an additional warning if you
still use it, but it's behaviour remains unchanged. Please change your procedures during this phase to
*not* use this script any more. If you find a use case where you cannot skip using this utility please
contact Ralf Schaulfer and Boris Feist.

After the move to production the `setupAccessToken.sh` will return with an error and will not do anything.

# Fetching SWAT Public SSH Keys

> **Access the Z Auth Webapp GUI [here](https://zauth-prod.z-auth-webapp.wdc.app.cirrus.ibm.com/)**

**_Before Submitting keys to SWAT, please generate SSH Key pair and how locate keys._** For details [here](../generatesshkey)

One of the main components of the ui, is fetching a users public SSH Keys from SWAT.

If you have public SSH keys, they should appear in the text area upon load.

At the top left of the homepage is a status tag, which lets you know if you have public SSH keys in SWAT.

![Status tags](./images/fetchSwatKeyImages/statusTags.png)

The blue status tag means the server is checking to see whether or not you have any public SSH keys in SWAT

The green status tag means you do have public SSH keys in your SWAT user profile and they can be displayed in the ui

The red status tag means you do NOT have public SSH keys in your SWAT user profile.

## Adding SSH Keys in SWAT

If you see a red status tag, that means no public SSH keys were detected. In order for z-auth-webapp to retrieve your public SSH keys, you must go to [SWAT](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2/) and add them to your user profile.

- Step 1: Access user profile on SWAT

![Swat user profile step 1](./images/fetchSwatKeyImages/userProfileStep1.png)

- Step 2: Once in the User Profile click SSH Keys.

![Swat user profile step 2](./images/fetchSwatKeyImages/userProfileStep2.png)

- Step 3: Once on the SSH Keys page, click on the **_Add SSH Key_** button and provide the name, ssh key, and description for your SSH Key

:::danger

Description \***\*must** include `server:hmcse` in order for the key to be displayed in the z-auth-webapp UI.

:::

![Swat user profile step 3](./images/fetchSwatKeyImages/userProfileStep3.png)
![SSH Key example](./images/fetchSwatKeyImages/exSshKey.png)

### Key Status in SWAT

Once a key is created, the status of the key (in SWAT) will be displayed under the key icon.

- A green bar and check mark indicates a non depicted key
- A grey bar indicates a depciated key but it is still functional

SWAT will **NEVER** remove the keys themselves

![key status in SWAT](./images/fetchSwatKeyImages/keyStatusInSwat.png)

## Refetching SWAT Keys

After adding a key to SWAT, you need to click the **Refetch SWAT Keys** button [here](https://zauth-prod.z-auth-webapp.wdc.app.cirrus.ibm.com/). If the **Refetch SWAT Keys** button is not clicked, z-auth-webapp will _not_ detect the newly added public SSH keys, therefore they will not be displayed in the ui. # Register and Deregister IP Addresses

One of the main components of the UI, is the ability to view, register, and deregister the IP addresses for SEs, HMCs, PAKs, and TCs.

## Usage

System owners need to register their HMC/SE/TKE IP to allow for continued system access.

System owners can deregister their IP if the system's IP changes or if the IP is no longer used for HMC/SE/TKE.

The register/deregister component is made up of two parts: the table and the register IP text inputs.

![Register and Deregister Components](./images/registerDeregisterImages/registerDeregisterComponents.png)

## IP Address Table

The table showcases all current registered IP Addresses. This information is separated into 2 columns:

- System Info: The system type/name
- IP Address: The IP Address associated with the given SEs/HMCs/PAKs/TCs

This table uses the [ag-grid react package](https://www.ag-grid.com/), which allows for detailed filtering, sorting, and grouping
### Table Functionalities

#### Quick Search

The table comes with the ability to perform quick search. Quick search filters the entire table based on the text you inputted in the quick search bar.

![Quick Search Text Input](./images/registerDeregisterImages/quickSearchTextInput.png)

#### Filtering

You can filter each column in the table based on specific criteria. The table comes with two places to filter a column:

- the filter icon at the header of each column

![Filter Column Header](./images/registerDeregisterImages/filterColumnHeader.png)

- the Column Filter tab found on the right side of the table

![Filter Column Side Panel](./images/registerDeregisterImages/filterColumnSidePanel.png)

In the filter toolbar, you will be able to select which rows are shown on the table. You deselect all and only showcase rows containing a specific system name or ip address.

![Filter Tool](./images/registerDeregisterImages/filterTool.png)

#### Sorting

You can sort rows in ascending or descending order in two ways:

- click next to the column header name

![Sort Column Header](./images/registerDeregisterImages/sortColumnHeader.png)

- click the menu tool in the column header and select "Sort Ascending" or "Sort Descending"

![Sort Menu Tool](./images/registerDeregisterImages/sortMenuTool.png)

#### Grouping

Grouping allows you to group the data in the table. There are two ways to group your data:

- click the menu tool in the column header and "Group by [column name]"

![Grouping Menu Tool](./images/registerDeregisterImages/groupingMenuTool.png)

- click the "Columns Properties" on the right side panel and inside the tool, drag the desired column name to the row groups section

![Grouping Side Panel](./images/registerDeregisterImages/groupingSidePanel.png)

#### Toolbar Actions

At the top of the table, next to quick search are several quick toolbar actions.

- **Display Group Toolbar** : Displays section where you can drag column header, allowing for quick grouping.

![Toolbar Action Grouping](./images/registerDeregisterImages/toolbarActionGrouping.png)

- **Display Filters Toolbar** : Displays the filter tools for each column for quick row filtering.

![Toolbar Action Filter](./images/registerDeregisterImages/toolbarActionFilter.png)

- **Switch Compacted/Expanded View** : Switches between showing rows in more compacted view or expanded view.

![Toolbar Action View](./images/registerDeregisterImages/toolbarActionView.png)

- **Refetch Query** : Refetches the query data for registered IPs. Comes in handy when an IP has been registered or deregistered and the change is not immediately reflected in the table.

![Toolbar Action Refetch](./images/registerDeregisterImages/toolbarActionRefetch.png)

## Register IP

The ui allows for you to quickly register an IP Address

![Empty Register IP](./images/registerDeregisterImages/emptyRegisterIP.png)

To register an IP, input the system info and the IP Address. It is **REQUIRED** to input both the **system info** (could simply be the system name) and the **IP address**.

Then click the Register IP button, and your newly registered IP should show on the table.

![Input Register IP](./images/registerDeregisterImages/inputRegisterIP.png)

# How to Generate SSH Key

For both Windows, Mac, and Linux users can use the command `ssh-keygen` to generate SSH Key pair.

The command ssh-keygen is part of the OpenSSH suite of tools and users will need them on their local system.

## Generate SSH Key on Local system

Note: the key gen is a onetime operation, they will remain on the system till removed by user

- Step 1: Open a local command window on your workstation, users can run `ssh -V` to check if they have OpenSSH on their system

![Check for OpenSSH step 1](./images/openssh.png)

- Step 2: Enter the command

```
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
```

A message will appear showing where the keys will be saved and prompt the user if they want to change were the keys are saved. By default, it will be placed in User/<$USER>/.ssh.
Leave it blank to use the default location, hit Enter.

![Run ssh-keygen select save location step 2](./images/keylocation.png)

- Step 3: A new prompt will appear asking if a passphrase should be implemented for the keys. It is recommended for users to setup a passphrase, this adds extra layer of security if someone gains access to your local system.
  Hit enter and you will get an output indicating that a new public and private key has been generated.

![Run ssh-keygen select save location step 3](./images/passphrase.png)

metadata.section_heading: Generate SSH Key on Local system

content:
## View SSH Key

To view ssh key go to the directoy the keys were saved(default is <$USER>/.ssh)
In the folder there will be a .pub file, print or view the file and there you will find the public key.
![Public SSH Key](./images/viewkey.png)
Copy the key and paste it into SWAT. To paste the key, go to [SWAT](https://jazzauth.rchland.ibm.com:9443/SWAT2/), click **User Profile**, select **SSH Keys** on the left hand pane, click **Add SSH Key**, and paste key there.

### Optional add SSH Key to ssh-agent

If user setup passphrase they will be prompted to enter the passphrase every time the key is used. User can add their key to the ssh-agent, afterwords users will not be asked for passphrase when the key is used.

- Step 1: Start the ssh-agent in the background

```
$ eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
> Agent pid 59566
```

- Step 2: Add your SSH private key to the ssh-agent, run the command `ssh-add`
  ![Run ssh-keygen select save location step 3](./images/sshadd.png)

You will be prompted for passphrase for keys that were setup with passphrase.
Afterwords when using the key, you will no longer be prompted for passphrase

content: ## installation via zDNF

### 1. Initial Setup - Install zdnf

First beegin by installing zDNF on your machine. Run the following commands as root user:

```bash
sudo rpm -U https://daisy.boeblingen.de.ibm.com/zdnf.noarch.rpm
```
This should only need to be done once

### 2. Enter your Jfrog Token

In order to run the tool, you will likely be prompted with supplying your Jfrog token, if you do not have one already, you can find instructions on doing so here: TBD. Keep in mind that these tokens expire, so if the token you are entering doesn't work, that could be the cause.

### 3. Identify the Snapshot Version

You can find the snapshot via 2 main methods, if you are updating tools on a D61C system, then this info can be found in the `#d61c-mcl-info-log` channel on Slack. and will look something like this: `se-D61C-S24-20260428_1945`.

If that information is unavailable, then you can look up the snapshot on daisy via the following steps:

1. Open [DAISY](https://daisy.pok.stglabs.ibm.com/index.html)
2. Select **zFirmware - Artemis+**
3. Near the top, select zFirmware Advisories under Advisories.
4. Select the desired driver stream under **BundleLayers**
3. Find the snapshot with the letters "tst" or "rel" - that is the snapshot currently in the respective directory
4. Copy the text under the **Target Snapshot Version** column

### 4. Run zdnf in Interactive Mode

Issue the zdnf tool without parameters like so(using sudo!), here is where it may ask you for your jfrog token.

```
[hmcmanager@LCST2B40-/home/hmcmanager]sudo zdnf

zFirmware Installation

  (1) install a certain advisory (driver snapshot or subsys package set)

  (8) show log of last installation
  (9) enable/disable EU-Proxy
  (x) exit
Please enter your choice (1-9 or x):

Choose action **5** (install the tools of a certain snapshot). Make sure that the "Driver" is set correctly and press enter to accept the defaults up to the point of entering the snapshot name. After entering the snapshot identified above, press enter again.

# JUPiTR-on-Demand2.0 (JOD)

JOD2.0 is an enhanced version of Jup on Demand that comes with a new UI, and additional features to make the defect opening process easier than before. The following guide will provide a walkthrough on how to use the tool and the features it entails
## Opening a ticket

### System Information
![](images/JOD2-1.png)

Begin by Selecting the system you wish to open a defect for in the system information dropdown. If the system isnt present on the list, click on the system registration button on the bottom right of this section.

### Defect Details

![](images/JOD2-2.png)

Begin Filling out the name of the defect you wish to write. JOD will automatically add in the system name and IP address, so don't include those in your title. Instead, provide a brief summary of the issue, include what the impact was (i.e. what state the system was left in and/or refcodes that logged), and what the apparent cause if the issue was if it is possible.

![](images/JOD2-3.png)

Take a moment to look at the possible duplicate defects listed, if you find one that looks highly similar, it's worth it to reach out to the defect owner and attach your data to the defect instead to avoid creating a duplicate ticket.

Afterwards, continue by filling out the problem description. A good problem description should include a sequence of events leading up to the error/failure, how it effected the system, what came up in the log involving the failure, and include what timestamps events happened. snippets of the iqyylog are always useful, as well as what your investigation has led you to believe what is causing the problem.

![](images/JOD2-4.png)

# Engineering Management

In this section you will find guides assisting with the Engineering Management tools ETM and EWM formerly known as RQM and Jupitr respectively.

We will also cover additional tools required to navigate lab "paperwork-like" activities such as the current line item database, or MCL STAT, etc.

## EWM Engineering Workflow Management (JUPiTR)
[EWM](/EngineeringManagement/EWM/README.md) is a defect tracking system for working on closing zFirmware change records on all driver streams. Still known as Jupitr, this tool is where EST opens defects to development groups, and tracks the progression of each defect until it is resolved

## ETM Engineering Testflow Management
[ETM](/EngineeringManagement/ETM/README.md) is our test plan tracking system used to assign groups of test cases to a test plan and track progress against some test iteration such as a GA1 or Continuous Delivery.

## epipeline Line Items
[ePipeline](/EngineeringManagement/epipeline/README.md) is our line item database, where offering management, development, and PM publish line item descriptions and tracks status of approval, sizing, etc.

## MclStat
[MclStat](/EngineeringManagement/MclStat/README.md) is a resource where you'll find MCL build information. Every bundle definition MCL and MCF content is defined here and the exact link to EWM change records can be found in the details.

## TEP Test Execution Process
The TEP is EST's formal definition of how a test cycle is planned, prepared for, and executed. It described how line items move from initial sizing to approval with affinity to a test iteration.  It then describes how EST pools test cases in association with verifying the set of line items comprising the GA deliverable in the form of test plans in each squad. It defines the entrance criteria for Final System Test (FST) acceptance, asserts empirical data analysis to predict the capacity of EST in a given number of weeks to aid in planning progress throughout GA while defects are opened and resolved. Finally exit criteria for GA is defined.

All kinds of skills contribute to becoming a great tester. Sometimes referred to as the "Tester's Art", every tester benefits from having a deeper understanding of what they are testing, but also how to test. The best testers feel a sense of play in what they do. They get into a flow state doing the deep work of testing.  Experienced testers and novice testers alike, need to be reminded of why they test, i.e. the purpose of testing.

With all this in mind, a selection of material awaits you here on how, what, why of the testing art. Enjoy!

## How to write effective defects
A panel of Z test experts were convened to discuss how they manage to earn such a high fix success rate with the defect tickets they open.  A quick summary of their thoughts:

1. Know and be known by your developers
2. Be methodical, deliberate, unhurried when opening a ticket
3. Take the time to search for duplicate tickets
Best way to do this currently is using JUPiTR "Full Text Search" query with the SRC or a keyword, e.g. checkstop, dump, loss
4. Take the time to collect the correct data
5. Seek out your team leader and test experts when you are uncertain
6. Know how to find and interpret system reference codes (SRCs)
